Steam, coal and the new economy (500–12 BG)

The Fire Nation's talent for invention was old, and its roots lay in the geography of its volcanic archipelago, its maritime economy, its mineral resources and the constant need to maintain food supplies across islands with little farmland. Gunpowder had been discovered in the Fire Nation in about 3000 BG and made a military weapon between 1000 and 700 BG, and for centuries its use was limited to fireworks and a few siege weapons. What changed after 500 BG was not a single discovery but the appearance of an industrial tradition.

Zenshin and the first engine (c. 500 BG)

For centuries the economy had depended on fishing, farming, inter-island commerce and maritime trade. These generated wealth in good seasons, but left the population vulnerable to natural disaster. A volcanic eruption could destroy settlements and farmland, a change in fish migration could ruin a coastal community, and a failed harvest or a disrupted shipping season could produce unemployment and local famine. The islands had coal, iron, other metals, natural gas and volcanic energy in abundance, but the capacity to exploit them was lacking until the inventor Zenshin built what the record identifies as the first steam engine, in about 500 BG. Its first purposes were not necessarily military. Steam machinery offered ways to pump water, run equipment and reduce dependence on human and animal labor, though its first performance was limited by the metallurgy of the day. Zenshin's descendants continued his work, refining the engine and applying mechanical principles to manufacturing and weapons, and what they built was less a collection of machines than a body of knowledge that could reproduce, improve and spread itself.

Firearms and the institutions behind them (440–300 BG)

Firearms developed alongside metalworking, chemistry and mechanical engineering: the arquebus in about 440 BG, the musket in 402 BG and the flintlock by 300 BG. They did not replace bending on the battlefield, and the early weapons were slow, inaccurate and dependent on training. Their importance was institutional. A state that wished to use firearms had to organize their manufacture, standardize ammunition, train soldiers and maintain supply, and, unlike a bender's gift, a firearm could be issued to any soldier after sufficient training. A state could possess advanced weapons and lose a war if it could not manufacture ammunition, transport supplies or maintain its equipment, and the Fire Nation's eventual advantage would lie in developing those supporting systems.

The Industrial Revolution (from c. 290 BG)

By about 290 BG, the cumulative effect of mechanical invention, resource extraction and better manufacturing had produced an Industrial Revolution. It was gradual. Early factories coexisted with workshops, family enterprises and farming communities, and steam engines at first served particular industries. Coal supplied concentrated energy and iron the machinery, and natural gas and volcanic energy offered further possibilities, though they were limited by the infrastructure needed to use them: the islands' geothermal power was not literally limitless, as the schoolbooks later said.

The new economy changed the relationship between the people and the environment. A poor fishing season could still hurt a coastal community, but the economy was less dependent on fishing alone, and factory work, mining, trade and manufacturing offered other incomes. It did not abolish poverty or crises, it changed their character. Workers became dependent on wages, factory owners gained influence, and industrial towns became vulnerable to unemployment and labor disputes. The benefits were unevenly spread, and merchants, industrialists, engineers, military contractors and well-connected families were best placed to profit. The state gained new powers, too: it could tax factories, invest in infrastructure, found technical schools and support military production on a scale that no earlier government could have afforded. Industrialization was both an economic transformation and a redistribution of political power, and, as noted above, it replaced the clans with a new elite.

Rails, rifles and aircraft (260–27 BG)

The first train entered service in about 260 BG. Rail carried coal, ore, machinery, grain and manufactured goods between industrial centers and ports, and it concentrated industry near mines, harbors and junctions. It also strengthened the central government, which could now move officials, tax revenue, equipment and troops faster, respond to emergencies and exert more control over distant provinces. Railways did not make the Fire Nation a centralized state, but they gave a centralized state the means to behave like one. The hot air balloon appeared in 220 BG, breech-loading rifles and the paper-cartridge bullet around 160 BG, and by 80 BG a four-round bolt-action rifle had been produced. A self-loading pistol followed in 29 BG. These weapons demanded precision manufacture and standardized ammunition, and they made military effectiveness depend less on exceptional individual fighters and more on the organization of large formations. They also had domestic implications, since armed citizens, workers and veterans could now possess capabilities once limited to an elite, and a government that wished to mobilize a society for war would have to decide how to equip it and how to keep it under control.

In 28 BG oil was discovered in the Si Wong Desert, in the Earth Kingdom, and the following year, 27 BG, the Fire Nation made the first flight of a plane. Early aircraft were limited in range, payload and reliability, and their first uses were observation, communication and experiment, but they needed specialized factories, mechanics, fuel and spare parts, and the ability to build one machine was only the beginning of the ability to operate a fleet. The discovery of oil in a foreign desert, and the invention of a machine that would eventually depend on it, created a connection that the Fire Nation's planners would not forget.

The race with Qianchan (26–2 BG)

From about 26 BG the Fire Nation and the Qianchan Republic were engaged in a technological race. The Fire Nation was an industrializing island power with maritime traditions, extensive minerals and growing central authority, and its factories and shipyards could support commerce and military modernization alike. Qianchan was a republic rooted in the overthrow of imperial rule, which valued administrative competence and national preparedness, and which saw its military as the guarantor of its constitution. Its republican character did not make it passive. Improvements in transport, production, firearms and organization in one country gave the other reasons to respond, and civilian and military technology shared foundations: better engines improved both transport and logistics, precise metalworking served factories and arms makers alike. By the end of the prewar period the two had become the leading industrial powers of the world, and their competition was a contest over which political and economic system could turn technological knowledge into lasting national power. The first tank followed in 2 AG.

An age of peace and prosperity

The technological transformation took place in a time of exceptional peace. By the last years of Kyoshi's life the world had experienced an extraordinarily long period without a great war, and it was a time of cooperation fostered by business and academia. Technological institutes sprang up around the world, and scholars, inventors and educators formed ties with one another in the name of progress. The Fire Nation embraced these changes wholeheartedly, became the most technologically advanced country in the world and excelled in trade and commerce while maintaining a powerful military.

  • Industrial employment grew, ports prospered and new industries gave work to engineers, merchants and skilled workers. The government could draw on a broader economic base than any earlier ruler had had.
  • The Four Nations Summit & Technological Symposium was held in the Fire Nation. Minister Khuchtei, who had been arguing that the unbreakable qualities of meteorite metal could be used to make armored machines, was furious when crates of it were stolen from the storehouse.
  • The Unity expedition, funded by the Southern chief Qanitt and the merchant Tiqriganiannig, carried the studies and technologies of the four nations around the world, though the governments suspected it of being a spy mission.
  • Disputes continued. The Earth Kingdom and the Water Tribes quarrelled in the Chenbao incidents (56–54 BG) over a resource-rich border region, and the Avatar Roku settled the dispute by diplomacy. There were Nomad incidents in 30 BG.
  • The spirits turned hostile. As the nations industrialized, spiritual disturbances grew, and the old pacts between families and spirits, like the Saowon's, were forgotten or broken.

National pride grew with prosperity. A population accustomed to growing employment, better transport and rising wealth could become conscious of the gap between its country's power and its place in the world, and engineers, industrialists, officers and politicians could take their technological progress as proof that their society had reached a new stage. Such pride was not inherently expansionist. But it could encourage a dangerous conclusion, that a country able to produce more wealth and better weapons was entitled to dictate how others should develop, and that idea would become central to Sozin's worldview.

Roku and Sozin

The Fire Lord Sozin, son of Taiso, and the Avatar Roku were born into this age of progress, and they were friends. Their relationship embodied two competing interpretations of the Fire Nation's rise.

Roku understood power through the responsibilities that came with keeping the balance. As Avatar, he had a role that extended beyond the interests of any one nation, and his authority was meant to restrain aggression and prevent disputes from becoming destructive wars. He became a force for balance and peace in the world.

Sozin believed that the prosperity of the Fire Nation should be shared with the rest of the world, and he dreamed of a global empire under his rule. To Roku, the Fire Nation's power obliged it to accept limits. To Sozin, limits were obstacles to a national mission. Industry created a demand for raw materials and markets, and nationalist rhetoric provided a justification for taking them by political domination. Industrialization did not make war inevitable, and the decisive change was the arrival on the throne of a man willing to turn national prosperity into a claim of entitlement over other peoples.

Reforms that militarized the country

Sozin's reforms militarized the country. His government increasingly coordinated industrial policy with strategic goals, and the existing industrial system provided the means: shipyards could build fleets, factories could make weapons and railways could move supplies. Procurement supported certain industries, naval expansion gave officers and contractors a stake in government spending, and a feedback loop was set up: industrialization increased the state's resources, the state invested in modernizing the military, procurement stimulated particular industries, and those industries became constituencies for continued spending and expansion.

  • The coal-powered fleet. The engineer Nyn Chei had designed a fast ship that was to have been a trade vessel, planned with the Water Tribe boatwright Massak, and not a patrol ship. Sozin turned the project into a fleet. It created hundreds of jobs for the poorest of society, and it required materials that were scarce, bringing the Fire Nation into repeated conflict with the Earth Kingdom over resources. The Fire Lord quietly used those conflicts to stoke anti-Earth Kingdom feeling. Steam propulsion reduced the dependence of fleets on the wind, and the fleet was equally able to protect commerce or to carry troops, blockade ports and support colonies.
  • Overland war machines. Sozin commissioned prototypes, and officials like Khuchtei theorized about meteorite-metal armor. The early designs faced serious engineering problems and produced no unstoppable force, but they showed that planners had begun to consider mechanization a general solution to battlefield problems.
  • Selective openness. Sozin encouraged his people to look to other nations for knowledge, but wished to preserve Fire Nation culture inside its borders, and talented individuals, such as the legendary archer Uzuku Yuyan, felt pressured to share their skills with the rest of their homeland.
  • Nationalist propaganda. To win the poorest to the cause, Sozin used propaganda to direct resentment toward the Earth Kingdom, the Water Tribes and the Air Nomads. It presented the Fire Nation as industrious and innovative, and others as obstacles to progress or as beneficiaries of Fire Nation leadership. It concealed the central contradiction of his program, that the nation which claimed to share its prosperity denied others the right to decide whether they wanted it. By turning discontent outward, the government could draw attention away from the unequal distribution of industrial wealth and the social costs of militarization, and workers in hard conditions were invited to see their hardships as sacrifices for national greatness.

The Fire and Air Center of Learning

Much of the nobility had in this period embraced the teachings and philosophy of the Air Nomads, who were then more involved with the other nations, and who wished to do all they could to help others. The nobles funded the Fire & Air Center of Learning, to teach Air Nomad ways in the Fire Nation, and all four air temples supported the idea. The renegade Air Nomad order known as the Guiding Wind, which wished to cut the ties between the Air Nomads and the elites of other nations, opposed it, and protested by sabotaging construction. Sozin responded by seizing the site from the nobility and posting his military guard there, saying that he would not leave until the Guiding Wind did, and the order had no intention of giving up.

The affair gave Sozin an opportunity to present the Air Nomads' influence as a threat to national security, and a dispute about one institution and one movement became evidence that foreign ideas were incompatible with the national interest. The seizure showed that he was willing to subordinate intellectual life to the state's priorities, and it demonstrated the danger of collective blame: the acts of the Guiding Wind could justify restrictions on a whole cultural tradition, though a dissenting order did not prove that all Air Nomads shared its methods. Having lost some nobles' support by taking the Center from them, he sought a way to win it back.

Zeisan

The troubles of the Fire Lord were compounded by his sister, Princess Zeisan, who proposed a political marriage to Khandro, the leader of the Guiding Wind. She had seen corruption growing in her family and sought to destabilize her brother's rule, with dynasty-toppling ambitions, and she announced that she was renouncing her wealth and titles to live in austerity. Sozin almost could not control his rage. He saw the Guiding Wind as a direct threat, because it opposed the idea of an aristocracy, and he tried to counter his sister's influence with nationalistic propaganda aimed at the poorest. There were reports throughout the nation of violent attacks by the Guiding Wind, though violence broke their pacifist principles, and Khandro began to suspect that the Fire Lord or his supporters had a hand in fabricating them. Opposition to Sozin came not only from foreigners but from the Fire Nation's own elite, from people who thought its development was being turned to a destructive end, and the way he dealt with it, by turning disagreement into a question of loyalty to the nation, set the character of his government.

The dragon hunts

To regain popularity and to appear more fearsome than his father, Sozin announced the Dragon Hunts. Few dragons were killed at first, but the nobility took up the sport voraciously. Whoever killed a dragon received the honorary title of "Dragon" from the crown, along with prestige and victory over competitors, and it was believed that the act would multiply one's firebending a thousandfold. The hunts redirected elite competition to an activity sanctioned by the Fire Lord, and tied honor to the royal program.

They also led to ethical debates between the nobles and spiritual leaders such as the Fire Sages, who were worried about killing sacred animals. The imbalance caused by killing ancient creatures drew spirits to the places where dragons had been slain, and strange events took place there. Sozin formed an elite task force to deal with them and keep them from the public. When an envoy from the Water Tribes sensed the disturbance and visited the death sites, Sozin responded with a propaganda campaign blaming spiritual disturbances on the presence of the Water Tribe's people. The Sun Warriors, the civilization that had learned firebending from the dragons, went into complete isolation, so that the Fire Nation and the world believed them extinct, and the Sages who objected lost standing. The hunts carried the dragons to the edge of extinction, and they showed a contradiction at the center of Sozin's idea of greatness: a nation that had mastered its volcanic environment took the killing of its own most sacred animal as a sign of superiority.

Claims, colonies and the sacred island

Sozin's imperial ambitions began with claims to uninhabited islands. Natsuo Island, one of the easternmost of the Fire Islands, was claimed by the crown for the first time after a large cache of ore was found there, and the calculating Earth King Jialun sent ships on training exercises near it, hoping to goad Sozin into conflict. The Fire Nation also claimed an island sacred to the Water Tribes, the halfway point between North and South near the Mo Ce Sea, which held deep spiritual and cultural significance. Chief Skiri of the North was furious and wanted to send most of his fleet to retake it, but he needed the consensus of the Southern chieftains, and they, unwilling to risk all-out war with the Fire Nation, could not agree. The case shows the Water Tribes' structural weakness, a divided and distant alliance that could not act against a single, determined power. The occupation of an uninhabited island and the seizure of a sacred one were different acts, but they implied the same principle: that the Fire Nation could extend its authority wherever its leadership found an area strategically or economically valuable.

In 37 BG the Fire Nation established its first colonies on the coast of the Earth Kingdom. The coast offered ports for shipping and supply, markets, resources and bases from which the Fire Nation could project power into the continent, and it marked a decisive escalation, since it was now directly challenging the territory of another major power. The colonies needed governors, police, taxes and defense, and they increased the strategic importance of the navy while placing long-term burdens on the government. They also created new interests at home. Merchants wanted the new ports, industrialists the resources and contracts, and officers the staging grounds, and once a state had settlements it could argue that they needed protection, and use that to justify further deployments and claims. The colonies quickly became local industrial centers, and they formed the basis of the Fire Nation's later continental empire.

Roku confronts Sozin

The Avatar opposed Sozin's expansion and confronted him over the direction of the nation. Roku stopped him, in 37 BG, and spared him, but he allowed the colonists to remain. It was a fundamental compromise. The immediate escalation was prevented, and the dispute was left unresolved. For Sozin, the survival of the colonies could be taken as proof that persistence brought results. For the Earth Kingdom and other powers, it was a worrying precedent, because a state that was determined enough might keep its gains in the face of the Avatar's opposition. It also showed the weakness of an order that depended on a single powerful individual: Roku could restrain Sozin in person, but he could not guarantee that his successors would share his sense of responsibility.

The Crescent Island disaster

The next episode turned the Avatar's own mistake into Sozin's opportunity. While trying to master the Avatar State, an impatient Roku triggered it with the winter solstice sun, destroying the upper half of the temple on Crescent Island and awakening the nearby volcano. The seismic instability that followed affected the surrounding islands, and the people there were left homeless, working to rebuild with the Avatar's help. Desperate for some stability, they began to believe Sozin's anti-Earth Kingdom propaganda, blaming the neighboring nation for its lack of support and for its greedy claim to Natsuo Island, and not looking for faults in their own government. It did not follow that the Earth Kingdom was responsible for the aftermath. It showed how public anger could be directed at a convenient target, and how a disaster, without being deliberately caused by anyone, could become a political turning point.

The end of restraint (12 BG)

The Avatar Roku died in 12 BG on Island Jezhi. Sozin, who could have helped him, left him to die. It removed the one individual who had most directly restrained the Fire Lord's ambitions, and for years the Avatar had shown that the Fire Nation could not pursue every strategic objective without regard for the wider world. The loss was not only of a person. The world's capacity to prevent a great war had rested heavily on one man, and there was no equivalent guarantee, nor any assurance that Sozin would voluntarily give up his plans. With the Avatar gone, the next one, Sozin knew, would be born among the Air Nomads, and Sozin resumed his policies.

By that time the Fire Nation had a substantial industrial base, a modernizing coal-powered fleet, advanced firearms, a growing technical sector and a leadership committed to expansion. Its institutions had been reshaped: propaganda had strengthened the government's power to mobilize opinion, the old nobility was broken, the Sages had been weakened, and elite prestige was tied to state-approved displays of strength. For twelve years the Fire Lord prepared, and he waited for a comet.

Why the war became possible

The Hundred Year War was not the automatic consequence of the Industrial Revolution. Industrialization created capabilities, incentives and political interests, but it did not determine how they would be used. Several developments, many of which this article has traced, came together:

  1. The crown had defeated its rivals. Zoryu's project and Oraso Eiko's victory removed the clans, the only force that had ever limited a Fire Lord.
  2. The state had the means. Szeto's ministries and coinage, the railways and the shipyards gave a centralized government the machinery to mobilize a country.
  3. The world was weakly defended. The Earth Kingdom was corrupt and agrarian after the Great Interregnum, the Water Tribes divided and poor, the Air Nomads pacifist and without an army, and the one republic that could match the Fire Nation was divided from Ba Sing Se by two centuries of hostility.
  4. The ideology was ready. Propaganda, the dragon hunts and the suppression of dissent had turned expansion into patriotism and opposition into disloyalty.
  5. The restraint was gone. The Avatar, the sole check on the Fire Nation's policy, was dead, and the next Avatar was unknown and unprepared.

The central historical change was not that the Fire Nation became powerful. It was that Sozin came to believe that its power entitled him to rule beyond its borders. That is what connects the Industrial Revolution to the Hundred Year War.

Why the Empire went to war

The Empire's own officials never described the Hundred Year War as a crusade. In the documents that survive, it is a problem of supply, and the arguments for it were assembled over the thirty-seven years between Roku's mercy and the Fire Lord's order. Later historians, in Qianchan and elsewhere, accept that the Empire believed these arguments and dispute whether they were true.

The rearmament (37 BG – 0 AG)

After the bombing at Zeisan on 10 June 37 BG, whose authors were never established, and Roku's decision to spare Sozin in the same year, the state rebuilt its armed forces in four phases:

The case for necessity

  • Fuel. The Research Bureau's forecast gave the Empire's domestic oil about a century. The only large field within reach lay in the Si Wong Desert, inside the Earth Kingdom.
  • A peer rival. From 26 BG the Empire and Qianchan were in a technology race, and the General Staff concluded that the Empire's lead would not last another generation.
  • The Avatar. Roku was the one figure the Empire could not outflank. After his death in 12 BG, the next Avatar would be born among the Air Nomads, and a war begun before that Avatar was found would face no restraint.

The opposition and its suppression

The case was never unanimous. Merchants argued that oil could be bought, naval officers that the fleet was not ready, and some in the royal family that the Tajisaki's honor lay in the peace it had kept. These voices were handled gradually: first by reassignment, then by the Diet's rules, then by the Ministry of Truth. By 0 AG no institution could stop the Fire Lord. The National Diet was formally intact, and it could not investigate the Fire Lord, the military or the Ministry of Truth.

Deterrence and its failure

The Earth Kingdom and Qianchan signed the Alliance Treaty in 3 BG. It created no joint command, and the Empire's staff knew it. The Empire judged that it could defeat its enemies one at a time.

Right outcome, wrong method

Later writers, especially in the United Republic of Nations, observe that Sozin foresaw a single world order and that the nations eventually joined one, without the war. The Empire was right about where the world was going and wrong about how to get there.

The Empire of Tajisaki (12 BG – 100 AG)

With Sozin the Tajisaki realm became an empire. In 0 AG he used the comet to destroy the Air Nomads in the Air Nomad Genocide and began the Hundred Year War. He then did to the nation's past what the Warring States Era had done by accident. He sealed the Dragonbone Catacombs, so that the nation's history would seem to begin with his reign, and since the wing of Wan Shi Tong's Library dedicated to the Fire Nation was also closed to visitors, very little about the nation's past was left in reach apart from what the state released. Textbooks were censored or rewritten to justify the war, and courses that allowed personal expression were removed from the curriculum as threats to the Fire Lord's unquestioned authority. The Sages, whose murals and scrolls had kept the older versions of the past, were put under government supervision and reduced to little more than an aging remnant of a time when spirituality came before military might, and some who remained loyal to the Avatar were executed as traitors. The state wrote an oath for schoolchildren, "The March to Civilization," and built a cult of personality around the Fire Lord, with his picture in every school and statues in the squares. Same-sex marriage, which the Fire Nation had long allowed, was outlawed. The Agni Kai, once a bloodless contest of honor, became a duel to the death.

The ideology of the Empire, which the Imperial Constitution called "the Truth," taught that the palace was the center of the world, and that the further a place lay from it, the lower its people stood. The Fire Lord's authority rested on the descent of the Tajisaki line, which the new histories presented as unbroken from the unification and divinely approved, and the clans and Sages that had once shared that authority were gone. After the Air Nomad Genocide the state added the Homeland Purity Initiative. After Sozin died in 20 AG his son Azulon took the throne and continued his policies, subjugating most of the Earth Kingdom and the former Air Nomad lands, and using their resources for further industrialization, railways, steamships and airships. The long process of expansion and militarization, followed by his successor Ozai, is told in the article on the Hundred Year War. The government of the Empire is described in the article on the Empire.

After the war

After the Fire Nation Civil War, Zuko, who was crowned in 118 AG, loosened the cult of personality, admitted the nation's mistakes and let the Sages return to their spiritual role under their own head, the Great Sage. In 168 AG he abdicated to his daughter Izumi. The flag of the Fire Nation went through four designs in the period: the three-tongued flame on red of the early age, the flower seal of the imperial era, a white banner with the same flower for the civil war, and the circular emblem of Zuko's reign. The Tajisaki line, which had ruled since the unification, continued on the throne under Zuko and his descendants.

Geography and society

The Fire Islands are volcanic, with a warm, humid climate, and the capital, Caldera City, lies inside the crater of a large volcano. The people are concentrated in cities. Fire Nation society is built on honor and respect for elders and authority, which shows in the bow with a fist in an open hand, in the status given to hair (a lost duel is marked by shaving the topknot) and in the Agni Kai. It has a long tradition of gender equality, with women as ministers, magistrates, mayors and Fire Lords, although women became rare in the army in the late war. The food is spicy, with noodles, meat, fish, rice and spiced tea, and chili is revered. The theater is popular, with Love amongst the Dragons performed every year, and the festivals include the Festival of Szeto, the Fire Lily Festivals in August and the traveling Fire Days Festival, which took the Empire's culture to its colonies.

Historiography

The history of the Fire Nation has been written four times over, and the later centuries are no less contested than the earliest. The Sages wrote it as a story of fire lent by the spirits and of a nation anointed to rule. The Tajisaki chroniclers wrote it as the story of a clan that won, and each dynasty improved it. The imperial historians of Sozin's age wrote it as a prelude to the Empire, and removed what did not fit. The modern scholars of the Academy of Caldera, working after the war, have tried to read all three against the archaeology and the foreign sources, and agree on very little before 4440 BG. They agree that the Warring States Era destroyed more of the record than any later event, that the unification was a political settlement and not a conquest of the islands, that the road to the war was the work of a state that had first defeated its own nobles, its own priests and its own memory, and that the name Tajisaki, which every Fire Lord has carried and which the people of the islands have used in law for forty-five centuries, is older than any document that mentions it.

history_of_the_earth_kingdom.title: History of the Earth Kingdom
history_of_the_earth_kingdom.html:
From the lion-turtle cities and the walls of Ba Sing Se to the Yellow Necks, Qin the Great, the Qianchan secession, the two collapses of the capital and the eve of the Hundred Year War.

For the republic that left the kingdom, see Qianchan Republic and History of Qianchan. For the kingdom as a modern state, see Earth Kingdom. For the Fire Nation's side of the road to war, see History of the Fire Nation.
History of the Earth Kingdom
HeartlandThe Earth Kingdom continent: the central plains, the northern mountains, the west coast, the Si Wong Desert and the eastern steppes
CapitalBa Sing Se
RulersThe Earth Kings (Earth Monarchs), fifty-four by 174 AG, the 52nd being Kuei
Constituent statesFifty-five by the later count, among them Omashu, Huamu, Shaozu and Ba Sing Se itself
Pre-war populationAbout 230,000,000 (0 AG)
Ruling linesThe first kings of Ba Sing Se; the Qin Dynasty in the south (270–255 BG); the line of Bao Kun (from the Great Interregnum)
Lost territoryThe southern provinces, which became the Qianchan Republic (255 BG)
FlagsPre-Warring States (4988–292 BG); Warring States (292–255 BG); Unification (255 BG–0 AG); Hundred Year War (0–100 AG)

The history of the Earth Kingdom is that of the largest nation in the world, a union of provinces under the kings of Ba Sing Se that was repeatedly torn by rebellion, warlords and civil war, and was held together by its capital's walls, its bureaucracy and, at critical moments, by an Avatar. Its central problem was never a lack of strength. It was that its rulers could not turn a nominal sovereignty over a continent into consistent control of it, and that every failure of the capital to protect, feed or listen to its people taught some province to rely on itself. Over some eight centuries that lesson produced the Yellow Neck Uprising, the conquests of Qin the Great, the secession of Qianchan, and two collapses of Ba Sing Se itself. It lost its southern provinces in the 3rd century BG, and it entered the Hundred Year War as a weak, corrupt, agrarian giant whose size could not be turned into an army.

The history is also contested, more than most. Ba Sing Se, the Qianchan archives and the Fire Nation's chroniclers each tell the story of the same events in a different way, and the disagreement over a single man, Qin, was the first great quarrel between the kingdom and the republic. This article follows the sequence that the sources share, and notes where they part.

Origins

The ancestors of the Earth Kingdom came from several traditions. In the era of Avatar Wan, in about 9,829 BG, some lived in fortified cities built on the backs of lion turtles, where they received the ability to earthbend through energybending. Others lived as nomads, crossing the Spirit Wilds and settling wherever the land would feed them, and the first earthbender armies fought other peoples and forced the Avatar to intervene. The lands that would become the Earth Kingdom were then a collection of warring states.

Among the early communities was the settlement of Lady Tienhai in the western part of the continent. Ba Sing Se's records would remember its people as nomadic barbarians, a label that later scholars read as evidence of a long habit in the capital of presenting independent peoples as uncivilized, and of describing as rebels whoever refused to pay it tribute.

Ba Sing Se began as a small underground city that earthbenders carved out of the rock, with catacombs that were abandoned as the city spread to the surface. It is one of the oldest settlements in the world, and a five-thousand-year-old map of it survives in Wan Shi Tong's Library.

A kingdom of provinces

The continent has three kinds of land: the fertile plains and river lands of the south and centre, whose peasants fed the kingdom; the mountains and deserts of the north and west; and the eastern steppes beyond Ba Sing Se, where nomadic horse peoples lived by herding and raiding, and sometimes traded with and served the kings. Their raids and the endless wars of the early states led the kings of Ba Sing Se to build the great Outer Wall in about 1000 BG, which they later extended into the inner walls and rings.

Unification

Over several centuries the rulers of Ba Sing Se, a proud warrior-king dynasty that valued its armies, conquered their neighbors, among them the northern mountain state of Yi and, in the end, Omashu and Gaoling, and one of them crowned himself the first Earth Monarch. The title was "Monarch of All the Earth Lands and Glorious Defender of Ba Sing Se". The monarchs governed from the royal palace in the city's Upper Ring, and usually never left it. They ruled through a loyal bureaucracy and, rather than abolishing the conquered governments, let the constituent states keep their own lords and kings in return for tribute, soldiers and recognition of the monarch's authority. The pre-Warring States flag (4988–292 BG) was a green field with a gold circle around a square, the symbol that still stands for the kingdom.

Sovereignty and control

The arrangement was a practical answer to the continent's size. Ba Sing Se could command large armies and run a sophisticated capital, but it could not govern every distant valley, and for centuries it did not try. The Earth Kingdom became a confederation of semi-autonomous territories, each with its own laws, ruling families and customs, and the extent of royal authority depended on the willingness of the provincial rulers to cooperate. When the capital was strong, the provinces obeyed. When it was weak they acted for themselves, and when it tried to impose direct control it met resistance from regional elites as well as from ordinary people.

This made the kingdom durable and brittle in the same measure. It also left a standing weakness in the way it dealt with poverty. Repeated peasant unrest exposed a political order that relied on royal legitimacy without regularly settling disputes over land, taxes and access to relief, and that the poorest subjects, who looked to a distant king for protection, tended to get no help from either the king or the lord.

The states

Omashu, in the Kolau Mountains of the south-west, was founded, according to legend, by Shu and Oma, who came from two warring towns and fell in love on the mountain that separated them. Its monarchs competed with Ba Sing Se for centuries, and its queen Guo Xun despised the Earth King Jialun. It was the second city of the kingdom.

Gaoling (4282–272 BG), Tongshui (4192–268 BG) and Yu Dao (4292 BG–4 AG) were kingdoms and regions of the south and west that kept flags of their own until they were absorbed or lost. Gaoling later became the capital of Qianchan. Huamu and Shaozu were large states of the later kingdom, with flags of their own, and Taku, the Hu Xin Provinces, the Si Wong Desert, Kyoshi Island and the Foggy Swamp were other regions, each with its own culture.

The age of unrest (531–292 BG)

The late Warring States period was a time of rebellion, regional wars, corruption and rivalry among the great powers of the continent.

  • Nong's rebellion (531 BG). General Nong led a peasant uprising against the Earth King Feishan, who was accused of being a tyrant and a puppet of the Fire Nation.
  • The Platinum Affair (530 BG). The Fire Nation and the Water Tribes secretly backed Nong with platinum ingots. Feishan won, kept the ingots and closed the Earth Kingdom's ports, and the other nations closed theirs, so that foreign trade passed for generations through a few shang cities. The kingdom learned that outside powers would buy its rebels, and that it could cheat them with impunity, and its neighbors learned to conduct such schemes more quietly.
  • The Unanimity Project (from 519 BG). A secret plan to unify the world by manipulating the Avatar was set in motion by a figure known only as the Mastermind.
  • The Fifth Nation (from 518 BG). A confederation of pirates from the neglected coasts of the eastern sea and the southern Earth Kingdom, which ravaged shipping for two centuries and later split into fleets. In the south and east it was known as the Yakuya Confederation, and its bases, supporters and tribute networks reached well onto the land.

The crown's neglect of the countryside, which let banditry and rebellion spread on the west coast and in the interior, was the common thread. The kingdom was not poor, and it was not weak in numbers. It was a state whose provinces had begun to ask what the capital was for.

The Yellow Neck Uprising (312–305 BG)

The Yellow Neck Uprising was the most devastating rebellion of the age, and its consequences outlasted it by centuries. It followed the death of the Avatar Kuruk at 33 in 312 BG. Kuruk had spent his last years dealing with the Spirit World and had left the nations to settle their own problems, and the failure to find his successor emboldened those whom an Avatar would normally have opposed, so that corrupt and ruthless people grew in power and the world became unstable.

The rebellion

In the interior, the large bandit groups known as daofei grew bolder. A charismatic and unbalanced man, Xu Ping An, who had mastered the almost extinct skill of generating lightning, gathered them as the Yellow Necks, after the scarves they wore, and styled himself "General of Pandimu", a land that existed only in his mind. His followers came to believe that their plundering served a higher spiritual cause. They marauded through the central Earth Kingdom, killing officials, soldiers and civilians whom they regarded as law-abiders, destroying whole settlements and leaving orphaned children to starve. In the northern warring states, a claimant named Xiang, who said he was the first king of Ba Sing Se reborn, took up the yellow scarf and carried the rebellion into the old royal territories, challenging a nobility that had long been corrupt.

The Earth Kingdom's army chose not to defend some of the remote hinterland, in part because the nobility's attention was consumed by the Wars of Secrets and Daggers, and the villages were left to the insurgents. The Earth Sage Jianzhu, a friend of Kuruk's, visited one destroyed settlement and was told by an emissary of the Earth King that no reinforcements would be sent. What he saw there, and the king's inaction, shaped his later decisions, among them the conspiracy to find Kuruk's successor by unconventional means.

Zhulu Pass (304 BG)

The rebellion's main phase is dated 312–305 BG, and the remnants of its army were broken at Zhulu Pass in 304 BG, where Jianzhu trapped them. He did not kill Xu Ping An, because the Fire Nation wanted to study his lightning, and the Earth Kingdom government traded him in a secret agreement. About five thousand of the other Yellow Necks surrendered. Jianzhu tortured the earthbenders among them to death, then told the others that those who dug a trench deep enough to hide in by sundown would be pardoned, and when the trenches were dug he buried them alive. He reported to the Earth King that Xu was dead, and the people were told that Jianzhu had buried the villagers whom the rebels had murdered. He became a hero of the kingdom, and to the daofei he was the Gravedigger of Zhulu Pass.

Legacy

The surviving Yellow Necks reorganized in the underground as the Autumn Bloom Society, and freed Xu Ping An in 296 BG before the Avatar Kyoshi killed him. The deeper consequence was political. The uprising destroyed what trust remained between the central government and many rural communities, and provincial rulers began to conclude that Ba Sing Se would defend them only when doing so served its own interests. A generation of orphans, passed between guardians or turned out into the streets, grew up knowing no authority at all. The monarchy survived, but its power increasingly depended on the cooperation of regional elites, who had learned that they could do without it.

The Yellow Neck Uprising was not the direct cause of Qianchan's independence. The two events are separated by decades, and the sequence is important: the uprising showed that the capital would not protect remote communities, Qin's conquests then showed that the regional order could be overturned, his death produced a succession crisis, and the southern army's survival produced a separate struggle for sovereignty. The uprising foreshadowed the later fragmentation, and was not its cause.

Qin and the loss of the south (296–255 BG)

The kingdom's southern provinces were lost in a single generation. After the Yellow Necks, the pirate Fifth Nation (the Yakuya Confederation) was broken in 296–292 BG, and the young Gaoling commander Qin made his name by destroying its eastern stronghold. As Qin the Great (to the court, "Chin the Conqueror") he built a coalition of provincial lords, the King of Omashu, the Lord of Yu Dao and the Avatar Kyoshi, marched on Ba Sing Se, and was killed outside its walls in 270 BG, in a duel in which the king cheated. Kyoshi then entered the Inner City and forced a written constitution on the court, which also ended the first of the capital's two peasant uprisings.

Qin's heirs proclaimed the Qin Dynasty and reduced Ba Sing Se to a tributary city, but the south rose against them in the War of Liberation (270–255 BG). A treaty of 255 BG recognized the independent Qianchan Republic, and the dynasty became one of its political houses. For the kingdom, the loss was permanent: the capital could still send an army, but it could no longer turn it into lasting political control.

The full account, including the Southern Army, the collective command council and the founding of the republic, is in History of Qianchan.

The Great Interregnum (255–230 BG)

Qin's war and the dynasty's collapse destroyed the continent's grain and administrative network. In the Great Interregnum (255–230 BG) two to three million people died of famine, and the provincial lords governed their own territories while the capital struggled to hold its place. The crisis was not caused by hunger alone. Food and relief were distributed unequally, officials were corrupt, refugees crowded the cities, and the authorities failed to respond, so that the anger of the common people deepened.

The second peasant uprising

Ba Sing Se survived because of its walls and granaries, but its walls could not protect it from its own people. In the worst years of the famine, in the decade after 255 BG (the exact year is disputed), a second peasant uprising broke out inside the city. The first, in 270 BG, had been settled by Kyoshi. This one grew out of the same failures that had weakened the monarchy: hunger, inequality, inadequate relief, and the belief that the court and the garrison protected themselves while ordinary people starved. Its leaders were workers, refugees who had fled the provinces, displaced families and parts of the urban population. It spread through the districts, disrupted the distribution of food and attacked the institutions on which the monarchy depended.

The government could not treat it as an invasion, because its enemies lived inside the walls, and many of the soldiers who were supposed to put it down came from the same hungry districts. Officials abandoned their posts, units became unreliable, and factions fought for the palace and the administrative centres. Ba Sing Se fell a second time, not to a foreign army, but because the political and social order inside the walls came apart. The monarchy's prestige, already damaged, did not recover, and the capital learned that its fortifications could hold off armies but not resolve the grievances that threatened its government.

Bao Kun

Out of the second collapse came the garrison commander Bao Kun. His control of the one body that was still organized, the army, let him impose authority where the court had failed, and he and his successors rebuilt a government centred on the city and then extended it outward. His descendants became the Earth Kings of the following centuries. They later claimed a mandate from the first kings of Ba Sing Se that the historical record does not support: their legitimacy rested on having restored order, and not on an unbroken line. The new dynasty inherited the old institutions, and with them the unresolved problems that had destroyed its predecessors.

The Long Cold Peace (255–12 BG)

For over two centuries there was no great war on the continent. It was a stable agrarian society of peasants, with minor industrialization in a few cities, whose government stayed corrupt, incompetent and prone to banditry.

The quarrel with Qianchan

Ba Sing Se would not accept the republic. It sent two armies, in 240 and 225 BG, both of which failed; the Preliminary Accord of 224 BG set a boundary without recognition; and about 215 BG the capital founded the Dai Li to stop republican ideas from reaching its own subjects. Qianchan's policy was "we govern ourselves; we do not export governance." The republic's side of the story is told in History of Qianchan.

Incidents of the long peace

  • The Night of Knives (66 BG). The Earth King massacred the sages who spoke out against him, abolished their order and took the religious power for the crown. The Fire Nation would do the same to its Sages more slowly.
  • The Chenbao incidents (56–54 BG). Border disputes with the Water Tribes over a resource-rich region, settled by Avatar Roku.
  • The Nomad incidents (30 BG). Raids and counter-raids on the steppe frontier.

An unindustrialized giant

The kingdom did not industrialize. It was agrarian and enormous, with provincial lords who kept their own armies, a monarch whose real authority hardly passed the city walls, and a bureaucracy that was loyal and unreformed. While the Fire Nation built its first railway (260 BG) and Qianchan its first coal engines (255 BG), the Earth Kingdom's engineers were few and its factories fewer, and the Earth Kingdom did not begin to industrialize in earnest until the 20s AG, with Qianchan's help. Its armies still believed in the mass charge, which would be the cause of staggering losses against machine guns.

The coast, the colonies and the oil (37 BG–0 AG)

The last decades of the peace were the beginning of the end of the kingdom's old world, and the events were mostly on its coast.

The Fire Nation colonies (37 BG)

In 37 BG the Fire Nation under Sozin established its first colonies on the Earth Kingdom's western coast, on land that would become the province of Yanakawa. It was an escalation: for the first time a major power had planted settlements in the territory of another, and the colonies, which needed governors, police, taxes and defence, quickly became local industrial centres. The Avatar Roku stopped Sozin's expansion but let the colonists stay. Ba Sing Se, which could not agree on a response, had been shown that persistence paid. A determined state might keep its gains in spite of the Avatar, and the capital had no army that could take the coast back. Colonies that had been admitted by default made the next step easier.

Two other incidents belong to the same years. The Fire Nation claimed Natsuo Island, one of the easternmost of its own islands, after a large cache of ore was found there, and the calculating Earth King Jialun sent vessels on exercises nearby in the hope of goading Sozin into a quarrel. And the Crescent Island disaster, in which Roku destroyed the upper half of the island's temple and set off its volcano, left homeless people on the Fire Nation's side who blamed the Earth Kingdom for not helping them, material that Sozin's propaganda would use.

Oil in the Si Wong (28 BG)

In 28 BG oil was discovered in the Si Wong Desert, in the west of the kingdom. The Si Wong held the only large oilfield within reach of the Fire Nation's armies. The following year the Fire Nation made the first flight of a plane, and its fleet was already burning coal. A kingdom that did not know how to use a field, and could not defend it, was sitting on the future fuel of its most dangerous neighbor, and it was the Fire Nation's planners, not Ba Sing Se's, who understood what it meant. The reasons for the war that follow in the next sections cannot be understood without this fact.

The Alliance Treaty (3 BG)

Alarmed by the Fire Nation's expansion, Ba Sing Se and Qianchan signed the Alliance Treaty in 3 BG. It was a suspension of tensions and not a reconciliation: Qianchan signed only on condition that Ba Sing Se revise its language of non-recognition, and neither side trusted the other. The treaty promised support and a common cause. It did not create a joint command, a common mobilization plan, an agreed estimate of the threat or a commitment to a preventive war, and it did not station a single soldier on the other's soil. An alliance in name could not, by itself, deter an enemy that was counting on the allies to be slow.

Why the kingdom could not stop the war

Historians of the Academy of Gaoling, who write more candidly about the Earth Kingdom than the kingdom does, give several reasons for the failure of deterrence, none of which depends on the kingdom's rulers being stupid.

  • The command problem. The monarchy had no national army to speak of. Its forces were provincial armies, commanded by lords who answered to the king in name and who would not send their troops across the continent to defend a coast that was not theirs. The capital could not mobilize the kingdom's population and wealth under one command.
  • The intelligence problem. Ba Sing Se saw Fire Nation colonies, a coal-fired fleet and a nationalist press, but it did not see the scale or timing of the rearmament. Its secret police was built to hunt republicans, not to read the Fire Nation's procurement. Qianchan had better information, and in the years before the war the allies disagreed over how serious the threat was.
  • The political problem. The monarchy's first fear was always internal. A kingdom that had fallen twice from within was reluctant to arm its provinces and commit its army abroad.
  • The surprise. No one expected that the first blow would fall on a people who had no army. The Air Nomads were not the kingdom's concern, and when the comet came, the kingdom had no part in the opening of the war.
  • The assumption of the Avatar. The old order had relied for four centuries on the Avatar to settle crises. Roku's death in 12 BG removed the one person who had restrained Sozin, and no state had a plan for the world without him.

The Earth Kingdom was, in sum, a rich and populous target that was too fragmented to organize its resources and too suspicious of its allies to let them help. That is not a judgment on its people, who paid for it with about 29.6 million lives.

The kingdom at 0 AG

MeasureEarth KingdomWhy it mattered to the Fire Nation
PopulationAbout 230,000,000Manpower, farmland and strategic depth, but also an enormous territory to hold
CommandProvincial armies under lords; no unified national commandA rapid strike on the coast would face only local resistance
IndustryAgrarian; industrialization only from the 20s AGNo means to match an industrial army, or to use its own oil
ResourcesThe Si Wong oilfield; coal, metals, timber and grainExactly what an industrial state forecast that it would need
AlliesQianchan (Alliance Treaty of 3 BG)The treaty brought no joint command; Qianchan entered the war only in 30 AG
Internal stateCorrupt court, the Dai Li and the memory of two collapsesThe capital feared its own subjects as much as its enemy

The case for necessity

The Fire Nation's own planners, as they were later quoted in captured papers, described the Earth Kingdom as the centre of the problem that they believed they had to solve. The argument, which the Empire's defenders repeated for a century, ran as follows. The Fire Nation's economy was the largest in the world, and it depended on fuel that its islands could not supply for ever: its engineers forecast, within about a hundred years, a shortage of accessible oil if industry and aviation went on growing. The only large oilfield within reach lay in the Si Wong, in a kingdom that could not use it, could not defend it and could not be trusted to sell it. The one rival that could match the Fire Nation, Qianchan, was growing, and was allied to the kingdom. Waiting would mean competing for the field later, from a weaker position. And the Avatar, who had stopped Sozin once and who would be born again among the Air Nomads, was the one thing in the world that could forbid it.

The argument was strategically comprehensible and morally disastrous. It mistook a resource problem for proof that conquest was the only solution, when the allies, in the years before the war, would have traded fuel, agreed on shipping rules and shared research if they had been asked. Qianchan said so repeatedly, and Sozin did not ask. The full account of this reasoning, and of Sozin's other motives, is in the History of the Fire Nation and the article on the Qianchan Republic. What matters here is that the Earth Kingdom's weakness was part of the reason it was chosen: a continent that could not mobilize, and held the fuel of the future, was both the prize and the opportunity.

The Hundred Year War (0–100 AG)

The Earth Kingdom entered the war with an army that still attacked in mass and a bureaucracy that could not feed or arm it. It lost Yanakawa and the west coast by 10 AG, the southern Omashu front by 25 AG, and the grasslands by 50 AG. It began to industrialize in 23 AG with Qianchan's help, and took part in the long fights over the Si Wong and Ba Sing Se, losing about 29.6 million people. After the coup attempt of 98 AG King Kuei centralized the war effort. The story is told in the article on the Hundred Year War.

After the war

The Sōen strike of 100 AG destroyed the Earth Kingdom's command, and the provincial lords and generals fought one another for twelve years, until Omashu, Ba Sing Se and Gaoling pacified them. About 13 million died in the warlord wars. The question of what the kingdom should be was argued in its flags. Proposals for a new flag included "Five Kingdoms under One Flag" (105 AG), the "Banner of the Kingdom" (112 AG), "Three Major Kingdoms and Six Major Battles" (121 AG), the "Earth States" and "Earth Republic" (138 AG) and the "Earth Confederation" (159 AG). King Kuei, the 52nd Earth King, died in 153 AG, officially in his sleep, and was in fact killed by his daughter Hou-Ting, who followed him as the 53rd monarch, who reversed his reforms at once and was hated by nearly everyone. In June 171 AG the Earth Queen was killed by a Red Lotus bomb, and the First Earth Civil War began, out of which the militarist Kuvira's Earth Empire emerged. An international coalition, with Qianchan, is still working to restore the kingdom, or the confederation of King Wu, 54th Earth King.

Historiography

The history of Qin, Qianchan and Ba Sing Se is politically contested, and the contest is a part of the history.

QuestionQianchan's traditionBa Sing Se's tradition
Who was Qin?A reformer from Gaoling who opposed arbitrary royal authority, and a people's man"Chin the Conqueror", a warlord who challenged the lawful monarchy
The Yakuya campaign (295 BG)An operation against a destabilizing power that restored security in the eastA pretext to accumulate territory, prestige and an army
The duel (270 BG)A betrayal with hidden crossbowmen and a poisoned bladeThe end of a dangerous rebellion and the restoration of royal legitimacy
The Qin DynastyA betrayal of Qin's principles by his heirsThe lawful continuation of Qin's territorial achievements
QianchanThe heir of the reform movement, which won its independence by popular resistanceA fragment of the continental state, and a dangerous precedent for separatism
Bao Kun's lineA military usurpation that happened to restore orderThe heirs of the first kings, with an ancient mandate

Neither tradition needs to be entirely false. Qin could have sought reform sincerely, enjoyed broad popular support and still expanded his power by conquest, and his followers could have believed in his principles while they profited from his victories. Ba Sing Se's rulers could likewise have feared the loss of control over the provinces while using the language of law and order to protect their own rule. The lesson that the Academy of Gaoling draws from the kingdom's repeated collapses is that walls and claims of ancient legitimacy cannot guarantee survival once famine, inequality and political exclusion have worn away the public's trust. Imperial Fire Nation histories, for their part, describe the Earth Kingdom as a state that was rescued from itself, and give no casualty or famine figures.

history_of_the_water_tribes.title: History of the Water Tribes
history_of_the_water_tribes.html:
From the first separation of the North and the South to the Kingdom of Two Poles, the Hundred Year War and the civil war that dissolved it.

History of the Water Tribes
HomelandsThe North Pole and the South Pole, with settlements in the Foggy Swamp and trade with Jasmine Island
Political formThe Kingdom of Two Poles (2098 BG – 174 AG), a Northern Chief over autonomous Southern chiefdoms
CapitalsAgna Qel'a (North); Taluqqriaq / Wolf Cove (South)
Pre-war populationAbout 8,000,000 in all (0 AG): about 6,000,000 at the poles
FlagsKingdom of Two Poles (2098 BG – 174 AG); Southern Federation (171 AG–); Kingdom of Agna Qel'a (174 AG–)

The history of the Water Tribes is the history of a people who began as one tribe, split in two, and lived for four thousand years as a kingdom of two poles in which the North ruled in name and the South governed itself. They were weaker than the Fire Nation and the Earth Kingdom in numbers, wealth and industry, and for most of their history they were isolated from the world. They fought the Hundred Year War as its victims, and lost about half their people.

Origins

The Water Tribe was originally one nation, centered on the North Pole. After a period of civil unrest in which its people could not agree on social and cultural practices, a large group of warriors, waterbenders and healers sailed south, and founded the Southern Water Tribe, a federation of autonomous chiefdoms. The South's chiefs eventually agreed to accept the Northern Chief as their ruler in return for self-government. The Kingdom of Two Poles (the flag dates to 2098 BG) was this arrangement: a Northern Chief with a ceremonial and representative role, a Southern Council of Chieftains and Elders that made its own laws, and a veto for the South if the North wished to go to war. Southern families married into the Northern ruling family, but the distance, which was thousands of kilometers of ocean, made the two cultures diverge.

The North was a hierarchical and patriarchal society, with a large city, Agna Qel'a, carved from the ice at the head of a fjord, which kept a navy and a strong tradition of waterbending, and kept women from fighting. The South was simpler and more egalitarian, with ice-walled towns, a high degree of gender equality and waterbending that women practiced in battle. The two sides sometimes saw each other as barbarians and oppressors.

The tribes shared a religion centered on the moon and ocean spirits, Tui and La, whose home was the Spirit Oasis in the North, and the southern lights, which a festival of the Glacier Spirits was meant to call. Southerners travelled: one group went to the Earth Kingdom and founded the Foggy Swamp Tribe, thousands of years before the war, and the South traded with Jasmine Island, which sold its tea almost exclusively through the Southern merchants for centuries, until a pirate attack that the South failed to repel led the island to put itself under the Earth Kingdom's protection.

Isolation, pirates and decline (530–12 BG)

The Platinum Affair of 530 BG, in which the four nations quarrelled over a rebel general in the Earth Kingdom's civil war, led the Water Tribes, like the others, to close their ports. Most of their trade then went through the shang city of Port Tuugaq, where a few go-betweens handled the movement of ivory, hides and dried fish. The South, which had no native timber and no deep-water navy, was easy prey. It was impoverished, and many of its people became pirates, who built the Fifth Nation, a confederation of sea raiders from the eastern sea and the southern earthlands (518–292 BG). The South disowned the family of the Fifth Nation's best-known leader, the pirate queen Tagaka, even though she presented herself as its protector. In 296 BG a force led by a man thought to be the Avatar defeated the Fifth Nation. The South asked for a loan to build a navy and did not get it, so it remained poor and weak, and many of its people left to work abroad. The Earth Kingdom and the Water Tribes also quarrelled in the Chenbao incidents (56–54 BG) over a resource-rich border region, which Avatar Roku settled by diplomacy.

By Roku's time the tribes were recovering and cooperating. Chief Qanitt of Whale Harbor and the rich merchant Tiqriganiannig promoted modernization in the South, and funded an international academic expedition, the Unity, that carried the studies and technologies of the four nations around the world, though the governments suspected it was a spy mission. At the same time the spirits turned hostile as the nations industrialized, and when the Fire Nation claimed a sacred island near the Mo Ce Sea, Chief Skiri of the North wanted to retake it by force, and the Southern chiefs, who did not want a war, would not agree.

The Hundred Year War (0–100 AG)

In 0 AG the Empire of Tajisaki, one week after destroying the Air Nomads, bombarded both poles on Sozin's orders to subjugate the Water Tribes and work them to death. The North repelled the Empire in the First Battle of Agna Qel'a, and was then bombed from its eastern-pole base for a century, until the Siege of the North in 99 AG, in which Agna Qel'a fell with about 800,000 dead. The South was invaded, its leaders captured and forced to cooperate, and for ninety-nine years it was an occupied country, where uprisings, the last in 29 and in 99 AG, cost most of its people. After the war about 70% of the South was dead or missing. The Foggy Swamp Tribe and the exiles of the South joined the Earth Kingdom's war. These events are described in the articles on the Subjugation of the Water Tribes, the Southern Uprising and the Siege of the North.

After the war

The two tribes were again united in the Kingdom of Two Poles under a Northern Chief, with a Southern Council, and rebuilt with the Northern help of the Southern Reconstruction Project. The North, an enormous modern state, and the South, with an expanding economy, drifted apart, and the South accused the North of having abandoned it in its worst years. The Water Tribe Civil War of 170–174 AG began over Chief Unalaq's proposal to make Agna Qel'a the sole capital of both tribes, which the South saw as an attempt to subjugate it. It ended in 174 AG when the South launched a naval bombardment of the Northern capital and a ground assault, and the Kingdom of Two Poles was dissolved. The South had been independent as the Southern Federation since 171 AG, and the North became the Kingdom of Agna Qel'a, whose rulers Desna and Eska signed a peace treaty that recognized the South's sovereignty. In 181 AG the Kingdom of Agna Qel'a sent an expedition to colonize parts of the northern Earth Kingdom.

The continental power of the south and east, a large agrarian monarchy based at Ba Sing Se. The principal victim of the Hundred Year War.

Earth Kingdom
CapitalBa Sing Se
GovernmentMonarchy (the Earth King) over provincial lords and kings
PopulationAbout {{stat:pop_ek_0|n}} (0 AG); about 200,000,000 (100 AG)
Armed forcesAbout 7,000,000 (80 AG)
War deadAbout 29,600,000 (Hundred Year War); about 13,000,000 more in the Post-War Conflicts

The Earth Kingdom is the largest nation in the world, a loose confederation of provinces and kingdoms, including Omashu, Huamu and Shaozu, under the Earth King in Ba Sing Se, which was a tributary city under the Qin Dynasty until it collapsed. The Earth King's real authority was limited to the city, and the provincial lords ran their own armies. In the Hundred Year War this fragmentation, the kingdom's agrarian economy, its mass-charge doctrine and the Empire's chemical weapons and air power explain why it lost about eight people for every one that the Fire Nation lost.

Current affairs, 170 AG

Inside the kingdom

  • The throne and the provinces. Queen Hou-Ting, the 53rd monarch, has ruled since about 153 AG. She reversed King Kuei's reforms at once, and her reign has been hated by nearly everyone from its first year. Her heir is her nephew Wu. Loyalists, Provincialists and Reformers argue over the capital's primacy, local government and an elected government, with Chancellor Du Mingzhe as her minister, and corruption in the provincial bureaucracies is worse than at any time since the war.
  • Recovery. The population has recovered about 40 million since 100 AG, to about {{stat:pop_ek_170|m}}. The economy is about {{stat:gdp_ek_170}} ({{stat:gdppc_ek_170}} a person), still largely agrarian but industrializing since 23 AG.
  • Unrest. The Collective revived in 169 AG among peasants and workers who are dissatisfied with the Earth Queen, and the Equalists are active in the cities. A faction around the metalbender Kuvira is the most prominent reform group in Ba Sing Se. See the unrest of 167–171 AG.

Geopolitical decisions

  • Qianchan. The alliance holds under the Treaty of Gaoling, and the army is equipped largely with Qianchan-licensed arms.
  • The Fire Nation. The kingdom is its principal trading partner, and the Rebuilding Fund pays for the recovery of the occupied provinces.
  • The United Republic. Relations are cool and respectful, since the republic sits on land the kingdom lost. See [[united_republic_of_nations|United Republic of Nations]].
  • The Water Tribes. Relations with the tribes are uncertain as their unity breaks down in the civil war of 170–174 AG.

History

Qin collapse (255–230 BG). The Qin Dynasty's collapse destroyed the continent's grain and administrative network, and killed two to three million people. Ba Sing Se survived, and its garrison commander Bao Kun held it and expanded outward. Bao Kun's line later claimed an ancient mandate that the historical record does not support. The south broke away as the Qianchan Republic.

The Long Cold Peace. Ba Sing Se fought two suppression campaigns against Qianchan (240 and 225 BG), ended by the Preliminary Accord of 224 BG, and founded the Dai Li in about 215 BG to suppress republican ideas. The Alliance Treaty of 3 BG united the two states against the Fire Nation.

The war. The Earth Kingdom lost Yanakawa and the west coast by 10 AG, its southern Omashu front was cut off by 25 AG, and it began to industrialize in 23 AG with Qianchan's help. The Eastern Push, the Desert War and the Siege of Ba Sing Se followed. King Kuei centralized command after the Dai Li coup attempt of 98 AG. The Earth Kingdom never had chemical weapons.

After the war. The Sōen strike destroyed Ba Sing Se's western walls, and the kingdom broke into warlord wars, which Omashu, Ba Sing Se and Gaoling ended by about 112 AG.

Kuei and Hou-Ting (81–171 AG). King Kuei rebuilt the kingdom and gave all adults the vote in 150 AG. His daughter Hou-Ting, who had him killed in 153 AG, succeeded him and reversed the reforms immediately and was hated for it. In 171 AG the Earth Queen was killed by a Red Lotus bomb, and the First Earth Civil War began, from which the Earth Empire emerged.

Country profile, 170 AG

The figures in this section describe the Earth Kingdom in 170 AG, seventy years after the end of the Hundred Year War. They are estimates; the provincial censuses on which they rest were taken to different standards.

Names

The kingdom takes its name from the Earth Kings of Ba Sing Se, the ruling house whose claim of descent from the first kings is not supported by the historical record. In Qianchan it is called "the Confederation", a name from the Alliance Treaty of 3 BG that the kingdom has gradually adopted for itself. Its citizens call it the Kingdom. See History of the Earth Kingdom.

Geography

The Earth Kingdom occupies most of the great continent: the central plains, the northern mountains, the west-coast ranges, the eastern steppes, the Si Wong Desert and the Foggy Swamp. It is the largest state in the world by area and, after the war, only the second largest by population. Its rivers, the Great Yellow and the Wei in particular, feed some of the oldest farmland on earth. The climate varies from alpine in the north to subtropical in the south, with a continental interior. The great cities, among them Ba Sing Se, Omashu, Huamu and Shaozu, are separated by long distances, which is one reason the kingdom has always been difficult to govern.

Government and politics

The Earth Kingdom is a federal monarchy in form and, since about 153 AG, the personal rule of the Earth Queen. The sovereign, who in 170 AG is the 53rd, is head of state and keeps the right to convene the Council of Provinces, to appoint a Chancellor and to ratify treaties, and Queen Hou-Ting uses all of them. The provincial kings and lords govern their own territories. The postwar settlement, built on the Ba Sing Se Treaty and the pacification of the warlords by 112 AG, gave the capital a standing army under a single command, a national treasury and a common code of law. The Council of Provinces has two chambers: the Council of Kings and Lords, composed of the fifty-five constituent states, and the Assembly of the Estates, elected by property owners from 114 AG and by all adults from 150 AG, repealed in 153 AG and, with the Assembly itself, suspended since 154 AG.

The old secret police, the Dai Li, was abolished in 115 AG after the two coup attempts of 98 and 100 AG, and its functions passed to the civilian Office of Public Security. Under the regency its Office of Public Security holds detainees without trial. Politics divides between the Loyalists, who defend the monarchy and the capital's primacy; the Provincialists, who favor stronger local government; and the Reformers, who look to Qianchan and ask for an elected government. Corruption in the provincial bureaucracies remains a standing complaint.

The reign of Hou-Ting

King Kuei ruled from 81 AG to about 153 AG and cleaned up the courts and the provincial bureaucracies, and gave the vote to all adults in 150 AG. His daughter \1 followed him, and had in fact killed him, and she undid his work at once: she repealed the vote, dismissed his ministers, restored the sale of offices and provincial tax farming and in 154 AG suspended the Assembly of the Estates. Her reign was unpopular from the start and hated by peasants, merchants, lords, officers and Reformers alike. The Reformers proposed an “Earth Confederation” in 159 AG. Her heir is her nephew Wu. See the First Earth Civil War.

Foreign relations

The kingdom's foreign policy is shaped by the war it survived. It is allied with Qianchan under the Alliance Treaty of 3 BG, and the Treaty of Gaoling of 113 AG finally ended the language of non-recognition that had divided them for three and a half centuries. It is the Fire Nation's principal trading partner, and its largest creditor for the Rebuilding Fund. It has a cool, respectful relationship with the United Republic of Nations, which sits on land the kingdom lost, and an uncertain one with the Water Tribes' successor states, as the Kingdom of Agna Qel'a (174 AG) emerges.

Military

The Royal Earth Kingdom Army has about 1,100,000 active personnel and a reserve of some 4 million. It is organized in provincial corps under a central staff established by King Kuei, and is equipped largely with Qianchan-licensed arms. It has an air arm, a small navy and a respected corps of engineers, who built the Ba Sing Se fortification works. Bending is integrated into the army as a supplementary capability. The Royal Guard defends the capital, with the Wall Garrison of Ba Sing Se as its oldest unit.

Economy

The kingdom is a large agrarian and, since the 23 AG industrialization with Qianchan's help, an increasingly industrial economy. It is the world's largest producer of grain, rice, tea, wool and timber, and a major producer of coal, iron, copper and oil from the Si Wong fields, which it operates through a national company. Its industry is concentrated in a handful of cities, and the contrast between them and the rural provinces is stark. The Rebuilding Fund and the war's dead have shaped the labor market: the kingdom has a young population and a shortage of men of working age. The currency is the yuan.

Science and technology

The kingdom's best research institutions are the Ba Sing Se Imperial Academy, the Omashu Polytechnic and the Wall Engineering Institute. It is a leader in agronomy, hydrology and geology. Its aviation and heavy industry still depend on Qianchan and the Fire Nation. The Library of Wan Shi Tong, in the Si Wong, is a pilgrimage site for scholars.

Demographics

About 205 million people live in the kingdom, a number that has recovered about 40 million since 100 AG. The census of 165 AG counted some 55 provincial identities, with Earth Common as the language of administration. The population is predominantly Earth Kingdomer, with minorities of Steppe peoples, Foggy Swamp tribes and Fire Nation settlers. Religion is mainly Earth Kingdom folk tradition and ancestor worship, with a strong tradition of Spirit veneration. The war left a generation of orphans and a sex ratio that did not normalize until the 140s AG.

Culture

Earth Kingdom culture is the oldest continuous civilization on the continent: its traditions include Pai Sho, tea houses, opera, brush painting, poetry, the great lion-turtle cities and the walled-city tradition. Its cuisine varies by province, from the noodle and dumpling traditions of the center to the spiced stews of the south. The cultural memory of the Hundred Year War, of the Siege of Ba Sing Se and of the famines is held in annual rites at the walls. The Earth Kingdom's war literature is among the largest in the world.

The federal republic of the south, born of the war that tore the southern provinces from the Earth Kingdom. Ba Sing Se's reluctant ally, and the industrial rival the Fire Nation feared most.

For the Qianchan Republic's origins as seen from the kingdom it left, see History of the Earth Kingdom. For the Empire's reasoning about the republic, see History of the Fire Nation.
Qianchan Republic
CapitalGaoling
GovernmentFederal republic with a President and a bicameral legislature (Parliament)
Founded255 BG, after the War of Liberation (270–255 BG)
Founder in spiritQin the Great (killed 270 BG)
Also calledThe "Fifth Nation" (by its own citizens and, bitterly, by Ba Sing Se's court)
