ba_sing_se.title: Ba Sing Se
ba_sing_se.html:
The capital of the Earth Kingdom, a vast walled metropolis in the northeastern continent.

Ba Sing Se
永固城
The Impenetrable City
LocationNortheastern Earth Kingdom
NationEarth Kingdom
PositionCapital and largest city
GovernmentEarth Monarch and royal administration
RulerKuei (during the final phase of the Hundred Year War)
EstablishedAncient period; inhabited by approximately 7,000 BG
Urban formWalled metropolis with concentric districts
Major divisionsOuter Wall, Agrarian Zone, Inner Wall, Lower Ring, Middle Ring and Upper Ring
Principal landmarksEarth Monarch's Palace, Ba Sing Se University, Lake Laogai, Inner Wall and Outer Wall
Pre-war populationPart of an Earth Kingdom population of approximately 230,000,000 in 0 AG
Major destructionSōen strike, 17 July 100 AG
Casualties of the Sōen strikeApproximately 380,000 killed

Ba Sing Se is the capital of the Earth Kingdom and one of the largest urban settlements in the world. Located in the northeastern part of the continent, the city is defined by its enormous concentric walls, extensive agricultural hinterland, monumental stone architecture and deeply stratified social order. Its name, commonly translated as the "Impenetrable City", refers to its historic reputation for resisting invasion. At its greatest extent, Ba Sing Se functioned less like an ordinary city than a fortified region containing farmland, settlements, lakes, military installations and an immense urban center.

The city's physical organization reflects its political history. Its outer defenses protect a broad agricultural zone, while the Inner Wall encloses the densely inhabited metropolis. Within the city, the Lower, Middle and Upper Rings divide residential and commercial districts by wealth and social position. At the center stands the Earth Monarch's Palace, the seat of a monarchy that once claimed authority over most of the continent. The result is a city of extraordinary scale and engineering, but also one in which physical boundaries reinforce political and economic inequality.

Ba Sing Se survived repeated rebellions, dynastic crises and the wars that reshaped the Earth Kingdom. During the Hundred Year War, it remained the kingdom's principal stronghold despite the loss of much of its territory. Its defenses were eventually subjected to increasingly destructive attacks by the Empire of Tajisaki. On 17 July 100 AG, the Empire's Sōen weapon destroyed the western sector of the Outer Wall and the Inner Wall, killing approximately 380,000 people and devastating the districts behind the breach. The attack became one of the defining catastrophes of the war.

Geography and natural setting

Ba Sing Se occupies a broad inland basin in the northeastern Earth Kingdom. The surrounding terrain includes mountains, uplands, river valleys and agricultural plains. Its position places it at the junction of major continental roads and administrative routes, allowing it to collect grain, taxes, manufactured goods and tribute from distant provinces. The city's size and centrality made it a destination for merchants, officials, soldiers, scholars and refugees from across the continent.

The city was built around the relationship between defensible terrain and dependable food supplies. Its enormous walls enclose not only buildings but also open land, water and productive fields. Rather than depending entirely on supplies entering through its gates, Ba Sing Se maintained a substantial agricultural zone within its defensive perimeter. This arrangement allowed it to sustain a large population during blockades and reduced the ability of an enemy army to starve the capital into surrender.

Lake Laogai lies within the city's wider defensive landscape. The lake, surrounding countryside and cultivated plains form part of the open space between the Outer Wall and the principal urban districts. These areas contrast with the dense neighborhoods of the Lower Ring and the monumental compounds of the Upper Ring.

Urban form and architecture

Ba Sing Se developed over many centuries, and its architecture reflects successive periods of expansion rather than a single unified construction plan. The oldest settlement is traditionally associated with subterranean chambers and excavated stone passages. As the city expanded above ground, these older spaces became less central to daily life, while the surface metropolis grew into a complex of walls, avenues, courtyards, markets, temples, government buildings and residential compounds.

The city is characterized by heavy masonry, broad defensive structures and an architectural language that emphasizes permanence. Stone buildings commonly incorporate timber supports, plastered surfaces, tiled roofs and enclosed courtyards. Earthbending allows builders to excavate foundations, move massive blocks, shape roads and erect defensive structures on a scale difficult to achieve through conventional labor alone. The resulting city combines ordinary residential streets with monumental walls and palace compounds that dominate the surrounding landscape.

Unlike cities organized around a single commercial waterfront or central market, Ba Sing Se is structured by nested defensive boundaries. Each wall creates a distinct urban threshold, regulating the movement of people and goods while communicating the authority of the state. The city's major roads, gates and transit routes connect these layers to the royal center, making its layout both a transportation system and an expression of political hierarchy.

Buildings vary significantly between districts. In the Lower Ring, houses are densely packed and often built from less expensive materials, with narrow streets and crowded courtyards. The Middle Ring has larger stone buildings, formal markets, public squares and more carefully maintained roads. The Upper Ring contains extensive walled residences, government compounds and ceremonial architecture, with tiled roofs and decorative details that signal wealth and rank.

The walls and defensive system

Outer Wall

The Outer Wall is Ba Sing Se's most recognizable structure and the principal symbol of its historical reputation for invulnerability. Rising approximately 600 feet (183 meters) in the original architectural accounts, it encircles the city and its agricultural hinterland. Its immense height and thickness make it one of the largest defensive constructions in the world.

The wall is not merely a barrier around a dense settlement. It protects an extensive territory containing farmland, open ground, water and routes needed to sustain the capital. Its gates are designed to be controlled by earthbending rather than conventional hinges and machinery, allowing defenders to open or close massive passages through the structure. Guard posts, internal chambers and defensive positions are integrated into the wall itself.

Its scale shaped Ba Sing Se's military doctrine. Invading armies had to overcome the Outer Wall before they could threaten the city's main population centers. Even a successful breach did not guarantee victory, since an attacker would still have to cross the agricultural zone and reach the Inner Wall. The city's defenders could therefore retreat to successive positions while using the open land to delay, observe and disrupt enemy movements.

Agrarian Zone

The Agrarian Zone occupies the broad territory between the Outer Wall and the Inner Wall. It contains fields, farms, open plains, water sources and scattered rural settlements. Much of the city's food supply originates here, and the zone is essential to Ba Sing Se's ability to withstand a siege.

The zone also serves a military purpose. Its open terrain separates the Outer Wall from the densely populated urban center, limiting the ability of an enemy to exploit a breach immediately. Defenders can observe movements across the fields, move troops between defensive positions and deny attackers the cover offered by dense urban districts.

Despite its strategic importance, the Agrarian Zone is not simply military land. Farmers work plots that supply the city's markets and granaries, and rural households remain economically tied to the capital. The fields demonstrate the unusual scale of Ba Sing Se: its urban government depends on land that would normally lie beyond the boundaries of a single city.

Inner Wall

The Inner Wall separates the agricultural hinterland from the principal urban settlement. It forms the second major line of defense, enclosing the districts where most residents live and where the city's commercial, administrative and cultural institutions are concentrated.

Access through the Inner Wall is controlled by gates and earthbending checkpoints. The wall also reinforces the city's social geography, since it separates the fields and outer settlements from the densely built residential rings. In periods of political stability, it represents the boundary between the city's food-producing hinterland and its institutional center. In wartime, it is a final major barrier protecting the urban population.

The Inner Wall was destroyed during the Sōen strike of 17 July 100 AG. Its destruction allowed the effects of the strike to extend into the districts immediately behind it and contributed to the fires and widespread collapse that followed.

Districts

Lower Ring

The Lower Ring is the largest and most densely populated of Ba Sing Se's principal urban divisions. It is home to laborers, craftspeople, small merchants, farmers who maintain residences inside the city, newcomers and refugees displaced by conflict elsewhere in the Earth Kingdom. Its streets are narrower and less formally paved than those of the wealthier districts, and residential buildings are often crowded together.

The district supports much of the city's everyday economy. Workshops, laundries, food stalls, neighborhood markets, lodging houses and small businesses serve the needs of a population that keeps the metropolis functioning. Its commercial life is varied and energetic, but residents have historically faced overcrowding, poor infrastructure and limited access to political influence.

The Lower Ring's position behind successive walls offers protection from external armies, but it does not guarantee equal treatment within the city. Restrictions on movement and unequal access to public services have made the district a recurring source of resentment. During periods of mass displacement, refugees have increased pressure on housing, sanitation and employment.

Middle Ring

The Middle Ring is the principal commercial and civic district of Ba Sing Se. It contains larger shops, markets, restaurants, financial offices, administrative buildings and educational institutions. Streets are generally wider and better maintained than those in the Lower Ring, and public squares and courtyards provide space for trade and civic gatherings.

Ba Sing Se University is among the district's most prominent institutions. The university serves as a center of scholarship, professional education and the preservation of historical records. The Middle Ring also contains markets that draw goods from across the Earth Kingdom, connecting the capital's consumers with agricultural and industrial production in distant provinces.

Although wealthier than the Lower Ring, the Middle Ring remains economically diverse. Merchants, civil servants, teachers, artisans and skilled workers live and work here. Its position between the poorer outer neighborhoods and the royal center makes it an important intermediary between ordinary urban life and the state's governing institutions.

Upper Ring

The Upper Ring is the wealthiest and most politically influential residential district of Ba Sing Se. It contains the estates of aristocratic families, residences of senior officials, military compounds, formal gardens and government buildings. Its streets and compounds are designed to project order, prosperity and authority.

Large houses are often organized around enclosed courtyards and surrounded by private walls. Yellow roof tiles and elaborate architectural details distinguish prestigious residences from the darker roofs and simpler structures of the Lower Ring. Security is more visible, and access to important compounds is controlled by officials, guards and household retainers.

The Upper Ring's privileges extend beyond architecture. Its residents enjoy easier access to the royal administration and greater freedom of movement through the city. The contrast between this district and the Lower Ring is one of Ba Sing Se's most enduring social divisions, making the city's concentric layout a physical representation of its class structure.

Earth Monarch's Palace

The Earth Monarch's Palace occupies the ceremonial and political center of Ba Sing Se. The immense compound contains audience halls, administrative offices, ceremonial courts, gardens, shrines, service quarters and residential buildings. Its scale allows it to function almost as a separate city within the Upper Ring.

The palace is enclosed by its own defensive walls and controlled gates. Its architecture emphasizes symmetry, formal axes, courtyards and monumental entrances. The principal halls provide the setting for royal audiences, appointments, state ceremonies and meetings with senior military and civilian officials.

The palace's location reinforces the relationship between the monarch and the capital. Roads and important urban routes lead toward the central government, while the palace's private grounds separate the royal household from the surrounding city. The compound is simultaneously a residence, a seat of administration and a symbol of the Earth Kingdom's claim to continental unity.

Lake Laogai

Lake Laogai lies within the wider territory enclosed by Ba Sing Se's outer defenses. Surrounded by open land and connected to the city's agricultural and water systems, it forms part of the landscape that distinguishes Ba Sing Se from a conventional walled settlement.

The lake and its surroundings are associated with the city's security apparatus and hidden state activities. Its name became particularly notorious through the operations of the Dai Li, whose influence extended beyond ordinary policing into surveillance, political repression and the management of information.

Transportation and infrastructure

Ba Sing Se's scale requires transportation systems capable of moving residents, workers, food and military personnel across long distances. Major roads connect the rings and lead toward the city's gates, while markets and public squares serve as local centers of movement and exchange.

Earthbending is central to the city's infrastructure. Benders operate gates, repair roads, excavate foundations and carry out large-scale construction. The manipulation of earth and stone allows the government to maintain defenses and infrastructure that would otherwise demand immense quantities of labor and time.

Earthbending-powered monorail systems were developed to improve travel between districts. Transit stations connect major urban routes and reduce the time required to cross the metropolis. These systems are especially important in a city whose size makes walking between distant districts a substantial journey.

Water systems, granaries, workshops and markets support the city's population. The agricultural zone supplies much of its food, while merchants bring in materials and goods from other parts of the Earth Kingdom. Ba Sing Se's ability to combine local production with continental trade is one of the foundations of its long-term importance.

History

Origins and early settlement

Ba Sing Se is one of the oldest continuously inhabited settlements in the world. Some traditions place an early settlement in the region around 7,000 BG, when major climatic changes and volcanic activity reshaped parts of the continent. The earliest city is associated with subterranean chambers excavated by earthbenders, who carved habitable spaces and extracted valuable minerals from the surrounding rock.

These underground settlements became important centers of trade. Luminous crystals extracted from the surrounding stone were valued as sources of light, and their distribution connected the settlement to distant communities. Trade wealth, population growth and the development of earthbending construction gradually encouraged expansion above ground.

By approximately 4,900 BG, the city had assumed much of the general form associated with its later history, including its great outer defenses and internal divisions. The walls were expanded and reinforced over successive centuries, as Ba Sing Se became a political center whose importance extended beyond its immediate surroundings.

Rise as the seat of the Earth Kings

As the settlement grew, Ba Sing Se became the center of an expanding political order. The monarchs who ruled from the city claimed authority over provinces scattered across the continent. The capital's walls and granaries gave it an advantage over rival cities, while its administrative institutions allowed rulers to collect tribute, appoint officials and coordinate military campaigns.

Control over such a vast territory was never complete. Distance, regional loyalties, banditry, competing rulers and the difficulty of maintaining reliable armies repeatedly weakened the capital's authority. The city could dominate the royal court and the surrounding provinces without necessarily exercising effective control over every region that recognized the Earth King.

The growing gap between the capital and the provinces contributed to repeated unrest. Rural communities and provincial elites often regarded Ba Sing Se as a center that demanded taxes and soldiers while providing insufficient protection in return. These grievances eventually contributed to the political crises of the late Warring States period.

The Warring States and Qin the Great

During the late Warring States period, the authority of Ba Sing Se was challenged by Qin the Great, a southern lord who advocated reform of the Earth King's absolute authority. Qin assembled a coalition of provincial rulers and military forces, with the support of Avatar Kyoshi, the King of Omashu and the Lord of Yu Dao.

Qin's forces expanded across much of the continent and reached the outer defenses of Ba Sing Se in 270 BG. The Earth King challenged Qin to a duel outside the walls, ostensibly to resolve the conflict without a prolonged siege. According to the account most widely accepted in the Qianchan Republic, the king used hidden crossbowmen and a poisoned blade. Qin was killed, although he mortally wounded the king in the same encounter.

Kyoshi remained at Ba Sing Se after the duel and used her authority to force reforms upon the royal court. These included a written constitution and limitations on certain royal privileges. The reforms stabilized the monarchy but did not transform it into a constitutional state. The struggle over Qin's death and the legitimacy of the capital's rule continued to shape the political divide between Ba Sing Se and the southern provinces.

The Great Interregnum and the rise of Bao Kun

The collapse of the Qin Dynasty in 255 BG caused widespread famine and disrupted the administrative and agricultural networks that had linked the continent. The ensuing Great Interregnum, dated approximately 255–230 BG, killed an estimated two to three million people and weakened the remaining political institutions of the region.

Ba Sing Se survived the crisis because of its defensive walls, granaries and capacity to retain control over the surrounding territory. Its garrison commander, Bao Kun, consolidated authority within the city and expanded outward during the collapse of neighboring administrations. His descendants became the Earth Kings of subsequent centuries, establishing a new ruling line whose legitimacy rested partly on the survival of the capital itself.

In the following decades, Ba Sing Se attempted to reassert authority over the southern territories, sending armies against the emerging Qianchan Republic. These campaigns failed to restore the former political unity. The Preliminary Accord of 224 BG established a boundary without fully resolving the dispute, and the capital subsequently supported the creation of the Dai Li to prevent republican political ideas from spreading into its territory.

The long peace and the centralization of power

For much of the period between the third century BG and the beginning of the Hundred Year War, Ba Sing Se experienced no conflict on the scale of the earlier continental wars. Its political system remained centered on the Earth King, the royal bureaucracy and the capital's military institutions. Agriculture continued to provide the foundation of the economy, while industrial development remained limited compared with that of the Fire Nation and Qianchan.

Stability did not eliminate corruption or political repression. Royal officials struggled to govern distant provinces, and the court repeatedly responded to dissent by suppressing opposition rather than reforming the structures that produced it. The Night of Knives in 66 BG, during which the Earth King massacred outspoken sages and abolished their order, became one of the clearest examples of the monarchy's hostility toward organized criticism.

In 3 BG, the Alliance Treaty tied Ba Sing Se to the Qianchan Republic despite the capital's long refusal to recognize the republic's legitimacy. The agreement reflected the growing threat posed by the Fire Nation and the practical necessity of cooperation between two states whose political relationship remained deeply contentious.

The Hundred Year War (0–100 AG)

Ba Sing Se entered the Hundred Year War as the capital of a vast but unevenly administered kingdom. Its population, agricultural resources and defensive works were formidable, but its military institutions were slow to adapt to industrial warfare. The Earth Kingdom suffered major territorial losses as the Empire of Tajisaki advanced along the western coast and into the kingdom's southern regions.

The capital remained a principal stronghold, and its defenses became a strategic objective for the Empire. The Outer Wall and Inner Wall forced attackers to confront successive defensive positions, while the Agrarian Zone provided the city with food and room to maneuver. Ba Sing Se's survival became central to the wider war because its fall would remove the Earth Kingdom's most important political and logistical center.

The city nevertheless suffered repeated attacks. Imperial forces developed increasingly heavy weapons and methods of breaching its defenses, while the Earth Kingdom struggled to modernize its army and coordinate operations across the continent. Qianchan assistance contributed to the kingdom's industrialization beginning in 23 AG, but the transformation came after decades of military setbacks.

The siege and the Sōen strike

During the later stages of the war, Ba Sing Se became the target of a renewed Imperial campaign. Conventional attacks damaged its outer defenses, and by 96–97 AG the western sector of the Outer Wall had been breached by heavy bombs. The city survived, but its defenses were weakened and reconstruction remained incomplete.

In 99–100 AG, the Imperial Research Bureau completed a forward Sōen array at Qinglan Port. The weapon was designed to release stored firebending energy in a concentrated beam and was intended specifically to break Ba Sing Se. Earth Kingdom intelligence did not establish the array's effective range before the attack.

On 17 July 100 AG, the Sōen was discharged against the western sector of the city. The beam destroyed the affected portion of the Outer Wall and obliterated surrounding structures. The Inner Wall was destroyed, while buildings in the districts behind it collapsed or caught fire. The resulting fires and blast damage devastated a wide area, and thousands of people suffered burns, blast injuries or blindness.

Approximately 380,000 people were killed in the strike. The weapon produced no lasting radiation, but its physical destruction was comparable in scale to the effects of a nuclear explosion. The loss of the walls and the damage to the capital's defensive system disrupted the Earth Kingdom's command structure at a critical moment in the war.

The strike was not the end of the conflict. On 18 July, allied forces attacked the Imperial position at Qinglan Port. The death of Ozai and the collapse of the Imperial command precipitated the final crisis of the Empire of Tajisaki. Ba Sing Se emerged from the war damaged and scarred, but its survival remained central to the continuation of the Earth Kingdom.

Reconstruction and the postwar kingdom

Reconstruction required the restoration of defensive walls, housing, roads, public buildings and the agricultural systems on which the capital depended. The scale of the destruction made recovery a national undertaking rather than a purely municipal project. Survivors were displaced across the city, and the loss of homes and livelihoods placed additional pressure on the already unequal urban districts.

The Sōen strike also weakened the symbolic authority of Ba Sing Se's defenses. The city had long been regarded as a place that no outside power could destroy. The destruction of the western wall demonstrated that its survival depended not only on the strength of its fortifications but also on intelligence, military adaptation and the political capacity to defend the wider kingdom.

Under Kuei, the monarchy pursued postwar reforms and reconstruction while attempting to restore the kingdom's authority over its provinces. Ba Sing Se remained the political center of the Earth Kingdom, but the war had exposed the limitations of a system in which a powerful capital governed a vast territory through a centralized court and uneven provincial institutions.

Government and administration

Ba Sing Se is governed as the seat of the Earth Monarch and the central administrative apparatus of the Earth Kingdom. The royal court appoints officials, directs military policy, receives provincial representatives and oversees the collection and distribution of resources. Ministries and bureaucratic offices manage taxation, public works, transport, trade and the maintenance of the city's defenses.

The Council of Five serves as a senior military body responsible for coordinating the kingdom's defense. Its relationship with the monarch has varied according to the political circumstances of each reign. During wartime, the council and the royal administration must coordinate the defense of the capital with military campaigns across a continent-sized state.

The Dai Li historically operated as the city's elite security and intelligence organization. Its responsibilities extended beyond conventional law enforcement to include political surveillance and the suppression of dissent. The organization's influence became particularly controversial when its leaders attempted to control information, manipulate the court and protect their own authority from scrutiny.

Ba Sing Se's administrative institutions are both a source of strength and a recurring weakness. The capital concentrates expertise, resources and authority in one place, allowing the kingdom to coordinate large projects and mobilize substantial forces. However, the same concentration makes the state vulnerable when the royal court is compromised, when the bureaucracy conceals military failures or when provincial communities lose confidence in the capital.

Economy

The city's economy is based on agriculture, commerce, crafts, government administration and the distribution of goods from across the Earth Kingdom. The Agrarian Zone supplies much of the food required by the population, while markets and merchants connect the capital with provincial production. The city's position at the center of the kingdom's road network makes it a major destination for grain, textiles, minerals, tools and manufactured goods.

Ba Sing Se's large population supports a diverse internal market. The Lower Ring contains workshops and small businesses that serve daily needs, the Middle Ring hosts major markets and commercial institutions, and the Upper Ring concentrates wealth in aristocratic estates and government employment. The royal administration itself is a major consumer of food, building materials, military equipment and specialist labor.

Despite its size, Ba Sing Se's economy remained predominantly agrarian for much of its history. Industrial development lagged behind the Fire Nation and Qianchan Republic, leaving the kingdom dependent on traditional production methods during the early decades of the Hundred Year War. Later modernization improved its capacity to manufacture and transport military supplies, but it could not immediately compensate for the kingdom's earlier failures to prepare for industrial warfare.

Society and culture

Ba Sing Se contains a wide variety of regional traditions, languages, occupations and social classes. Its markets bring together merchants from distant provinces, while its schools, temples and administrative institutions attract scholars and officials. Tea houses, restaurants, poetry houses, public gardens and neighborhood markets provide spaces for recreation and social life.

Tea drinking is a prominent part of the city's everyday culture. Shops and tea houses serve as places to rest, conduct business and discuss local affairs. The city's food culture reflects its role as a continental market, combining agricultural produce from the surrounding countryside with ingredients and cooking traditions brought by travelers and migrants.

Education is concentrated in institutions such as Ba Sing Se University, while the royal court supports ceremonial traditions intended to reinforce the authority of the monarchy. Architecture, clothing and domestic decoration communicate social position. Roof tiles, compound walls, the scale of a residence and its proximity to government institutions all help distinguish the wealthy from the poor.

The city's social divisions have also shaped its political culture. The walls between rings limit movement and reinforce unequal access to employment, housing and government. The ideal of Ba Sing Se as a safe and orderly refuge has often coexisted with the exclusion of poorer residents and the suppression of unwelcome information. The city can therefore be understood both as an extraordinary achievement of urban engineering and as a system in which security and hierarchy are closely linked.

Military significance

Ba Sing Se's military importance derives from its size, central location, population, food supply and defensive works. Its walls protect more than a palace or a single urban district. They enclose a large territory capable of sustaining a substantial population, making the city difficult to defeat through a short blockade or a single conventional assault.

The city also serves as the administrative center of the Earth Kingdom. Its capture or destruction threatens the continuity of the monarchy, the coordination of provincial armies and the distribution of resources. For this reason, an attack on Ba Sing Se has consequences far beyond the city's immediate boundaries.

Its history demonstrates the limits of fortification when separated from effective intelligence and military modernization. The Outer Wall delayed attackers for centuries, but the Sōen strike showed that a weapon designed to concentrate overwhelming energy against a narrow section of the defenses could inflict catastrophic damage. Ba Sing Se's survival depended ultimately on the resilience of its people and institutions as much as on its walls.

agna_qela.title: Agna Qel'a
agna_qela.html:
The capital of the Northern Water Tribe, an ice city at the head of a fjord.

Agna Qel'a
Capital city of the North
[Panoramic image: the ice city rising in terraces from a frozen fjord, with immense ice cliffs, bridges, canals and the royal palace above the harbor]
LocationSouthern coast of the North Pole continent, at the head of a fjord on the Northern Sea
CountryNorthern Water Tribe (until 174 AG); Kingdom of Agna Qel'a (from 174 AG)
PositionCapital and largest city
GovernmentSeat of the Northern Chief; later the royal seat of the Kingdom of Agna Qel'a
Head of stateChief of the Northern Water Tribe; Desna and Eska from 171 AG
EstablishedAncient; founded during the unification of the northern tribes
PopulationNot established
LanguageNorthern Water Tribe languages
Major featuresRoyal Palace, Spirit Oasis, inner harbor, fjord gates, canal network, ice terraces and cliff districts
Historical significanceSite of the First Battle of Agna Qel'a (0 AG), the Siege of the North (99 AG), and the Water Tribe Civil War (170–174 AG)

Agna Qel'a is the capital and largest city of the Northern Water Tribe, situated at the southern edge of the North Pole continent where a deep fjord opens into the Northern Sea. One of the oldest continuously inhabited urban settlements in the polar regions, the city is renowned for its enormous ice architecture, tiered districts, intricate waterways and monumental structures carved directly into the surrounding glaciers.

Unlike settlements in the southern polar regions, Agna Qel'a developed into a dense, permanent metropolis. Its buildings, fortifications and public spaces form a continuous architectural landscape, with towers, domes, vaulted halls and bridges rising from the frozen ground. Much of the city appears to grow out of the ice itself: natural cliffs become foundations for residential districts, glacial ridges form the city's upper terraces, and water channels cut through the lower city before reaching the harbor.

The city serves as the political, commercial, religious and military center of the northern tribes. Its location within a sheltered fjord, together with its immense ice defenses and controlled waterways, made it exceptionally difficult to attack. Nevertheless, Agna Qel'a suffered extensive bombardment during the Hundred Year War, fell to the Empire of Tajisaki during the Siege of the North in 99 AG, and became the principal battleground of the Water Tribe Civil War in 170–174 AG.

Description

Geography and natural setting

Agna Qel'a occupies a natural basin at the head of a large polar fjord. The surrounding landscape consists of towering glaciers, steep ice cliffs, frozen plateaus and an extensive tundra extending inland toward the mountainous interior of the North Pole. The fjord provides access to the open sea while offering shelter from the worst ocean swells and drifting pack ice.

The city is built across several elevations. Its lowest districts occupy the relatively flat ice shelf around the inner harbor, while the central city rises along natural ridges and the upper slopes of the fjord. The highest districts are incorporated into the cliffs themselves, where large structures emerge from the glacial walls. From the sea, the settlement resembles a continuous wall of blue-white ice punctuated by towers, arched openings and illuminated windows.

Its scale is difficult to appreciate from within the lower city. The royal palace and the highest towers can be seen from distant sections of the fjord, while the outer residential districts disappear into the surrounding cliffs. During clear weather, sunlight reflects from the pale architecture across the harbor. During blizzards, the upper city is frequently obscured, leaving only the lights of the major waterways and public buildings visible through the snow.

Architecture and urban form

Agna Qel'a is constructed primarily from ice, although timber, animal products, stone and imported materials are also used where available. Waterbending is central to the city's construction. Builders shape water into walls, columns, vaulted ceilings, stairways and entire buildings, then maintain the structures through repeated freezing, carving and reinforcement.

Rather than following a uniform grid, the city developed organically around its geography. Older buildings cluster around the original settlement and the Spirit Oasis, while successive generations expanded outward along the fjord, up the cliffs and across the surrounding ice shelves. The result is an irregular but interconnected urban landscape in which narrow residential lanes open into broad ceremonial squares, enclosed courtyards and monumental public spaces.

Buildings are frequently joined by covered bridges, elevated walkways and archways that cross streets and waterways. In the older districts, closely spaced buildings form sheltered corridors against the wind. Newer districts have wider streets and larger communal structures, reflecting the city's growth and the increasing concentration of its population.

Residential buildings are rarely simple blocks of ice. Their facades incorporate carved reliefs, projecting balconies, rounded windows, layered roofs and decorative ridges. Family histories, ancestral figures, marine animals and spiritual motifs are commonly carved into walls and entrances. Wealthier families commission elaborate facades, while communal housing and working districts favor simpler, more practical forms.

The use of ice as a building material gives the city a distinctive appearance. Light passes through thin walls and translucent arches, producing blue and turquoise tones in enclosed spaces. Thick structural walls appear almost opaque, while polished floors and frozen surfaces reflect the light of lamps and braziers. The city is therefore not a uniform white expanse, but a layered composition of pale blue, deep turquoise, silver and shadow.

Despite its apparent fragility, much of the architecture is massive. Buildings are integrated into the natural ice wherever possible, and major structures use thick supporting walls, interlocking forms and carefully maintained foundations. Waterbenders continuously repair weather damage, restore eroded surfaces and reinforce critical sections of the city's infrastructure.

Canals, bridges and harbor

The canal network is one of Agna Qel'a's defining features. Waterways connect residential districts, markets, public squares and the inner harbor, allowing small boats and canoes to move through much of the lower city. In colder periods, portions of the canals freeze at the surface, while maintained channels and enclosed passages continue to carry water and traffic.

Bridges range from narrow residential crossings to enormous ceremonial arches spanning the principal waterways. Some are covered to protect travelers from snow and wind; others are open and decorated with carved balustrades, columns and statues. At the largest intersections, several waterways converge beneath terraces of buildings, producing the impression of a city layered over its own canals.

The fjord entrance is protected by enormous ice walls and fortified gates. Ships entering the harbor must pass through controlled approaches, where waterbenders operate locks that regulate water levels and prevent unauthorized vessels from reaching the inner city. The arrangement serves both commercial and military purposes, allowing the capital to receive fishing fleets, trading ships and visitors while maintaining control over its principal maritime entrance.

These waterways are more than a means of transportation. They also supply water, support fishing and facilitate the movement of construction materials. During an attack, the canals and locks can be altered by waterbenders to obstruct vessels, flood approaches or isolate sections of the city.

Districts and landmarks

Agna Qel'a has no single architectural style or perfectly regular plan. Its principal districts developed at different times and reflect the city's changing political, religious and economic roles.

  • The Royal District. Located on the upper terraces, this district contains the royal palace, administrative halls, residences of senior officials and ceremonial grounds. Its buildings are among the largest in the city and dominate the skyline.
  • The Spirit Oasis. An ancient sanctuary associated with the Moon and Ocean Spirits, Tui and La. The oasis lies within a sheltered area of the city and is distinguished by its living water and vegetation, which contrast sharply with the frozen landscape outside.
  • The Old City. The oldest continuously occupied part of the settlement, characterized by narrow lanes, closely spaced buildings, carved family facades and small bridges. Its irregular layout reflects generations of construction around the original settlement.
  • The Inner Harbor. The principal maritime center, containing docks, warehouses, boatyards and the controlled waterways connecting the city to the fjord. It is also a critical part of the city's defenses.
  • The Lower City. A broad collection of residential, commercial and working districts around the harbor and lower canals. These districts accommodate merchants, fishermen, artisans, laborers and many of the city's service industries.
  • The Cliff Districts. Residential and institutional neighborhoods built into the natural ice cliffs above the central city. Elevated walkways and carved passages connect them to the lower terraces.
  • The Healing Quarter. A concentration of healers, medical schools, treatment halls and teaching facilities. Its location within the capital reflects the importance of healing in Northern Water Tribe society.
  • The Warrior Grounds. Training yards, armories, barracks and military facilities associated with the defense of the city and the Northern Water Tribe.

The districts are connected by a dense network of stairs, ramps, bridges, tunnels and canals. The result is a city that is simultaneously vertical and horizontal: movement along the fjord connects the major districts, while climbing through the terraces leads into progressively higher residential and administrative areas.

History

Foundation and unification

Agna Qel'a was founded during the unification of the independent tribes of the North Pole. Before the establishment of the city, northern communities were dispersed across the tundra and coastline, following seasonal hunting grounds, fishing routes and the movements of marine animals.

The construction of a permanent capital represented an attempt to unite these communities through a common political and religious center. Its position on the Northern Sea allowed the settlement to connect otherwise isolated communities, while the fjord offered a sheltered harbor and access to inland routes. The city gradually became the meeting place of tribal leaders, spiritual authorities, hunters and traders.

The unification did not eliminate every political or cultural disagreement. Some groups eventually departed for the South Pole, contributing to the development of the Southern Water Tribe. Nevertheless, Agna Qel'a remained the dominant northern settlement and the principal seat of the Northern Chief.

In its earliest centuries, the city was smaller and less commercially important than it would later become. Its principal functions were political, religious and communal. Pilgrims visited the Spirit Oasis, while hunters exchanged hides, fish, animal products and tools with neighboring communities. As its population increased, the settlement expanded along the fjord and incorporated the surrounding ice formations into its architecture.

Trade and urban growth

Agna Qel'a gradually developed into a major center of polar trade. Its harbor connected northern hunters and fishermen with merchants from other regions, and the city became an important market for animal products, seafood, crafted goods and imported materials.

Trade encouraged the growth of permanent workshops, warehouses, markets and specialized occupations. Artisans developed increasingly elaborate techniques for carving and reinforcing ice, while healers and spiritual authorities established institutions that attracted students from across the North Pole.

The growth of commerce also increased the political importance of the capital. Northern chiefs and wealthy families increasingly concentrated their resources in Agna Qel'a, while smaller communities remained dependent on the city for trade, medical services and political representation. The resulting concentration of wealth and authority strengthened the capital's position within the Northern Water Tribe.

Over time, migration from rural and semi-nomadic communities accelerated. Families seeking security, employment and access to the city's institutions settled in its expanding outer districts. The resulting urban growth transformed Agna Qel'a from a fortified tribal center into a large, densely populated metropolis.

The Hundred Year War (0–100 AG)

Agna Qel'a became a principal target of the Hundred Year War after the Empire of Tajisaki began its campaign against the Water Tribes in 0 AG. One week after the destruction of the Air Nomads, the Empire launched simultaneous attacks against the North and South Poles, seeking to subjugate the tribes and destroy their ability to resist.

The first major assault against the northern capital took place during the First Battle of Agna Qel'a, from 11 to 19 September 0 AG. The Imperial Northern Battlegroup attacked the city with naval forces, airships, incendiary weapons and a landing force intended to establish a foothold on the coast.

The defenders used the terrain, severe weather and waterbending to resist the invasion. Ice barriers were repaired or reconstructed as they were damaged, while riflemen and waterbenders attacked the Imperial landing force on the exposed ice shelf. Fog and blizzards disrupted the attackers' coordination, and the landing force was isolated before it could establish a secure position.

The Imperial force withdrew on 19 September. The battle nevertheless caused extensive damage, particularly in the lower city, and approximately 52,000 people were killed. The ice walls were repaired in the following weeks. The Empire abandoned attempts to capture the capital at this scale and instead established a forward base farther east, from which it conducted periodic bombing raids.

The North's survival came at the cost of increasing isolation. The Empire's naval superiority and air attacks weakened trade and inflicted continued civilian losses. Northern communities increasingly sought refuge within the capital and other fortified settlements, strengthening the city's dominance over the surrounding region.

The decisive attack came in November 99 AG during the Siege of the North, also known as the Second Battle of Agna Qel'a. The Empire launched a combined air and naval operation using chemical weapons, incendiary bombs and winter-trained mechanized troops. Unlike the first assault, the offensive was designed to overwhelm the city's defenses and destroy the Northern Water Tribe's remaining capacity to resist.

The city fell in December 99 AG after five weeks of fighting. Approximately 800,000 people died in the siege, including large numbers of civilians. The Chief and much of the Northern leadership were evacuated by Qianchan submarines, while surviving defenders and residents fled into the surrounding tundra or were captured. Agna Qel'a suffered severe destruction, and the Northern Water Tribe's population fell dramatically during the final year of the war.

The capital's fall did not immediately end the war. The Empire continued operations against the poles until the collapse of its central authority in July 100 AG, following the Sōen strike on Ba Sing Se and the death of Fire Lord Ozai at Qinglan Port.

Reconstruction and reunification

Following the war, Agna Qel'a underwent extensive reconstruction. Damaged ice walls, canals, residential districts and public buildings were restored, while new neighborhoods expanded into surrounding ice cliffs and previously undeveloped ground. The city's population grew as northern communities returned and new residents moved into the capital.

The postwar period also brought greater political and economic centralization. Agna Qel'a remained the seat of the Northern Chief and the principal center of administration for the northern territories. Reconstruction was accompanied by renewed trade, institutional development and the expansion of medical and educational facilities.

Under the postwar arrangement known as the Kingdom of Two Poles, the North and South were formally united under a Northern Chief, with a Southern Council intended to represent the interests of the southern population. The Northern capital played a central role in reconstruction efforts, including assistance to the South. However, the relationship remained unequal, and disputes over political authority, economic resources and the limits of southern autonomy persisted.

The capital continued to expand through the following decades. New districts spread across the surrounding cliffs and ice shelves, while the older city retained its dense network of canals and monumental architecture. Agna Qel'a became a symbol of northern recovery, but also of the concentration of power that increasingly alienated southern leaders.

Water Tribe Civil War (170–174 AG)

The city's modern political role was transformed by the Water Tribe Civil War of 170–174 AG. The conflict emerged from longstanding tensions between the North and South and escalated after Chief Unalaq proposed making Agna Qel'a the sole capital of both tribes. Southern leaders regarded the proposal as an attempt to subordinate the South to northern political authority.

The Southern Water Tribe declared independence in 171 AG, establishing the Southern Federation. The conflict escalated into mechanized warfare, including naval operations, attacks on fortified positions and fighting across the polar settlements. The North retained Agna Qel'a as its principal political and military center, while the Southern Federation developed its own command structure and territorial administration.

In 174 AG, Southern forces launched a naval bombardment of the capital followed by a ground assault. The attack marked the decisive final phase of the civil war. The Kingdom of Two Poles was dissolved, and the northern territories reorganized as the Kingdom of Agna Qel'a. Desna and Eska became its rulers and signed a peace treaty recognizing southern sovereignty.

The war reinforced the city's importance as both a strategic stronghold and a symbol of northern political identity. It also left a lasting division between the two poles, ending the long-standing ambition to govern the Water Tribes from a single capital.

Defenses and strategic importance

Agna Qel'a's defensive strength derives from the combination of geography, architecture and waterbending. The fjord narrows the approaches to the city, while the surrounding ice cliffs restrict movement across the landward side. The outer ice walls, fortified gates and controlled canal locks force ships and landing forces into predictable approaches.

The city's waterways can be modified during combat. Defenders can raise barriers, freeze channels, flood low-lying approaches and obstruct vessels attempting to pass through the locks. The ice walls can also be repaired rapidly by trained waterbenders, making conventional bombardment less effective when defenders retain control of the surrounding waters.

These advantages helped the city survive the First Battle of Agna Qel'a. They were less effective against the Empire's later combination of sustained air attacks, chemical weapons and mechanized infantry. The fall of the capital in 99 AG demonstrated that the city's defenses depended not only on its physical structure but also on its ability to maintain supplies, communications and control of the surrounding sea.

In the postwar period, Agna Qel'a remained a major military center. Its harbor, workshops and central position in northern administration supported the development of modern defensive forces. During the Water Tribe Civil War, however, the same concentration of infrastructure and political authority made the capital a decisive target for the Southern Federation.

Economy and society

Agna Qel'a is the principal commercial center of the northern polar region. Fishing, hunting, boatbuilding, trade, craftsmanship and the maintenance of the city's ice infrastructure form important parts of its economy. The harbor connects the capital to coastal communities and foreign merchants, while its markets distribute food, clothing, tools and imported goods throughout the northern territories.

The construction and maintenance of the city support specialized occupations. Waterbenders work alongside architects, carvers, engineers and builders to preserve major structures and extend the canal network. The city's scale also requires extensive public services, including transport, sanitation, storage, heating and emergency maintenance during severe weather.

Healing is a particularly important profession. The capital houses experienced healers and medical schools, and its institutions serve residents from across the North Pole. The concentration of these services reinforces Agna Qel'a's status as a destination for education and employment.

The city's population includes political officials, religious authorities, merchants, artisans, fishermen, soldiers, healers and laborers. Wealth and social status vary considerably between districts. The monumental upper city and the residences of influential families contrast with the crowded working neighborhoods around the lower harbor, reflecting the inequalities that accompanied the city's commercial growth.

Culture and religion

The Spirit Oasis occupies a special position in the religious life of Agna Qel'a. Its living water and sheltered vegetation distinguish it from the frozen environment beyond, and its association with Tui and La makes it one of the most important spiritual sites of the Water Tribes.

Religious symbolism is incorporated throughout the city. Carved motifs of the moon, ocean, marine animals and ancestral figures appear on public buildings, bridges and residential facades. Ceremonial spaces are concentrated around the older districts and the royal precinct, where political authority and spiritual tradition have historically overlapped.

The architecture also functions as a record of family and community history. Carvings commemorate ancestors, important events and local legends, allowing buildings to preserve traditions across generations. In the older districts, the accumulated decoration gives the city an appearance of continuous historical growth rather than a single planned construction project.

Despite destruction during the Hundred Year War and the Water Tribe Civil War, Agna Qel'a retained its status as the principal symbol of northern identity. Its scale, distinctive ice architecture and association with the Spirit Oasis made the capital central to the political imagination of the Northern Water Tribe and, later, the Kingdom of Agna Qel'a.

omashu.title: Omashu
omashu.html:
A prominent autonomous kingdom and mountain city in the western Earth Kingdom, known for its industrial development, political reforms and role in the Hundred Year War.

Omashu
LocationWestern Earth Kingdom, among the high mountains
CountryEarth Kingdom (autonomous kingdom)
GovernmentMonarchy under its own king
Political statusConstituent kingdom of the Earth Kingdom
Known forIndustrialization, reform movements, mountain defenses and the southern Omashu front
Major allyQianchan Republic
Strategic importanceWestern mountain approaches and southern war front
Major conflictHundred Year War (0–100 AG)
Postwar roleOne of three powers that ended the Earth Kingdom's warlord wars by 112 AG
Associated eventsEarly Land War; southern Omashu front; postwar pacification

Omashu is a major mountain kingdom and city in the western Earth Kingdom. Although it recognizes the Earth Monarch, Omashu retains its own king and a substantial degree of political and administrative autonomy. Its mountainous geography, established commercial networks and tradition of local government have made it one of the most prominent constituent states of the kingdom.

Omashu is distinguished by its role in the development of industry and political reform within the Earth Kingdom. Its urban economy combines traditional earthbending construction with workshops, manufacturing, transport infrastructure and trade across the western mountain routes. Its rulers and administrators have periodically pursued reforms intended to improve the efficiency of government, strengthen the kingdom's defenses and reduce its dependence on the distant court at Ba Sing Se.

During the Hundred Year War, Omashu became one of the Earth Kingdom's principal military strongholds. By 25 AG, the Empire of Tajisaki's advance through the high mountains had severed the southern Omashu front's land connection with the rest of the kingdom. The Qianchan Republic subsequently supplied the front by sea and committed its entire air force to supporting operations in the region during the late war.

Following the destruction of part of Ba Sing Se's defenses by the Sōen in 100 AG, the Earth Kingdom fragmented into competing regional powers and warlord territories. Omashu, Ba Sing Se and Gaoling became the three principal powers responsible for ending the ensuing warlord wars by approximately 112 AG. Omashu's position in the western mountains, its military experience and its independent political institutions made it essential to the reconstruction of the kingdom.

Geography

Omashu lies among the high mountains of the western Earth Kingdom. Its terrain consists of steep slopes, narrow valleys, elevated plateaus and passes connecting the interior to western and southern routes. These geographical features have shaped the kingdom's political development, economy and military organization.

The mountain approaches restrict the movement of large armies and make the kingdom difficult to invade through conventional means. Narrow roads and passes can be defended by relatively small forces, while elevated positions provide observation over surrounding valleys. The same terrain, however, complicates the movement of agricultural goods, industrial materials and military supplies, making transportation infrastructure particularly important.

Omashu's position gives it access to trade routes linking inland settlements with western ports and the southern regions. These connections supported its growth as a commercial center and later became essential to its industrial development. During the Hundred Year War, the mountain routes also determined the shape of the front, as Imperial advances sought to isolate the kingdom from the wider Earth Kingdom.

Urban form and architecture

The city of Omashu is built into a mountainous landscape of steep cliffs and elevated terraces. Residential districts, markets, workshops and administrative buildings occupy different levels of the terrain, connected by roads, stairs, bridges and engineered transport routes. Rather than spreading uniformly across a plain, the city rises and descends with the mountain, producing a dense urban settlement in which topography determines the arrangement of neighborhoods.

Earthbending plays a central role in the city's construction. Buildings are founded directly into rock, terraces are cut into slopes, and retaining walls support roads and residential districts. Stone structures are often combined with timber, tiled roofs, courtyards and covered walkways. Fortifications and elevated platforms are integrated into the urban landscape, allowing defensive works to serve as part of the city's ordinary infrastructure.

Omashu's architecture reflects the practical demands of a city built on difficult terrain. Broad ceremonial spaces are concentrated where the mountain permits them, while narrow streets and stepped lanes follow the contours of the slopes. Bridges and elevated roads link neighborhoods separated by ravines, and the movement of goods depends on transport systems capable of overcoming large differences in elevation.

The city is also notable for its delivery-chute system, which uses gravity and engineered channels to move packages through the urban landscape. The system illustrates Omashu's long-standing interest in practical engineering and efficient movement. Its later industrial development built upon this tradition, expanding the use of mechanical systems and organized transport to serve workshops, markets and military supply depots.

Government and political status

Omashu is a hereditary kingdom within the wider Earth Kingdom. Its king governs local affairs through a royal administration, with authority over the city's institutions, regional security and the surrounding territory. The kingdom's relationship with Ba Sing Se is based on membership in the Earth Kingdom rather than direct administration by the capital.

This arrangement gives Omashu considerable room to pursue policies suited to its own geography and economy. Local officials can manage infrastructure, trade, industrial projects and defensive preparations without requiring every decision to originate at the royal court in Ba Sing Se. The extent of this autonomy has varied according to the strength of the Earth Monarch and the political circumstances of the wider kingdom.

Omashu's political tradition has periodically placed it at the forefront of debates over reform. Its leaders have had to reconcile the authority of the monarchy with the practical demands of governing a major commercial and industrial center. Administrative efficiency, public works and the organization of local resources have therefore been important concerns, particularly during periods of military crisis.

Omashu's autonomy has not always meant opposition to the Earth Kingdom. The kingdom has participated in wider continental affairs when its interests aligned with those of the monarchy, and it has contributed to the defense of the Earth Kingdom during the Hundred Year War. Its political position is best understood as a powerful constituent state that supports a common kingdom while maintaining its own institutions and regional priorities.

Industrialization and economic reform

Omashu became one of the Earth Kingdom's important centers of industrial development. Its commercial networks, access to mountain resources and tradition of earthbending engineering provided favorable conditions for the expansion of workshops and manufacturing. The city's transport systems also encouraged experimentation with mechanisms designed to move goods efficiently through steep and crowded urban districts.

Industrial development in Omashu was not simply a response to the Hundred Year War. The kingdom's geography had long required practical solutions to the movement of people, food and materials. Roads, retaining walls, bridges, delivery systems and storage facilities formed the foundation for more specialized engineering. As demand grew, workshops could supply tools, construction materials, transport components and equipment for the kingdom's defenses.

The emergence of industrial production placed Omashu among the Earth Kingdom's most forward-looking states. While the kingdom as a whole remained predominantly agrarian for much of its history, Omashu's commercial and engineering traditions made it a natural center for efforts to modernize production. Its experience also demonstrated that industrialization did not require the complete abandonment of traditional earthbending methods; instead, bending could be integrated into construction, manufacturing and infrastructure.

Political reform accompanied these economic changes. Industrial and commercial growth increased the importance of reliable administration, predictable trade rules, infrastructure investment and the coordination of labor and resources. Reform-minded officials and local interests had reasons to favor more systematic government over arbitrary royal intervention. Omashu consequently became associated with practical reforms that sought to strengthen state capacity and make its institutions more responsive to the needs of a growing economy.

These developments did not make Omashu a modern industrial state on the same scale as the Qianchan Republic or the Empire of Tajisaki. Rather, they distinguished Omashu within the Earth Kingdom, where industrialization proceeded unevenly and central government often struggled to coordinate development across distant provinces.

Trade and transportation

Trade has been central to Omashu's prosperity. The city connects mountain settlements with regional markets and routes leading toward the western and southern parts of the continent. Merchants exchange agricultural goods, stone, timber, metal, tools and manufactured products, while the city itself supports a large market for transport services and specialist labor.

Omashu's steep terrain encouraged the development of unusual transportation systems. Its delivery chutes allow packages to descend between elevations quickly, reducing the need to carry every item along winding roads and stairways. Roads and bridges connect the principal districts, while storage facilities and market yards allow goods to be collected and redistributed.

During peacetime, these systems support commerce and urban life. During war, they become part of the kingdom's logistics network. The same engineering capacity used to move commercial goods can support the transport of equipment, food and military supplies, although the city's dependence on mountain passes makes it vulnerable when those routes are cut.

Military significance

Omashu's military importance derives from its defensible terrain, autonomous administration and position along the western approaches to the Earth Kingdom. The mountains provide natural barriers, while roads and passes concentrate movement into routes that can be defended. The city itself combines elevated positions with fortified approaches, making a direct assault costly for an invading army.

Its industrial and engineering capabilities also contribute to its defense. The kingdom can maintain fortifications, repair transport infrastructure and support the production of equipment needed by its forces. Its ability to organize local resources is particularly important when communications with Ba Sing Se are disrupted.

Omashu's military tradition is closely connected to its autonomy. A kingdom responsible for defending difficult mountain territory cannot depend entirely on decisions made far away by a central court. Local command, knowledge of the terrain and the capacity to maintain supply routes are essential to its survival.

The Hundred Year War

The early war and the mountain approaches

During the early decades of the Hundred Year War, Omashu became one of the principal western strongholds of the Earth Kingdom. The Empire of Tajisaki's continental advance placed increasing pressure on the kingdom's approaches, as Imperial forces sought to cross the high mountains and reach the southern and western territories.

The kingdom's terrain slowed the advance and complicated the movement of large formations. However, the Empire's industrial and military advantages allowed it to continue applying pressure through the mountain corridors. Omashu's strategic position meant that its defense was important not only to the kingdom itself but also to the wider balance of the western front.

The southern Omashu front (25 AG onward)

By 25 AG, the Empire's advance through the high mountains had severed the southern Omashu front's land connection with the rest of the Earth Kingdom. The isolation threatened the front's supply of food, ammunition, equipment and reinforcements. Maintaining the position required a supply system capable of bypassing the Imperial-held territory between Omashu and the kingdom's other forces.

The Qianchan Republic supplied the front by sea. Qianchan's navy and commercial infrastructure allowed it to move supplies along maritime routes that remained accessible despite the loss of the land connection. The relationship made Omashu an important recipient of Qianchan support and demonstrated the strategic value of cooperation between the two states.

The supply effort was difficult and vulnerable to interdiction. Ships had to move goods through contested waters, and cargo then had to be transferred to routes leading inland toward the mountain front. The ability to sustain the position depended on coordination between naval escorts, port facilities, transport units and Omashu's own logistical organizations.

Qianchan air support

In the later stages of the war, Qianchan committed its entire air force to the Omashu front. This concentration reflected the front's strategic importance and the need to sustain the Earth Kingdom's western resistance against the Empire's superior industrial and aerial capabilities.

Air support supplemented maritime supply and the kingdom's ground defenses. Aircraft could support operations along the mountain approaches, help protect critical positions and respond to Imperial pressure in areas where difficult terrain limited the movement of ground forces. The commitment also placed substantial demands on Qianchan's wider military effort, since aircraft assigned to Omashu were unavailable for other fronts.

Omashu's survival during the later war therefore depended on a combination of local defensive capacity and external support. Its terrain made it difficult to conquer, but geography alone could not sustain a front cut off from the rest of the kingdom. Qianchan's supply network and air force helped preserve the position until the final phase of the war.

The Sōen strike and the postwar crisis

The destruction of part of Ba Sing Se's defenses by the Sōen on 17 July 100 AG marked a turning point in the final phase of the war and the beginning of a severe political crisis within the Earth Kingdom. The capital survived, but the loss of approximately 380,000 people and the destruction of key defensive structures weakened the authority of the central government.

The end of the Empire's war did not restore order automatically. With the monarchy's institutions damaged and the kingdom's regional powers already accustomed to independent military organization, competing warlords attempted to establish control over territories and supply routes. The conflict that followed threatened to replace Imperial occupation with prolonged internal fragmentation.

Omashu's experience as an autonomous kingdom made it one of the principal regional powers capable of responding to this crisis. Its military institutions, industrial capacity and established administration provided a foundation for sustained operations beyond its immediate territory. Its position in the western mountains also gave it strategic leverage over routes connecting several regions of the kingdom.

Pacification of the warlord wars (100–112 AG)

After the Hundred Year War, Omashu joined Ba Sing Se and Gaoling as one of the three principal powers responsible for ending the Earth Kingdom's warlord wars. The three centers represented different sources of authority: the monarchy and central institutions of Ba Sing Se, Omashu's autonomous kingdom and military position, and Gaoling's role as the capital of the Qianchan Republic.

The campaign against the warlords required more than defeating individual armies. Regional authorities had to be displaced or reconciled, roads and trade routes reopened, and local administrations restored or reorganized. The struggle also involved competing ideas about the future of the Earth Kingdom, including the relationship between the central monarchy and the powerful states that had assumed greater responsibility for their own defense.

Omashu's contribution was particularly important in the western regions, where its geographic position and military experience allowed it to project power beyond the city. Its participation helped prevent the postwar settlement from being determined solely by Ba Sing Se and ensured that the autonomous kingdoms remained significant actors in the restoration of order.

By approximately 112 AG, the three powers had ended the principal phase of the warlord wars. The result was not an immediate return to the political conditions that had existed before the Hundred Year War. Instead, the kingdom emerged from the crisis with a changed balance of power, in which regional states such as Omashu had demonstrated that they could play a decisive role in the survival and reconstruction of the Earth Kingdom.

Legacy

Omashu occupies a distinctive place in the history of the Earth Kingdom. It is a major autonomous kingdom whose political identity is rooted in its own monarchy, mountain geography and tradition of local administration. Its commercial and engineering systems helped it develop an industrial base unusual for the wider kingdom, while its reform movements challenged the assumption that continental government had to be directed exclusively from Ba Sing Se.

The Hundred Year War transformed Omashu from a prominent regional power into a central component of the Earth Kingdom's military survival. The isolation of the southern front and its dependence on Qianchan supply demonstrated the importance of maritime logistics and international cooperation. Qianchan's commitment of its entire air force to the front further cemented the relationship between the two powers.

Omashu's role in the postwar pacification of the kingdom gave it an enduring place in the settlement that followed the Empire's defeat. Alongside Ba Sing Se and Gaoling, it helped end the warlord wars and restore a measure of continental order. Its history illustrates the importance of regional institutions in a state whose size and diversity repeatedly strained the authority of its capital.

yu_dao.title: Yu Dao
yu_dao.html:
A region and city of the Earth Kingdom's west coast, the site of the opening landing of the Yanakawan Campaign.

Yu Dao
RegionEarth Kingdom (4292 BG – 4 AG)
BattlesYu Dao (3–6 January 1 AG); Relief of Yu Dao (March 101 AG)

Yu Dao was the site where the Empire landed on 3 January 1 AG, at the river landing of Yuhe, and used mustard gas for the first time in the war. The region fell in 4 AG, and its flag was retired. It was relieved in the War of Independence in March 101 AG.

City of the United Republic

After its relief Yu Dao is part of the United Republic: a harbor city of mixed Fire Nation and Earth Kingdom settlement (the sources say a hundred and fifty years of it) whose financial district on Nanaka island, with its exchange building (renovated 158 AG) on the back of the fifty-yuan note, trades with Qianchan. Councillor Ilama is from Yu Dao. Yu Dao Central Police Station, on Harbor Front, was built in 128 AG.

Bombings of 170 AG

About 11 September 170 AG a bomb destroyed the lower floors of the exchange building, and on 18 September another destroyed the police station. The Assembly was told that at least 237 were dead; the martial law vote followed on 22 September. A reconstruction fence on the harbor front became a memorial of names painted in red, among them Dava's. See Republic City crisis of 170 AG.

Destruction, December 182 AG

After the fall of Republic City, Yu Dao became the seat of the Republic’s government. It was destroyed by an atomic air burst on 19 December 182 AG. See Strikes of December 182 AG.

taluqqriaq.title: Taluqqriaq
taluqqriaq.html:
The Southern Water Tribe's cavern capital, the Wolf Cave beneath Wolf Cove.

Taluqqriaq
CountrySouthern Water Tribe
DestroyedNovember 99 AG

Taluqqriaq is the Water Tribe name for Wolf Cove, "the wolf cave." After the surface town was shelled, it became the resistance's capital, a city of caverns beneath the glacier. The Southern Garrison shelled the glacier above it from 13 November 99 AG, and Breaker units dug into the tunnels. It was destroyed, and the Avatar was found in the ice near it.

qinglan_port.title: Qinglan Port
qinglan_port.html:
A harbor of Yanakawa (Imperial name Seiran Harbor), the site of the Sōen's forward array and the death of Ozai.

Qinglan Port
RegionYanakawa
Imperial nameSeiran Harbor
EventsSeiran Bay landing (1 AG); Battle of Qinglan Port (18 July 100 AG); the Provisional Council (18 September 100 AG); Treaty of Qinglan (105 AG)

Qinglan Port was the site of the second Imperial landing of 1 AG, at Seiran Bay. In 99–100 AG the Empire built the forward Sōen array there, from which Ozai fired on Ba Sing Se. The allies took the port on 18 July 100 AG, and the Yanakawan Liberation Front formed its Provisional Council there.

si_wong_desert.title: Si Wong Desert
si_wong_desert.html:
A vast desert of the western Earth Kingdom, and the source of the oil that fueled the Fire Nation's war.

Si Wong Desert
OilDiscovered 28 BG; used as vehicle fuel from 5 AG
WarsDesert War (50–79 AG); Si Wong Offensive (80–88 AG)
Oil cityTongba

The Si Wong Desert held the only large oilfield within reach of the Imperial armies. The Empire reached its edge in 27 AG, fought for it in the Desert War (50–79 AG) and held it from the Si Wong Offensive until Ozai's death. After the war it was used for nuclear testing.

air_temple_island_chains.html:
The island chain south-west of the continent, with the Southern chain, occupied by the Empire from 1 AG.

Southern Air Temple island chain
LocationSouth-south-west of the Earth Kingdom
Occupied1 AG (Empire)
LaterDivided with Qianchan (50 AG); Qianchan-occupied supply route for the Royalists

The Southern Air Temple island chain was razed in the Air Nomad Genocide, and was occupied with the Southern chain by the Empire, which built forward bases and airfields there. They were the launching point for the invasion of Yanakawa in January 1 AG. A Qianchan civilian ship was sunk in its waters in 27 AG, and by 50 AG the chain was divided between the Empire and the Qianchan Navy. In the civil war, Qianchan occupied it and used it to supply Zuko.

The Earth Kingdom's western coastal province, the land of the United Republic of Nations.

Yanakawa was the first province that the Empire took on the continent, in the ten-year Yanakawan Campaign. It was the base of the Imperial Eastern Territories for ninety years, until the Yanakawan War of Independence made it the core of the United Republic of Nations.
