siege_of_caldera.title: Siege of Caldera
siege_of_caldera.html:
Siege of Caldera
Part ofThe late stage of the Fire Nation Civil War
Date22 August 117 – April 118 AG (about nine months); ended with the Duel of the Palace on 9 May 118 AG
LocationCaldera City, capital of the Fire Nation
ResultRoyalist victory. The Court’s defenses collapse
Belligerents
Royalists
Salvationists (the committees)
Ozai loyalists (the Court)
Commanders and leaders
RoyalistsGeneral Ito Shigeru; Zuko
SalvationistsCentral Salvation Committee (Tanaka Kenji, Ono Sayuri)
CourtAzula; General Hirata Gensai
Strength
Royalistsabout 120,000
Salvationistsabout 50,000
Courtabout 25,000 (Flame Guard, Ministry of Truth detachments, cultists), with about 800,000 civilians in the city
Casualties and losses
About 260,000 killed, mostly civilians

The Siege of Caldera was the last great battle of the Fire Nation Civil War. For about nine months, from 22 August 117 AG to the spring of 118 AG, Royalist, Salvationist and Court forces fought one another across the Fire Nation capital, Caldera City, which at the start of the siege held about 800,000 civilians. About 260,000 people died, most of them civilians, which makes it the deadliest battle of the war. It is the nineteenth of the war's twenty defining battles.

The siege was unusual in that it was fought by three parties inside a single city, none of which was strong enough to remove the others. The Royalists, under General Ito Shigeru and, from May 118, Zuko in person, attacked from the south and east. The Salvationists, whose field army had been destroyed at the Nagare River, held the western wards. The Court, under Azula and General Hirata Gensai, held the central ministries and the Palace district. The fighting was conducted street by street, and it was accompanied by famine, cold and, in the last months, epidemic disease. The failure of the city's gas and water supply in December 117 is generally regarded as the point at which the civilian death rate overtook the military one.

The Salvationist forces ended their part in the siege by negotiation in March 118. The Royalists took the ministries, the harbor and the Imperial Archive in April, and the Court was reduced to the Palace district, where the siege ended with the Duel of the Palace on 9 May 118 AG. The siege has been the subject of more civilian testimony than any other event of the war, and its register of the dead, compiled ward by ward by the Royalist administration in the summer of 118, was used in the accountability hearings that followed.

Background

Strategic position in 117 AG

By the summer of 117 AG the war had been a three-sided conflict for a year and a half, since the Salvationist committees broke with the Court at Kuroshio Mills in March 116. The Court had lost its factories with the fall of Sakuragawa in 115 and most of its field army with the mutinies and defections of 111 to 116. It retained the capital, a number of fortified ministries, the Flame Guard, the detachments of the Ministry of Truth and the cultists who revered the late Fire Lord Ozai. The Royalists, who held the south and the east with the support of the Qianchan Republic, had the largest field army but were short of heavy artillery and of rail transport west of the river. The Salvationists had been the strongest party in the field until the summer, when the loss of the Western Corps at the Nagare River ended their ability to fight a mobile war.

After the Nagare River the Royalist command faced a choice. The army could pause for the winter and rebuild its supplies, or it could advance on the capital while the Salvationists were disorganized and the Court was without allies. Ito Shigeru, who commanded the Southern Army, favored the second course. Zuko, who was in the south, gave his approval in July, and in the same month Ito issued the order for the concentration of the army on the river line south of the capital. The Qianchan expeditionary command agreed to supply an air wing for the transport of bread and medicine into the districts that the Royalists were expected to capture, a decision that was later credited with saving about 60,000 lives.

The city

Caldera was built on a crater lake and the plain around it, and its center, the Palace district, stood on the ridge above the harbor. Its principal quarters were the Palace district and its ministries, the Imperial Archive on the east side of the ridge, the harbor and the warehouses below it, and the residential and industrial wards that surrounded the center in an arc from the southern suburbs to the western rail yards. The river that ran through the city divided it into a northern and a southern half and was crossed by eleven bridges, of which seven were of stone. The wards were numbered, from the First Ward around the Palace to the Twelfth at the outer edge, and the numbering is used in most of the siege accounts.

Before the siege the city had about 800,000 people, a number that had increased by about 150,000 during the war because of refugees from the provinces. Many of its factories had closed in 115 and 116, when the Court lost its supply of coal. Its food had been requisitioned by the Court since 116, and the granaries, which were in the harbor district and at the northern rail yard, were held by the Flame Guard. The city had no reserves, and the roads to the countryside were cut by the Royalists in the first week of the siege. The evacuation of civilians, which the Salvationist and Royalist commands proposed to the Court in August, was refused.

The Court's decision to hold the capital

Azula, who held the Court's title, decided in July to defend the capital. According to the records of the Ministry of Truth, which survive in part, her reasoning was that the Court could not survive as a government outside the capital, and that the Royalists and the Salvationists would not be able to agree on the division of the city. The decision was opposed by Hirata Gensai, who held the Court's command, and who argued that the Court should withdraw to the north with the Flame Guard and the remaining armor. Azula overruled him. Hirata remained in his post, and the records show that from August he conducted the defense in accordance with the order, while preparing plans for withdrawal that he did not use.

The decision has been the subject of dispute among historians. Royalist histories regard it as a decision to sacrifice the civilian population of the capital for the sake of the Court's survival. Court records, which are mostly the work of former Ministry officials, describe it as a necessary act to protect the capital from capture by forces that had themselves killed Fire Nation civilians. Salvationist accounts present it as a decision by a government that no longer had any means of governing.

Forces and commanders

Royalists

The Royalist Southern Army numbered about 120,000 at the start of the siege, organized in nine divisions and two independent brigades. Its commander, General Ito Shigeru, was 58, a career officer who had held Shu Jing in 107 and had commanded the army since the Royalist victory at Iwakura Plain. His chief of staff was Colonel Mori Hayato, and his principal subordinates were Lieutenant General Kuroda Masaru, who commanded the three divisions of the southern group, and Major General Sasaki Toru, who commanded the eastern group. The army included the Engineer Corps, with the 4th and 9th Pioneer Regiments, which were responsible for the construction of the bridges and for the clearing of obstacles, and a Household Guard that was attached to Zuko and numbered about 4,000.

The army's equipment was a mixture of Royalist-made and Qianchan-supplied. It had about 400 field guns, of which about 60 were heavy, 150 tanks, a number of armored rail carriages and the requisitioned river barges that were used for transport and for the movement of the wounded. The army's air support consisted of the Qianchan Air Wing, which operated from a field south of the city and which had about 80 aircraft, most of them transports. Its pilots flew about 1,100 supply sorties during the siege, and the Royalist command credited the bread drops with the feeding of about 400,000 civilians in the districts that the Royalists held.

Zuko was present with the army from the beginning of the siege, but in the first months he did not exercise operational command. He was in the Royalist headquarters at the southern suburb of Minato-Ura, where he conducted the political work of the Royalist government and, according to the staff diaries, visited the field hospitals on most days. He entered the city on 2 May, after the Royalists had taken the harbor, and took command of the final operations against the Palace district.

Salvationists

The Salvationist forces in the city numbered about 50,000. They consisted of the remnants of the Fourth Army and the Ryuusei Facility garrison, the Tetsuken battalions that had survived the Nagare River, and ward militias that had been raised from the factory workers of the western districts. The political direction of the movement was in the hands of the Central Salvation Committee, of which Tanaka Kenji, Ono Sayuri, Fujiwara Daigo, Matsuda Reiko and Kuga Ren were the members. At Caldera the members were separated: Tanaka held the military command and the northern part of the western wards, Ono ran the Western Wards Committee, and Fujiwara, Matsuda and Kuga were responsible for the supply, the workshops and the security of the western wards respectively.

The Salvationists' weapons were in short supply. The Tetsuken systems that remained were few and their generators were unreliable, and the last of the Ryuusei missiles had been fired at the Third Battle of Shu Jing. By January the committees' stocks of small-arms ammunition were down to about twenty rounds a man, and by February the artillery had no shells. The Western Wards Committee, which had about 300 members, controlled the distribution of food and fuel in the western wards, and its work in the winter is the principal basis of the later Salvationist claim that the committees had organized the relief of the city.

The Court

The Court's forces numbered about 25,000. They consisted of Flame Guard battalions, which were the best-trained and best-equipped troops in the city; detachments of the Ministry of Truth, under General Hirata Gensai, which served as a security force and as the garrison of the ministries; and companies of cultists, who were recruited from among the supporters of the late Fire Lord Ozai and who held the Palace district. The Court's heavy weapons consisted of the fortress guns on the Palace walls and the harbor chain, and a small number of tanks that were used as mobile pillboxes.

Azula, who exercised the Court's authority, did not take the field. According to the Ministry's records, she lived in the Palace and conducted the Court's business from the throne room. Hirata held the command and directed the defense from the Ministry of War, on the First Ward ridge. His deputy, Colonel Ando Takeru, commanded the Flame Guard in the central ministries and was responsible for the defense of the Imperial Archive until its fall in April.

The Court did not issue rations to the civilian population. According to Court records, this was because its stocks were required for the troops, and because it expected the Royalists and the Salvationists to feed the districts they held. Royalist and Salvationist sources hold that the Court's granaries contained enough grain to feed the city for about three months, and that the Flame Guard used it to feed only its own troops and the Palace staff.

Course

The southern suburbs (August–September 117)

The Royalist Southern Army reached the southern suburbs of Caldera on 22 August 117 AG, after a march of eleven days from the Nagare River line. The first contact was made by the Royalist 14th Division, which found the outer ring of earthworks around the suburbs abandoned. The Court had withdrawn its forces into the inner city, and the suburbs were held only by a scattering of ward militias and by civilians who had refused to leave. The Royalists took the suburbs in three weeks, in a series of small engagements in which most of the fighting was in the rail yards of Minato-Ura and in the brickworks along the southern road.

The army's advance was slow by design. Ito, who had been criticized for the casualties at Hira and Sakuragawa (later Joha), ordered that the suburbs be cleared by infantry with limited artillery support, and that the civilian population be moved to the rear in organized columns. About 90,000 people were moved by this means in the first month. The refugees were housed in camps south of the river, where the Qianchan Air Wing delivered bread on most days from the second week of September. The Royalist command recorded that about 40,000 refugees in the camps received food from the air drops in the last week of September, a figure that rose to about 120,000 by the end of October.

During the same weeks the Salvationist forces withdrew from the southern wards into the west. Tanaka Kenji, who had arrived in the city with about 6,000 men from the Nagare River, was reluctant to give up the southern wards, because they contained the municipal waterworks, and he left a rear guard of about 2,000 men in the pumping station at the edge of the Eighth Ward. The rear guard held for six days against the Royalist 9th Division, and was withdrawn on 14 September after the Royalists brought up two heavy guns. The pumping station was damaged in the fighting, a point that is cited in the later disputes over the responsibility for the failure of the water supply.

The river districts (September–November 117)

From the middle of September the Royalists advanced on the river districts, which lay between the southern suburbs and the Palace ridge. They were the most densely populated part of the city, with about 300,000 people, and they were the area in which most of the heavy fighting of the autumn took place. The Royalists advanced from the south along three axes, with the eastern group on the harbor road, the central group on the avenue that led to the river bridges, and the western group on the factory road that led to the Salvationist wards. The Court's forces held the line of the river on the north side of the central group's front, and the Salvationists held the factory district to the west.

The fighting in the river districts was a series of local actions, mostly at the bridges and in the blocks of tenements and workshops that lined the river. The Royalists took the Third and Fifth Bridges in the first week of October. The Court held the Seventh, which led directly to the Palace ridge, and the Salvationists held the Ninth and Tenth, which led to the western wards. The Royalist engineers built three pontoon bridges, of which two were destroyed by the Court's guns within a day, and the third, near the Fifth Bridge, remained in use until the end of the siege.

The battle of the Seventh Bridge, which lasted from 11 to 26 October, was the principal action of the autumn. The Royalist 4th Division, under Major General Aizawa Kenji, attacked the bridge from the south, and the Court's Flame Guard defended it from the north with the support of the guns on the ridge. The bridge changed hands three times. The Royalists took it on 19 October, lost it the next morning to a counterattack by the Flame Guard, and finally took it on 26 October after the Engineer Corps had blown a hole in the embankment that allowed the Royalist infantry to flank the Court's positions. The 4th Division lost about 3,800 men, about a third of its strength, and the Court lost about 1,500.

By the end of October the Royalists held about a third of the city, mainly the southern and southeastern wards, the river districts south of the Seventh Bridge, and the eastern part of the harbor. The Court held the central ministries, the northern part of the river districts, the Palace ridge, and the part of the harbor that lay under the guns of the ridge. The Salvationists held the western wards, from the Ninth Bridge to the rail yards.

The three-sided front

The front lines that formed in October and November were unusual in that each party was in contact with both of the others. The Royalist front with the Court ran along the river and the foot of the Palace ridge. The Royalist front with the Salvationists ran along the boundary between the Eighth and Ninth Wards, where the factory road entered the western district. The Salvationist front with the Court ran along the Tenth Ward, in the northwest, where the Court's guns on the ridge overlooked the Salvationist positions.

The three-sided character of the front limited the scale of the fighting. According to the staff diaries of Mori Hayato, Ito's chief of staff, the Royalist command avoided attacking the Salvationist wards in the autumn because it believed that an attack would drive the Salvationists back into alliance with the Court. The Salvationist committees, for their part, did not attack the Court, because they lacked the ammunition and because their command expected the Royalists and the Court to exhaust each other. Contacts across the Royalist-Salvationist line were frequent and informal. Ono Sayuri met Royalist officers under flag of truce at least seven times between October and December, and the Royalist command allowed the committees to move food from the harbor to the western wards under a local arrangement.

The fighting continued nonetheless. The Court's Flame Guard raided the Salvationist positions in the Tenth Ward in November, and shot about 140 civilians in the course of the raids. The Royalists, who had received reports of the killings, increased their patrols of the river and shelled the ridge with their heavy guns. By the end of November about 45,000 people had died in the city, of whom about 30,000 were civilians.

The winter (December 117 – February 118)

The winter began with the failure of the city's gas and water supply. The gasworks, which was in the Eighth Ward and which had been damaged in September, ran out of coal in the first week of December. The pumping station in the Eighth Ward, which supplied the river districts and the harbor, had been out of service since September, and the water in the pipes was contaminated by the end of November. The Royalists and the Salvationists dug wells in the districts that they held. The Court, which had its own supply in the Palace district, did not.

The temperature in December fell below freezing for twenty-three days, and in January the lake froze at its edges. The city's heating fuel had been exhausted, and the civilians burned furniture, doors and the wood of the houses in the abandoned wards. The fires that resulted destroyed about a fifth of the housing in the river districts, and the fire in the Fourth Ward on 17 January, in which about 2,000 people died, was the worst single disaster of the winter.

Food was in short supply in all parts of the city. In the Royalist districts the ration was supplemented by the bread drops, and the Royalist command issued about 200 grams of bread a day to each registered civilian in January. In the Salvationist wards the Western Wards Committee issued about 150 grams of grain and a ration of salted fish, and the committee's kitchens served about 80,000 people a day. In the Court's districts there were no rations. The people who lived in the northern river districts and the harbor under the Court's guns survived on what they could scavenge, and the death rate there was the highest in the city.

By the end of January the deaths from cold and starvation had reached about 3,000 a day across the city, and the number remained at that level through February. The bodies were collected by burial parties in the Royalist and Salvationist districts and buried in mass graves in the parks and the lakeshore. In the Court's districts the dead were left in the streets, and in February the Royalist guns were turned on the northern river districts to destroy the buildings in which the dead lay, a decision that was later criticized as an attempt to hide the extent of the casualties.

The crossing of the lines became a major feature of the winter. About 60,000 people crossed from the Court's districts to the Royalist lines in the period from December to February, usually at night, across the river ice and through the ruins. The Royalists received them in reception points near the Fifth Bridge, where they were given food and medical care. The Court's Flame Guard shot at the crossings, and the Royalist command estimated that for every person who reached the lines, another died on the way. About 15,000 people also crossed from the Court's districts to the Salvationist wards.

The Salvationist collapse (March 118)

By the end of February the Salvationist forces had no ammunition and the Western Wards Committee had exhausted its stocks of food. On 28 February the committee met in the Tenth Ward to consider its position. Tanaka Kenji, who presided, proposed that the committees withdraw from the city to the north with the remaining troops, and Ono Sayuri proposed that they negotiate a truce with the Royalists on the basis that the civilians of the western wards would be fed. The committee voted for the truce, by a margin of nine to six, and Tanaka declared that he would not be bound by the vote.

A truce between the committee and the Royalist command was agreed on 6 March. Its terms were that the Salvationist forces would cease fire, that the Royalists would deliver food to the western wards by air and road, and that the committee would hold its positions until the end of the month. Tanaka left the city on the night of 6 March with about 1,500 men of the Iron Column, by the northern road, and after a march of nine days reached the foothills north of the capital. He did not return.

The committee's negotiations with the Royalists continued for six days. Ono Sayuri conducted them in person, with Ito Shigeru and, on the last day, Zuko, who came to the lines under a white flag. The agreement that they reached on 12 March provided for the surrender of the western wards to the Royalist administration. The committee's forces were to lay down their arms, the civilians of the western wards were to be fed by the Royalists, and the committee members who stayed in the city were to be held in custody and to be tried for any crimes that they had committed. Ono signed the agreement in the Tenth Ward on 12 March, and the Royalist 11th Division entered the western wards on the following day.

The surrender of the western wards brought about 120,000 civilians under Royalist protection. The Royalist command began the delivery of food on 13 March, and by the end of the month it had delivered about 800 tons, a quantity that was sufficient to stop the deaths from starvation in the western wards within about three weeks. The Salvationist soldiers, who numbered about 28,000, were disarmed and held in the Twelfth Ward. The committees' remaining weapons were collected at the rail yard, and about 4,000 Tetsuken sets and discharge units were found. They were not used again.

The Royalist assault on the Court (April 118)

With the western wards secured, the Royalists turned their full strength on the Court. The assault began on 1 April, with a bombardment of the ministries by about 300 guns, and was carried out by the eastern and central groups. The Royalist plan, which Ito had drafted in January, was to take the ministries one at a time, beginning with the harbor, which controlled the supply by sea, and the Imperial Archive on the eastern ridge. The Court's Flame Guard, which had about 12,000 men in the ministries, held the buildings in strength.

The harbor was taken in nine days. The Royalist 6th Division, supported by a Qianchan naval contingent that had come up the coast in the second week of March, landed on the harbor mole on 3 April and attacked the warehouses and the harbor chain. The Court's guns on the ridge shelled the mole, and the Royalists lost about 1,100 men. The harbor chain was cut on 8 April by Royalist divers, and the Court's last coastal ships, which had been lying in the harbor since the autumn, were sunk or captured on 11 April.

The ministries of the central ward were taken in the second half of April. The Ministry of Truth, a fortified building on the First Ward ridge, was attacked on 16 April by the Royalist 4th and 9th Divisions and fell on 21 April after the Engineer Corps had blown a hole in its north wall. Its garrison, about 800 men, was killed or captured. The Ministry of the Interior, the Ministry of War and the Treasury were taken in the following days, and by 26 April the Royalists held every ministry building except the Palace itself.

The Imperial Archive was the scene of the most dramatic episode of the assault. The Archive, which held the records of the Empire from the time of Fire Lord Sozin, had been defended by Ando Takeru and about 600 Flame Guard. On 19 April, when the Royalists had broken into the lower levels, Ando ordered that the records be burned. The Archive staff refused, and the records show that about thirty of them locked themselves into the main stacks. According to the diary of Watanabe Shin, a senior archivist, a platoon of Royalist infantry under Sergeant Hasegawa Mei reached the stacks on the evening of the same day, and the fire, which had destroyed the north gallery, was put out by the soldiers and the archivists working together. About a fifth of the collection was lost. Ando was captured, and he later testified at the hearings.

The Palace district (late April – May 118)

By the end of April the Court was reduced to the Palace district, an area of about two square kilometers on the First Ward ridge, with the Palace itself at its center. Hirata Gensai had been killed in the fighting on 21 April, in the Ministry of Truth, and the command of the remaining forces passed to Azula. The Court's troops numbered about 4,000, of whom about 1,500 were Flame Guard and the rest cultists and Ministry staff. The Palace walls were intact, and the Royalists, who wished to avoid a battle in the Palace, halted their advance at the foot of the ridge.

Zuko entered the city on 2 May and took command of the Royalist forces. In the week that followed, the Royalist command sent two messages to the Palace, offering terms of surrender. They were refused. The second of them was answered on 7 May by Azula's challenge to an Agni Kai, which Zuko accepted. The duel was fought on 9 May in the courtyard of the Palace, and its outcome is described in the article on the Duel of the Palace.

Supply and the air bridge

The supply of the Royalist districts by air was the most extensive operation of its kind in the war. The Qianchan Air Wing operated from a field south of the city, at Minato-Ura, where the Royalist engineers lengthened a farm road into a runway of about 1,400 meters. The wing's aircraft were mostly twin-engined transports, of which about 50 were serviceable at any time, and its pilots flew by day and, from December, by night, using lamps and flares set out by the reception teams. The loads were dropped by parachute into the Royalist districts, and the bread was baked in the field ovens of the Royalist army, at Minato-Ura, and in the Qianchan bakeries on the coast.

The wing flew about 1,100 supply sorties between September and May, which delivered, according to its logbooks, about 6,400 tons of food, 700 tons of medical supplies and 400 tons of fuel. The aircraft losses were light until February, when the Court's anti-aircraft guns on the ridge shot down six of them in two weeks, and the Royalists shifted the drops to the south and east of the city. About 40 of the wing's aircrew were killed during the operation. The commander of the wing, Colonel Gu Mingzhe, was awarded a Royalist decoration after the siege and later became the head of the Qianchan military mission in the Fire Nation.

The committees' supply was by land and by the lake. The Western Wards Committee organized convoys of carts and barges that brought grain and salted fish from the western provinces across the lake to the west shore, and the convoys were allowed to pass by the Royalist patrols under the local arrangement made in October. The arrangement was ended by the Royalist command in January, after the discovery that some of the grain was being sent to the Court's forces in the Tenth Ward, but it was restored in February after a protest by the committee and by the Qianchan mission. The committee's kitchens served the grain with rice and a thin soup of fish and seaweed, and the ration was reduced to about 100 grams a day in the second half of February.

The Court's supply was the smallest. It depended on the stocks that had been collected in the harbor district and the northern rail yard in 116, and on what the Flame Guard could take from the districts that it held. In January the Court's forces took about 1,200 tons of grain from the warehouses of the harbor, and the Royalists, who learned of the removal from the crossers, shelled the warehouses in February. The remaining grain was burned or looted in the following weeks.

Defense of the Palace district

The Court's preparations for the defense of the Palace district began in the autumn. The Palace stood on a ridge about 90 meters above the lake, and the approaches to it were limited to three roads and a stair that led from the harbor. The Flame Guard fortified the roads with barricades and gun positions, mined the stair, and pulled down the buildings on the slopes to give clear fields of fire. The Palace walls, which were of stone and about eight meters high, were reinforced with sandbags and with steel plate taken from the Ministry of War.

The garrison of the district in May consisted of about 1,500 Flame Guard, a number of cultists and about 800 staff and servants. The cultists, who held the outer walls, were organized in companies of about a hundred and led by former officers of the Ozai household. Their discipline was poor, according to Ando's testimony, and about a quarter of them deserted in the first week of May. The Flame Guard, who were better disciplined, held the inner courtyards and the Palace itself.

The Palace had food for about three weeks, and its well and cisterns provided water. The Royalist command, which knew the extent of the stocks from the deserters, expected the garrison to hold for about a month, and made preparations for a siege. The challenge to the duel on 7 May, a few days after the arrival of Zuko, ended these preparations.

The negotiations of March

The negotiations that ended the Salvationist participation in the siege were conducted over six days, from 6 to 12 March, in a room of a school in the Tenth Ward that stood on the line between the Royalist and the Salvationist positions. They are recorded in the minutes of Mori Hayato, Ito's chief of staff, and in the account of the committee's secretary, Takagi Noriko, who was present throughout. The two accounts agree on the main points, but differ on the atmosphere. Mori describes the Salvationist delegation as "tired, correct and unwilling to be thanked." Takagi writes that the Royalists "arrived with bread in their pockets and apologized for the smell of it."

The principal points at issue were the treatment of the civilians, the fate of the soldiers and the status of the committee members. Ono Sayuri asked, first, that the Royalists feed the western wards without conditions, and, second, that the Salvationist soldiers be treated as prisoners of war and not as rebels. Ito agreed to the first immediately, and referred the second to Zuko, who arrived on 11 March. Zuko's reply, which Takagi recorded, was that the soldiers would be released after the war and that the committee members would be tried by a civil court, and not by a military tribunal. Ono accepted the terms on 12 March, with the reservation that the Salvationists' weapons be surrendered to the Royalist administration and not to the Court.

The agreement was signed by Ono, Ito and Zuko, and witnessed by the Qianchan relief mission. Its text was published in the Royalist press on 15 March. Tanaka, who had left the city six days earlier, issued a statement from the north on 20 March that described the agreement as a surrender, and called on the Salvationists to continue the struggle. The statement had little effect on the soldiers in the city, but it was the beginning of the insurgency.

Weapons and urban tactics

Royalist methods

The Royalist army had learned the methods of street fighting at Shu Jing, Hira and Sakuragawa, and applied them at Caldera in a systematic form. Its infantry advanced in groups of about thirty men, each with a rifle section, a machine-gun team, a demolition team and a flamethrower. The demolition teams, which were drawn from the pioneer regiments, breached the walls of buildings with shaped charges so that the infantry could move through them without exposing themselves in the street. This method, which the staff called "mouse-holing," was used in almost all the actions in the river districts, and was credited with reducing the infantry's losses by about a third.

The army's heavy guns were used mainly against fixed positions. The 150mm guns that had been brought from the Black Rail line were placed south of the river and fired on the Palace ridge and the ministries, while the field guns were used in direct fire against barricades. The Royalist tanks, which were few, were used in the support of the infantry in the wider avenues and were generally withdrawn at night. Their losses were light, about 20 vehicles in the whole siege, mainly to the Court's gun positions on the ridge.

Salvationist methods

The Salvationist forces relied on the defense of prepared positions in the factories and the tenements of the western wards. The committees' engineers had fortified the factory blocks with sandbags, barbed wire and mines, and had cut communication trenches between the buildings. The remaining Tetsuken sets were distributed among the strongpoints, where they were used against armor and, in a few cases, to disable the field telephones of the Royalists. Their generators, which depended on batteries that could not be recharged after November, were mostly out of service by the end of the year.

The ward militias, which were organized by the committees from the workers of the western wards, were armed with rifles and grenades, and were used mainly as a screening force. About 14,000 men and women served in them at the peak. Their casualties were heavy in the first months, but after the three-sided truce of October they were mostly employed in the maintenance of order and in the guarding of the food stores.

Court methods

The Court's defense was based on the possession of the high ground, from which its guns could cover the river and the approaches to the ridge. The fortress guns of the Palace walls and the harbor chain were of old design but had a long range, and their fire on the Royalist and Salvationist districts caused many of the civilian casualties of the autumn. The Flame Guard, who were mostly firebenders, used their abilities at close range in the street fighting. According to the Royalist reports, they were effective against infantry in the open and in the clearing of rooms, and they were also the main cause of the fires that destroyed the northern river districts in the autumn.

The cultists, who had no formal training, were used as sentries and as auxiliaries. They fought with a fervor that impressed the Royalist soldiers, and their reputation for refusing to surrender is reflected in the casualty returns: of about 1,300 cultists in the ministries in April, only about 200 were captured alive. The Ministry of Truth's detachments, which acted as a political police, were used to enforce the Court's orders in the districts it held, and they conducted the shootings of civilians in the Tenth Ward in November and the executions of suspected deserters in the winter.

Effects on the city

The tactics of all three parties destroyed the city's fabric. The mouse-holing of the Royalists, the fortification of the buildings by the Salvationists and the use of the heights by the Court meant that nearly every block in the river districts was fought over, and the damage was cumulative. The bombardments of the ministries in April reduced the central ward to rubble. The fires, which began in the autumn and reached their height in January, were the worst cause of the destruction, and the Royalist engineers' reports show that about 60 percent of the damage to the housing was caused by fire.

Civilian experience

Refuges and wards

Most of the civilians who survived the siege did so in organized refuges. The Royalist, Salvationist and Court authorities each ran a system of ward offices, and in the Royalist and Salvationist districts these offices issued ration cards, registered the dead and organized the collection of water and fuel. The ward offices of the western districts were run by committees of residents, and the Western Wards Committee supervised about 140 of them. The Royalist offices were staffed by administrators of the provisional government and by volunteers from the Qianchan relief mission. In the Court's districts the ward offices were closed in October, and the civilians depended on neighbors and on a number of church and temple kitchens that operated until January.

Schools, temples, warehouses and the cellars of public buildings were used as refuges. The best documented is the primary school in the Seventh Ward, where the teacher Aoki Yuki received about 900 people in the first week of October. The school, a two-story brick building near the river, had a deep cellar that had been built as an air-raid shelter, and Aoki recorded in her diary that the shelter held 340 people, with the others on the ground floor. The refuge ran a communal kitchen from a boiler in the school's laundry, and the pupils' desks were burned for fuel in December. By the end of February about 220 of the refugees had died, most of them from cold and illness, and the survivors were evacuated to the Royalist reception points in March.

Water and fuel

The loss of water was the principal cause of the epidemic that followed. After the failure of the municipal supply in December, the civilians drew water from the lake, from wells and from the river, and the water in the river was contaminated by the dead who had been left in the northern districts. Dysentery and typhoid appeared in January, and in February the Royalist and Qianchan medical services recorded about 400 cases a day in the districts south of the river. The Qianchan relief mission set up water-purification points at the Fifth Bridge, and by March it had purified about 60,000 liters a day, which was enough for about a fifth of the civilians in the Royalist districts.

The fuel shortage affected the civilians in a different way. In the absence of coal and gas the people burned wood, and the wood of the city was soon exhausted. The tenements in the river districts were stripped of their floors and doors, and the timber houses in the Fourth and Sixth Wards were pulled down by their occupants. The fires that resulted were the main cause of the loss of housing. About 90,000 people were left without shelter in January, and many of them died of exposure in the weeks that followed.

Medical services

The city's medical services were overwhelmed in the first month. The municipal hospital, in the Ninth Ward, held about 1,200 patients at the start of the siege and about 4,000 by December, and by the end of January its staff had been reduced to about forty doctors and nurses. The hospital was hit by a Court shell on 2 December, and in the following week about 300 patients were moved to the cellar of the nearby bathhouse. The Royalists set up field hospitals in the southern suburbs, with about 6,000 beds, and the Qianchan relief mission added another 2,500 beds in tents on the lake shore.

The Salvationist committees operated a medical service of their own, run by Dr. Saito Hiroshi, who had survived the Nagare River and who joined the Western Wards Committee in October. Saito, who kept a notebook of his work during the siege, organized the western wards' clinics, and trained about 200 volunteers in the dressing of wounds and the management of dysentery. His notebook records that his clinics treated about 70,000 patients between October and March, and that about 9,000 of them died.

Children

The siege left a large number of orphans. The Royalist registry recorded about 31,000 children who had lost both parents, and about 80,000 who had lost one. Most were cared for by relatives, and about 12,000 were placed in the temples and orphanages that the Royalist administration organized in the summer of 118. A group of about 300 children was found in the cellar of a sealed warehouse in the harbor district in May, having survived on a store of dried fruit; its discovery was widely reported in the Royalist press. The orphanages that were established in 118 continued to operate into the 120s.

Notable people

Aoki Yuki (born 83 AG) was the head teacher of the primary school in the Seventh Ward. She kept a diary from the beginning of September 117 until the end of April 118, in which she recorded the daily numbers of the refuge, the food supply and the deaths. The diary, which she gave to the Royalist relief committee in May, was published in 126 AG with an introduction by a Qianchan historian. She continued to teach in the rebuilt school until 140 and died in 151. Her last entry, written on 30 April 118, reads: "There is bread today. Nobody has the strength to eat it."

Watanabe Shin (born 74 AG) was a senior archivist at the Imperial Archive. His diary covers the last three months of the siege, and describes the Court's attempt to destroy the records and the intervention of the Royalist infantry. He was among the staff who locked themselves into the stacks on 19 April. After the war he became the director of the restored Archive, and the first to publish a catalog of the records that had survived the fire. He died in 133.

Hasegawa Mei (born 92 AG) was a sergeant in the Royalist 9th Division, and the leader of the platoon that reached the stacks of the Imperial Archive on 19 April. She was born in the harbor district of Caldera and had joined the Royalist army in 111, after the death of her family at Hira. Her platoon of 28 men put out the fire in the north gallery, and the platoon lost four dead. She was decorated by the Reformation government in 119, and later served as an officer of the Archive's guard.

Ono Sayuri (born 80 AG) was a schoolteacher from the western provinces and the political member of the Central Salvation Committee. At Caldera she ran the Western Wards Committee and negotiated the surrender of the western wards. She was held in the harbor barracks from March 118 and was tried in 121 by a civil court, which found that her conduct in the western wards had been lawful and that she had acted to prevent loss of life. She was sentenced to four years for her part in the movement's earlier acts and released in 122. She later taught in a village school in the western provinces.

Tanaka Kenji (born 76 AG) was the military member of the Central Salvation Committee. He left Caldera on the night of 6 March and led the remnants of the Iron Column in the north until his death at Hanegawa Pass in March 120. His role in the western wards is the subject of the sharpest dispute among the historians of the movement, because he refused to be bound by the committee's decision on the truce.

Aizawa Kenji was a major general in the Royalist army and the commander of the 4th Division. His division bore the heaviest losses of the siege, and he was wounded in the fighting at the Seventh Bridge. He was later the first chief of the postwar army staff.

Ando Takeru was a colonel of the Flame Guard and the commander of the Court's forces in the central ministries. He was captured at the Imperial Archive on 19 April. He was tried by a military court in 120, which sentenced him to fifteen years for the order to burn the Archive and for the shooting of civilians in the Tenth Ward in November, and was released in 130.

Dr. Lin Wei, a Qianchan medical officer, led the relief mission's medical staff in the Royalist districts. His reports, which were published by the Qianchan Congress in 119, are the principal contemporary source for the epidemic in the river districts.

Casualties

The Royalist register of the dead, compiled by the provisional administration in the summer of 118, recorded about 260,000 deaths in the city between 22 August 117 and 9 May 118. Of these, about 220,000 were civilians, about 18,000 were Royalist soldiers, about 12,000 were Salvationists and about 10,000 were members of the Court's forces. The register was based on burial returns, ward lists and the records of the hospitals and the refuges, and its compilers estimated that about 15,000 of the dead had not been identified. The civilian dead included about 120,000 who died of starvation and exposure, about 40,000 who died of disease, about 45,000 who were killed by shelling, fire and small-arms fire, and about 15,000 who died in the crossings of the lines.

The register has been criticized by Court and Salvationist authors. Court writers argue that it overstates the Court's responsibility by assigning the dead of the northern river districts to the Court, although the Royalist guns were responsible for a large part of the destruction there. Salvationist authors argue that it understates the number of deaths in the Royalist reception points, where the mortality in February was high. The Qianchan relief mission's own estimate, which was published in 119, gave the civilian dead as about 205,000, but the mission's coverage of the Court's districts was incomplete.

The city's population fell from about 800,000 to about 450,000. About 90,000 people had fled before or during the first weeks of the siege, about 60,000 had crossed the lines to the south and about 40,000 had been evacuated by the Royalists in the summer of 118. The destruction of housing was extensive: about 35 percent of the city's buildings were destroyed or damaged beyond repair, and the river districts and the northern harbor were almost entirely in ruins.

Aftermath

The end of the Court

The Court's forces in the Palace district surrendered on 9 May 118, on the day of the duel. Their commanders were taken into custody and the cultists, about 800 men, were disarmed and held in the harbor barracks. The Palace itself was occupied by the Royalist Household Guard, and the staff of the Court were registered and questioned. About 2,200 Court officials and officers were later tried, of whom about 140 were sentenced to death, and the others received prison terms or were released in the amnesty that followed the coronation.

Relief and burial

The Royalist administration began the work of relief in the first week of May. Zuko ordered the distribution of the Royalist reserves, and the Qianchan Air Wing delivered about 2,000 tons of food in May. The ration was raised in June to about 500 grams a day. The reopening of the harbor allowed the unloading of grain from the Qianchan and the United Republic, and the first deliveries from the southern provinces reached the city in July.

The burial of the dead took the whole of the summer. Burial parties, which numbered about 6,000 men, many of them Salvationist and Court prisoners, collected the bodies from the streets and the ruins and buried them in about 130 mass graves, of which the largest was at the lakeshore park in the Twelfth Ward. The work was complicated by the presence of unexploded shells and by the danger of epidemic disease, and about 400 of the workers died. The register of the dead was compiled in parallel, and its completion in August allowed the first families to claim the bodies of the identified.

The surviving forces

The Salvationist forces in the city, about 28,000 men, were held in the Twelfth Ward until July and then released under the terms of the surrender. The leaders were held. Tanaka and the Iron Column withdrew to the north, where the column surrendered at Suiko in August. The Salvationist movement continued as an insurgency, which is described in the article on the Salvationist insurgency.

The hearings

The register of the dead became the basis of the accountability hearings, which began in the autumn of 118 and continued until 121. The hearings were conducted by civil courts of the provisional government, and their findings on the Siege of Caldera were that the Court's decision to refuse the evacuation of civilians and the retention of the granaries were crimes, that the Royalist command's shelling of the northern river districts in February had been unlawful in part, and that the Salvationist committees' conduct in the western wards had been in most respects lawful. The findings were criticized by all three sides. Royalist veterans objected to the criticism of the shelling, Court officials to the findings on the granaries, and Salvationist authors to the finding that Tanaka had been responsible for the decision to withhold ammunition from the western wards.

Analysis

Military assessment

Military historians have generally described the Siege of Caldera as a failure of all three commands, with the Royalists' decision to conduct a slow, cautious siege prolonging the suffering of the civilians, the Salvationists' decision to make a stand in the city exposing the western wards to the same fate, and the Court's decision to hold the capital condemning the city to destruction. The Royalists' caution, which is usually attributed to the heavy losses at Hira and Sakuragawa, is the most debated point. Some historians argue that a faster assault in the autumn would have ended the siege before the winter, at the cost of heavy military casualties. Others argue that the Court's defense would have been stronger and the civilian losses greater.

The three-sided character of the siege is the other main subject of analysis. The absence of a clear front between the Royalists and the Salvationists limited the fighting in the autumn but meant that neither party could bring its full force against the Court. The conversations across the lines, which the Royalist and Salvationist commands conducted from October, are generally regarded as the main reason for the peaceful end of the Salvationist part of the siege. Historians note that the agreement of 12 March was concluded without the knowledge of the Court, and that the Court had no means of preventing it.

Humanitarian assessment

The question of responsibility for the civilian deaths has been disputed since the end of the siege. All parties requisitioned food, and none of them was able to feed the city. The Royalist bread drops and the Western Wards Committee's kitchens saved an estimated 150,000 to 200,000 lives, according to the Qianchan report, but the delivery of food was limited by the weight that the aircraft could carry and by the distances that the committees' carts could travel. The Court's retention of the granaries is regarded by most historians as the greatest single failure, since the grain stored in the harbor district would have fed the city for about three months. The Royalist shelling of the northern river districts is regarded by many as a breach of the usages of war, though the Royalist command argued that the buildings were being used by the Flame Guard as firing positions.

The Concord of Nations, in its first resolutions on the protection of civilians in sieges, referred to the Siege of Caldera as one of the three cases that had shown the need for a rule that civilians be allowed to leave a besieged city. The rule that was adopted in 125 AG is known in several histories as the "Caldera rule."

Legacy and memory

The rebuilding of Caldera was the principal task of the first years of the Reformation government. The city's population returned to about 600,000 by 125 AG and to its prewar level by 140. The river districts were rebuilt on a new street plan, with wider avenues and public water systems, and the Seventh Ward school was reconstructed in 121 as the first public building of the new administration. The ridge was left as a park, and the Palace, which had been damaged in the final days, was restored and reopened in 123.

The memorial to the dead of the siege was unveiled in the Seventh Ward in 124 AG, on the site of Aoki Yuki's school. It consists of a low wall of dark stone that bears no names, and a register hall, which holds the register of the dead in about 40 volumes, and is open to families who wish to look up a name. A second monument, in the Twelfth Ward, marks the lakeshore graves. The anniversary of the beginning of the siege, 22 August, is observed in Caldera as a day of mourning, and the date of the surrender of the western wards, 12 March, is marked by an annual ceremony in the Tenth Ward that is attended by Salvationist veterans and by Royalist officials.

The siege has been widely treated in literature and art. Aoki's diary is used as a school text in the Fire Nation. Watanabe's diary and the account of the rescue of the Imperial Archive are the subject of several popular histories. The siege is the setting of the first postwar novels, and the episode of the sealed warehouse has been dramatized in at least two plays. Historians of the postwar period note that the memory of the siege shaped the Fire Nation's attitude to the use of force in internal disputes, and that it was cited in the debates of the Reformation government over the army's powers.

Historiography

Royalist accounts

Royalist histories, most of which were written in the 120s by officers of the army staff, describe the siege as a necessary operation to end a war that the Court and the Salvationists had refused to end by negotiation. They emphasize the care that Ito took to protect civilians, the organization of the bread drops and the evacuation, and they note that the Royalists fed more civilians than they killed. They generally accept the register of the dead, and attribute most of the deaths to the Court's refusal to allow the evacuation and to the Court's retention of the granaries. Their treatment of the shelling of the northern river districts is cautious: most describe it as a military necessity, while a minority, including the later memoirs of Aizawa Kenji, admit that the shelling continued longer than was required.

Court accounts

The Court's records are incomplete, since most of the Ministry of Truth's archives were destroyed in April. The surviving accounts, which are mostly the testimony of former officials at the hearings and the memoirs of Ando Takeru and others, hold that the Court's decision to defend the capital was a legitimate act of government, and that the responsibility for the deaths lay with the Royalists and the Salvationists, who had brought war into a city that the Court had not attacked. They deny that the granaries were withheld, and say that the grain was needed to feed the Flame Guard and the Palace staff, and that the Court had asked the other parties for a ceasefire in November. The Royalist and Salvationist sources do not mention any such request, and no copy of it has been found.

Salvationist accounts

Salvationist accounts, which were mostly written in exile or in prison in the 120s, describe the committees as having organized the relief of the western wards and the negotiation of the surrender as a deliberate act to save civilians. Their authors argue that the Royalists would have starved the city if the committees had not held the western wards, and that the surrender of 12 March was a victory of the committees' principles. They differ on the role of Tanaka, whom some describe as a hero who refused to surrender the movement's honor and others as a commander who abandoned the committee in the hour of its decision. The younger generation of the Salvationists, in the unrest of the 160s and 170s, treated the western wards as a model of the movement's government, and the claim is disputed by historians who note that the committee's kitchens depended in part on food supplied by the Royalists under the local arrangement.

Other sources

The diaries of Aoki Yuki and Watanabe Shin, and the notebook of Saito Hiroshi, are the principal civilian sources for the siege. They are widely read, and none of them supports any of the three parties' accounts in full. Aoki's diary records the help that her refuge received from soldiers of all three parties, and it records two occasions on which Court soldiers took food from the school. Watanabe's diary criticizes the Court's attempt to burn the Archive and praises the Royalist soldiers, but also records the looting of the Archive's storerooms by the Royalists in the week after the rescue. Saito's notebook is the main source for the committees' medical services, and it contradicts the Salvationist claim that the western wards were spared the epidemic.

The Qianchan relief mission's reports, which were published by the Qianchan Congress in 119 and 120, are regarded as the most neutral of the primary sources, although they were produced by a party that supported the Royalists and that had no access to the Court's districts. The register of the dead is the basis of all the casualty figures, and the criticisms of it have not produced a generally accepted alternative.

duel_of_the_palace.title: Duel of the Palace
duel_of_the_palace.html:
Also known as the Last Stand of Caldera and, in Royalist usage, the Reckoning. The final engagement of the Fire Nation Civil War.

Duel of the Palace
Date9 May 118 AG
LocationMain courtyard of the Imperial Palace, Caldera City
ResultZuko kills Azula in an Agni Kai to the death under the Way of the Warrior, after she breaks its rules with lightning. The Court Government ends.
Belligerents
Zuko (Royalists)Azula (Court Government)
WitnessesRoyalist commanders, the surviving Flame Guard, members of the Diet, and Qianchan observers

The Duel of the Palace was the single combat that ended the Fire Nation Civil War. It took place on 9 May 118 AG in the main courtyard of the Imperial Palace in Caldera City, after the collapse of the Court's defenses in the Siege of Caldera. Azula, the last holder of the Court's throne, blamed her brother Zuko for everything that had befallen the Court and the Empire and called a traditional Agni Kai to the death under the Way of the Warrior. She declared that it would end the matter once and for all, and that whoever lived would be the true inheritor of the lands. Zuko accepted. In the course of the duel Azula broke its rules by using lightning, which Zuko redirected. Zuko then beheaded her with a single stroke of his sword. The Court's remaining forces surrendered the same day, and Zuko was crowned Fire Lord later in 118 AG.

Background

By spring 118 AG the Court Government had been reduced to the Palace district of Caldera City. Most of its field army had passed to the Salvationists in 111–113 AG and had broken with it in 116 AG, and the Court's defenses in the capital gave way in the months after the siege began in 117 AG. Royalist forces held the outer city, and the Salvationists were closing from the west. Azula, who had held the Court's title since the rigged succession of July 100 AG, was left with the Flame Guard, remnants of the Ministry of Truth and the cultists who revered her father.

The Way of the Warrior is the Fire Nation's tradition of honor in combat. Under it, a challenge to a formal duel cannot be refused without dishonor, and the result decides the quarrel. Neither Azula's nor Zuko's supporters disputed that it applied.

The challenge

On 7 May 118 AG, Azula sent a herald under truce to the Royalist command with a challenge. In it she charged Zuko with responsibility for the war and its ruin: for the Diet's defiance in 100 AG, for the division of the army, for the Court's fall, and for the loss of her father's empire. She wrote that the quarrel between them was the only one left to settle, that it should be ended once and for all, and that whoever lived would be the true inheritor of the lands. She asked that her forces and his stand down while it was fought.

Zuko's advisers, including several Diet members, urged him to refuse and to take the Palace by assault, since the Court was nearly beaten. He accepted the next day. He said afterwards that the war had been fought in the name of the throne, and that the throne's holder should answer for it. Royalist officers and later accounts also note that the Salvationists were nearing the city, and that a delay would have given them the Palace.

The duel

The Agni Kai was fought on the morning of 9 May in the Palace's main courtyard, with both sides' forces drawn up at the edges under truce. Qianchan observers and Diet members were admitted as witnesses. Under the old rules of a duel to the death, the fighting is done with firebending only, and each duelist carries a sword for the final stroke. It lasted about twenty minutes, according to the most common account. Witnesses report that before the fight began the two traded insults across the courtyard, Azula raving and talking to people who were not there, and Zuko calm.

Witnesses describe Azula as fighting without restraint and Zuko as giving ground. Several accounts record that the two traded insults throughout, and that she asked him to finish it after the lightning failed. Late in the fight she drew and fired lightning, which the rules do not permit, and which is held to be a sign that a duelist has stopped believing she can win. Zuko, who had been taught the technique by Iroh, redirected it into the Palace's north wall, and was burned in doing so. Azula stood still for a moment. Zuko closed in a flash and beheaded her with a single stroke of his sword, so quickly that those nearest did not see it. By the old rules a duelist who cheats forfeits an honorable death. The courtyard was silent for some time afterwards. Azula's remaining officers stood down, and Court forces in the Palace district surrendered during the day.

Aftermath

Zuko was crowned Fire Lord later in 118 AG. At the coronation an assassin in the crowd aimed a gun at his chest and was shot dead by a loyal guard before he could fire. His reign (118–168 AG) is conventionally dated from the duel. Salvationist forces continued their insurgency until 120 AG.

Historiography

Royalist and most neutral sources treat the killing as lawful and consistent with the Way of the Warrior, and as the only possible end to a war in which the Court would not yield. They point out that Azula chose a duel because it let her die with her honor, and gave her a chance of killing her brother, and that she forfeited the honor by breaking the rules. Court survivors deny that she used lightning. Salvationist accounts condemn it as a family quarrel settled at the cost of millions of lives. Court survivors remember Azula as a martyr, and her challenge is quoted as her final act of defiance. Zuko rarely spoke publicly of the duel.

the_devastation.title: The Devastation (Jasmine Island Mutiny)
the_devastation.html:
Also known as the Jasmine Island Mutiny (Imperial legal designation) and the Night of the New Moon (island usage). Part of the Hundred Year War, western island chain.

The Devastation (Jasmine Island Mutiny)
DateNight of 7 June 90 AG, the New Moon Celebration (approx. 2100 to 0900 the following day)
LocationJasmine Island, western island chain, Empire of Tajisaki
ResultMutiny suppressed. Rear Admiral Yueya and Captain Zhao arrested by Army and loyal Navy personnel, and sent to the mainland for court-martial. Heavy civilian losses and destruction on the island.
Belligerents
Loyal Imperial forces
Jasmine Island garrison ("the protectors"), Army detachment, Navy personnel who refused Yueya's orders, including the imprisoned crew of the battlecruiser		Mutineers
Rear Admiral Yueya's loyalists
Commanders and leaders
Lt. Akataa (garrison, acting commander); Captain Lu Ten (Army liaison); the battlecruiser's captain and executive officerRear Admiral Yueya; Captain Zhao
Strength
Garrisonapprox. 300, about half on leave for the celebration
Army detachmentone company
Squadronapprox. 1,900 personnel, of whom approx. 250 followed Yueya. One battlecruiser (outside the harbor) and two destroyers
Casualties and losses
Garrison: 41 killed. Army detachment: 9 killed. Loyal sailors: 31 killed. Mutineers: approx. 100 killed. Civilians: an estimated 1,900–2,400 killed and 4,500 injured. About 80% of the island's fields and half of its main settlement destroyed. All figures disputed.

The Devastation was the destruction of the harbor town and farmland of Jasmine Island, an Imperial possession in the western island chain, by the loyalists of Rear Admiral Yueya of the Imperial Navy on the night of 7 June 90 AG, the island's New Moon Celebration. It was a mutiny. The island had been part of the Empire for decades and had never rebelled. Yueya, who had petitioned for the garrison command and been refused, took her squadron into the harbor in the absence of the garrison's colonel, declared the island in rebellion, and destroyed it. The killing did not stop at any point in the night: it grew as Yueya seized the squadron's battlecruiser and turned its guns on the hillside where the refugees had gathered. It was stopped by the island's own garrison, led by a junior officer, with the help of Army troops under Captain Lu Ten and Navy sailors who refused to follow her. Those sailors, who had been locked in the battlecruiser's brig, blew their way out and fought to the ship's bridge. Yueya's troops surrendered to Lu Ten at dawn, and she was arrested and sent to the mainland. The event led to her court-martial and, afterwards, to Lu Ten's Address on Conduct.

Background

Jasmine Island

Jasmine Island is a small island with a population of about 25,000, known for its tea and its golden jasmine. It was governed by a three-member island council under Imperial supervision and defended by a garrison of Army troops, mostly recruited locally, who were known as the protectors. The garrison's commander was an Army colonel. The island had no history of resistance, and during the war its main contribution to the Empire was tea. In 90 AG the island's economy was in decline because of the war's effect on shipping.

Yueya's petition

Rear Admiral Yueya commanded a Navy squadron in the western islands. She claimed descent from a man who had been humiliated in an attack on the island in the third century BG, and her family had carried the shame of it for centuries. In early 90 AG she petitioned the Admiralty and the War Council to be made garrison commander of Jasmine Island, which would have given her military authority over it.

The petition was denied. The garrison command was an Army post, the colonel in post had reported no difficulties, and the Directorate saw no operational reason to move it. The refusal was administrative and not personal. Officers who served with her later said that she took it as an insult, that she spoke of the island constantly afterwards, and that she began to prepare a plan to take it by force.

The plan

Yueya told the War Council that the island was a potential base for enemy agents and requested a force to "secure" it, which would be one battlecruiser, two destroyers and some troops. The Council, which believed that it was agreeing to a reinforcement of the garrison, approved. Yueya's real plan was to destroy the island and to describe it afterwards as a suppressed rebellion, in the expectation that her superiors would sanction the result after the fact. She timed it for the New Moon Celebration, when the town would be crowded and a part of the garrison on leave, and for a day when the garrison's colonel was away from the town, on a scheduled visit to the tea estates in the island's interior.

An Army company was embarked with the squadron, as is usual in reinforcement operations. Captain Lu Ten of the Armored Corps, then serving as an Army liaison officer, accompanied it. Yueya briefed him that the island's council had been infiltrated, that the garrison might be compromised, and that the celebration was a cover for an uprising. Lu Ten doubted the account and asked to lead the Army company ashore with the first assault, in order to see for himself.

Course of events

Approach and the first attack (2100–0030)

The squadron arrived at dusk and anchored off the harbor. At about 2100, Yueya transferred her flag from the battlecruiser to a destroyer, so as to command the harbor action herself, and left the battlecruiser under its captain outside the harbor mouth. The captain was told that the ship's main guns would be used only on her order.

At about 2330, Captain Zhao, Yueya's second-in-command, landed with a team of elite firebenders in launches, and placed explosive charges in the market square, under the Monument to Peace. At about midnight the charges were fired. The monument fell onto the council chambers and on the homes of the council members beside the square. Two of the island's three councillors, Shio-Ming and Kai, were killed. The blast and the collapse also killed a large part of the celebration crowd in the square. Yueya's landing parties then spread out through the town and the fields, setting fire to buildings and crops, and shooting at people who tried to put out the fires.

The garrison (0000–0100)

The garrison's commander was out of town, and about half of the garrison was on leave in the crowd. The senior officer present was Lieutenant Akataa, a young officer from the island who had been left in charge for the day. Akataa had a few dozen men in the barracks. He gathered them, organized a response, and sent a group to find the surviving councillor, Yuming, and her son Caishen, and to get them out of the square. The garrison fought in the streets with the rifles and light weapons it had, protected civilians, and was driven back. No one in the garrison knew what was happening beyond the fact that Imperial naval troops were attacking.

Lu Ten meets Akataa (approx. 0100)

Lu Ten had landed with his Army company in the second wave. By about 0100 he had found no rebels and a burning town. At about that hour, near the fish market, his squad met a group of the garrison, Akataa, Aiko, Basalt, Siku and Fu Meili, who had taken a position in a warehouse. The two groups nearly fired on each other. Akataa, who had seen the council chambers collapse, asked who had ordered the attack. Lu Ten told him that the order had come from the Rear Admiral, that he had been briefed on a rebellion, and that he could see no sign of one. Akataa showed him the dead in the square and the garrison's wounded. Lu Ten said that he would go back to Yueya and demand an end to the attack. He warned Akataa that she might not stop.

Lu Ten and Yueya (approx. 0130–0200)

Lu Ten went back to the harbor and confronted Yueya on the quay beside her destroyer. She told him that the rebels were hiding among the civilians. He asked where they were. She did not answer. He told her that he would report to the Western Command by radio if she did not stop, and that the garrison, whose commander would return in the morning, would not take the order to stand down from a Navy officer. Yueya refused to halt. At about 0150 Lu Ten sent his report from the Army company's radio, and Yueya, who learned of it, ordered the attack widened and sent for the battlecruiser's guns.

The battlecruiser (0200–0430)

The battlecruiser's captain, who had learned that no rebellion existed, refused to bring the ship's guns to bear. Yueya sent her flag lieutenant and a party of loyalist marines to the ship. They arrested the captain, the executive officer and about 60 officers and sailors who backed them, and locked them in the brig on the lowest deck. The loyalists then fired the secondary battery on the market district, and at about 0300 the main guns, in two salvos, on the hillside where the refugees had gathered. The shelling lasted until about 0430 and was the greatest single cause of civilian deaths after the explosion in the market square.

On the shore the killing grew through the same hours. Landing parties went through the town street by street and burned the farms in the lower valley, where many farmers were trapped. The garrison, which had lost its commander's authority and a part of its men, held the area around the barracks and the hospital, and Lu Ten's Army company, which had dropped any pretense of taking Yueya's orders, covered the evacuation of the wounded. Navy medical staff from the second destroyer, who had been instructed by their own captain to help, went ashore, and Lu Ten set up an aid station. Yuming took charge of the emergency response. The island's magistrate, Jin Bo, tried to organize the evacuation of the island's library and archive, and the innkeeper Saya took refugees to her inn in the interior.

The brig (approx. 0430–0520)

The imprisoned sailors had listened to the shelling through the hull for two hours. At about 0430, the damage-control ratings among them, using the demolition charges that the brig's compartment shared with the ship's flooding-control stores, blew the brig's door and the bulkhead behind it. About 60 sailors, armed with the loyalist guards' rifles, fought their way up three decks, compartment by compartment, to the bridge. The firefight inside the ship lasted about 50 minutes. They took the bridge at about 0520, at a cost of 31 killed. About 40 loyalists were killed. The battlecruiser's executive officer took command in place of the captain, who had been wounded, and ordered the guns to cease fire and secured the main battery. A signal was sent to the garrison and to the Western Command.

The harbor (approx. 0500–0630)

With the battlecruiser's guns silent, the island's response was prepared. Akataa's garrison, with the Army detachment and a group of sailors who had refused to follow Yueya, took the pier and the harbor boom. The captain of the second destroyer, who had stood down earlier, moved his ship across the harbor mouth, so that Yueya's ship could not leave. The garrison's two coastal guns, which Akataa had manned during the night, hit the destroyer's forward gun mount and steering, and she could not move. Zhao's landing party, cut off in the market area, fell back to the quay and was surrounded there by the garrison and the sailors. The destroyer was boxed in, and by about 0630 she had stopped firing.

Surrender and arrest (0630–0900)

Lu Ten walked onto the quay, with his company behind him, and called on the mutineers to lay down their arms. He did it as an Imperial officer acting under the law against mutiny, and he told them that the Rear Admiral had no authority for what she had done and that those who stopped would be treated as men who had obeyed an unlawful order. The loyalists, who had been fighting for hours against their own comrades, surrendered to him, and Zhao, who was on the quay, surrendered with them. Yueya remained on the destroyer's bridge for some time. She was arrested there by Lu Ten, with the Army detachment and officers of the Navy who had refused to follow her, including the executive officer of the battlecruiser and the captain of the second destroyer.

The garrison's colonel returned to the town at about 0900 and assumed command. Yueya and Zhao were held in the garrison's stockade, and were sent to the mainland under guard the following day, on the second destroyer, with the battlecruiser as escort.

Casualties and damage

Civilians were the largest group of casualties, an estimated 1,900–2,400 killed. The explosion in the market square and the collapse of the council chambers killed an estimated 150–200 people at once. The shelling of the market district and the hillside, mostly by the battlecruiser's main guns, killed about 600. The rest died during the fires, from shooting in the streets, and in the burning of the farms. Fire destroyed about half of the main settlement and about 80% of the island's fields. The garrison lost 41 killed, the Army detachment nine, the loyal sailors 31, and the mutineers about 100. The island's recovery took years.

Aftermath

Yueya and Zhao were court-martialed in the summer of 90 AG. Yueya was convicted of exceeding her orders, deceiving the War Council and the unlawful killing of Imperial subjects, and sentenced to imprisonment. Zhao was convicted on lesser charges and reduced in rank. In July 97 AG, a few days after his coronation, Fire Lord Ozai pardoned both, restored their ranks, and sent them to the south to help suppress the Southern Water Tribe insurgency, which was then a low-level conflict of small-scale skirmishes. The Diet and a part of the military regarded this as a mockery of the court-martial, and Ozai answered that the Empire should concentrate on the insurgency and bury the past (see Pardon Crisis of 97 AG). The sailors of the battlecruiser who had broken out of the brig were commended, and its captain and executive officer were decorated. Jasmine Island was placed under a civilian administrator, and the Directorate granted reconstruction aid. After the trial, Lu Ten submitted the Address on Conduct to Fire Lord Azulon and the National Diet. Lt. Akataa was commended and promoted.

The pardon (97 AG)

After his coronation in 97 AG, Fire Lord Ozai pardoned Yueya and Zhao and sent them to the South Pole, where an insurgency was under way, to pacify it. Lu Ten had been killed the year before, in the siege of Ba Sing Se. The pardon was widely read as a repudiation of the Address on Conduct, since it gave an officer convicted of the unlawful killing of Imperial subjects a command in occupied territory, which was the kind of abuse the Address had warned against.

Historiography

Imperial Navy accounts describe the event as an excess of zeal by one officer, put the number of civilian deaths lower, and do not mention the brig. Army and island records give higher figures, and emphasize the role of the garrison. The sequence of the night, and in particular the shelling and the brig breakout, are known mainly from the court-martial transcripts and from the accounts of Lu Ten, Akataa and the Navy officers and sailors who stood with them.
