war_demographic_ledger.title: Demographic ledger of the Hundred Year War
war_demographic_ledger.html:
A single accounting of the Hundred Year War's human cost, 0–100 AG: about 81 million excess deaths (range 75–90 million), of which about 41 million were violent and about 40 million indirect, together with the war's consequences for population, health and society.

This page revises the death toll given on Demographics of the Hundred Year War and Hundred Year War, which counted only direct deaths (about 41 million). The two figures do not conflict: this page adds the indirect deaths. Deaths of the Post-War Conflicts (100–120 AG) are counted separately.
Demographic ledger of the Hundred Year War
Period0–100 AG
Direct deathsAbout 40,840,000 (fighting, bombardment, massacre, genocide, engineered famine, reprisal)
Indirect deathsAbout 40,000,000 (famine, epidemic, displacement, collapse of medicine, detention, late injury)
Total excess deathsAbout 80,840,000 (central estimate); range 75,000,000–90,000,000
Direct casualties (dead, wounded, missing)About 77,000,000 (range 75–80 million)
Population, 0 AGAbout 501,000,000
Population, 100 AGAbout 547,600,000
Share of 0 AG population killedAbout 16%

The demographic ledger of the Hundred Year War is the accounting that reconciles the war's campaign totals, national totals and overall figures without counting the same death twice. Earlier tallies counted the dead in battle, in sieges and in the Empire's atrocities, and arrived at about 41 million. Those tallies were correct for what they measured, but they left out a second category of death which, in a war that destroyed harvests, cities, hospitals and the roads between them, was nearly as large as the first. A century of war killed about 81 million people, about one in six of the people alive when it began.

Method and definitions

  • Excess deaths are deaths above those that would have occurred in the same populations without the war, estimated from the 0 AG populations and the pre-war death rates of each nation.
  • Direct deaths are deaths caused by violence: combat, bombardment, chemical attack, massacre, genocide, execution, reprisal and the deliberate starvation of districts. These are the front tallies of Demographics, which are mutually exclusive: each death appears under one front only.
  • Indirect deaths are deaths caused by the war's conditions but not by an act of violence: starvation from collapsed harvests, epidemic disease, exposure among refugees, collapse of medical care, and deaths in detention or forced labor that the front tallies did not capture. Each is counted once, in the cause that best explains it.
  • Not included: the dead of the Post-War Conflicts (100–120 AG), about 19 million; and births that did not happen (see below).

The central estimate is the sum of the direct tally and the reconstructed indirect deaths. The low estimate (75 million) counts only deaths documented in Imperial, Qianchan or Earth Kingdom registers and assumes the lower end of the indirect range. The high estimate (90 million) assumes that the Empire's records, which were burned in the civil war, understated the death rate in the occupied lands. Estimates cannot be narrower than this because the occupied territories kept no reliable registers, the Empire concealed casualty figures from its own people, and large numbers of civilians were never recorded at all.

Direct deaths

FrontYearsDead
Earth Kingdom land war (including genocide and famine in the northwest, chemical weapons)0–79 AGabout 24,000,000
Air Nomad Genocide0–20 AGabout 3,400,000
Subjugation of the Water Tribes0–79 AGabout 1,680,000
Naval war30–79 AGabout 1,200,000
Si Wong Offensive80–88 AGabout 880,000
Siege of Ba Sing Se96–97 AGabout 3,500,000
Southern Uprising99 AGabout 480,000
Siege of the North and occupation99–100 AGabout 1,080,000
Sōen strike on Ba Sing Se17 July 100 AGabout 380,000
Occupation, famine and unlisted campaigns80–100 AGabout 4,200,000
Total, directabout 40,800,000

By nation the direct dead were: Earth Kingdom about 29.6 million, Water Tribes about 3.64 million, Fire Nation about 3.51 million, Air Nomads about 3.0 million, Qianchan about 1.09 million (total 40.84 million; the front tally rounds to 40.8).

Indirect deaths

The indirect dead were concentrated where the war lasted longest and where the Empire's occupation policies, fighting and blockades destroyed the means of life: the Earth Kingdom.

CauseEarth KingdomWater TribesFire NationQianchanTotal
Wartime famine (collapsed harvests, blockade, requisition, scorched earth)13,000,000350,000800,000200,00014,350,000
Epidemic disease (typhus, cholera, dysentery, influenza in camps, sieges and refugee columns)9,000,000200,0001,200,000300,00010,700,000
Refugee and displacement mortality (exposure, marches, camps)5,500,000100,000005,600,000
Medical and infrastructure collapse (untreated wounds, chronic illness, excess infant and maternal deaths)4,200,000100,0001,000,000300,0005,600,000
Detention and forced labor deaths not counted in the front tallies2,400,000150,000200,00002,750,000
Late deaths from chemical injuries and burns950,00050,000001,000,000
Total, indirect35,050,000950,0003,200,000800,00040,000,000

Why the Earth Kingdom's indirect toll was so high

  • The occupation economy. The Empire requisitioned grain, conscripted farmers into labor battalions, burned fields in contested districts and starved those that resisted. Harvests that fell by a quarter in a good year fell by half in a bad one.
  • The collapse of transport. Rail lines, canals and roads were cut, so that famine in one province could not be relieved from another. Provincial lords, each with their own supply, hoarded.
  • Siege and refugee conditions. Typhus and cholera followed the sieges and the refugee columns that walked out of the occupied zones. Water supplies in the cities were bombed or poisoned.
  • The lack of medical services. The Earth Kingdom's levies had no professional medical corps, and civilian hospitals were bombed, requisitioned or abandoned.
  • No growth. A population that had been growing slowly stopped growing, and its remaining families bore the costs for decades.

The Fire Nation's indirect toll

The Fire Nation lost about 3.2 million people to indirect causes, almost as many as it lost in the fighting. The causes were disease in barracks and camps, shortages in the later decades of rationing, the diversion of civilian health resources to the war and superweapon programs, and the blockade by Qianchan's submarines on the islands' import supply.

Total deaths by nation

NationDirectIndirectTotalShare of 0 AG population
Earth Kingdom29,600,00035,050,00064,650,000about 28%
Water Tribes3,640,000950,0004,590,000about 57%
Fire Nation3,510,0003,200,0006,710,000about 5.6%
Air Nomads3,000,00003,000,000about 100%
Qianchan1,090,000800,0001,890,000about 1.4%
World40,840,00040,000,00080,840,000about 16%

The Earth Kingdom lost almost ten people for every one the Fire Nation lost, a wider gap than the 8:1 ratio of the direct tally. The Air Nomads were destroyed as a people. About 400 survivors, among them those with airbending, remained in 100 AG.

Casualties other than death

The direct casualty figure of 75–80 million that appears on earlier pages counts the dead, the wounded and the missing from the war's fighting and atrocities. It is a measure of injury, not of mortality, and it should not be confused with the death toll of this page. The ledger divides it as follows:

CategoryNumber (central)Notes
Dead (direct)40,840,000As above
Wounded and maimedabout 31,500,000Includes the blind, burned, amputees, and those with gas injuries
Missing, unreconciledabout 4,700,000Includes deportees and conscripted laborers never accounted for. Many are later reclassified as dead
Direct casualtiesabout 77,000,000Within the 75–80 million of the earlier estimate

The two ranges overlap by coincidence. Direct casualties (including the wounded) were about 77 million; total deaths, including indirect, about 81 million. A historian who quotes "75–80 million" without saying which she means is almost always understating the war's deaths or overstating its injuries.

Population effects

Revised population in 100 AG

The populations given on the Demographics page were calculated after direct deaths only. With indirect deaths subtracted, the nations stood as follows in 100 AG:

NationPopulation, 0 AGExpected 100 AG without the warActual, 100 AG
Empire of Tajisaki (Fire Nation)120,000,000178,800,000about 172,100,000
Qianchan Republic140,000,000208,600,000about 206,700,000
Earth Kingdom230,000,000230,000,000 (no growth)about 165,350,000
Water Tribes8,000,0008,000,000 (without growth)about 3,410,000
Air Nomads3,000,0003,000,000about 400
World501,000,000about 547,600,000

The world's population was about 9 percent larger in 100 AG than in 0 AG, and not 17 percent as the earlier figure implied. The growth was entirely in the Fire Nation and Qianchan. The Earth Kingdom, which had been the largest nation in the world, was smaller than Qianchan by 41 million and smaller than the Fire Nation by about 7 million. It had lost more than a quarter of its people.

The shortfall against the counterfactual

The population a nation would have had without the war exceeds its actual population by more than its dead. The remainder are births that did not happen: couples separated by conscription or deportation, families too poor to raise children, women who died before their children were born. On the growth rates of the Demographics page (0.4% a year for the industrial states, 0.25% for the Water Tribes and for the Earth Kingdom's world average) the ledger estimates:

NationCounterfactual 100 AGActualShortfallOf which deathsOf which births not occurring
Fire Nation178.8 M172.1 M6.7 M6.7 Mnone (growth held)
Qianchan208.6 M206.7 M1.9 M1.9 Mnone
Earth Kingdom (at 0.25%)295.0 M165.4 M129.6 M64.6 Mabout 65 M
Water Tribes (at 0.25%)10.0 M3.4 M6.6 M4.6 Mabout 2 M
Air Nomads3.0 M0.0004 M3.0 M3.0 Ma people

The Earth Kingdom's shortfall is the largest single demographic loss in the world's history.

Other indirect consequences

Displacement

At its peak, around 90 AG, the war had displaced about 55–70 million people. Most were Earth Kingdom civilians who fled the occupied provinces for the cities of the interior and, later, for Qianchan, which took in refugees in large numbers and accounts for part of its population growth. Others were deported by the Empire to the Eastern Territories and the Southern colony. The Civil War and the Post-War Conflicts added another 7–10 million displaced from the Fire Nation alone.

The generation of orphans and widows

An estimated 18–22 million children lost one or both parents. The Earth Kingdom's adult sex ratio was skewed for two generations, because conscription and massacre took more men than women. Orphanages, religious houses and, in the Fire Nation, military schools raised a large part of the generation that rebuilt the world.

Disability and chemical injury

The 31.5 million wounded included many who lived with permanent injuries. The Empire's chemical weapons, which only the Empire possessed, left survivors with blinded eyes, scarred lungs and cancers that were still killing people decades later. The Sōen strike blinded thousands and burned many more.

Land and food

The Earth Kingdom's farmland was ruined in wide areas by scorched earth, abandoned irrigation and unexploded ordnance. Famine did not end with the war. In the Post-War Conflicts, the warlord wars and famine killed millions more. The memory of the engineered famines is one of the foundations of the Earth Kingdom's modern politics.

Economic and social effects

  • The Earth Kingdom's economy, which had been a large agrarian state, was reduced to a fraction of its prewar output and was rebuilt, from 23 AG, with Qianchan's help.
  • The Water Tribes lost the majority of their population and much of their oral tradition.
  • Qianchan and the Fire Nation emerged as the two largest societies in the world, with the Empire's economy distorted by the war.
  • The Air Nomads' culture survives only in the memory of the 400 who live, in the archives of Qianchan and in the practices of the airbenders whom Qianchan sheltered at the Southern Air Temple.

Reconciliation with campaign pages

Campaign and battle pages continue to give direct deaths for their own fronts. They should be read as follows:

  • A campaign page's dead are in the direct tally of this page, once.
  • Famine and disease in the same districts are in the indirect tally, once.
  • Deaths in a front's occupation or reprisals appear on that front's page if they were violent, and in "detention and forced labor" if they were not.
  • No death appears in both the direct and indirect tallies.

Historiography

The figure of 41 million was the standard figure for the first decades after the war, and it was an undercount that many historians knew to be incomplete. Qianchan's archives, the registers of the Earth Kingdom's provincial governments and, after 118 AG, the Fire Nation's own opened records allowed the indirect deaths to be reconstructed. The low estimate of 75 million is favored by those who accept only documented deaths; the high estimate of 90 million by those who argue that the occupied lands' registers were incomplete. The debate over the toll is also a debate about responsibility: some Earth Kingdom historians count all famine in the occupied lands as an act of the Empire, which would place almost all of the indirect deaths on the direct side of the ledger.

See also

  • Post-War Conflicts

occupation_and_resistance.title: Occupation and resistance
occupation_and_resistance.html:
How imperial control operated across the occupied Earth Kingdom, the Southern and Northern Water Tribes and the former Air Nomad communities, and the many forms of resistance and collaboration it produced, 0–100 AG.

For individual campaigns, see Yanakawan Campaign, Subjugation of the Water Tribes, Southern Uprising and Air Nomad Genocide. For the human cost, see Demographic ledger of the Hundred Year War.
Occupation and resistance
Period0–100 AG (and into the Post-War Conflicts)
Occupying powerThe Empire of Tajisaki
Administered byThe Ministry of Colonial Affairs; the Ministry of National Harmony (population policy); the War establishment (garrisons); the Ministry of Truth (security)
Legal basisImperial Constitution, Arts. 42–44; the Homeland Purity Initiative
Main territoriesThe west coast and Yanakawa (the Eastern Territories); the northern mountains and plains; the South Pole; the island chains; the north (99–100 AG)
ResistanceProvincial armies; guerrillas; the Southern Water Tribe; the Coastal Resistance Council and the Yanakawan Liberation Front; Qianchan-supplied cells; hidden Air Nomads

The Hundred Year War was a war of occupation as much as of battles. For most of the century large parts of the world lived under the Empire's rule, and the way that rule worked decided how many people died, who collaborated and who resisted, and what kind of societies emerged when the Empire fell. Imperial control was not uniform. It differed by region, by period and by the Empire's purposes: the west coast became a colony, the Water Tribes a labor reserve, the former Air Nomad lands a chain of bases, and the Earth Kingdom's interior a battlefield that the Empire tried to hold with garrisons.

The structure of imperial control

Law and classification

Colonial administrators held combined executive, legislative and judicial powers within their jurisdictions (Arts. 42–43), and the Homeland Purity Initiative authorized "integration, resettlement and, in cases of irreconcilable resistance, removal" (Art. 44). The Ministry of National Harmony classified populations in four categories:

CategoryWhoTreatment
Recognized Imperial PersonsTajisaki citizens and settlersFull legal protection, preferential access to land and posts
Enrolled Colonial SubjectsLocals registered and found cooperativeLimited rights; ration and work permits; obliged to labor and levy
Unenrolled PopulationsThose not yet registered or who evaded registrationNo protection; subject to resettlement and forced labor
Designated Threat PopulationsCommunities judged hostile or harboring resistanceRemoval, collective punishment, detention or elimination

Classification determined food, movement, work and survival. Registers of waterbenders, of able-bodied adults and of families were among the first things the Empire compiled in each occupied district.

Garrison, settlement and occupied city

The Empire ran three kinds of place, and the differences mattered.

TypeCharacterExample
Military garrisonA fortified base with a military governor, no settled civilian population beyond camp followers and laborThe island-chain bases; forward fields in the north; the Northern Air Temple base
Colonial settler townNew or expanded towns populated by Fire Nation settlers, with their own police, courts and services, and a subject labor population outsideThe coastal towns of the Eastern Territories; the port districts of Yanakawa
Occupied native cityAn existing city under an Imperial governor, with its municipal institutions kept in place under supervisionCities of the west coast and the north; the captured Council of the South Pole

Who administered

Governors-general ran the larger territories and reported to the Ministry of Colonial Affairs. Practical authority was divided: National Harmony oversaw population policy, the War establishment controlled garrisons, and the Ministry of Truth ran security and the press. The division often produced conflicting priorities, because officials were required to manage a local population, respond to the security demands of the army and carry out the population policies of the center at the same time.

The occupied Earth Kingdom

The west coast and Yanakawa (1–10 AG)

The Empire invaded Yanakawa in January 1 AG from the occupied island chains, using mustard gas at Yu Dao, and conquered the whole west coast by 10 AG. It became the core of the Eastern Territories, which the Empire held for ninety years. The territory was developed as a colony: the Fire Nation colonies of 37 BG were the first settlements, and after the conquest the coast was divided into districts with settler towns, ports and rail lines built to carry the northern and southern pushes. The population was registered and classified, and large numbers were deported to labor sites.

The north, the mountains and the interior

The Empire pushed north along the mountain chain and south toward Omashu. It did not try to administer the whole continent. In the northwest it practiced extermination policies against the people of the occupied lands, and in resisting districts it starved the population as a matter of policy. In the interior it held the towns it needed for rail, supply and the Si Wong oil, and relied on garrisons, movable columns and air power to keep the rest of the countryside uncertain and afraid.

Policy toward civilians

  • Genocide and elimination. In the northwest, in "Designated Threat" districts, whole communities were removed or killed.
  • Engineered famine. Grain was requisitioned, fields burned, and districts that resisted were cut off.
  • Forced labor. Laborers built rail lines, roads, airfields and depots, and worked in mines and processing plants.
  • Deportation. Populations were moved to the Eastern Territories and, in the case of Water Tribe deportees, to colonies elsewhere.
  • Collective punishment. A raid, an ambush or a cut cable could bring the destruction of the nearest village.
  • Chemical weapons. Used in the occupied lands from the first week of the war against cities and strongholds.

Local elites: collaboration, neutrality and resistance

The Earth Kingdom's provincial lords were not a single body. Some fought for their own provinces, some withdrew with their troops, some bargained, and a few collaborated. The Empire needed local administrators and offered them security, posts and land in return for cooperation.

ResponseWhoReason
Armed resistanceProvincial armies and some lords, often for their own rulers and territoriesLoyalty to the province; revenge; fear of what occupation meant
WithdrawalLords who moved their court and levies to the interiorPreserving the army; avoiding a decisive battle
Cooperation under duressOfficials and notables who kept administration running to protect their peopleTo prevent worse; to keep food and order
CollaborationA minority who took posts, contracts or landProfit, ambition, or belief that the Empire would win
NeutralityMany small towns and villagesSurvival

Daily life

Schools taught the Empire's version of history, and the press was controlled by the Ministry of National Enlightenment. Courts applied imperial law, local courts were limited to petty cases, and municipal governments were reduced to executors of the governor's orders. Registers, permits and checkpoints regulated movement, and the ration was a means of control. In settler towns, an Imperial school, an Imperial court and an Imperial police force worked beside a native quarter with none of them.

The Water Tribes

The South Pole (0–99 AG)

About a week after the Air Nomad Genocide began, the Empire bombarded both poles. In the South the landings succeeded, and the Council of Chieftains and Elders and the leading chieftains were captured in the first weeks. Those who refused to cooperate were executed in front of their people; the rest were forced into an Imperial administration under a Governor-General. The Council issued the Governor's orders as its own, drew up registers of waterbenders and able-bodied adults and supplied laborers, with a hostage system and collective punishment to compel it. Some chieftains collaborated and others cooperated to protect their people, and generations disputed the difference.

The occupation's central feature was forced labor: laborers built harbors, dry docks and ice-cut channels, laid rail lines across the ice, quarried ice and worked in seal and whale processing plants. Waterbenders were used to cut ice and clear channels, and the captured were kept in prisons and denied water but for drinking. Talekeepers and elders were killed in large numbers, and much of the oral tradition was lost. By 99 AG the South had become a colony and a research base, with a permanent garrison, ice mines and settlements.

The North

The Northern Water Tribe repelled the landings of 0 AG, and the Empire settled for a forward base on the far eastern pole, from which it bombed Agna Qel'a periodically for a hundred years. The North was never occupied until the combined operation of 99 AG, when the Northern Fleet took Agna Qel'a in December. The occupation of the North lasted from the fall of the city to the Coalition Northern Offensive of 100 AG, and it was short and brutal: persistent blister agents were used in the ice cellars, killing people in their shelters, and about a million died in the siege and the occupation. See Siege of the North.

Waterbenders and the Southern Raiders

The Empire's special concern was waterbenders, who were the most valuable and the most closely watched, and who were hunted so that no new Avatar could rise among the Water Tribes. By 99 AG the Southern waterbenders had dwindled to a handful.

The former Air Nomad lands

The Empire occupied the four Air Temples and their island chains in 0 AG. It killed or removed their inhabitants, and made the sites bases rather than settlements.

SiteUse
Southern Air Temple island chainRazed; forward operating base and airfields; the launch point for the invasion of Yanakawa. Divided between the Empire and the Qianchan Navy by 50 AG
Southern Air Temple chainOccupied completely; forward base and airfields. Preserved after the war by Qianchan, which granted the airbenders autonomy there
Eastern Air TempleDestroyed; whole islands razed, including civilian villages
Northern Air TempleFirebombed; the ruin kept as an airbase, resupply depot and supply hub for the rest of the war

The Air Nomads who lived elsewhere were hunted for twenty years along the pilgrim routes and at sea, and the last organized group, a community of monks, children and refugees, was killed in the snow of the South Pole in 20 AG. In 99 AG about 300–400 people with airbending lived in the interior of Qianchan or the Earth Kingdom, most of them without knowing what they were. They survived by hiding, and by being unknown. There was no organized Air Nomad resistance. Their resistance, if the word applies, was survival, and the preservation of what could be remembered.

Resistance

Resistance was not one movement. Different communities had different objectives, and they rarely cooperated.

FormWhereAims and methods
Provincial armiesThe Earth KingdomFighting for their own lords and lands; conventional warfare; after 98 AG under King Kuei's centralized command
Local guerrillasOccupied districts of the Earth KingdomRaids on railways, depots and collaborators; ambushes; sabotage
Qianchan-trained and -supplied cellsThe south, Omashu front, the polesSurplus rifles by sea; training in desert and guerrilla warfare; political consequences of foreign support
Southern Water Tribe insurgencyThe South PoleRaids on convoys, ice mines on the roads, attacks on rail and industrial sites, ships trapped in the ice; uprisings in 29 AG and 99 AG
Coastal Resistance Council, then Yanakawan Liberation FrontYanakawa and the Eastern TerritoriesFrom 97 AG a council of the coast; the YLF from June 100 AG; took Qinglan Port on 18 July 100 AG
Hidden Air NomadsThe interiorConcealment and survival
Dissenters inside the Fire NationThe EmpireThe Army's reform wing and, later, the Salvationists

Resistance that harmed its own people

Not all resistance behaved well. Some groups attacked collaborators on rumor, took food from villages that could not spare it, or fought rival groups more savagely than the Empire. Imperial reprisals fell on the villages near the attacks, which gave the movements a reason to restrain their raids, and sometimes a reason not to.

Intelligence and suppression

The Ministry of Truth and the military intelligence services infiltrated resistance networks, relying on informers whose reports led to ambushes. In the Southern Uprising of 99 AG, informers and mortar bombardment destroyed the resistance capital, Taluqqriaq. Reprisals were harsh and open: about 90,000 killed in the South after the uprising, and about 240,000 conscripted, deported or missing by the end of the war. The Empire's own people were told little. The state suppressed casualty figures, described the Air Nomad Genocide as a "purification" and kept the occupation out of the press.

The resistance had its own intelligence and propaganda. Qianchan's and the Earth Kingdom's newspapers reported defeats and atrocities, and the Qianchan archives, the most detailed outside source on the genocide, hold the registers of the Air Nomad dead.

Qianchan's role

Qianchan could not occupy or defend the poles, and distance limited its support. It supplied Omashu by sea after 25 AG, the Southern guerrillas with surplus rifles, and the Earth Kingdom with rifles, machine guns and doctrine from 30 AG. It evacuated the Northern Water Tribe's leaders by submarine in 99 AG. See History of Qianchan.

The end of the occupation

The death of Ozai on 18 July 100 AG collapsed the Empire's central authority. The YLF took Qinglan Port on the same day and formed the Provisional Council in September. The Court faction continued naval skirmishes until 110 AG, and the Treaty of Qinglan of 28 April 105 AG ended the land war in Yanakawa and recognized its independence. Garrisons in the occupied lands surrendered, withdrew or, in some cases, became warlords. The Water Tribes' occupation ended with the Coalition Northern Offensive and the end of the war, and the Southern Federation was formed in 171 AG. See Yanakawan War of Independence.

Historiography

The history of the occupation has been written late and by the survivors. Imperial records, which the Empire concealed during the war, were not published until after it. Local memories differ from provincial ones, and resistance narratives often ignore the fact that most people neither resisted nor collaborated, but tried to survive.

history_of_qianchan.title: History of Qianchan
history_of_qianchan.html:
The history of the Qianchan Republic from the southern grievances of the old kingdom to the peace after the Hundred Year War, with the history of the southern fronts of the war: Omashu, the South Pole, the southern seas and the southern rebellions against the Empire.

This page is the long history. For the state as it stood, see Qianchan Republic. For its origins as seen from Ba Sing Se, see History of the Earth Kingdom.
History of Qianchan
CapitalGaoling
Founded255 BG (constitutional process 270–255 BG)
PeriodsLiberation (270–255 BG); the Long Cold Peace (255 BG – 0 AG); the war (30–100 AG); the aftermath (100 AG –)
Southern frontsOmashu (south); the South Pole; the Western and Southern island chains; the southern seas
Entered the war30 AG (after the sinking of a civilian ship in 27 AG)
War deadAbout 1,090,000 (direct); about 1,890,000 with indirect deaths

The history of Qianchan is the history of a state that was founded by a rebellion and that spent two centuries defending its existence, first against the kingdom it had left and then against the empire that wanted to rule the world. It also includes the history of the southern rebellions: the struggles of the southern earth lands, of Omashu, of the Southern Water Tribe and of the island chains against Imperial occupation, in most of which Qianchan took a part, and in some of which it was the only outside power that did.

Origins (before 270 BG)

The south of the Earth Kingdom was always a different country from the capital: wetter, richer in coal and iron, closer to the sea and farther from the Inner City. It paid the same tribute as the north and received less protection. Its lords and merchants shared the view that the kingdom existed for its capital. The Yellow Neck Uprising of 312–305 BG, in which the capital put down a peasant rebellion with little regard for the provinces that bore the cost, left a memory of betrayal. The Yakuya Confederation, whose people the court later called the Fifth Nation, left the south a legacy of eastern merchants and an idea of its own status. See History of the Earth Kingdom.

The Yakuya Confederation and Qin's eastern campaign (296–292 BG)

The Fifth Nation was the worst of the kingdom's coastal afflictions. It was a multigenerational society of pirates, waterbenders, firebenders and nonbenders, whose leader, Tagaka, had made it a power that no state could easily afford to ignore. Its fleets threatened the coastal trade, and its commanders held bases and networks of supporters along the eastern and southern coasts, which showed how little Ba Sing Se could protect its distant ports. In 296 BG a force led by a man then believed to be the Avatar, Yun, defeated the main fleet at sea, and the Earth Kingdom allowed the Tajisaki Navy to patrol the Eastern Sea to restore order and rescue the people the pirates had kidnapped.

The land bases remained. In 295 BG a young commander from Gaoling, Qin, led a detachment against the Confederation's principal stronghold, the political and logistical centre of its power, in the eastern territories of what would become Qianchan. The expedition was meant to be limited. Qin's forces broke through the defences and took the city, and the Confederation lost its ability to coordinate its fleets on land or to protect its bases, feed its followers or compel its constituent groups to obey. Its remnants dispersed into small fleets and local communities, and by 292 BG it had ceased to exist as a power.

The victory made Qin famous. To the communities that the Confederation had threatened, he had done what Ba Sing Se had repeatedly failed to do, and to soldiers and provincial lords he had shown that a coordinated regional army could defeat a power that lived off the kingdom's fragmentation. It tied his name to the east, which would later become Qianchan, and it gave him the prestige to build a coalition. The capital read it differently, and its chroniclers said that Qin had used a crisis to acquire territory and renown beyond his lawful authority. The two readings were the first sign of the quarrel that would divide the south from the north for ever.

Qin the Great (292–270 BG)

Qin, remembered in the south as Qin the Great and in Ba Sing Se, with a sneer, as Chin the Conqueror, was a lord of Gaoling who rose in the chaos that followed the Yellow Necks. He cultivated an image as a leader who understood the conditions of ordinary people, and argued that the kingdom's troubles were not the inevitable result of its size but of a capital that had abandoned its provinces. The provinces were expected to pay taxes and give soldiers, and the capital too often failed to protect them from banditry, predatory officials and political violence. His programme was administrative reform, more accountable provincial government, relief for the poor and an end to the capital's arbitrary interference in local affairs. Gaoling became a gathering place for reformers, discontented officers, merchants and communities that had lost confidence in the crown.

His enemies said that he exploited popular discontent to build a personal following, and later royal historians made that charge the heart of their portrait of him as a warlord. The coalition grew regardless, because the crisis was real. Its members were:

  • the Avatar Kyoshi, who thought the reform just;
  • the King of Omashu, who disliked Ba Sing Se's pretensions to supremacy;
  • the Lord of Yu Dao;
  • the lords of Tongshui and the western ports, who wanted protection for their trade.

Their motives differed, and Qin supplied the centre round which they could unite. He subdued the northwest, and by 272 BG Gaoling's banner had merged into his. He did not at first present himself as the founder of a new dynasty. But his armies grew, and with them the expectation that he would eventually impose a settlement on Ba Sing Se itself. The Earth King, who feared that any concession would destroy the monarchy, refused all reform, and in 270 BG Qin marched on the capital. At the height of his conquests only Ba Sing Se and Kyoshi's peninsula were beyond his control.

The duel

Qin reached the outer walls in 270 BG and almost forced the city to surrender. The king, to avoid a siege he might lose, challenged him to a duel outside the walls, presenting it as a means of settling the quarrel without further bloodshed. In the Qianchan account, which is the most widely accepted, it was a betrayal: the king fought with hidden crossbowmen and a poisoned blade and killed Qin before his followers could intervene, and Qin, in the last exchange, mortally wounded the king. Both died on the field. Some rumours place Qin's death elsewhere, saying that he fell from a cliff on the Yokoya peninsula while trying to fight Kyoshi, when she separated it from the mainland. The accounts were never reconciled, and the surviving record establishes his campaigns, alliances and death more securely than it does his private intentions.

Kyoshi in the Inner City

Kyoshi, who had come to the walls with Qin, did not leave. With the king dead and his heirs weak, she went into the Inner City and used her authority as Avatar to force through reforms of the royal court: a written constitution, the ending of some of the king's privileges, and a promise to attend to the peasants, which also ended a peasant uprising in the city, the first of the two that Ba Sing Se would suffer in that century. The reforms made the monarchy more stable but not more humane, and they never made the kingdom a constitutional state. For Qin's followers his death proved that the old order would never reform itself. For Ba Sing Se it was a chance to restore royal authority and to recast the whole movement as the rebellion of a dangerous warlord.

The Qin Dynasty and the War of Liberation (270–255 BG)

Qin's death left a vacuum across the territories he had brought under his banner. His heirs proclaimed the Qin Dynasty, kept much of his administrative and military system, and reduced Ba Sing Se to a tributary city. The Earth King's death and Kyoshi's intervention had left the capital unable to reverse his territorial gains.

The south did not stay united behind the dynasty. Qin's movement had drawn its strength from communities that resisted arbitrary power, and a hereditary dynasty threatened to reproduce the concentration of authority that he had meant to reform. In 270 BG the southern lands rose against Qin's heirs, in the War of Liberation (270–255 BG). It began in Qianchan, where local communities, former officers and political organizations refused to recognize the heirs, and it spread across the south as provincial forces defected and peasant uprisings cut the dynasty's supply routes. Many Earth Kingdom soldiers defected, among them many who had served under Qin and who would not serve under his sons. The Avatar took no part, and dealt instead with the warlords in the northwest.

It was not a single rebellion under one command. It was a series of overlapping campaigns, local revolts, quarrels among former commanders and negotiations, fought over fortified towns and grain routes while armies requisitioned the harvests. The rebels' core, the Southern Army, was made of Qin's surviving formations and the forces that had joined the revolt, and it was held together by a collective command of regional officers and civil administrators instead of a single chief. Its organization is described below.

The Southern Army and its council

The army that fought the war was assembled from Qin's surviving regiments, from Earth Kingdom units that deserted the capital and from village militias. It had no single commander. A collective command council of officers and delegates governed the territory it held, collected taxes and appointed administrators, which is why the republic distrusts any person holding a sword and a treasury at once. In fifteen years the Southern Army took the coalfields and river ports, and in 255 BG a settlement recognized the south's independence.

From council to republic

  1. The provisional council (270–262 BG). Officers governed by decree.
  2. Pressure from below (c. 262–258 BG). Peasant organizations and merchants demanded land titles, a currency and courts.
  3. The district conventions (258–255 BG). Delegates drafted a constitution: a legislature of districts, a civilian executive, regular taxation and an army subordinate to civilians.
  4. The settlement of 255 BG. The first President took office and the council dissolved itself.

The Qin house survived as a political house, with estates and seats in the legislature but no claim to rule.

255 BG

By 255 BG the war had exhausted the remaining authorities. Famine and the breakdown of the dynasty's grain and transport networks had destroyed the Qin Dynasty in the north, and the last loyalist stronghold on the west coast fell. A treaty recognized the independence and autonomy of the new Qianchan Republic, which for a time called itself the Fifth Nation, a name that echoed both the pirate confederation whose eastern lands it had inherited and the republic's claim to be a new power among the four. Qianchan did not say that it inherited the dynasty's hereditary right to rule. It said that it was the successor of the institutions that had survived Qin's death and resisted the restoration of hereditary rule.

The Qin Dynasty did not disappear. It gave up its claim to sovereignty over the south, accepted the republican order, and became one of Qianchan's major political houses, keeping its wealth, estates and military connections, and entering the republic's legislature, ministries and officer corps. It is the strangest feature of the settlement, and it is discussed in the article on Qianchan.

The first centuries (255 BG – 100 BG)

Industry

The republic adopted coal-fired engines in 255 BG, and its coal, iron, rivers and ports made it an industrial state within generations. Its universities, centered on the Academy of Gaoling, trained engineers and scientists. By 130 BG it had the repeater.

The Long Cold Peace

Ba Sing Se's two suppression campaigns of 240 and 225 BG failed. The Preliminary Accord of 224 BG set a boundary without recognition, and the kingdom founded the Dai Li around 215 BG to stop republican ideas from spreading north. For two centuries the relationship was one of trade and hostility. Qianchan's policy was "we govern ourselves; we do not export governance," and it refused requests for help from Earth Kingdom reformers, from principle (a republic that exports itself by force is an empire) and prudence (any support for northern rebels would give Ba Sing Se the pretext for another war).

Politics

The republic's governments were coalitions of veterans, merchants, agrarian assemblies and federalists, and its politics were noisy and slow. It strengthened a federal system as a precaution against invasion, and kept a citizen-militia tradition, in which every adult was expected to have trained.

The race with the Fire Nation (26 BG – 0 AG)

From 26 BG Qianchan and the Fire Nation were in a technology race. The republic's journals printed freely, and the Empire's researchers read them. It was a rivalry of steel, rail, ships and, by the 20s BG, of sciences. Qianchan's intelligence on the Empire was the best in the world, because its engineers could see what the Fire Nation built. Its leaders concluded that the Empire was building the largest army and fleet in its history, and they disagreed with Ba Sing Se about what that meant. They offered an oil-sharing discussion in the late 20s BG that went unanswered, proposed a combined staff, a standard railway gauge and a naval convention with the North, and signed the Alliance Treaty in 3 BG only after Ba Sing Se agreed to revise its language of non-recognition. See Prewar diplomacy.

The war (0–100 AG)

Neutrality and watching (0–25 AG)

When the comet came, Qianchan was not at war. Its government was in session, its fleet in port, and its leaders were as surprised as anyone that the blow fell on a people with no army. Its archives became the most detailed outside record of the Air Nomad Genocide, and the registers of the dead were kept in Gaoling. It was not at war, but it was not neutral in sympathy. It received refugees, and in the 10s AG it began to supply the Earth Kingdom's southern front through its sea routes.

The Empire, which held naval superiority alone, raided small settlements along Qianchan's coast and in the polar regions. These raids terrorized communities and disrupted trade, but could not neutralize Qianchan's capacity to supply its ally. They are part of the reason that Fire Lord Azulon, after 20 AG, moved the Empire's budget towards the land war. See Imperial military budget.

The Omashu front (10–100 AG)

The kingdom of Omashu, in the west of the Earth Kingdom, was the southern anchor of the war. The Empire pushed south from Yanakawa from 10 AG, was foiled in its attempt to break east, and pushed instead into the high mountains. By 25 AG it had cut the southern Omashu front off from the rest of the Earth Kingdom by land. Omashu held, because Qianchan supplied it by sea.

PeriodOmashu front
10–25 AGThe Empire's southern push; foiled; the front cut off by 25 AG
25–30 AGOmashu supplied by sea by Qianchan under Imperial naval superiority and blockade; losses in the convoys
30–50 AGQianchan's formal entry; convoys escorted; the sea route secured
50–80 AGQianchan's air force expands; Omashu becomes the base for the southern air war
80–100 AGQianchan's whole air force committed to the Omashu front in the late war

After the Sōen strike, Omashu, Ba Sing Se and Gaoling were the three powers that ended the Earth Kingdom's warlord wars, by 112 AG.

The ship, the battle and the entry (27–30 AG)

In 27 AG an Imperial vessel sank a civilian Qianchan ship in the waters of the Southern Air Temple island chain, and a naval battle that followed was a draw. Qianchan's Parliament debated for three years. In 30 AG it entered the war, after the Empire's first engagement with the Qianchan Navy, at the Southern Air Temple Waters, ended in a draw. The date marks both a formal declaration and the start of sustained combat.

The middle war (30–80 AG)

  • The submarine war. Qianchan fought a submarine campaign against Imperial shipping that became one of the long conflicts of the middle war, and drove the Navy's carriers onto the defensive.
  • The island chains. By 50 AG the Western and Southern island chains were divided between the Empire and the Qianchan Navy.
  • Arms and doctrine. It supplied the Earth Kingdom with rifles, machine guns and doctrine, taught it desert warfare, and from 23 AG helped it industrialize.
  • The Eastern Push and the Desert War. Qianchan's forces fought alongside the Earth Kingdom on the central plains and in the Si Wong.

The late war (80–100 AG)

Qianchan lost about 150,000 dead in the Si Wong Offensive and about 40,000 at the siege of Ba Sing Se, where it refused to commit troops until King Kuei was evacuated. It supplied the Southern guerrillas with surplus rifles by sea before the uprising of 99 AG, evacuated the Northern Water Tribe's leaders by submarine in 99 AG, and in 100 AG put its army under a single command with the Earth Kingdom's, under the Ba Sing Se Treaty. Its fission program, Tieshan, ran in parallel to the Empire's.

The southern rebellions in the Empire

The Empire's southern territories, and the southern lands that resisted it, produced a series of rebellions across the century. The list below gathers them with the republic's part in each.

DateRebellion or frontQianchan's part
0–40 AGThe Southern Water Tribe's insurgency: raids on convoys, ice mines, attacks on rail and industrial sitesMoral support; refugees; later arms by sea
10–25 AGOmashu's resistance to the southern pushSea supply from 25 AG
29 AGThe last great early uprising of the South Pole; crushed; the population falls to about three quartersNone possible at the distance
1–50 AGThe Southern and Western island chains: Imperial bases, then contestedNaval war; divided with the Empire by 50 AG
50–79 AGThe southern flank of the Desert WarTroops, advisers, arms
97–99 AGSkirmishes and missing patrols in the SouthSurplus rifles supplied by sea
12 May – 9 Dec 99 AGThe Southern Uprising from Taluqqriaq; crushed. The Avatar found and evacuated to GaolingArms; the Avatar's party reached Qianchan by sea
100 AGThe Yanakawan rebellion (Coastal Resistance Council, YLF)Arms and recognition
100–112 AGThe warlord wars of the Earth KingdomWith Omashu and Ba Sing Se, ended them

The South Pole and Gaoling

The Southern Water Tribe, a federation of chiefdoms, fought the Empire for a hundred years and lost about 70 percent of its people. Qianchan, whose reach did not extend to the pole, could do little before the 90s AG. But it was in Gaoling that the resistance's leaders and its Avatar found refuge in 99 AG, and it was Qianchan that gave the Southern survivors a place to rebuild. The Imperial intelligence services heard rumors that the surviving leadership was building a new capital far to the south.

Why Qianchan was never occupied

The Empire raided Qianchan's coasts but never held ground there. Its navy was contested after 30 AG, its air force was tied down at Omashu, and its Army found the republic's armored forces, citizen militia and industry too heavy to break at the price it was willing to pay. The republic was the one major power that was never invaded, and that is why it could be an arsenal for the others.

After the war (100 AG –)

After the Sōen strike and the death of Ozai, Qianchan helped end the Earth Kingdom's warlord wars from Gaoling, supplied the Yanakawan rebels with surplus weapons and preserved the Southern Air Temple, granting the airbenders autonomy there. It occupied the island chains in the civil war, taking the port of Shiza from Court loyalists in the winter of 100–101 AG, and used them to supply the Royalists. Its population grew from about 140 million to about 207 million by 100 AG, partly through refugees. Its fission program, Tieshan, outlived the war.

Historiography

Qin's legacy is disputed. The republic's schools remember Qin the liberator, Ba Sing Se's court histories Qin the usurper, and modern historians Qin the symbol, a name attached to the collective work of the Southern Army's council and the district conventions. Historians also disagree on whether the republic was founded in 270, 258 or 255 BG, and whether the Empire's attack could have been avoided by an earlier, firmer alliance.

army_navy_divide.title: The Army–Navy divide
army_navy_divide.html:
The rivalry between the Army and the Navy of the Empire of Tajisaki: a quarrel over money, prestige and class that began under Sozin and never touched the services' cooperation in the field.

For the budget shares behind the rivalry, see Imperial military budget. For the institutions, see Political institutions of the Empire.
The Army–Navy divide
PartiesThe Imperial Army (the larger, conscript service); the Imperial Navy (the smaller, aristocratic service)
NaturePolitical and institutional: appropriations, prestige, appointments, class. Not operational
OriginThe Sozin Rearmament (37 BG – 0 AG): Navy 70%, Army 30%
ReversalAzulon's reallocation: Army 60%, Navy 40% (from the early 20s AG)
ArenasThe annual General Appropriations Act in the National Diet; cabinet formation; garrison appointments
ConsequencesThe Pardon Crisis; the reform movement; the split of the Navy by squadron in the Civil War

The Empire had one Fire Lord and two services that were rivals from the reign of Sozin. They quarreled over appropriations, status and class. They did not quarrel in the field: when the two operated together, there was no friction. That is the main difference between the Empire's rivalry and the interservice quarrels of other militarized states, in which the services also fought over strategy, fuel, aircraft, intelligence and who commanded joint operations. In the Empire, the rivalry stayed at the budget table, in the Diet, in the press and at the dinner table.

Origins: Sozin's era

Sozin spent the last twelve years before the war, and twenty-five before them, militarizing the Fire Nation. One of his first projects was a fast ship, originally a trade vessel, which he turned into a fleet. The Navy was his favored service from the start, because it was the instrument of an island empire's reach: it transported troops, protected commerce and supported overseas campaigns.

Under Sozin about 70 percent of military funding and research went to the Navy and 30 percent to the Army. The division was not necessarily a fixed statute, but it reflected the government's preference. The Navy received the best shipyards, the first call on steel and the best engineers, and built the carriers, the submarines and the Kaienha incendiary torpedoes (by 99 AG, eight carriers and 94 submarines). The Army had to innovate and cut corners. It built cheap, mass-produced solutions because it could not afford expensive ones, and the Army's own explanation of its tank, aircraft and powered-armor programs is that necessity produced them. It gave the Army a grievance that it never lost.

The appropriations fight

Each year the Diet passed the General Appropriations Act (GAA). The Diet could not investigate military operations (Art. 28), but it controlled the budget, so the GAA was where the services fought.

Who held the larger share

PeriodReignArmyNavyResult
37 BG – 20 AGSozin30%70%Navy primacy; the origin of the Army's grievance
20 AG – 97 AGAzulon60%40%Army primacy; the Navy defends its 40% and its prestige
97–100 AGOzai60%40%Unchanged, plus 30% of the civilian budget to superweapons

The Navy held the larger cut only under Sozin. After Azulon's reallocation the Army was the main recipient of state resources, because the war's demands had changed and the strategic center of gravity was the land front. The Navy's response was not to resist the reallocation but to defend what it had: its prestige, its patronage and its claim that the war could not be won without sea control. The dispute therefore changed character. It was no longer about which service had the larger cut, but about who deserved it, who held the posts and whose war it was.

The Diet maps onto the services

  • House of Representatives. Its voters are men who completed their service (Arts. 20–22), most of whom served in the Army, since the Army is by far the larger service. The lower house leans toward the Army.
  • House of Lords. The heads of the thirteen noble houses hold permanent seats, and naval officers come disproportionately from those houses and their coastal clients. The Lords lean toward the Navy.

These were tendencies, not blocs. Members of either house could support the other service, and officers did not necessarily share the political preferences of their institution. But it meant that every GAA needed a deal: the lower house could vote the Army more money, and the Lords could cut it back.

The active-duty rule

By constitutional convention, the Ministers of War, the Navy and Aviation had to be serving officers. If a service's budget was cut, it could withdraw its minister, and the cabinet fell until a Prime Minister could be found whom both services would accept. The convention gave each service leverage over the cabinet and a reason to treat the budget as a question of survival. Its precise constitutional status is unsettled.

Si Wong oil

After the Si Wong Offensive (80–88 AG), oil production reached about 140,000 barrels a day by 90 AG, and it paid for the Army's mechanization. Because the money came from outside the annual appropriations, the Army grew without winning the appropriations fight, and the Navy resented it as a loophole.

The carriers and the Army's case

Qianchan's submarines drove the Navy's carriers onto the defensive. From the Eastern Push and the Desert War onward, the Army argued that the Navy's share no longer matched the war the Empire was actually fighting. The Navy answered that the sea lines supplied the army, and that without the blockade the Earth Kingdom could not be starved.

Class

ArmyNavy
Rank and fileConscripts from every part of the EmpireVolunteers and conscripts from coastal communities
NCOsPredominantly commonersMixed
OfficersAcademy graduates who rose from the people, with the old military houses holding the top commandsCoastal noble families, some tied to the thirteen houses; commissions through family and patronage
Self-imageThe people's service; the one institution in which a commoner and an aristocrat serve in the same chain of commandThe Empire's technical and aristocratic elite
PoliticsCarries the reform movementCarries the Court's loyalty

The Army was the base of the reform movement associated with Lu Ten, the People's Prince, and, after his death, Iroh. The veterans who later formed the Salvationists, whose base was the non-bender Kern infantry, came from it. The Navy sided with Ozai in the Pardon Crisis. Neither was uniform: there were Court officers in the Army and a minority of naval officers who put discipline and the law above personal loyalty.

Where there is no divide: operations

Whenever the two services worked together, it went smoothly.

  • Sealift and landings. Navy transports carried Army divisions, and nobody counted whose ships they were.
  • Garrisons. Army garrisons held the islands that the Navy took, and relied on its supply lines.
  • Planning. The Army and Navy sections of the General Staff Directorate planned jointly and signed off together.
  • Failure. Failures were not blamed on the other service. The Siege of Ba Sing Se (96–97 AG) was blamed on the Planning Directorate and cost Iroh his rank, and neither service blamed the other.
  • Jasmine Island. In 90 AG, naval officers who refused Rear Admiral Yueya's orders stood with Lu Ten and the Army detachment and helped arrest her.

The services cooperated in the field, and despised each other at the budget table.

The marines

The marines are the elite units of the Empire. On paper they belong to the Navy, but they are recruited from both services and trained to the Army's standards. They are the one body both services claim and admire.

The divide in the record

DateEventEffect on the divide
90 AGJasmine Island and the Address on Conduct. Yueya had been denied garrison command of an Army post because the Directorate "saw no reason to move an Army post to the Navy." The Address proposed "a clearer division between Army and Navy in garrison appointments"Garrison posts are prestige as well as money, and a denied petition from a Navy admiral could be read as an insult. The Chronicle calls the divide "the center of the story" and "not as clean as either service would like"
97–99 AGThe Pardon Crisis: Ozai restores Yueya and Zhao by prerogativeThe Navy read it as proof that the Fire Lord was on its side; the Army's reform wing read it as a Navy privilege
98 AGIroh forced to retire; Zhao promoted to AdmiralThe shift of favor was visible to everyone
99 AGThe Navy's Northern Fleet takes Agna Qel'aAfter the Army's failure at Ba Sing Se, the Navy used it to argue for keeping its share
100 AGQinglan PortNeither regular service fought there: Ozai's force was the Flame Guard, a Ministry of Truth detachment, and Breaker and mechanized elements
Nov 100 AGThe Civil WarThe Navy split by squadron, along the houses of each squadron's senior officers, not by service. The Army split along reform and Court lines

Legacy

Sozin's preferential investment in the Navy set the initial conditions. The Army's manpower and its mechanization then gave it grounds to challenge the allocation, and Azulon agreed. The rivalry persisted as a dispute over funding, appointments and political influence, not as a breakdown in joint operations, and became one of the enduring institutional tensions of the Empire. It helps explain the Pardon Crisis as a service quarrel as well as a political one, why the General Staff was both powerful and unable to settle the quarrel, and why the Civil War's military split looked like something that had always been there.

How the three Fire Lords of the Hundred Year War divided the Empire's military resources: Sozin's naval reach, Azulon's continental war and Ozai's superweapons, and why each allocation made sense for the war its author faced.

SozinNavy 70%, Army 30%
AzulonArmy 60%, Navy 40%
OzaiArmy 60%, Navy 40%; plus 30% of the civilian budget for superweapons
ShorthandSozin builds the empire's reach; Azulon concentrates its strength; Ozai tries to turn that strength into absolute supremacy through terror, and overreaches

The Empire's military evolution across the Hundred Year War follows a coherent progression. Each Fire Lord inherited the imperial war machine built by his predecessor but faced a different strategic problem. They did not run three unrelated military systems. They changed the priorities of one machine as the strategic situation changed.

Fire LordArmyNavySuperweaponsStrategic emphasis
Sozin30%70%No separate allocationNaval expansion and the construction of an imperial power-projection capability
Azulon60%40%No separate allocationContinental warfare, mechanization, sustained offensives, occupation
Ozai60%40%30% of the civilian budgetConventional war plus terror weapons to force a decisive outcome

Sozin: naval power projection (to 20 AG)

Sozin prioritized naval expansion and overseas power projection. A strong navy lets an island empire transport expeditionary forces, supply distant colonies, control sea lanes, threaten coastlines, support amphibious operations and protect maritime commerce. The allocation fits an empire in its expansion phase. Sozin was building the capacity to project power across the world and establish a far-reaching colonial system, and the Navy was the principal instrument of reach, while the Army supplied the forces needed to seize and hold territory.

The 30 percent Army share did not mean the Army was irrelevant. The balance was plausible because the early campaigns had limited objectives, because naval transport and fire support mattered, and because the Army could rely on expeditionary formations, colonial forces and the industrial base that the state was developing. The Navy received priority access to shipyards, steel and engineers, and its carriers, submarines and Kaienha torpedoes were the visible result. The first years of the war, in which the Empire held naval superiority alone, were won on that investment. See The Sozin Rearmament.

Azulon: continental conquest (20–97 AG)

Azulon shifted the balance toward the Army because the continental land war mattered more than raids against small settlements in the polar regions or Qianchan's coastal villages. The Earth Kingdom was too large and too important to be defeated by naval raids or peripheral operations alone.

Why Azulon shifted the budget

  • The decisive front was on land. The Earth Kingdom was the principal theater. Taking territory required sustained offensives, siege warfare, infantry, artillery, armor, engineers and enormous logistical networks.
  • Naval raids were not strategic victories. Attacking settlements in the polar regions or along Qianchan's coast could destroy supplies, terrorize communities and disrupt trade. It could not substitute for defeating the Earth Kingdom's field armies or capturing its industrial and administrative centers.
  • The Army needed to sustain its offensives. Every advance inland created new demands for troops, ammunition, railways, roads, fuel, replacement vehicles and garrisons. The allocation reflected the cost of maintaining a continental occupation.
  • Qianchan was a military-industrial adversary. Raiding its coastal villages was not enough to neutralize its capacity to supply the Earth Kingdom. The Empire needed to prioritize the campaigns, logistics and mechanization that could change the balance on the main front.
  • The Navy still mattered. At 40 percent, it retained substantial funding for sea control, amphibious operations, coastal bombardment, blockade and the protection of maritime supply lines. Azulon changed the priority; he did not abandon naval warfare.

The reallocation reflects a change in the Empire's center of gravity. The central question was no longer how to reach distant targets but how to defeat and occupy a continental power. Sozin's military was designed to project Fire Nation power across the world; Azulon's was increasingly organized to break the Earth Kingdom on its own territory. That gave the Army–Navy rivalry its material basis: the Navy had enjoyed budgetary primacy under Sozin, and under Azulon the Army became the principal recipient because the war's demands had changed. See The Army–Navy divide.

The Sōen begins

In 47 AG Azulon initiated the Sōen program, after his staff asked whether the destructive power associated with the comet could be stored and used on demand. It began as research on fire crystals and firebender-fed batteries, and it was funded within the existing military and research structure. The first charged cell reached about one ton of explosive equivalent in 58 AG, and the first multi-crystal array about 100 tons in 72 AG. The program was not an invention that appeared under Ozai. It was part of the Empire's long-term development, built over decades.

Ozai: conventional war plus superweapons (97–100 AG)

Ozai kept Azulon's conventional allocation, because he still needed the Army to capture and occupy territory and the Navy to sustain operations. He did not replace conventional warfare with superweapons. He tried to combine conventional conquest with a weapon capable of producing a decisive shock.

The additional 30 percent of the civilian budget was separate from the 60/40 Army–Navy split. It should not be described as 30 percent of the total state budget. It made the superweapon program a parallel state priority, competing with civilian spending.

Ozai's strategic logic

Sozin wanted to remake the world. Azulon wanted to conquer it. Ozai wanted to terrorize it into submission. His reasoning ran:

  • Conventional warfare has dragged on for generations.
  • The Earth Kingdom continues to resist despite enormous territorial and human losses.
  • If the Empire can show that even its greatest cities are vulnerable to annihilation, the remaining resistance may collapse.
  • The Fire Nation can then present itself as the unquestioned supreme nation-state.

The consequences of the allocation

  • Civilian infrastructure and public services lost resources or grew more slowly.
  • Scientific and industrial institutions were redirected toward military priorities.
  • Secrecy and coercion grew in order to protect the program.
  • Ministries and senior officials competed over a reduced pool of civilian resources.

The concentration of authority was as important as the money. A program meant to produce a war-ending weapon gave Ozai every reason to centralize secrecy and decision-making, which strengthened the court and the security apparatus at the expense of ordinary oversight, and the more he invested in a spectacular strike, the greater the pressure to use it to justify the cost.

The Sōen, 97–100 AG

DateEvent
86 AGThe comet's expected return is calculated; the program gets a target date
95 AGConventional work yields a wall-breaking bomb, used at Ba Sing Se in 96 AG
97 AGOzai succeeds Azulon and redirects the program toward a strike on Ba Sing Se
99 AGResearchers propose a fission weapon and refuse to develop it, and are executed. The Research Bureau's report says the Sōen can break Ba Sing Se
99–100 AGA forward array is built at Qinglan Port
17 July 100 AGOzai fires the Sōen at Ba Sing Se, and proclaims himself Tentei
18 July 100 AGAllied forces attack Qinglan Port; Ozai is killed before a second discharge

The AU figures are: a main array of about 9.4 kilotons during the comet window, with 2–3 kilotons on ordinary recharge; a portable version carried by a Koometsu bomber of about 2.1 kilotons with a range of about 80 km; a full array range of about 420 km; a firebender trigger and a crew of about 40 to charge it. The strike atomized Ba Sing Se's western Outer Wall, destroyed the Inner Wall, killed roughly 380,000 people, blinded thousands and disrupted Coalition command for about 36 hours.

Why the strategy failed to guarantee victory

Superweapons cannot solve the problem of occupation. Destroying a capital does not destroy all enemy armed forces, and political leadership, local administration, resistance networks and military formations may survive. Mass destruction can harden resistance and give enemies a reason to prioritize capturing the weapon. The Empire still needed conventional forces, logistics and a functioning political authority to exploit gains, and it needed to hold what it had destroyed.

The strike was a tactical catastrophe for Ba Sing Se but did not deliver the strategic result Ozai wanted. It gave the Coalition an urgent reason to capture or destroy the weapon, and, with Ozai's death the next day, it left the Fire Nation exposed to a succession crisis. The core irony is that Ozai's attempt to bypass the limits of conventional warfare produced a spectacular tactical success without securing a political result, and he could not turn the destruction into stable victory before his death. The distinction between tactical destruction and strategic victory is the lesson of the century.
