political_institutions_of_the_empire.title: Political institutions of the Empire
political_institutions_of_the_empire.html:
The administrative, legislative, military and security organizations through which the Fire Lord governed the Fire Nation and its imperial territories during the Hundred Year War.

Items marked "proposed" below are reconstructions of institutional arrangements whose exact constitutional status is unsettled in the sources.
Political institutions of the Empire
FormHereditary monarchy with a restricted-franchise legislature and an autonomous military command
SovereignThe Fire Lord (Art. 1: "in perpetuity")
LegislatureNational Diet: House of Lords; House of Representatives (proposed 375 seats)
ExecutiveThe Cabinet, serving at the Fire Lord's pleasure
Military commandGeneral Staff Directorate (Art. 32)
Security and informationMinistry of Truth; Ministry of National Enlightenment
DissolvedThe Diet, 8 August 100 AG

The political institutions of the Empire of Tajisaki combined hereditary monarchy, aristocratic privilege, restricted electoral representation and a centralized military command. Although the National Diet had legislative and budgetary powers, its authority was limited by constitutional restrictions on military oversight, by the prerogatives of the Fire Lord and by the independence of the General Staff Directorate. Over the century of war the system became increasingly dependent on military institutions and state-controlled information. Tensions between the court and reformers inside the armed forces grew in the later years, and they ended in the Pardon Crisis of 97–99 AG and the succession crisis of 100 AG.

Historical development

Sozin and the centralization of authority

Under Sozin the Fire Nation went through military expansion, industrial development and political centralization. His government coordinated industrial policy with strategic goals and invested heavily in naval construction and research. The Navy received preferential funding, in a division of military funding of about 70:30 in its favor, a pattern whose status as an official rule or an informal habit remains unspecified. The disparity gave the two services different institutional cultures and competing claims over appropriations, prestige and senior appointments. Sozin's reforms also strengthened the General Staff Directorate, which became the central institution of strategic planning and the base on which later Fire Lords governed the military, the colonies and domestic life. See The Sozin Rearmament.

The war and the growth of the state

The war accelerated centralization. The size of the armed forces and the administration of occupied territories increased the importance of military planning, security, public information and population policy. The General Staff gained influence through its direct relationship with the Fire Lord. The war did not eliminate the Diet. The legislature continued to pass laws and budgets while remaining unable to investigate the military or several central institutions, an arrangement that let the government preserve the appearance of constitutional administration.

The later war and the reform movement

As the Army grew, and especially after the oil of the Si Wong paid for its mechanization (about 140,000 barrels a day by 90 AG), it challenged the Navy's position of financial and political privilege. The Army's conscript base and mixed officer corps gave reformist veterans and junior officers a social foundation, while the Navy kept stronger associations with the aristocracy and the court. The Address on Conduct of 90 AG and the Pardon Crisis of 97–99 AG, in which the House of Representatives censured Ozai's pardon of Yueya and Zhao by 214 votes to 161 without overturning it, showed the limits of legislative opposition. See The Army–Navy divide.

The Fire Lord

The Fire Lord was the hereditary sovereign and highest authority. The office combined executive, military and dynastic powers: authority over the Cabinet, direct access to the General Staff, and a decisive role in succession. Under the constitution the Fire Lord ruled in perpetuity (Art. 1), was sacred and inviolable (Art. 2), commanded the armed forces and alone made war and peace (Art. 5), and could issue Rescripts and Proclamations that overrode all other law (Art. 7). A reigning Fire Lord designated his successor, and a designation was final. If none had been made, the Privy Council had to meet within 72 hours, and the claimant had to produce fire at a confirmation ceremony within seven days (Art. 3).

The Cabinet served at the Fire Lord's pleasure and was not accountable to the Diet. Succession lay outside the Diet's authority (Art. 25), and this was the system's structural weakness: when a succession was disputed, the legislature had little means to intervene.

The National Diet

The Diet had two chambers and held legislative and budgetary powers.

House of Lords

The Lords represented the hereditary and appointed establishment. Under the proposed composition, the heads of the thirteen noble houses each held a permanent seat that passed with the headship of the house, imperial princes of sufficient age sat ex officio, and about sixty royal appointees served for life. The house gave the aristocracy continuity and influence over legislation and military appropriations, and limited elected representatives' ability to enact reforms the noble houses opposed. The rules for its dissolution and for the removal of members need further clarification.

House of Representatives

The elected house, whose voters were men who had completed three years of military service (Arts. 20–22). The proposed reconstruction assigns it 375 seats, consistent with the recorded 214–161 vote of the Pardon Crisis, with four-year terms and a Fire Lord who could dissolve it. Veterans were therefore its principal constituency. The status of women, colonial residents, disabled veterans and those exempt from service is not fully established.

Powers and limits

Article 28 forbade the Diet to investigate military operations, the Ministry of Truth or the Fire Lord. Its most consequential power was the budget: the General Staff could not simply establish and fund an entirely new army without authorization, and the annual General Appropriations Act became the arena in which the Army, the Navy, their allies and the court competed. It could not independently remove the Cabinet, investigate the security apparatus or compel the sovereign to reverse a decision protected by prerogative.

Origins and phases

The Diet began as a clan council about 295 BG, after the Camellia–Peony War, because the Fire Lord was tired of putting down clan rebellions, and for 250 years the disarmed clans fought through the budget, the offices and the land. The last clan revolt of about 40 BG ended armed resistance. About 29 BG Sozin modernized the council, adding an elected House of Representatives with a franchise tied to completed service, and the constitution of 12 BG locked in Article 28. From about 80 AG the Army's conscript base made the veterans the electorate, and the reformists gained a footing in the House. The Diet's collapse in 97–100 AG is described below. See National Diet.

Parties

The Court Concord, the clan-and-Navy majority, held the Lords and most of the House before the Pardon Crisis. The Commerce League, of merchants and bankers, argued that oil could be bought. The Reform bloc, of veterans, Army reformists and colonial delegates, took Lu Ten's Address on Conduct as its platform and Iroh as its figurehead. The banned left of veterans' committees stood outside the Diet and was the root of the Salvationists.

The Privy Council

The Privy Council was the Fire Lord's private advisory body, and the body that confirmed a successor when none had been designated. A proposed reconstruction puts its membership at about twelve individuals, appointed for life by the Fire Lord, drawn from the aristocracy, the court and the senior state establishment.

The succession crisis of 100 AG

After Ozai's death at Qinglan Port on 18 July 100 AG, the General Staff Directorate produced a sealed designation naming Azula, and troops took control of the Council's chamber. Seven councillors were arrested between 23 and 25 July, and on 25 July the remaining members confirmed Azula under guard. The legitimacy of the designation and the circumstances of the confirmation became the center of the dispute between Azula's supporters and the faction supporting Zuko. The episode showed how the succession process could be coerced by whoever controlled military force and access to the court. See Succession crisis.

The Cabinet and ministries

The Prime Minister and the ministers of National Enlightenment, Truth, National Harmony, War, the Navy, Aviation, Colonial Affairs and others served at the Fire Lord's pleasure.

A proposed constitutional convention required the Ministers of War, the Navy and Aviation to be serving officers. A service's refusal to provide a minister, or the resignation of one under military pressure, could prevent a government from forming or bring down an existing Cabinet. Its precise constitutional status remains to be confirmed.

MinistryRole
TruthInternal security, political policing, censorship enforcement, loyalty investigations. Outside judicial review (Art. 33) and outside Diet investigation (Art. 28). Enforces the state ideology, "The Truth". Supported the Court faction in 100 AG
National EnlightenmentThe press, schools and public information; the official historical narrative. On 19 July 100 AG it announced that Ozai was wounded and recovering, and on 20 July retracted the claim
National HarmonyAdministers the Homeland Purity Initiative (Art. 44): integration, resettlement, removal and the four-category classification of populations
Colonial AffairsColonial territories; administrators hold combined executive, legislative and judicial powers (Arts. 42–43). Responsibilities are divided with National Harmony (population policy) and the War establishment (garrisons)
War, the Navy, AviationAdministration of the services. The precise relation of the Aviation ministry to Army and Navy aviation remains to be established

The General Staff Directorate

The Directorate planned the Empire's campaigns and, under Article 32, stood outside the Cabinet with a right of direct audience with the Fire Lord. A proposed structure divides it into a Planning Directorate, an Army Section, a Navy Section and departments for operations, intelligence and logistics. The Planning Directorate prepared Plan Yellow, the Si Wong Offensive and the later campaign against Ba Sing Se. The two sections had equal standing and planned jointly; the separation reflected the services' identities and their competition for resources, and did not prevent them coordinating operations.

In the succession crisis the Directorate produced the sealed designation naming Azula and helped the Court government consolidate authority. A proposed account estimates that about half of the military followed the Directorate and the Court, and the remainder supported Zuko.

The Army, the Navy and the guard

The Army and Navy are the subject of The Army–Navy divide. In summary: the Army is the larger service, built on conscription, with commoner NCOs and a mixed officer corps, the base of the reform movement; the Navy is smaller, closer to the aristocracy and the court, and the favored service under Sozin. The marines belong administratively to the Navy but recruit from both. The Army and Navy cooperated in joint planning, transport, landings and garrisons; Army transports and Navy supply lines were components of a common system.

The Flame Guard

The Flame Guard was the Fire Lord's household guard, separate from the Army and Navy and tied to the protection of the sovereign and the palace at Caldera City. A proposed account says its members were exclusively firebenders and that its oath was to the person of the Fire Lord, not to the Empire or the constitution. That made it a personal instrument of the monarchy. In 100 AG it supported the Court faction and helped enforce its authority in the capital, and it formed part of Ozai's force at Qinglan Port.

The Salvationists

The Salvationists were a radical movement that grew out of veterans' committees in the Army during the collapse of the Empire in 100 AG. Unlike the royalist reformers, they wanted to abolish the monarchy and nobility and found a people's republic. Their early support came from the non-bender infantry of the Kern regiments, who interpreted the war as one fought by ordinary people for the benefit of the imperial ruling class. They rejected the legitimacy of the monarchy and the Diet, and opposed the Ministry of Truth, the General Staff and the nobility. A Central Salvation Committee directed them, with local committees controlling the Army units that came under their authority.

By the established chronology, they killed Iroh in a bombing in 101 AG, took over much of the Court's field army between 107 and 113 AG, seized the western complex of the Imperial Research Bureau in 109 AG, broke openly with the Court in 116 AG, and were suppressed by about 120 AG.

The dissolution of the Diet

After Ozai's death the House of Representatives urged the confirmation of Zuko. On 2 August 100 AG it convened in defiance of the Court and declared Azula's confirmation unlawful, and the House of Lords did not join. The Diet was dissolved on 8 August after a shooting in its galleries. It had retained meaningful powers over the budget but lacked the independence and the protections to resolve a succession dispute when the sovereign's supporters controlled the military and the security apparatus.

Constitutional character and legacy

The system was not wholly without limits. The Diet could legislate and control appropriations, and the services competed for resources through established political channels. But the Fire Lord's prerogatives and the Directorate's direct relationship with the sovereign restricted any representative oversight. The system's central contradiction was the coexistence of constitutional structures with institutions that operated beyond public accountability. The Diet could influence the funding of the armed forces and could not investigate their operations. The elected chamber represented veterans but did not form a government accountable to voters. The Privy Council provided a succession procedure and could be coerced. The ministries served the Fire Lord and, in several areas, stood outside judicial or legislative review.

By 100 AG these arrangements had failed to provide a stable way to resolve disputes over succession and the legitimacy of imperial authority, and the dissolution of the Diet and the fragmentation of the armed forces showed how little independence the constitutional institutions had from the sovereign and the military that enforced his authority.

yakuya_confederation.title: Yakuya Confederation
yakuya_confederation.html:
This article is a stub. 'Working on the lore smh' - Ren. Most surviving accounts of the Yakuya Confederation were written by its enemies or by the states that inherited its territory. Its own records, including the Red Articles, survive only in fragments and later Qianchan maritime tradition.
Yakuya Confederation
"The Fifth Nation"
TypeMaritime confederation of raiders, traders, exiles and coastal settlements
Existedc. 518–292 BG
TerritoryHarbors and island strongholds on the eastern sea and south-eastern coast of the Earth Kingdom; later incorporated into the eastern lands of Qianchan
SeatPort Yakuya, the "Red Harbor", in the eastern Earth Kingdom
GovernmentCouncil of Captains; Tide Captain during wartime
Last leaderPirate Queen Tagaka
PopulationPerhaps 600,000 at its height, including waterbenders, firebenders and non-benders
LanguagesHarbor Cant, a maritime trade creole
CurrencySalt and silver tallies; ransom bonds
Preceded byCoastal piracy of the Platinum Affair period
Succeeded byLocal fleets and communities; later Qianchan control of its eastern territories
Defeated296 BG (main fleet); 295–292 BG (principal strongholds), by Yun's expedition and Qin's eastern campaign

The Yakuya Confederation, known to its members as the Fifth Nation, was a multigenerational maritime confederation of raiders, traders, exiles and coastal communities that dominated parts of the eastern sea and south-eastern Earth Kingdom coast from approximately 518 to 292 BG. Its society brought together waterbenders, firebenders and non-benders who had abandoned, fled or been expelled from the established nations. At its height, the Confederation possessed a powerful fleet, fortified harbors and a network of trading partners that made it a force neither the Earth Kingdom nor the Southern Water Tribe could afford to ignore.

The Confederation emerged partly from the collapse of trust in the states around it. Corruption among Earth Kingdom officials, neglect of southern coastal communities and the inability or unwillingness of established authorities to protect ordinary people encouraged sailors, fishermen, deserters and fugitives to seek security outside conventional political structures. The Yakuya initially presented itself as an alternative to these systems. Over time, however, its leaders developed their own hierarchies, coercive practices and forms of exploitation, creating a lasting contradiction between the Confederation's founding grievances and its conduct as a maritime power.

Origins

The Confederation developed in the aftermath of the Platinum Affair of 530 BG, when the four nations restricted their ports and disrupted trade between them. The resulting commercial vacuum affected the eastern sea and the south-eastern coast of the Earth Kingdom particularly severely. Coastal settlements lost access to established trading networks, while smaller communities had little protection against larger raiding fleets. The Southern Water Tribe, whose southern settlements lacked abundant shipbuilding timber and a powerful deep-water navy, was especially vulnerable to maritime predation and economic isolation.

The political conditions behind the Confederation's formation were as important as the disruption of trade. Southern Water Tribe sailors and coastal families increasingly resented officials who demanded taxes and obedience while leaving remote settlements exposed to raiders and poverty. In the Earth Kingdom, corrupt magistrates and local authorities exploited coastal communities, while access to justice often depended on wealth or political connections. For people who had no influential patrons, leaving could seem more practical than seeking reform from institutions they no longer trusted.

The first Yakuya crews included Southern Water Tribe exiles, Earth Kingdom fishermen, smugglers, fugitives and deserters from the Tajisaki Navy. Some had been displaced by conflict or debt; others had abandoned their communities after disputes with local authorities. They did not share a single ancestry or political tradition. What united them was their distrust of the states that had failed or mistreated them, alongside the practical need to defend their ships and livelihoods.

Around 518 BG, several captains pooled their fleets to resist larger raiding groups and protect their access to the eastern sea. Their alliance became known as the Yakuya, a name traditionally translated from Harbor Cant as "the shared tide". What began as a defensive arrangement gradually expanded into a wider network of harbors, crews and settlements. Its members increasingly identified with the Confederation rather than with the nations from which they had come.

The Fifth Nation

The name Fifth Nation reflected the Confederation's growing claim to political independence. It was not one of the four established nations, but neither was it merely a collection of unrelated pirate crews. Its members maintained their own rules, elected leaders, divided resources and defended territory. The name was also used derisively by opponents, particularly officials who considered the Confederation an illegitimate rival to the established political order.

The Yakuya's appeal rested on its willingness to accept people across national and bending divisions. Crews were organized around maritime skill and allegiance rather than ancestry alone. Waterbenders, firebenders and non-benders served together, while women and men could rise to positions of command. For those excluded from conventional institutions, the Confederation offered the possibility of status and belonging unavailable in their former communities.

This relative openness did not make Yakuya society universally egalitarian. Authority depended heavily on captains, fleet strength and personal loyalty. The freedom of a crew could coexist with the coercion of captives, and the independence of a harbor could coexist with the exploitation of surrounding settlements. The Confederation's political ideals were therefore neither wholly fictitious nor consistently upheld. Its history was shaped by the struggle between mutual protection and the ambitions of those who commanded its ships.

Organization

The Confederation was governed by a Council of Captains, whose members commanded fleets and harbors. In wartime, the council elected a Tide Captain to coordinate military operations. Individual captains retained considerable authority over their crews, making the Confederation flexible at sea but vulnerable to factional disputes and competing ambitions.

Its written code, the Red Articles, regulated the division of spoils, the care of wounded crew members and the punishment of those who betrayed their shipmates. The Articles helped create a shared political identity among people from different nations. Their surviving traditions also influenced later maritime customs in Qianchan, particularly the division of profits by agreed shares.

The Confederation's decentralized government made it difficult for an enemy to destroy all its forces in a single engagement. Individual fleets could continue operating after a defeat, and scattered harbors could shelter survivors. The same decentralization, however, complicated strategic coordination. Captains might cooperate against an external enemy while refusing to submit to another captain's authority once the immediate threat had passed.

Economy

The Yakuya economy combined trade, tolls, protection payments, ransom and raiding. Its harbors occupied an important position in maritime commerce during a period when formal trade between the nations was restricted. Merchants and travelers could exchange goods there that were difficult to obtain through official channels, making the Confederation an intermediary between otherwise disconnected markets.

Yakuya captains collected tolls at strategic passages, sold protection to merchant ships and held hostages for ransom. The Earth Kingdom and the Water Tribes accused the Confederation of kidnapping and enslaving captives, practices that became more prominent under its later commanders. Although some communities benefited from trade and protection arrangements, others suffered from extortion and raids.

Port Yakuya, known as the Red Harbor, became the principal center of this maritime network. Its population was mixed and its trade language reflected the many peoples who passed through its docks. Salt and silver tallies facilitated ordinary transactions, while ransom bonds recorded obligations arising from the capture and release of prisoners.

The Confederation's commercial importance strengthened its position but also created a growing dependence on the continuation of maritime trade. Its leaders needed secure ports, timber, supplies and loyal crews. As the fleet expanded, competition for these resources encouraged further raids and territorial consolidation, gradually turning a movement founded by displaced communities into a power capable of imposing its own demands on others.

Rise of Tagaka

The Confederation reached its greatest military prominence under Tagaka, who presented herself as a defender of the Southern Water Tribe despite the tribe's rejection of her family. Under her leadership, Yakuya forces became increasingly aggressive toward coastal shipping and settlements. Its fleets challenged the Earth Kingdom Navy, captured prisoners and extended their influence along the eastern and southern coasts.

Tagaka's leadership represented a hardening of the Confederation's original contradictions. The Yakuya had emerged from the grievances of people who believed that established governments protected the powerful at the expense of ordinary communities. Tagaka invoked those grievances to justify the Confederation's independence, yet her own power rested on military coercion and the exploitation of captives. Her claim to defend the Southern Water Tribe did not mean that the tribe had accepted her authority, nor did it prevent her forces from harming people they claimed to protect.

By the late third century BG, the Confederation had become a major threat to regional commerce. Its military success convinced its leaders that the Earth Kingdom could be defeated or forced into concessions. That confidence would contribute to its downfall when its fleet confronted a coalition capable of exploiting the weaknesses of its decentralized command.

Fall of the Fifth Nation

In 296 BG, a force associated with the Earth Kingdom and the young man believed to be the Avatar, Yun, confronted Tagaka's fleet near the South Pole. Tagaka had planned to ambush the delegation and proceed with a raid on Yokoya. The meeting took place on an iceberg, where the lack of solid earth appeared to limit the Earth Kingdom party's ability to resist her forces.

Tagaka's ships had been concealed among the ice. During the confrontation, her forces gained the upper hand, killing or immobilizing members of the delegation and restraining Yun. The fleet then set course for Yokoya. Kelsang attempted to intercept the ships with his glider, but Tagaka damaged it and prevented him from stopping the fleet by himself.

Kyoshi confronted Tagaka and rejected her invitation to join the Confederation, citing the abandonment she and her fellow orphan had suffered at Yokoya. In the ensuing battle, Kyoshi unconsciously drew upon the power of previous Avatars and raised enormous columns of earth from the seafloor. The resulting destruction shattered Tagaka's flagship and devastated the main fleet. Hei-Ran and Rangi helped subdue Tagaka, while Jianzhu attacked the remaining ships and completed the fleet's destruction.

Tagaka was captured, and many of her followers were killed or taken prisoner. The defeat destroyed the Confederation's main concentration of naval power, although it did not immediately eliminate its scattered fleets or distant strongholds. The Earth Kingdom subsequently permitted the Tajisaki Navy to patrol parts of the eastern sea. Tajisaki Navy operations also helped rescue captives, although some missions encountered surviving Yakuya factions that continued to resist.

The defeat exposed the vulnerability of the Confederation's reliance on its fleet. Its decentralized organization allowed individual crews to survive, but it could not easily replace the ships, experienced captains and coordinated strength lost in the battle. Tagaka's capture also deprived the remaining factions of a leader capable of commanding their collective loyalty.

Qin's Eastern Campaign

The destruction of the main fleet did not end the Confederation's territorial presence. Its fortified harbors, inland allies and eastern strongholds continued to resist the authorities seeking to eliminate its power. In 295 BG, Qin of Gaoling began a campaign against the Yakuya's principal stronghold and its territorial base in the eastern lands.

Qin's campaign differed from the naval defeat of 296 BG. Where the earlier battle had broken the Confederation's main fleet, the eastern campaign targeted its ability to maintain ports, supply crews and exercise authority over territory. The capture of its principal stronghold weakened the remaining factions and disrupted the network that had connected its maritime operations to its inland possessions.

By 292 BG, the principal strongholds had fallen and the Confederation had ceased to function as a unified political and military organization. Its surviving members dispersed into local fleets, settlements and independent communities. Some continued raiding, others entered ordinary maritime trade, and still others sought accommodation with emerging regional powers.

The campaigns of 296–292 BG therefore marked the end of the Yakuya Confederation in stages: first its principal fleet, then its territorial network, and finally its capacity to act as a single confederated power. The defeat strengthened Qin's position and helped establish his reputation as a leader capable of bringing the eastern lands under a new political order.

Legacy

The Yakuya Confederation left three major legacies. The first was its name. When the eastern lands later separated from the Earth Kingdom and established the Qianchan Republic in 255 BG, the republic's printers adopted the name Fifth Nation. The term, originally used by Ba Sing Se's court as an insult against the maritime confederation, was repurposed as a declaration that the eastern lands represented a political community distinct from the four established nations.

The second legacy was its maritime culture. The Confederation's mixed crews, trade practices and traditions of dividing spoils influenced the development of Qianchan's later naval institutions. Harbor Cant survived in a creolized form along parts of the eastern coast, while elements of the Red Articles endured in maritime custom and commercial law.

The third was its political example. The Yakuya demonstrated that people alienated by corrupt or ineffective governments could build a competing community across national and bending divisions. It also demonstrated the dangers of such a movement when military necessity, wealth and the ambitions of its leaders displaced its original promises. The Confederation's history remained a warning both to governments that neglected their populations and to rebels who believed that overthrowing an unjust authority was enough to guarantee a just successor.

For Qianchan, the Confederation became both predecessor and cautionary ancestor. The republic inherited the name and parts of its maritime tradition, but its eventual political institutions developed from a different struggle over territorial sovereignty and government. The Yakuya had been defeated decades before Qianchan's independence; its legacy survived not as a continuous state, but through the people, customs and political memory that outlasted it.

about_new_red_dawn.title: About Avatar: New Red Dawn
about_new_red_dawn.html:
This is the lore wiki of Avatar: New Red Dawn, a fan-made alternate universe (AU). It is fiction, written in the voice of an in-universe encyclopedia. Dates use the BG / AG calendar, and figures are estimates that the in-universe sources dispute.
About Avatar: New Red Dawn
TitleAvatar: New Red Dawn (NRD)
TypeAlternate-universe lore wiki
SettingThe world of the four nations, from the age of the lion turtles to the 170s AG
CalendarBG (Before the Genocide) and AG (After the Genocide); 0 AG is the year of the comet
Core eventThe Hundred Year War, 0–100 AG
Great powersEmpire of Tajisaki (the Fire Nation); Earth Kingdom; Qianchan Republic; the pirate state of the Yakuya Confederation (extinct)
Other peoplesThe Water Tribes; the Air Nomads (destroyed in 0 AG); the United Republic of Nations (from 105 AG)
World populationAbout 501,000,000 (0 AG); about 548,000,000 (100 AG)
Started2022
Pages100

Avatar: New Red Dawn (NRD) is an alternate universe of the world of Avatar: The Last Airbender in which the age of the four nations ends not in a quiet century of conquest but in the first industrial total war. Its Fire Nation is the Empire of Tajisaki, the richest, most industrialized and most centralized state in the world, led by a Fire Lord who comes to believe that its prosperity entitles it to rule everyone else. Its war, the Hundred Year War, begins in 0 AG with the destruction of the Air Nomads and ends a hundred years later with a weapon of mass destruction, a collapsing dynasty and a world that has been rebuilt on the ruins of its old order.

The wiki records that world as its own historians would: in the voice of an encyclopedia, with tables, disputed figures, rival national narratives and sources that disagree. It is meant to be read as history, not as a story with a single protagonist, and most of its pages are about institutions, decisions and consequences.

The premise

The AU rests on a handful of changes to the world that its audience knows.

  • The world has industrialized. It is about the size of Earth and thinly settled, with about 501 million people in 0 AG. Steam, rail, steel, repeating rifles and early aircraft are in use, and over the century of the war the world acquires tanks, jets, powered armor and fission research. See the Technology timeline.
  • The Fire Nation is a modern state. After an industrial revolution beginning about 290 BG, it becomes an empire under Fire Lord Sozin, with a restricted legislature, a General Staff that answers only to the throne, and ministries of Truth and National Enlightenment. See History of the Fire Nation and Political institutions of the Empire.
  • There is a fifth great actor. The Qianchan Republic, a federal republic that broke away from the Earth Kingdom in 255 BG after the War of Liberation led by Qin the Great, is the Empire's industrial rival and, from 30 AG, a combatant in the war.
  • The war has reasons. It is the product of an energy forecast, an industrial race, a ruler's ideology and the death of the Avatar Roku, and it is traced across thirty-seven years of rearmament. See The Sozin Rearmament and Prewar diplomacy.
  • The war is total. The Empire uses genocide, engineered famine, chemical weapons, forced labor and occupation, and kills about 41 million people directly and about 81 million counting indirect deaths. See the Demographic ledger.
  • The Avatar comes late. The next Avatar, Aang, is found only in 99 AG. The war is not won by one hero, but by a coalition, a collapsing regime and the choices of people inside it.

Calendar and dating

The wiki counts years from the comet. AG (After the Genocide) years count up from 0 AG, the year the Empire attacked the Air Temples. BG (Before the Genocide) years count down to it, so a larger BG number is earlier: 300 BG is before 12 BG. The Hundred Year War is 0–100 AG, and the latest dated events in the lore fall in the 170s AG.

The world at a glance

PowerGovernmentPopulation, 0 AGIn the war
Empire of Tajisaki (Fire Nation)Absolute monarchy with a limited Diet and a military command beyond the CabinetAbout 120,000,000The aggressor; the world's strongest military
Earth KingdomMonarchy over provincial lords and kingsAbout 230,000,000The principal victim; about 29.6 million direct dead
Qianchan RepublicFederal republicAbout 140,000,000Industrial rival; enters in 30 AG
Southern and Northern Water TribeA kingdom of two polesAbout 8,000,000Subjugated; about half destroyed
Air NomadsNo state; four temples and scattered communitiesAbout 3,000,000Destroyed in 0 AG
United Republic of NationsCouncil republic, later presidential republicFounded 105 AGBorn from the Empire's former colonies

A short history

EraDatesSummary
The age of clansto about 300 BGThe Tajisaki clan wins the Warring States and names a state after itself. Centuries of clan strife follow. See History of the Fire Nation
The kingdom and the southto 255 BGThe Earth Kingdom rises, tears itself apart and loses its southern provinces. See History of the Earth Kingdom and History of Qianchan
Industry and the long peace290–37 BGThe Fire Nation industrializes; Qianchan competes; the Water Tribes and Air Nomads withdraw from world politics. See Fire Nation economy and society
The road to war37 BG – 0 AGRoku halts Sozin; the Empire rearms; Roku dies in 12 BG; the Alliance Treaty is signed in 3 BG. See The Sozin Rearmament
The Hundred Year War0–100 AGThe comet; the genocide; the invasion of the west coast; Qianchan enters in 30 AG; the Desert War; the Si Wong Offensive; the siege of Ba Sing Se; the Sōen strike; the death of Ozai on 18 July 100 AG. See Hundred Year War
The collapse and the settlement100–120 AGThe Fire Nation Civil War, the Yanakawan War of Independence (the Treaty of Qinglan, 105 AG) and the Earth Kingdom's warlord wars. See Post-War Conflicts
The reign of Zuko118–168 AGThe Fire Nation is rebuilt under Fire Lord Zuko
The late lore170s AGThe Southern Federation (171 AG), the Raiko Amendment of the United Republic (171 AG) and the Kingdom of Agna Qel'a (174 AG)

Themes

  • Prosperity and aggression. The Empire's industrial lead, its oil forecast and its ideology of a Fire Nation-led world combine into a war, and the wiki asks whether the war was necessary or chosen.
  • Institutions. Most decisive moments, such as the Pardon Crisis, the succession crisis and the dissolution of the Diet, are about who held the power to say no.
  • Occupation and memory. The occupied Earth Kingdom, the Water Tribes and the former Air Nomad lands each have their own history of survival. See Occupation and resistance.
  • Tactical destruction and strategic victory. The Sōen destroys a capital and does not win a war.
  • Rival histories. Ba Sing Se, Qianchan, the Empire and the survivors tell the same events differently, and many pages end with a historiography section.

Where to start

  • The war in brief: Hundred Year War, Timeline and Major Battles and Sieges.
  • Why it began: The Sozin Rearmament, Prewar diplomacy, Prewar military balance.
  • The cost: Demographic ledger and Demographics.
  • The Empire's machinery: Political institutions, Imperial military budget, The Army–Navy divide.
  • People and the end of the war: Ozai, Iroh, Aang, Sōen strike, Battle of Qinglan Port.
  • Literature of the world: The Chronicle: The Prince Who Asked Why and Cinders in the Furnace.

Why I created Avatar: New Red Dawn

I made this because I was pissed off at the worldbuilding, especially in The Legend of Korra. During the pandemic, when I was watching and reading about Avatar, I kept thinking about how much more seriously its history and technology could have been developed. I was more frustrated with Korra than Aang, particularly with the lead-up to the Equalist Revolution and the ending of the first season. I wanted to see what would happen if those conflicts were explored further instead of being resolved so quickly.

My starting point was simple: what if the Avatar world took gunpowder seriously? What if firearms developed much earlier and contributed to an earlier industrial revolution? What if that led to modern military institutions, mass production, railways, aircraft and industrial-scale warfare? I wanted to take that idea seriously and follow it beyond the introduction of a few new weapons.

I also wanted to explore a more violent history than the relatively child-friendly presentation of the original franchise. The Avatar world already has imperialism, genocide, political oppression and war. I wanted to examine what those things would look like when industrialization and modern state power made them more destructive. Genocide should leave scars. Occupation should create resistance. Revolutions should have consequences. Wars should change societies long after the fighting ends.

And honestly, the guns were never the entire point. Take firearms away and people will still find ways to kill each other with swords, bending or whatever else they have. The problem is not the weapon itself. It is what people, governments and institutions are willing to do with the power they possess.

That is what Avatar: New Red Dawn became: my attempt to rebuild the political, technological and historical logic of a world I liked but whose worldbuilding frustrated me. I wanted to explore what might happen if its nations industrialized earlier, developed different institutions and experienced the consequences of those changes on a much larger scale.

Basically, I wanted to take the premise seriously and see just how ugly its history could get.

point_of_divergence.title: Point of divergence
point_of_divergence.html:
This page records where the world of New Red Dawn departs from the source series. Dates are in BG (Before the Genocide); 0 AG is the year of the comet.
Point of divergence
Datec. {{stat:pod_year}} BG
PlaceA clan household on the southern Fire Islands
DiscovererTorao Yagen, an apothecary (disputed)
DiscoveryThe formula for black powder
EraThe long strife (4440–300 BG)
First military use1000–700 BG
Years to military useAbout {{stat:pod_gap}}
Before the warAbout {{stat:pod_year}} years

The point of divergence of the world of New Red Dawn is the discovery of the black powder formula in the Fire Islands, about {{stat:pod_year}} years before the war began. In the source series nobody fields firearms, and explosions come from bending and a few rare mixtures. Here the formula exists, and the long delay before it matters shapes the Fire Nation's politics, its industry and the weapons of the [[hundred_year_war|Hundred Year War]].

The discovery

The temple ledgers credit Torao Yagen, an apothecary serving a clan household on the southern islands. His work was ordinary: boiling saltpeter out of cave floors and curing-house earth for preserving fish and meat, grinding volcanic sulfur for salves and incense, and burning charcoal. A badly proportioned batch of the three flashed violently, and he wrote down the proportions that did it. Some chronicles credit a guild of saltpeter-boilers instead of one man, and nothing independent confirms either.

The Fire Islands supplied everything he needed: sulfur from the volcanic vents, charcoal from the forests, and saltpeter from the caves and the cured-fish trade. This is why the formula was found there rather than on the mainland.

Why it took two thousand years

  • Fire was already cheap. A firebender needed no powder, so the nobility had little use for it as a weapon.
  • Politics. A tube and a charge let a commoner kill a bender. Under the [[history_of_the_fire_nation|three-sided settlement]] of crown, clans and Sages, none of the three wanted that spread. The Sages kept the recipe as a temple craft for festivals, and the clans guarded their own supplies.
  • Materials. Bronze and cast-iron tubes burst, and uncorned powder was weak and absorbed damp in the island climate. Reliable guns waited for corning and better founding.
  • Culture. Fireworks became a festival art. A powder-maker was a ritual craftsman before he was a soldier.

Chain of consequences

DateDevelopmentEffect
c. 3000 BGThe formula for black powder (saltpeter, sulfur and charcoal) is written down in the Fire Islands.The point of divergence.

The result by 0 AG

A three-thousand-year-old powder, foundry and mining tradition left the Fire Nation as the richest and most industrialized state at the start of the war. By 0 AG its economy was about {{stat:gdp_fn_0}}, or {{stat:gdppc_fn_0}} a person. Qianchan was second at {{stat:gdp_qc_0}}, and the Earth Kingdom, the largest nation by population, had {{stat:gdp_ek_0}}. See [[statistics|Population and economy statistics]].

Disputed points

  • Whether one man or a guild found the formula, and whether 3000 BG is the date of the discovery or of the first surviving record.
  • Whether the Sages deliberately suppressed military use or simply had no army to use it.
  • When the formula reached the Earth Kingdom and the poles. The earliest foreign evidence is from the 1000–700 BG period.

warring_states_wars.title: Warring States wars
warring_states_wars.html:
This is a stub. It gathers what the wiki already records about this war and will be expanded.
Warring States wars
DateFire Islands: from before the records to about 4440 BG. Earth Kingdom: the late Warring States, about 531–255 BG
LocationThe Fire Islands; the Earth Kingdom
ResultThe Tajisaki clan unifies the Fire Islands under the first Fire Lord. In the Earth Kingdom the wars end in Qin's conquests, the Qin Dynasty and the secession of Qianchan
Casualties and losses
Not established. Reconstructed estimates run to tens of millions across all the wars, mostly from famine and plague. Counted as the second most deadly series of wars in history, after the Hundred Year War

The Warring States wars is the collective name for the two long ages of warlord and clan warfare that shaped the Fire Nation and the Earth Kingdom before the industrial age. The Fire Islands and the Earth Kingdom each had a Warring States era, and the wiki treats them together because later historians in both countries counted their dead together. Very little of the evidence survives.

The Fire Islands

For several thousand years the islands were ruled by warlords, clans and the Sages of the temples. The Tajisaki clan won the era, and its chief was raised by the Sages as the first Fire Lord about 4440 BG; the realm took the clan's name. The Warring States era destroyed much of the evidence, and later rulers, Sozin most thoroughly, rewrote what survived. See History of the Fire Nation.

The Earth Kingdom

After the Platinum Affair the kingdom entered an age of unrest, with rebellions, regional wars and corruption, among them the Yellow Neck Uprising, the Wars of Secrets and Daggers and Nong's Rebellion. The late Warring States ended when Qin the Great conquered the continent outside Ba Sing Se, and the war that followed his death produced Qianchan. See History of the Earth Kingdom.

Legacy

The wars gave the Fire Nation its tradition of clan rule and the Earth Kingdom its distrust of the capital. The Hundred Year War later overtook them in scale, and the Post-War Conflicts ranked third.

camellia_peony_war.html:
This is a stub. It gathers what the wiki already records about this war and will be expanded.
Camellia-Peony War
Datec. 312–295 BG
LocationThe Fire Nation: the capital, the Saowon lands and the great clan estates

The Camellia-Peony War was the succession struggle between Fire Lord Zoryu and his illegitimate half-brother Chaejin. It was called a war only in retrospect, and the word is a poetic exaggeration: open war was narrowly avoided, but enough violent clashes occurred for the name to stick. It was the last great struggle between the throne and the clans.

Background

Avatar Kuruk died in 312 BG, Chaeryu was on the throne and Zoryu was about to succeed him. The Sages, who had anointed the first Fire Lord and never forgot it, backed Chaejin, and the Saowon clan, whose fortunes after the Ma'inka affair decided the balance, followed them.

Course and end

Zoryu held power with the Keohso and with the help of the Earth Sage Jianzhu and the young man then believed to be the Avatar, Yun, who mediated and advised him to keep doubles. The struggle ended around the Festival of Szeto in 295 BG with the purge of the Saowon. The war's last pitched battle was the Battle of Kinbara of about 300 BG, which the throne won with flintlock muskets. Zoryu then began the project that took the armies from the clans.

Tajisaki dating

The Fire Nation counts years in Tajisaki dating, with year 0 at the Battle of Kinbara of about 300 BG, so that 0 AG is 300 and the census of 467 is 167 AG. The count marks the end of the age of clan war that this conflict closed.

Aftermath

It led, as the sources put it, directly to Sozin: a state with no armed clans and a strong centre, which industrialized from about 290 BG. The Sages were watched by every later Fire Lord.

yellow_neck_uprising.html:

Not established; whole villages were destroyed

The Yellow Neck Uprising was a bandit rebellion in the Earth Kingdom that began when Avatar Kuruk died in 312 BG. The Avatar's authority to mediate between nations was absent for a generation, and the daofei, the bandit armies of the interior, filled the vacuum.

Origins

Xu Ping An, a charismatic and unbalanced man who could generate lightning, a skill that had nearly died out, gathered the daofei into the Yellow Necks, named for their scarves. They marauded through the heartland and killed officials, soldiers and civilians alike.

Course

The kingdom's army did not defend the remote hinterland, partly because the nobility was occupied with the Wars of Secrets and Daggers. The Earth Sage Jianzhu broke the rebels at Zhulu Pass in 304 BG and ended the uprising by burying thousands of captured Yellow Necks alive, reporting a different story to the Earth King.

Consequences

The Fire Nation took a practical interest in Xu Ping An's lightning and made a secret deal for him. The uprising is a recurring example in the histories of the kingdom's failure to protect its own people.

wars_of_secrets_and_daggers.html:

The Wars of Secrets and Daggers was the name for the feuds of the Earth Kingdom's nobility in the early 4th century BG, fought with forged letters, hired blades and poison more than with armies. They are known mainly because they distracted the court at the time of the Yellow Neck Uprising.

Character

The feuds were conducted in the capital and in provincial courts through patronage and murder. Chroniclers named them for the weapons their victims died of.

Effect

The nobility paid little attention to the hinterland, which was left to the bandit armies. Later critics cite the wars as proof that the kingdom's elite governed for itself.

Sources

The wars are mentioned in passing by Fire Nation and Earth Kingdom chroniclers. No full account survives.

Nong's Rebellion was a prolonged rising in the Earth Kingdom against King Feishan, who was accused of tyranny and of being a puppet of the Fire Nation. It is remembered mostly for how it ended.

Course

During the childhood of Avatar Yangchen the Fire Nation and the Water Tribes secretly agreed to back the rebel General Nong with ingots of platinum, in the hope of a friendlier government in Ba Sing Se.

The Platinum Affair

Feishan won. He kept the ingots and closed the Earth Kingdom's ports in the diplomatic blunder known as the Platinum Affair (530 BG). The Fire Nation isolated itself, the South was left without a navy, and the coastal neglect that followed is one root of the Yakuya Confederation.

Legacy

The affair was a precedent for foreign money in the kingdom's wars, and the Empire later remembered it.

The Yakuya War was the campaign that ended the Yakuya Confederation, the pirate state that called itself the Fifth Nation, in two stages: a naval defeat in 296 BG and a land campaign from 295 to 292 BG.

The fleet, 296 BG

A force associated with the Earth Kingdom and the young man believed to be the Avatar, Yun, met Tagaka's fleet near the South Pole, on an iceberg where the pirates expected to ambush the delegation. The main fleet was broken, and after it the Tajisaki Navy took a recognized role patrolling the Eastern Sea, with the kingdom's permission.

Qin's eastern campaign, 295–292 BG

Qin of Gaoling attacked the principal stronghold and the territorial base of the Confederation. By 292 BG the strongholds had fallen. The victory made Qin's name, and the eastern lands later passed to Qianchan.

Aftermath

The survivors dispersed into local fleets and independent communities. The name Fifth Nation was later taken up by Qianchan.

Qin's conquests

Qin's conquests were the campaigns by which Qin the Great, a southern lord who wanted to reform the absolute authority of the Earth King, brought the continent, apart from Ba Sing Se and Kyoshi's peninsula, under his banner.

Rise

Qin rose in the chaos of the late Warring States, and his reputation grew with his campaign against the Yakuya stronghold in 295–292 BG. With Kyoshi, Omashu and Yu Dao he took the northwest.

The duel, 270 BG

At the outer walls of Ba Sing Se Qin fought the Earth King in a duel. The king cheated, with hidden crossbowmen and a poisoned blade, and Qin was killed, though he mortally wounded the king. Kyoshi then went into the Inner City and forced the reforms of the court.

Aftermath

His heirs ruled as the Qin Dynasty, which the south overthrew in the War of Liberation.

war_of_liberation.html:

War of Liberation

The War of Liberation was the revolt of the southern lands against the heirs of Qin the Great, which created the Qianchan Republic. It began in 270 BG, when Qin was killed outside Ba Sing Se.

Causes

Qin's movement drew its strength from communities that resisted arbitrary power, and a hereditary dynasty threatened to reproduce the concentration of authority that he had meant to reform.

Course

It began in Qianchan, where local communities, former officers and political organizations refused to recognize the heirs, and spread as provincial forces defected and peasant uprisings cut the dynasty's supply lines. Many Earth Kingdom soldiers who had served under Qin would not serve his sons. The Avatar took no part, and dealt with the warlords in the northwest.

Result

The dynasty collapsed in famine in 255 BG. Ba Sing Se, under Bao Kun, used the collapse to recover; the Great Interregnum followed. Ba Sing Se did not recognize the republic.

Ba Sing Se fought two suppression campaigns against the Qianchan Republic, in 240 BG and 225 BG, to bring the seceded south back under the Earth King. Both failed.

Campaigns

The first campaign, in 240 BG, was launched when the capital had recovered from the Great Interregnum. The second, in 225 BG, followed the same plan and failed for the same reason: the republic's lines were shorter and its people were willing to fight for it.

The Preliminary Accord, 224 BG

The accord set a boundary but did not recognize the republic, which is why the kingdom's court has been able to claim Qianchan ever since. About nine years later the Dai Li were founded to suppress republican ideas at home.

Effect

The failure ended the kingdom's attempts to reconquer the south and began the Long Cold Peace that lasted until the Hundred Year War.

great_interregnum.html:

Great Interregnum

The Great Interregnum was the quarter-century of civil conflict and famine in the Earth Kingdom that followed the collapse of the Qin Dynasty in 255 BG. It destroyed the continent's grain and administrative network.

Course

With the dynasty gone, the provinces fought one another and the capital. A second peasant uprising inside Ba Sing Se, about 255–245 BG (the date is disputed), ended with the garrison commander Bao Kun in control of the city.

Recovery

Bao Kun held Ba Sing Se and expanded outward. The capital then turned south in the suppression campaigns.

The Fire Nation

The Fire Nation was a spectator and a beneficiary. It took no part in the fighting, and its controlled trade profited from a continent in disorder.

The First Uprising of 29 AG was the last and largest of the early risings against the Imperial occupation of the South Pole, and the first to unite the Southern chiefdoms under a single command.

Background

The occupation met resistance from the first year: raids on convoys, ice mines on the roads and attacks on rail lines. The resistance hid in caves, chiefly Taluqqriaq, the Wolf Cave.

Course and reprisals

The Empire answered with the destruction of villages and towns, mass executions and the starvation of districts that sheltered guerrillas. The Qianchan Republic, which entered the war in 30 AG, could do nothing at that distance.

Legacy

It left the South with about three quarters of its population, and its memory fed the Southern Uprising of 99 AG.

The naval war was the war at sea of the Hundred Year War: first an Imperial monopoly, then, after Qianchan entered the war in 30 AG, a contest that neither side could win.

Imperial naval superiority, 1–30 AG

Under Sozin the Navy took 70% of the military budget and the Empire held naval superiority alone. The southern and western chains were taken as Imperial bases and contested later.

Qianchan enters, 30–79 AG

A Qianchan civilian ship was sunk in 27 AG, and the republic entered the war in 30 AG. The first Qianchan-Imperial naval battle, in the Southern Air Temple waters in 30 AG, was a draw. By 50 AG the island chains were divided between the two.

Cost

Both sides lost about 600,000 dead in the naval war. It tied down Imperial ships in escorting convoys and kept the Water Tribes' guerrillas supplied.

The Hu Xin Provinces campaign was the Imperial advance into the northwest of the Earth Kingdom after the conquest of the west coast. It is one of the campaigns the demographic tables count with the unlisted fighting of 0–79 AG.

Course

After the west coast fell in 10 AG the Army advanced north. Battles such as Han Tui (12 AG), the destruction of Taku (15 AG) and Garsai (21 AG) opened the road, and several provincial lords opened their gates.

Occupation

The Empire practiced extermination policies against the people of the occupied northwest and starved districts that resisted. The provinces remained Imperial colonies until the end of the war.

Later role

The Coalition Northern Offensive of 100 AG aimed to reach the Empire's colonies in the Hu Xin Provinces and to cut the western army's supply line.

earth_kingdom_warlord_wars.html:

Earth Kingdom warlord wars
Also known asThe Famine Wars (Earth Kingdom usage)
Part ofThe Post-War Conflicts
Date17 July 100 AG – about 112 AG (main phase); holdouts to 120 AG
LocationThe Earth Kingdom, chiefly the central plains, the northwest and the Hu Xin Provinces
Result
  • Provincial and Imperial-remnant warlords defeated or bought into the settlement
  • The Hundred Year War formally ended, and the United Republic recognized, by the Treaty of Qinglan (28 April 105 AG)
  • The kingdom reorganized as a union of fifty-five states under a standing army and a national treasury
Belligerents
Warlords
provincial marshals, Imperial garrisons left behind, auxiliary commands and revived bandit armies		Order
Omashu, Ba Sing Se and Gaoling (Qianchan)
Commanders and leaders
King Kuei; the King of Omashu; the President of Qianchan, Zhou Qin; many local strongmen
Casualties and losses
About 13 million dead: about 8.5 million of famine, about 3 million of disease and about 1.5 million of violence. Part of the {{stat:hyw_postwar_deaths}} killed in the Post-War Conflicts

The Earth Kingdom warlord wars (called the Famine Wars in the kingdom) were the part of the Post-War Conflicts fought in the Earth Kingdom after the war's command collapsed in July 100 AG. They were less a war than a long breakdown of order, in which provincial armies, Imperial remnants and bandit bands fought one another for food, rail lines and territory, and in which hunger killed far more people than battle. They ended when three powers, Omashu, Ba Sing Se and Gaoling, pacified the warlords by about 112 AG, and left the kingdom a different state from the one that entered the Hundred Year War.

Background

The kingdom entered 100 AG as a nation that had been starved for a century. Occupation had emptied the northwest, the siege of Ba Sing Se had broken the capital's food supply, and the population, which had been {{stat:pop_ek_0|n}} in 0 AG, was about {{stat:pop_ek_100|n}} by the war's end. Provincial lords had held to the Coalition because the war required it, and the Council of Five had given the capital the means to command them. Two failed attempts by the Dai Li, in 98 and 100 AG, had by then wrecked the one institution that could have kept the provinces in line.

The Sōen strike on Ba Sing Se of 17 July 100 AG took the capital's command away for thirty-six hours, and Imperial authority disappeared the next day with the death of Ozai at Battle of Qinglan Port. Garrisons in the occupied northwest were cut off from their orders and their pay. The Hundred Year War had ended in fact, and nothing had taken its place.

The collapse, 100–101 AG

The first winter was the worst. Provincial marshals who had marched to the northern front in 99 AG took their armies home, and in many places kept them fed by requisitioning the harvest. The railway network, which the war had built and then half destroyed, stopped working as a system and became a set of local lines held by whoever held the stations. The grain of the central plains no longer reached the cities, and Ba Sing Se, whose agrarian zone had been wrecked by the Sōen, could not feed itself.

Gaoling sent food by sea and by the southern roads, and was the main reason the winter killed millions rather than tens of millions. Even so, the kingdom's own historians put the deaths of 100–101 AG at about four million, most of them in the cities of the plains and in the northwest.

The warlords, 101–104 AG

By 101 AG the fighting had settled into a pattern. The kingdom was divided among perhaps two hundred armed polities, most of them small, and the historians sort them into four kinds.

KindWho they wereWhat they held
Provincial marshalsRegular officers of the old army who kept their commands and ruled as governorsProvincial capitals, granaries and the nearest rail lines
Imperial remnantsGarrisons and auxiliary commands left behind in the occupied northwest, which became the Hu Xin Free Command and similar bandsThe Imperial forts, depots and company towns of the Hu Xin Provinces
Grain lordsLandowners, merchants and former officials who raised private armies to protect or seize storesMills, river ports and storage towns
Bandit armiesThe revived daofei, with deserters and the dispossessedRoads, mountain passes and the countryside between the others

Few of these fought for a political idea. The marshals claimed to defend the king, and some of them did. The Imperial remnants had no orders and no government to obey, because the Court at Caldera was busy with the Fire Nation Civil War. Fighting centered on grain, and the most important battles of the period were over mills and rail junctions, not cities.

The end of the Hundred Year War, 105 AG

The warlord wars were still raging when the Hundred Year War was brought to a formal end. On 28 April 105 AG, at Qinglan Port, the Royalist Restoration Government of Zuko, President Zhou Qin of Qianchan and King Kuei signed the Treaty of Qinglan, with the delegates of the Yanakawan Provisional Council. The treaty ended the state of war that had existed since 0 AG, recognized the United Republic of Nations as a sovereign state, and set out the concessions each party made. The Court faction under Azula did not sign. See the Treaty of Qinglan.

It mattered to the warlord wars in three ways. The Fire Nation promised to withdraw its garrisons and to give up its claims to the Hu Xin Provinces and the other occupied territories, which removed the Imperial remnants' reason to exist and left many to be bought out or defeated. The kingdom, with the war formally over, could ask its allies for food and arms without the fiction of a front. And the Rebuilding Fund it created gave Ba Sing Se money, in coal and steel, for the first time since the war began.

The three powers, 105–112 AG

PowerMethodArea
OmashuKept its army and its mountain kingdom intact, and moved out of the mountains along the western roads. The King of Omashu offered terms and garrisons in the places that accepted themThe west and the Hu Xin Provinces
Ba Sing SeUsed the single command that Kuei had built after 98 AG, rebuilt the rail lines that fed the capital, and bargained with the marshals one at a timeThe center, the plains and the capital's hinterland
GaolingRan food convoys north from the southern states, paid for by Qianchan's harvests and its credit, and sent advisers and arms to the governments that accepted the settlementThe south and the southern plains

The campaign was mostly persuasion backed by force. A marshal who accepted the king's authority kept his province as a state, with a seat in the new Council of Provinces. One who refused was cut off from the railway and from grain, and then attacked. By about 112 AG all of the larger warlords had been defeated or had come in, and what remained were small bands that took until 120 AG to disappear.

Casualties and displacement

CauseDeadNote
FamineAbout 8.5 millionThe winter of 100–101 AG, and the later failures of the harvest in the northwest
DiseaseAbout 3 millionCholera and typhus in the cities and camps
ViolenceAbout 1.5 millionBattles, reprisals and massacres
TotalAbout 13 millionAbout 8 percent of the kingdom's population in 100 AG

The kingdom's population was about {{stat:pop_ek_100|n}} in 100 AG and about {{stat:pop_ek_125|n}} in 125 AG, after twenty-five years of recovery. About 20 million people were displaced during the wars, many of them to Qianchan, the United Republic of Nations and the cities of the south.

Settlement and legacy

The kingdom that came out of the wars was different. The marshals who accepted the settlement became the governors of what are now the fifty-five constituent states, the capital kept a standing army under one command, and a national treasury and a common code of law followed. The Council of Provinces gave the states a voice, and the monarchy kept its place at the cost of its old claim to rule the provinces directly. Omashu's part in the settlement left the autonomous kingdoms with a permanent say in the kingdom's government. The Treaty of Gaoling in 113 AG ended the old language of non-recognition between the kingdom and Qianchan, and the Dai Li were abolished in 115 AG.

The wars are remembered in the kingdom as the Famine Wars, not as battles. They are what Earth Kingdom historians mean when they say that the Hundred Year War lasted twelve years longer than the Fire Nation admits.

salvationist_insurgency.title: Salvationist insurgency
salvationist_insurgency.html:
Salvationist insurgency
Part ofThe final phase of the Fire Nation Civil War
DateMarch 118 – March 120 AG
LocationNorthern provinces and the western belt of the Fire Nation
ResultInsurgency suppressed; survivors flee abroad; accountability hearings follow
Belligerents
Salvationistsremnant committees, the northern column, urban cellsRoyalist governmentArmy, Home Guard, Qianchan advisers (limited)
Commanders and leaders
SalvationistsTanaka Kenji (killed March 120); Fujiwara Daigo; Matsuda ReikoRoyalistsZuko; General Ito Shigeru; Colonel Mori Hayato
Casualties and losses
About 22,000 killed on both sides; about 9,000 members arrested

The Salvationist insurgency was the final phase of the Fire Nation Civil War, fought by the Salvationists against the Royalist government from the fall of Caldera in 118 AG to the death of their field commander in March 120 AG. The movement, which had broken with the Court in 116 AG, lost its field army at the Nagare River and its last stronghold at Suiko, and fought on as a network of cells in the north and in the cities of the west.

Origins

The Salvationists began as veterans' committees inside the Court's own army. From about 113 AG they controlled most of its field armies, with the help of captured and prototype Imperial Research Bureau weapons. Their members had earlier killed Iroh with a bomb at Shu Jing on 9 March 101 AG. After the break of 116 AG they were an independent army, and after the Siege of Caldera they had lost most of it.

On 12 March 118, Ono Sayuri surrendered the western wards of Caldera, and Tanaka Kenji, who had refused the truce, left the city with about 1,500 men for the north. The People's Iron Column, the other organized force, surrendered at Suiko in August. What remained was Tanaka's northern column, a handful of committees in the western belt and the cells that the movement had kept in the cities since 101.

Insurgency

The northern column, which grew to about 6,000 as soldiers from disbanded units joined it, held the high valleys north of Shu Jing through the winter of 118–119. It lived by requisition and by raiding rail depots, and its tactics were those of the earlier war: short attacks on supply lines, then withdrawal. In the western cities the cells carried out about forty bombings and assassinations in 119, mostly against Royalist officials and against former committee members who had accepted the amnesty.

The Royalist government, which was occupied with famine relief and with the accountability hearings, first treated the insurgency as a matter for the police. In the spring of 119, Ito Shigeru, now the chief of the army staff, assigned four divisions to the north, and the column was pushed from its valleys in the summer.

End

Tanaka was killed at Hanegawa Pass on 11 March 120, in a clash with a Royalist patrol that did not know who he was. His body was identified by his sword and by a notebook carried on him. The northern column dispersed within a month, and the last cell in the west was arrested in June. About 9,000 members were arrested over the two years; most were released under the amnesty of 120, and the committee members who were named at the hearings were tried in the civil courts. Kuga Ren, captured in 119, was tried in 121 AG.

Many members escaped abroad, to the United Republic or to the southern island chain of the Qianchan Republic, and kept the ideas alive.

Historiography

Royalist accounts describe the insurgency as banditry by the remnants of a defeated army, and note that it had no popular support after Caldera. Salvationist memoirs, most of which were written in exile, describe it as a resistance that kept the movement's ideas alive in a country that wanted to forget them. Historians of the later unrest point out that the cells' bombings in 119 had a significant effect on the Royalist government's views on security, and led to the permanent police apparatus that the Reformation government later inherited.

The Water Tribe Civil War was the war between the North and South in the Kingdom of Two Poles, which ended the union of the two tribes that had been rebuilt after the Hundred Year War.

Causes

The North, an enormous modern state, and the South, with an expanding economy, drifted apart, and the South accused the North of having abandoned it in its worst years. The war began over Chief Unalaq's proposal to make Agna Qel'a the sole capital of both tribes, which the South saw as an attempt to subjugate it.

Course

The Southern Water Tribe declared independence as the Southern Federation in 171 AG. The war ended in 174 AG when the South launched a naval bombardment of the Northern capital and a ground assault.

Settlement

The rulers of the new Kingdom of Agna Qel'a, Desna and Eska, signed a peace treaty that recognized the South's sovereignty.

battle_of_kinbara.title: Battle of Kinbara
battle_of_kinbara.html:
This is a stub. It gathers what the wiki records about this battle and will be expanded.
Battle of Kinbara
Datec. 300 BG (Tajisaki 0); the day is disputed
LocationThe Kinbara plain, a river flat in the Saowon lands north of the capital (the exact site is not established)
ResultDecisive victory for the throne. The Saowon army is destroyed; no clan army ever again meets the throne in the field
Belligerents
Throne
Fire Lord Zoryu's household troops, the Keohso, with flintlock muskets		Clans
the Saowon levy and allied clan retainers, loyal to Chaejin
Strength
Not established. Fire Nation chronicles give figures that cannot be reconciled and are probably embroidered
Casualties and losses
Not established; the clan army was broken in an afternoon and the pursuit was short

The Battle of Kinbara was the decisive battle of the Camellia-Peony War and the last pitched battle of the age of clan war. Fought in about 300 BG, it was the first large battle won by flintlock musketry, and the Fire Nation counts its years from it: this is the epoch of Tajisaki dating.

Background

By 300 BG the Camellia-Peony War had dragged on for twelve years. The clans still kept private armies of lacquered cavalry and matchlock arquebusiers, a weapon known since 440 BG, and the Saowon, the richest of them, held the river lands that fed the capital. The musket, in its snaplock form, had been in the Keohso's hands since about 402 BG, but it was slow and unreliable.

The flintlock

The flintlock, a lock that strikes a flint against steel and needs no lit cord, is credited by tradition to armourers of the Keohso workshops, whose names are not recorded. Its advantage was that it fired in weather in which a matchlock could not. Kinbara is remembered as its first massed use and as the first battle in which firing by ranks decided the day. It is the entry for 300 BG in the technology timeline.

Battle

The Saowon advanced across the plain in rain, expecting the Keohso to stand and be ridden down. Their cord matches went out. The Keohso, in ranks that fired and reloaded in turn, shot the horse and the first lines to pieces, and the clan army broke before it reached them. Chaejin, who had accompanied it, left the field. The chronicles disagree about whether Zoryu was there in person. The Saowon histories later called the day the Rain of Kinbara.

Aftermath and Tajisaki dating

It was the last pitched battle of the clan wars. The Saowon were besieged and negotiated, and the war was closed around the Festival of Szeto in 295 BG with the purge of the clan. Zoryu then began the project that took the armies from the clans. Afterwards the throne reckoned the years from the battle, so that Kinbara is year 0 of Tajisaki dating and Tajisaki year = AG + 300. The count was adopted later, by edict, and the choice of Kinbara over the unification at about 4440 BG was deliberate: it dated the throne's authority from the day the clans lost the power to challenge it.

Open questions

The wiki does not yet settle who commanded at Kinbara, what became of Chaejin, whether the Sages or the Avatar-claimant Yun took any part, or whether the Keohso had help in perfecting the flintlock. Later pages may fill these in.

Izumi is the Fire Lord in 170 AG. She is the daughter of Zuko, who abdicated to her in 168 AG, and the third sovereign of the postwar Fire Nation.

Reign

Izumi came to the throne at about forty-seven, after fifty years in which the throne had been rebuilt as a constitutional office. The cabinet of Prime Minister Ryoko Sato governs with the National Diet, and the Fire Lord's role is ceremonial and moral more than executive.

Family

Her husband is Ryota Kōga, and her children are the Crown Prince, Iroh, and Princess Kiko, a pop singer. Her mother's name for Kiko, “hope”, was chosen for the nation's stability during the Joha Crisis of the mid-150s AG, which is not yet written.

The Earth Kingdom

In 171 AG she agreed to send medical supplies and outdated firearms from the Hundred Year War to the Royalists in the First Earth Civil War.

Open questions

Her view of the Salvationists and the Joha Crisis are not yet written.

See also

  • Zuko
  • Fire Nation (Empire of Tajisaki)
  • Kiko
  • Ryoko Sato
  • National Diet

Later reign

Izumi reigned through the Earth Empire’s attack on the kingdom. She chaired the Concord’s forum at Caldera City in September 176, received the Empire’s ambassador on 14 March 180, was evacuated from the Palace on 10 December 182 eleven days before the atomic strike on the old city, and broadcast from Shinja on 22 December: “Caldera is not the Fire Nation. The Fire Nation is the people who are listening to this.” See History of Tajisaki, 171–190 AG.

After the Zaofu raid of 24 December 180 she took the wounded Opal Beifong aboard a ship to the island regions and told her of Suyin's death. She paid for Opal's care at the Shizu City Hospital out of her own purse, in gratitude to Suyin for her work in advancing the technology of mankind.

hou_ting.title: Hou-Ting
hou_ting.html:
This is a stub. It gathers what the wiki records and will be expanded.
Hou-Ting
OfficeEarth Queen; 53rd monarch of the Earth Kingdom, 153–171 AG
Bornc. 126 AG
PredecessorHer father, Kuei, whom she had killed
BrotherYuhan
HeirPrince Wu, her nephew
Died8 June 171 AG, killed by a bomb at the founding parade in Ba Sing Se
ReputationHated by nearly every class from the first year

Hou-Ting was the 53rd monarch of the Earth Kingdom. She had her father King Kuei killed, and the court called it a natural death. She took the throne in 153 AG and reversed his reforms at once. Her reign was hated from the start, by peasants, merchants, lords, officers and reformers alike.

Succession

Hou-Ting was about twenty-seven and spoiled and power-hungry when she inherited the throne. Her brother Yuhan, sickly and naive, had been made a diplomat to the Fire Nation. She had been kept out of government in her father's reign and held his reforms in contempt.

Her father's death

Kuei died in 153 AG, officially peacefully in his sleep. In fact Hou-Ting had him killed. The court physician who certified the death left the palace and disappeared, and the few who knew said nothing while she held the guard. The year was that of Avatar Aang's death, when the world had no Avatar to ask questions. The rumor that the king was murdered was told in the capital from the first week, and the Collective and the Equalists repeated it in later pamphlets. How she did it is not settled.

The reversal, 153–154 AG

Within months she repealed the vote that Kuei had given to all adults in 150 AG, dismissed his ministers, restored the sale of offices and provincial tax farming and raised the land tax. In 154 AG she suspended the Assembly of the Estates and gave the Office of Public Security the power to hold prisoners without trial. Kuei had spent his reign cleaning up the war years' corruption, and she put it back.

A hated reign

She was unpopular from the first year. Peasants resented the taxes, merchants the licenses and monopolies sold to the court, the provincial lords and kings the loss of their voice, officers the sale of commissions, and Reformers the end of the Assembly. Even the Loyalists defended the throne more than they defended the queen. The Reformers proposed an “Earth Confederation” flag and constitution in 159 AG, and she buried it. The revival of the Collective in 169 AG and the movements of the unrest of 167–171 AG all grew out of her rule. The kingdom's later histories treat it as the cause of the collapse.

Death

On 8 June 171 AG the queen was killed by a bomb at the annual parade in Ba Sing Se Square, which celebrated the founding of the Earth Kingdom. The Red Lotus leader Zaheer is named as the assassin. Her nephew, Wu, succeeded her as the 54th monarch, and her death began the First Earth Civil War. The Ba Sing Se press ran the headline “The Kingdom Has Fallen!”, and mourning was small.

Open questions

Her method, her accomplices, her consort and the details of her laws are not yet written.
