republic_city_crisis_of_170_ag.title: Republic City crisis of 170 AG
republic_city_crisis_of_170_ag.html:
Dates marked c. are reconstructed. The sources give most events only relative to one another ("three weeks after", "six weeks since"), and they disagree in places; see Sources and discrepancies. Casualty figures are in-universe estimates.
Republic City crisis of 170 AG
Datec. 7 July – c. 1 October 170 AG
PlaceRepublic City (Jianyu, Longshore, Asagawa, Wada); Yu Dao; the Fujishihoro highlands and the Hengdong agricultural belt
ContextThe unrest of 167–171 AG; the constitutional reform of the United Republic
PartiesThe Republic Council and National Assembly; the Metropolitan Police and the United Forces; the Equalists under Amon (Yan)
AttacksAsagawa transit hub (16 Aug); Pro-Bending Arena (17 Aug); Yu Dao exchange (c. 11 Sep) and police station (18 Sep); a device in a bending school
Deaths31 at the arena; at least 237 at Yu Dao; 412 in a month by the Council President's count; the real total is unknown
OutcomeMartial law in three zones (22 Sep); the Raiko Amendment in 171 AG

The Republic City crisis of 170 AG was a twelve-week sequence of a police killing, mass demonstrations, bombings and emergency measures in the United Republic of Nations. It began with the death of the textile worker Dava in early July and ended, in the sources that survive, with a police raid on an Equalist communication hub in the Longshore district. In between, the republic passed the constitutional reform that bears the name of Raiko, put its army on the streets of its own capital and received the Avatar Korra, who had come to learn airbending and spent the autumn trying to find a place in the argument. It is the immediate background of the civil wars of 171 AG.

Background

The Council and the reform

The United Republic was governed in 170 AG by a Republic Council of six: Tarrlok (Northern Water, Council President), Viku (Southern Water), Ilama (Fire, from Yu Dao), Zi (Earth), Tenzin (Air) and Ujo, the only non-bender, who sits for the non-bending majority. Five of the six seats belong to benders, and by 170 AG it was the Equalists' loudest complaint that the republic's non-benders had one voice in six.

Raiko, a member of the National Assembly, proposed to replace the council with a presidential system modeled on the Qianchan Republic, without Qianchan's federal states. He had first proposed a single-chamber parliament; the final text kept the Assembly and added a Senate elected by proportional representation. The opposition, led by the firebender Zoltan, called him a would-be dictator; the independent Xinwan thought the reform right but risky. A referendum and several months of review by the Supreme Court preceded the Council's vote on 18 July. The Council had governed for "seven decades" by Tarrlok's reckoning, counting from the start of the War of Independence in 100 AG.

The eastern districts

The districts east of the city centre (Jianyu, Longshore, lower Asagawa) are mill and dock districts with a non-bender majority, bordered on the north by Kennouchi, which is old Fire Nation heritage and voted against the reform, and on the east by the Hengdong agricultural belt, which is of Earth Kingdom heritage. The Fujishihoro highlands, a range that runs east to west across the main island, were the stronghold of the resistance of the War of Independence and of the highland insurgencies of 118–124 AG. Officials who knew the map saw that the attacks of 170 AG did not fall on one side of that line.

Chronology

DateEvent
c. 7 July 170 AGDeath of Dava. Dava, a twenty-three-year-old non-bender textile worker from the mill on Harbor Approach, is shot dead by Officer Han of the Metropolitan Police at a labor demonstration over shift lengths at Jianyu Square. The government says she rushed a police line; her coworkers say she had her hands raised. A blurred photograph and four and a half minutes of footage circulate and every side reads them as proof. Han is suspended and sent out of the city to relatives near Juniper. See Dava.
Early July 170 AGThe Equalists send a coordination notice to their eastern-district cells four days before the demonstration is announced publicly. It describes the demonstration as an opportunity and names the pharmacy corner of Jianyu Square, where Dava and her friend Fen will stand.
18 July 170 AGConstitutional vote. The Speaker of the National Assembly announces that the Republic Council has voted 4–2 for the constitutional reform proposed by the Assembly member Raiko. Councillors Tenzin (Air), Ujo (non-bender), Ilama (Fire, of Yu Dao) and Zi (Earth) vote in favor; the Council President Tarrlok (Northern Water) and Viku (Southern Water) vote against. The Supreme Court had found the reform constitutional after several months of review. The Council of Six signs the text the same day on Air Temple Island. The reform replaces the council republic with a presidential system, adds a proportionally elected Senate beside the Assembly, and takes effect after a transition period. Raiko challenges the opposition leader Zoltan, a firebender, to a presidential election.
18 July 170 AGThe Avatar Korra lands at Republic City and is flown to Air Temple Island with Varrick and Zhu Li and a White Lotus escort, to begin airbending with Tenzin. A crowd of children and fans meets her. RCNN broadcasts the signing and her arrival in the same bulletin.
c. 28 July 170 AGJianyu Square demonstration. A permitted gathering, estimated at 400–500 by dispatch, grows to 600–800 by nightfall and chants Dava's name; leaflets reading Equality. Rights. Dava. and bearing a circle-and-wheel symbol have been left in an alley behind the pharmacy. After dark a sharp sound from the western side sends the crowd into motion; a mill worker is taken to Republic City General at 21:47 and three people are arrested. The press, the police and the demonstrators disagree about what started it. (In a separate incident, three shots were heard near Jianyu and Sixth on a morning in the same weeks.)
c. 1–5 August 170 AGAt a closed meeting on paper maps, Chief Lin Beifong tells General Tao of the city garrison, Councillors Ilama and Zi and Tenzin that there have been eight incidents in four districts in three weeks: five on infrastructure (substations, a rail switching station, Hengdong water pumps), three on benders, and a device in the ventilation of a bending school in the Fujishihoro foothills, found by a twelve-year-old student. It is judged "meant to be found". Tao says the pattern recalls the highland resistance networks of the War of Independence. Tenzin names Yan; Beifong answers that Yan is the name used while the structure is not understood. Tarrlok's chair is empty. Korra, who attended, then watches rival crowds, Equalist and pro-bending-fan, chant across Jianyu boulevard.
16 August 170 AGAsagawa transit hub bombing. A bomb wrecks the eastern dispatch building of the metro authority. The first reports call it a gas line failure; the casualty figure is never stated and rumors range from 12 to 40. Metro service is suspended in the east.
17 August 170 AGPro-Bending Arena bombing. At about 08:47, on a match day, a device explodes in the VIP level, followed by a secondary device. The radio gives 19 dead, then 43; the press runs Dozens feared dead. At 14:00 Beifong confirms 31 dead and about 104 injured, both devices in the VIP level, no claim of responsibility. The tournament is suspended. Asami Sato and the pro-benders Mako and Bolin leave through the maintenance exit.
18 August 170 AGBeifong sends units into three zones (Jianyu, Longshore, lower Asagawa) with target lists: twelve detentions, four with actionable links and eight by proximity. She releases six. At 22:00 she orders a curfew in the eastern districts for an initial 72 hours. The curfew is renewed four times by the end of September. A night patrol recalls the Wada district emergency of 155 AG, which lasted three weeks and left two dead on each side.
c. 11 September 170 AGYu Dao exchange bombing. The lower three floors of the Yu Dao exchange building, on Nanaka island on the harbor front, are destroyed; the trading floor is lost. A fourth-floor office loses eleven people. The exchange moves to Shicheng, volume falls by sixty percent, and Qianchan institutions begin to route trade around it.
14 September 170 AGIn closed session the transitional authority amends Article 14, subsection 3 of the transitional constitutional framework: the 72-hour civilian review of emergency deployments is removed and unilateral authorization extended. The amendment is not published.
18 September 170 AGYu Dao station bombing. At about 07:55 a bomb destroys the front of Yu Dao Central Police Station on Harbor Front, built in 128 AG. Sergeant Polo dies in the second-floor briefing room; Constable Park is hurt; Constable Hwan was upstairs; Officer Sera Lim, seven minutes late, is on the pavement. The Assembly is later told that the Yu Dao toll stands at 237 and will rise.
22 September 170 AGMartial law vote. The Assembly meets at 09:03 before three foreign missions, with Korra in the public gallery. Ilama calls the attacks an act of war; Zoltan demands full authorization without review; Assemblyman Cho and Assemblywoman Dae speak; Raiko, citing "over four hundred" dead in a month, supports it "with oversight"; Tenzin opposes it, warning against turning the army on citizens. Tarrlok, who has had his motion drafted for three days, moves martial law in the eastern districts, the Fujishihoro highland zone and the Hengdong agricultural belt, with a 72-hour review. It passes with 81 percent. Tenzin is the only councillor against; the Assembly members from Hengdong (three), Longshore (two), Shicheng (one) and Jianyu vote no. It is signed at 10:47; orders go out at 11:00 and troops are in the eastern districts by noon. (A General Staff colonel gives the interval after the bombing as 41 hours, which would make it 20 September.)
23 September 170 AGAt 06:03 military personnel carriers relieve the police at the Jianyu-adjacent checkpoint; Officer Kwan's unit is reassigned at 07:00. The photographer Yuna photographs the handover. In the Longshore district she interviews Sera Lim, whose brother farms in Hengdong.
Late September 170 AGAt the Caijia facility General Ta Min of the United Forces' southern theater, Colonel Fenn and the civilian Shen ask Hiroshi Sato for the current mechanized suits in six weeks at reduced specification, and for a new-generation exosuit (¥8,000,000). On 28 September Asami Sato confronts him with the ¥20,000 the company gave the police memorial fund, proposes that ten percent of defense revenue go to victims, and demands that the posted notice at the mill be taken down. Hiroshi locks the blueprint in a drawer.
c. 29 September 170 AGA typewritten Equalist leaflet found at the Jianyu checkpoint at 06:15 cites the unpublished Article 14 amendment and states that Dava "was there about wages". The journalist who finds it, Yuna of Republican Daily, reasons that the author has a source in the government and one in the movement, and that Yan "is deciding what you find".
c. 30 September 170 AGRepublican Daily publishes Who Was Dava, 800 words, built on the account of Fen and on the labor notice, the mill's shift logs and a coworker's injury report. The Equalists claim the story as theirs. The notice about "personal responsibility" posted at the mill after the injury comes down on the Tuesday, following a telephone call to the floor supervisor from a source never identified. Beifong orders the two Jianyu detainees she had held reviewed for release.
c. 1 October 170 AGAn Equalist, Rill, of the Longshore cell, comes to the paper with three things: the coordination notice and its pharmacy corner, the district and type of the network's communication hub (Eastern Longshore, a commercial building with a ground-floor business as cover) and a warning that something operational is coming. Her building matches the middle of three possible sites that Beifong has been narrowing, which a four-line intercept now confirms. The hub is a laundry on Fengdao Street. At 22:00 Beifong briefs Dren's unit and Korra, who has left the observer pass behind; they move forty minutes later. The sources end here.
171 AGThe Raiko Amendment takes effect and the United Republic becomes a presidential state under President Raiko. The Equalists are a declared terrorist organization. See Unrest of 167–171 AG.

Casualties

No complete count exists. Beifong confirmed 31 dead and about 104 injured at the arena by 14:00 on the day. The transit hub toll was never stated. The Assembly was told on 22 September that Yu Dao had cost at least 237 lives, a provisional figure. In the same debate Tarrlok gave 412 deaths in a month across three coordinated strikes and Raiko "over four hundred"; the two do not agree with the arena and Yu Dao figures when summed, and no source reconciles them. The Metropolitan Police treated figures from the radio (19, 43) as unreliable from the first day.

The Equalist network

The police believed the attacks came from the Equalists, whose leader, Amon, appears in police briefings as Yan. The Equalists did not claim the arena or Yu Dao attacks. Beifong and her intelligence officer Sho told her superiors that the structure was unknown: it could be Yan, someone near him, or someone using his name and network to a different end. The network distributed through a laundry on Fengdao Street in Longshore, whose owner Chu asked no questions in return for a share of his rent, and was organised in cells of about seven people. Rill, a Longshore organiser who had joined through the dockworkers, concluded from the pharmacy-corner notice that the leadership had known where Dava would stand, and asked for a week to find out; she took her evidence to the press before the week was over.

The government response

Three measures followed one another: the police detention drive and curfew of 18 August, the Assembly authorization of 22 September and the deployment of the United Forces to the eastern districts, the highlands and the Hengdong belt. The authorization rested on the amended Article 14, subsection 3, adopted in closed session on the 14th, four days before the Yu Dao station was bombed. The veteran constitutional correspondent Hemi, of Republican Daily, confirmed from a source in the government that the amendment was real and described it as housekeeping; the source did not address the timing. A later claim that Tarrlok had written his motion three days before the Yu Dao station bomb is recorded, but not documented.

The deployment reached the Hengdong villages within weeks. Checkpoints lengthened the farmers' market runs; a village school ran half days; children drew soldiers beside their houses and animals. A farmer there told the Avatar to "work faster".

Industry

The United Forces' demand for mechanized equipment, first placed with Future Industries before the crisis, was accelerated after the arena bombing. The company's chairman, Hiroshi Sato, suspected that his contact in the military coordination office, Shen, represented a faction inside the government with its own interest in the "post-deployment settlement". His daughter Asami persuaded him to withdraw the exosuit proposal from the table and to review the shifts at one of his supplier mills, the mill where Dava had worked.

The press

Republican Daily's photographer Yuna, embedded with the police, photographed the transfer of the checkpoint to the army and a portrait of Sera Lim's hands that was widely reprinted. Her story Who Was Dava changed what the republic thought the demonstrations had been about, from the Equalists and the police to twelve-hour shifts and a posted notice about personal responsibility. Rao, her editor, noted that Yan had left the leaflet where she would find it and that the story was true.

Consequences

  • Constitutional. The emergency provisions of 170 AG became part of the presidential constitution that took effect in 171 AG; the Raiko Amendment is the best known of them.
  • Political. The Equalists were declared a terrorist organization; Raiko, who had supported the deployment "with oversight", won the presidency.
  • Social. The curfew and checkpoints taught a generation in the eastern districts that the republic and its army were the same thing. The movements in the unrest recruited there.
  • The Avatar. Korra concluded that observing was not enough and that the Avatar ought to be "in the room".

Sources and discrepancies

The main narrative source is the serial Dawn of a New Revolution, which this article follows wherever the wiki's other pages differ; see About Avatar: New Red Dawn. The accounts disagree on a few points:

  • The place of Dava's death. Official statements say the harbor district; Fen and the leaflets say Jianyu Square.
  • The vote. The press gives 22 September; a colonel's briefing gives 41 hours after the bombing.
  • Seven decades. The Council counted from 100 AG, the start of the War of Independence; the formal union dates from 105 AG (Treaty of Qinglan).
  • Korra's time in the city. "Four months" in one briefing; the raid is only about two and a half months after her arrival.

See also

  • Raiko

tarrlok.title: Tarrlok
tarrlok.html:
Tarrlok
OfficeCouncil President of the Republic Council (Northern Water seat), 170 AG
NationUnited Republic of Nations; of the Northern Water Tribe
ServiceAbout thirty years in public life by 170 AG

Tarrlok is a waterbender of the Northern Water Tribe and the Council President of the United Republic in 170 AG. He presides over the six-member Republic Council and has served the republic for some thirty years.

Positions

In the reform debate of 170 AG he and Tenzin voted against Raiko's constitution, the 4–2 vote of 18 July. Tenzin voted on principle, against concentrated power, and Tarrlok because the reform ended the Council he presided over. His speech on the republic's origins described it as the child of a war of independence between the remnants of Ozai's regime and Earth Kingdom generals, "not Avatar Aang's creation".

The crisis

He was absent from the closed police briefing of early August. On 22 September he moved martial law in the eastern districts, the Fujishihoro highlands and the Hengdong belt, with an address that said he was "sick" of debating proportionality, and carried it with 81 percent. The Equalist leaflet and the press asked who had told Yan about the closed-session amendment of 14 September; the reporter Yuna's notes put Tarrlok's name against the question, with a question mark. He gave no statement after the story Who Was Dava. See Republic City crisis of 170 AG.

See also

  • Tenzin
  • Raiko
  • Republic City crisis of 170 AG

lin_beifong.title: Lin Beifong
lin_beifong.html:
Lin Beifong
OfficeChief of the Metropolitan Police of Republic City, 170 AG
FamilyBeifong

Lin Beifong is the Chief of the Metropolitan Police of Republic City in 170 AG. She is the daughter of Toph and bears the name of the Beifong family of Zaofu; her relation to Suyin Beifong is not recorded.

In the crisis of 170 AG

She was the first official to see a pattern. In early August she briefed Councillors Ilama and Zi, Tenzin and General Tao on paper maps, without records; she told them that Yan was "the name we use when we don't understand the structure yet". After the arena bombing she ordered the detention drive (12 detained, 6 released) and, to keep the parameters in her own hands, proposed the curfew of 18 August herself. She held two of the detainees on thin evidence and released them after Who Was Dava appeared. She briefed Korra and Dren's unit for the raid on the Fengdao Street laundry on the night of c. 1 October. See Republic City crisis of 170 AG.

See also

  • Suyin Beifong
  • Republic City

dava.title: Dava
dava.html:
Dava
Bornc. 147 AG
Diedc. 7 July 170 AG, Jianyu Square, Republic City
OccupationTextile worker, mill on Harbor Approach, Longshore district

Dava (c. 147–170 AG) was a non-bending textile worker from the Longshore district of Republic City whose death at a labor demonstration became the focus of the crisis of 170 AG.

Life

She worked for nine years at a textile mill on Harbor Approach, four of them on the same line as her friend Fen. In the summer of 170 AG the mill ran twelve-hour shifts and more. A coworker, Pei, caught her hand in a conveyor after thirteen hours on her feet and lost two fingers; management posted a notice about personal responsibility by the time clock. Dava read it for a long time and said to Fen, I'm going to the demonstration on Saturday. You should come.

Death

She died at the demonstration, on the pharmacy corner of Jianyu Square, shot by Officer Han of the Metropolitan Police. Fen reports that Dava raised her hands first, "like I'm not doing anything, look". The police said she had rushed a line. Han was suspended. A photograph and four and a half minutes of footage became the evidence on every side.

The notice about personal responsibility posted by the time clock reflected the republic's harsh treatment of newcomers, who were left to bear the consequences of their own choices.

After her death

Her face was painted on walls across the eastern districts, ten feet high, with Say her name. Demonstrations chanted it. The Equalists took it as a slogan. For nearly three months nobody said why she had been there. On c. 30 September Republican Daily ran Who Was Dava, and the name began to carry the facts of her life: the hours, the injury and the notice. Her name was among those painted on the Yu Dao reconstruction fence.

See also

  • Republic City crisis of 170 AG
  • Equalists

republic_city.title: Republic City
republic_city.html:
Republic City
NationUnited Republic of Nations
StatusCapital; National Capital Region (governor: Ailani, 170 AG)
Seat ofThe Republic Council, the National Assembly, the Supreme Court

Republic City is the capital of the United Republic of Nations, on the Ikiri Sea. Tradition says that Sokka, the friend of Aang, helped design it.

Districts

  • Government quarter. The council hall and the Assembly chamber, with press and diplomats' galleries.
  • Jianyu, Longshore, lower Asagawa. Mill, dock and tenement districts of the east with a non-bender majority; the site of the 170 AG demonstrations, bombings and curfew. Harbor Approach, where Dava's mill stands, and Fengdao Street are in Longshore.
  • Wada. The border district on the edge of the eastern zone. Rail yards; the site of the labor emergency of 155 AG; the offices of Republican Daily.
  • Kennouchi. A northern district of old Fire Nation families.
  • Shicheng. A district whose Assembly member voted against the martial law authorization.

Landmarks

Air Temple Island, in the bay, the home of Tenzin's family and of the airbender acolytes. The Pro-Bending Arena, wrecked on 17 August 170 AG; the tournament resumed on a temporary stage in Republic City Park. Republic City General. Police headquarters. Republic City Park. The metro, a rail network with its surface lines.

Hinterland

East of the city the Fujishihoro highlands run east to west across the main island; beyond them lies the Hengdong agricultural belt of Earth Kingdom heritage. Yu Dao is four hours south by air, and the Caijia region on the southern coast has Future Industries' research facility.

Destruction of 118 AG

On 27 September 118 AG, in the sixteenth year of the republic, the Denied under Tagah attacked the city while Jharana hung above the harbor. By the Council’s count of 4 October, 41,200 people were dead and about three-fifths of the built-up area had been destroyed or condemned. It is the only time the capital has been largely destroyed. Unity Tower, a few weeks old, was one of the few large buildings left standing. By 126 AG the docks had been rebuilt, because the International Port was working when it was bombed. See Unity Tower attack.

See also

  • Republic City crisis of 170 AG
  • Yu Dao
  • Dock Bombing of 126 AG

future_industries.title: Future Industries
future_industries.html:
Future Industries
ChairmanHiroshi Sato
HeirAsami Sato
SeatRepublic City; research facility at Caijia (c. 159 AG), 400 staff
ProductsCars; pro-bending sponsorship; defense equipment

Future Industries is the republic's largest private manufacturer, run by Hiroshi Sato. Its public face is its cars, its factories and its sponsorship of pro-bending teams; its Caijia research facility, which has a doubled security complement, holds the defense work.

The Sato family

Hiroshi has built the company since the death of his wife, who objected to the defense work. His daughter Asami reads the contracts, visits the factories and knows the arena and mill. In the crisis of 170 AG she learned that the company's supplier mill in Longshore, where Dava worked, posted the notice about personal responsibility; she demanded it be taken down, the hours reviewed and a company officer sent to the mill.

The contract

The company's United Forces contract covers a mechanized suit retrofitted from a Hundred Year War design. In August and September 170 AG General Ta Min of the southern theater asked for the current generation in six weeks at reduced specification, and for a new exosuit built for highland terrain (¥8,000,000 for development and first production). Hiroshi accepted the first and put the second in a desk drawer after Asami's proposal that ten percent of defense revenue go to victims. The company had given ¥20,000 to the police memorial fund. See Republic City crisis of 170 AG.

See also

  • Republic City crisis of 170 AG
  • United Republic of Nations

republican_daily.title: Republican Daily
republican_daily.html:
Republican Daily
TypeNewspaper of record
SeatWada district, Republic City, in the same building since 132 AG
EditorRao

Republican Daily is the United Republic's paper of record, occupying the fourth and fifth floors of a building in the Wada district. It still develops film in its fifth-floor darkroom, although the staff use digital cameras.

Staff in 170 AG

  • Rao, editor, who tells reporters to be careful what they conclude.
  • Yuna, photographer and reporter, embedded with the Metropolitan Police and later the army. Her camera, a Korin K3, is secondhand.
  • Hemi, constitutional affairs, thirty-four years at the paper.
  • Soo, legal correspondent.

The crisis of 170 AG

In late September the paper published Who Was Dava and held the Article 14 story until it could verify it without leaflets or a single source. The telephone line took 47 calls before noon, most from readers, one from a threat. See Republic City crisis of 170 AG and Dava.

See also

  • Republic City
  • Equalists

naniporo_directive_716.title: Operational Directive 716 (Naniporo Sector)
naniporo_directive_716.html:
Operational Directive 716 was an order issued to the Imperial Southern Garrison in the winter of 99–100 AG. It declared the mountain settlements of the Naniporo Sector hostile and called for their total destruction. It was issued during the Southern Uprising and is one of the clearest statements of intent for the Empire's final clearance of the South's interior.

Operational Directive 716 (Naniporo Sector)
DateWinter 99–100 AG (undated in the source)
LocationThe Naniporo Sector, the mountain valleys of the South Pole
Issued byImperial high command, through the Southern Garrison
Carried out bySouthern Garrison units, the 3rd Armored support, and a column under Prince Zuko
ResultNot recorded in the source; see Outcome

The order

The directive was read aloud at a briefing in a Southern Garrison compound, over a tactical display. It classified the settlements Red-Zone Alpha through Gamma as “hostile strongholds” and set the “primary objective” as “total eradication of insurgent presence.” It authorized incendiary clearance, ordered mobile artillery to seal the valley exits, and warned that any unit bypassing the burn sectors would answer to a tribunal. The speaker closed: “This is not a war of attrition. This is annihilation.” Hesitation, it said, would be treated as treason, and “Ozai's will is absolute.”

The briefing's final slide gave the measure of success: “80% hostile neutralization.”

Plan of attack

The phases were assigned by valley. Alpha took the northern approach, where the 42nd had been lost the previous winter. Bravo pushed through the village cluster. Charlie, the southern gulch, went to Zuko's column, where two companies had “melted” the month before, with no bodies recovered.

Conduct and reception

Officers at the briefing objected that a sweep-and-freeze had become an extermination order and that orders had changed twice in a week. Captain Jun of the 9th Company complained that the ice had been “eating battalions” for generations. Major Taoru ended the discussion: “Orders stand.”

Zuko's own scouting had described the village in his sector as having perfect firing angles and children who moved through practiced drills. The directive did not separate the fighters from the villages that sheltered them, and it treated the settlements as a single military target.

Outcome

The sources do not record how many settlements were destroyed under the directive or how many people died. The reprisal figure for the Southern Uprising, about 90,000 killed, is the nearest recorded total and may include this campaign.

See also

  • Southern Uprising
  • The Southern Vault
  • Zuko
  • Ozai

Source: Ash on Ice, ch. 20.

southern_vault.title: The Southern Vault
southern_vault.html:
The Southern Vault was a classified Imperial research complex under a mountain at the South Pole, built in 35 AG to study the Southern spirit portal. It was decommissioned on paper and sealed in practice. For the rest of the Hundred Year War it was used as a hiding place by the surviving top officials of the Southern Water Tribe's pre-war government, until the Empire broke into it during the fall of the Southern capital in December 99 AG. In the 180s AG it was reopened by Avatar Korra, with consequences that are still remembered.

The Southern Vault
Built35 AG, by the Empire of Tajisaki
TypeClassified research complex; later a hiding place and hidden administrative centre of the Southern chiefdoms
LocationThe South Pole. The source does not name the complex; this wiki identifies it with the Imperial bunker complex of the Southern Uprising.
OccupantsImperial researchers (from 35 AG); then the surviving officials of the Southern Water Tribe's pre-war government
FateBreached and sealed during the fall of Taluqqriaq, December 99 AG; reopened in the 180s AG

Purpose

The vault was built to study the Southern spirit portal, one of the two original gateways between the physical world and the Spirit World. The portal had been sealed since the Harmonic Convergence of 9,829 BG and lay in the heart of an ancient forest at the South Pole. It could be opened and closed only by the Avatar, and only at the solstices. The Empire's researchers could not open it, and the work in the vault was an attempt to do it by other means.

An Imperial officer, Xin, later found the site in the Empire's own archives. It was listed as “one of ours,” dated to the early occupation, and classified “six levels down.” Its files were “decommissioned on paper. Buried in practice.” Xin summarized the work as spirit-energy experiments, “the kind you test on rats, then lie about for twenty years.” The records the Empire recovered described black projects, spirit-engineered systems, failed rituals and containment protocols. The Empire publicly called the Avatar extinct, but the vault's files showed that it privately knew the Avatar's role in the portals, and later knew he was alive.

Hiding place of the old government

When the program ended, the Empire sealed the vault and treated it as empty. It was not. In the first weeks of the war the Empire had captured the Council of Chieftains and Elders and the leading chieftains of the Southern Water Tribe, but some of the pre-war government's top officials had escaped, and their successors found the abandoned complex. Its two-meter door, its depth and its Imperial classification made it the safest place in the South, since the garrison had been told that it was closed and dangerous.

The remnant of the pre-war government used the lower levels as a hiding place for decades. It kept the chiefdoms' records, seals and agreements there, and ran a hidden administration for the resistance. By 99 AG the resistance was using the complex as its administrative centre, which an Imperial officer complained about when he found the archive entry.

The breach (December 99 AG)

During the fall of Taluqqriaq in December 99 AG, Imperial breaker teams cut at the vault's locking seams with thermal torches. The door was about two meters thick, curved like a submarine hatch, and of Fire Nation make. The Avatar fought at the breach against Breaker units and infantry, and the complex was sealed again with the fighting still underway. The elders who ran the hidden administration were among those ordered out in the evacuation of the South. A Qianchan army squad held a bunker to cover the withdrawal, and its officer had warned the elders that the bunker was a tomb.

Casualties

The Imperial record of the assault lists three Breakers destroyed, twelve infantry killed on site, five further deaths during the evacuation, and three officers knocked out.

Later history (180s AG)

The vault's spirit-engineered systems, containment protocols and conduits were never dismantled. In the 180s AG, Avatar Korra reopened the complex, and the consequences of that decision are the reason the vault is remembered outside the South. The wiki does not yet record the incident.

See also

  • Southern Uprising
  • Evacuation of the South
  • Southern Water Tribe
  • Subjugation of the Water Tribes
  • Taluqqriaq
  • Korra
  • Aang

Source: Ash on Ice, ch. 25, 26, 32. Spirit portal details follow The Legend of Korra.

southern_evacuation.title: Evacuation of the South (99–100 AG)
southern_evacuation.html:
The evacuation of the South was the removal of the Southern Water Tribe's surviving fighters, leaders, wounded and children from the South Pole after the fall of Taluqqriaq. It ran from December 99 AG into early 100 AG. It took the surviving resistance to the Qianchan Republic, where refugee districts were built for the South's people.

Evacuation of the South (99–100 AG)
Date9 December 99 AG to early 100 AG
LocationTaluqqriaq; the sea route to Qianchan; Yulugak; Gaoling
ParticipantsSouthern Water Tribe resistance; Qianchan naval and army forces; Qianchan civil command
ResultSurviving resistance and refugees resettled in Qianchan. The South was occupied; within about three weeks of the evacuation the coast fell.

From the capital

As the capital fell on 9 December 99 AG, the wounded and the children were taken out through the tunnels and by sea. A Qianchan army squad of five earthbenders and five nonbenders held a bunker to cover the withdrawal. Its officer had warned the elders in advance that the bunker was “a tomb.” The escape counts disagree: Hama counted about fifty-six saved, and Hakoda said more than a hundred had died before the hall broke.

By sea

The fleet left on a Qianchan destroyer painted with false red and gold to pass as a Fire Nation merchant ship. It made for Yulugak, a Qianchan port that had “not fired a single shot this war” and sat in fog. Hakoda watched the coast burn from the stern. He had read the reports, and he said: “We never should've gone for the capital.”

Reception in Qianchan

Qianchan sorted the arrivals by bending. Waterbenders went to Sector Three, a settlement built by Zaofu engineers under the Gaoling Bureau of Displaced Affairs. Earthbenders went to the Yanjin community near the steelworks. Officials promised that Sector Three would become a full district within six months, with permanent housing, schools and a controlled water supply.

Some refugees had hoped to return home rather than rebuild in Qianchan. A separate district, Sector Six, was built with food carts, murals and a carpentry co-op. Refugees there had begun to call it their own. Qianchan officials used the districts for press visits.

The South after

Three weeks after the evacuation, the coast fell and half the South went dark. The Empire ran the South through permits, cut rations, burned fishing nets and arrested elders. It hunted inland fighters, torched towns and executed cells that were found.

See also

  • Southern Uprising
  • The Southern Vault
  • Qianchan Republic
  • Gaoling
  • Hakoda

Source: Ash on Ice, ch. 27, 29–31, 39.

southern_air_temple_last_stand.title: Last stand at the Southern Air Temple
southern_air_temple_last_stand.html:
Also called the Fall of the Southern Air Temple. Part of the Air Nomad Genocide.

Last stand at the Southern Air Temple
Date0 AG (the day is not recorded in the source), three days after Aang left the temple
LocationThe Southern Air Temple, South Pole: the courtyards, the west wing and the central atrium
ResultImperial victory. The temple was taken and its monks killed or captured. About two dozen children were sent out through a tunnel beneath the atrium.
AttackersThe Empire of Tajisaki: an unmarked airship, artillery, and a ground force with four-round bolt-action rifles, bayonets, revolvers, grenades and firebenders. The atrium assault used a detachment of seventy.
DefendersThe monks and nuns of the temple, who had no weapons at the start of the attack. Eleven made the last stand in the atrium, led by the elder monk Gyatso.
Casualties and losses
Imperial: thirty-two of the atrium detachment never walked out, and more fell in the courtyards and the west wing. Defenders: all the adult monks killed, apart from two captured alive; about a dozen of the children reached the southern valley.

The last stand at the Southern Air Temple was the defense of the temple by its monks against the Empire's attack of 0 AG. It lasted for hours, and its final phase, a fight for the central atrium that covered the escape of the temple's children, is the best-documented single action of the Air Nomad Genocide. It is remembered above all for the elder who held the atrium to the end. The Imperial Navy's after-action report records that it took a detachment of seventy soldiers and a pile of dead to bring him down.

Background

For about two days before the attack, the monks had noticed a low, steady vibration in the floorboards from the northwest quadrant, at the same hour each day. It was not Earth Kingdom machinery and not farm equipment, and the pitch did not skip. On the morning of the attack the elder Gyatso said that “the mountain is trying to tell us something.” Three days earlier he had sent Aang out on a glider, before first light, because the boy “needed to breathe.” Pasang thought he should have been kept at the temple and disciplined, and the elder Dorje said that he would come back.

That morning the sound of gunfire came up from the valley floor, and then the heavy thump of artillery. Pasang guessed that it was the Earth Kingdom, and Gyatso guessed the Qianchan, whose warning had reached the temple three days before. Nobody had opened the letter.

The bombardment

The first shell, the size of a barrel, fell from an unmarked airship hidden in cloud, and struck the library annex. The bell tower and the south spire followed, then the meditation hall. The airship carried no insignia and no flag. Shrapnel killed monks and novices in the courtyard before any soldier appeared.

Imperial infantry then climbed the steps from the valley, men in red and black who had been marching in the mountains for weeks. They opened fire on novices who were pulling the wounded behind walls. The monks had no weapons and no formation. One of them cried that they were being attacked as if they were a threat, and another said that it was an execution, not a raid.

The courtyard and the west wing

The first soldier to reach the top of the steps was lifted by a blast of air together with three others and thrown against the courtyard wall. Gyatso told the first officers that he did not want to kill them but would not let them defile the place, and when they fired, he moved “like a storm.” After one soldier was thrown through the far archway and killed, the Imperial troops shouted that the monks were fighting back and opened fire.

Gyatso then ordered the surviving monks to take the soldiers' weapons. Some tackled fallen riflemen and fired their rifles badly, including a boy, Tenga, who fumbled the bolt. Master Dashi broke the stone beneath two gunners on the west walkway, and Sister Malu cut through a squad at close range, using vacuum and pressure and without taking a weapon. Pasang was shot dead in mid-stride as he ran to Gyatso. An Imperial grenade was deflected by Gyatso down a corridor, where it collapsed the west wing and killed an unknown number of soldiers and monks. Fire Nation firebenders, with bayonets fixed, then pushed in from the western corridors, and Gyatso crushed their lead with a compressed blast, but bullets grazed his arm and thigh.

The atrium

By then the monks' purpose had changed. The temple's children, about two dozen of them, the youngest seven years old, had been gathered behind the pillars. Gyatso ordered them to go through the atrium and down the lower stairs, to a crawlspace beneath the dais, and to keep going until they saw the roots of the mountain and daylight. A sixteen-year-old monk, Yulren, led them. The rest of the surviving monks formed up behind Gyatso at the atrium's doors, eleven in all, including two nuns, with a few stolen rifles among them.

For the next several hours the eleven held the corridor leading to the atrium. They threw soldiers into walls, crushed bayonets, turned flame back on the firebenders who made it, and fired captured rifles into the breach. The monks died one at a time, and by the end only Gyatso stood. His left arm hung useless, and the bullet wounds at his shoulder and thigh had bled through his robe. The Imperial survivors, seventeen of them at the last count, closed in on him in the smoke.

The master

Imperial officers who survived the atrium gave the Imperial Navy an account that its reporters did not at first believe. According to the after-action report, the elder was struck by about fifty rifle rounds in the course of the fight. The majority of them did not pass through his air shield: the bullets bent away in the air in front of him, spent themselves on the walls, and were later picked out of the stone as flattened slugs. Only the rounds that struck when he was exhausted, or when he turned away to protect the doorway, got through. Soldiers who were in the room later described him in terms they otherwise used for fortified positions. The shield held through hours of fire, and every man who rushed him was thrown back.

The report counted thirty-two of the seventy men of the atrium detachment as dead, some of them never found. Most of them were torn apart by wind, and a few were crushed by stone that folded inward, in a way that the investigators called too clean to be random. He is credited with the deaths of two full squads and with at least one firebender cut down in the fight. Gyatso's last words, spoken to the soldiers who had surrounded him, were: “You'll die trying to erase us.” One of them then shot him in the head from close range, after the fight, and the Imperial Navy's public logs omitted the shot. A photograph of the body survived in the archives, and the original draft of the report said that the soldiers had been afraid he would get back up.

Aftermath

The Empire captured two monks alive. One died on the way to Ba Sing Se, and the other was held in a military hospital under a pseudonym and was never reported dead. A report form found later confirmed the tunnel beneath the atrium, with an exit near the southern ridge. The tunnel collapsed halfway through, but footprints smaller than an adult's led down it, and Qianchan archivists concluded that about a dozen children reached the southern valley. A remote village on that route, founded by refugees after the war, does not discuss it.

The Empire held the temple for most of the war. It catalogued the monks' remains in crates with identity tags written in military shorthand, painted Imperial scripture over the carvings, and used the courtyards as a stage for ceremonies and decrees. Qianchan reclaimed the temple later, and kept it as a ruin, with the scorched frescoes, the bullet holes and the blackened ring on the atrium floor. A single wooden staff still stands upright on its end in the middle of the dais.

Source notes

  • The Imperial Navy's report counts eight monks confirmed in the atrium, and the narration of the fight counts eleven. The report names no one, and the identification of its “older master” with Gyatso comes from the sequence of events.
  • The rifle that fired the rounds is given in this page as the standard four-round bolt-action rifle of the Imperial infantry, which the wiki dates to 80 BG. The source does not give its type number.
  • The sources disagree on dates. Azula is quoted placing the killing of the monks at “20 AG,” at the Southern Pole, and an Eastern Temple massacre at “1 AG.” Qianchan is said to have reclaimed the temple “eleven years” before the Avatar's visit, which does not sit easily with Hakoda's “almost a hundred years.” This page follows the wiki's date of 0 AG and does not reconcile the other dates.

See also

  • Air Nomad Genocide
  • Air Nomads
  • Aang
  • Hakoda

Source: Ash on Ice, ch. 37–40.

glass_chapel.title: Observation and Research Outpost 9
glass_chapel.html:
Observation and Research Outpost 9, known unofficially as the Glass Chapel, was a Fire Nation surveillance and research site built into a converted mountain temple above a city. The source does not name the temple or the city.

Observation and Research Outpost 9
TypeSurveillance and research outpost
Official nameObservation and Research Outpost 9
Unofficial nameThe Glass Chapel
LocationA mountain temple above a Fire Nation city; the city is not named

Conversion

The original stone walls still stood, but they were webbed with cables. The temple's domes had been replaced with radar dishes, its archways braced with rebar and sensor towers. The building clung to the cliff “like a scab grown around something trying to get out.”

Security

Fences, sandbag checkpoints and motion sensors surrounded the site. Its signs did not name it. The temple had no tourists, no monks and no flags. Nobody called it holy anymore, but people spoke more quietly when they parked.

Function

The source describes the site only as an observation and research outpost. At night an antenna on the spire blinked red, and glass plates beneath it lit faintly.

See also

  • Caldera City
  • Empire of Tajisaki

Source: Ash on Ice, ch. 17.

flame_in_her_heart.title: Flame in Her Heart
flame_in_her_heart.html:
Flame in Her Heart was an Imperial propaganda film of the war's late years. It was screened in the working districts of a Fire Nation city, and its premiere was attended by a full house that gave a standing ovation.

Flame in Her Heart
TypeFilm, propaganda
DateLate war, undated in the source
ScreeningsDistricts 3 and 5 of a Fire Nation city, among others

Premiere

At the premiere the lead actress, a former rig acrobat, gave the audience a speech. She said that four years before she had been “hanging from silk ropes,” and that the film was “not subtle. But then again, neither is this war.” The house roared. In the balcony, Mai stayed seated, kept her arms folded and did not clap.

Screenings and slogans

Loudspeakers on the streets played the film's victory anthem, slowed to a drag, in the city's working quarters. On a bridge over a black river, a red banner read: “THE WAR ENDS WHEN WE CRUSH THE REBELS.” The slogan was displayed as a public line. It is not identified as a quotation from the film.

Source notes

The sources give the film's title and the premiere speech. They do not describe its plot.

See also

  • Empire of Tajisaki
  • Hundred Year War

Source: Ash on Ice, ch. 16–17.

kanbukyoku.title: Kanbukyoku
kanbukyoku.html:
Kanbukyoku (literally the “Cabinet Bureau”) is the Empire's secret police, an internal bureau that operated in the occupied and home territories. The source identifies it by its insignia, a red circle with barbed spokes, which is painted on the body of a black Type-9 transport. In early 100 AG, Ozai gave control of it to Azula, who then ran Caldera.

Kanbukyoku
TypeSecret police
Formed2 AG, during the conquest of Yanakawa, by Sozin
InsigniaA red circle with barbed spokes
TransferEarly 100 AG, undated in the source; before the death of Ozai on 18 July 100 AG
Controlled byAzula, from early 100 AG

On 9 March 101 AG a Kanbukyoku squad came to the Lily House at Shu Jing, minutes after a Salvationist bomb, and was killed with Iroh.

Background

The Yanakawan Campaign began on 3 January 1 AG with a landing at the site of later Yu Dao. Within months the Empire held the coastal ports, but the interior of the peninsula was not secure. The Eastern Army's regional commands were stretched across hundreds of villages, and the provincial levies that Earth Kingdom officials had raised to resist them were scattered and poorly led. In the spring of 2 AG, villages across the peninsula began to rise. Supply convoys were ambushed in the passes, garrison posts went silent for days, and the army's reports showed a pattern that its own officers could not explain.

Formation (2 AG)

Sozin's answer was to take the problem away from the army. In 2 AG he issued an Imperial edict creating Kanbukyoku as a bureau of the Cabinet, reporting to the Fire Lord's council rather than to the General Staff or the regional commands. The Cabinet Bureau's remit was intelligence and the suppression of sedition in occupied territory. Its first officers were drawn from the civil administration and the old internal police, not from the army, which made it an object of resentment among the generals from the start.

The same edict created the Naikaku Jōhōkyōku (Cabinet Intelligence Bureau) as the intelligence branch of the new Cabinet Bureau, formed at the same time. Kanbukyoku was the security and policing arm, and Naikaku Jōhōkyōku gathered and analyzed the information on which its operations depended.

The reasons Sozin gave were practical. Army commanders reported what they could hold, not what they had lost, and the rebellions were growing in the gaps between commands. A bureau that answered only to the throne could compare reports across regions, pay informers directly, and question prisoners without the army's chain of command slowing or shielding it. The edict named the Cabinet Bureau's purpose as the “restoration of order and the identification of enemies of the throne.”

Early operations (2–10 AG)

In its first years the bureau built registers of every village on the peninsula, paid informers in grain and tax exemptions, and tracked the families of men who had gone into the hills. After each ambush, villages near the attack were searched, and those found to have shelter or supplies were punished collectively. The bureau's interrogations were not recorded, and its prisoners were usually sent to the Eastern Territories as labor, which is why many of the rebels' names survive only in the bureau's files.

The bureau did not end the rebellion. Its reports gave the Eastern Army the names of villages to burn, and the resulting reprisals drove more people into the hills. Yanakawa's rebels, later organized as the Yanakawan Liberation Front, traced their own origins to the reprisals of these years.

The transfer

Azula arrived at a Fire Nation outpost in a Type-9 transport with the Kanbukyoku insignia on its body. She wore the black coat of the internal bureau, with officer's silver on the sleeves. She told Zuko that their father had called it a “handoff,” that the city needed oversight, and that he had given her the Kanbukyoku. “I run Caldera now,” she said.

Facilities

A later scene refers to Kanbukyoku chambers in the south quarter of a Fire Nation facility, a room with red stone walls. The source does not say where the chambers are or what they were used for.

See also

  • Naikaku Jōhōkyōku
  • Azula
  • Ozai
  • Caldera City
  • Imperial Research Bureau

Source: Ash on Ice, ch. 34, 37.

naikaku_johokyoku.title: Naikaku Jōhōkyoku
naikaku_johokyoku.html:
Naikaku Jōhōkyoku (the Cabinet Intelligence Bureau) was the intelligence branch of the Empire's Cabinet Bureau. It was formed in 2 AG by the same Imperial edict as Kanbukyoku, the secret police it served.

Naikaku Jōhōkyoku
TypeIntelligence branch of the Cabinet Bureau
Formed2 AG, at the same time as Kanbukyoku
Reports toThe Fire Lord's council, not the General Staff
RoleGathering, analysis and counter-intelligence

Formation

The bureau was created in 2 AG by the same edict that formed Kanbukyoku, during the Yanakawan campaign. Where Kanbukyoku arrested, searched and interrogated, the intelligence branch collected reports from the provinces, compared them across commands, and told the throne which villages were dangerous and which officers were misreporting. It was the first Imperial body to combine these tasks in one place.

Work

The bureau ran informers in the occupied territories, intercepted correspondence between rebel villages, and kept files on commanders whose reports did not match what was happening in the field. Its analysts were the main source of the complaints that reached the Cabinet about army conduct, which made it unpopular with the General Staff from the start.

Comparison

For readers from outside the wiki's setting, the bureau's role resembles the American CIA in its intelligence work and the German Abwehr of the 1930s and 1940s in its counter-intelligence and informer networks. The name and structure follow Japan's Cabinet Intelligence Bureau of the 1940s.

See also

  • Kanbukyoku
  • Yanakawan Campaign
  • The Army–Navy divide

Source: user lore notes, 18 October 2026. Date of formation follows the Kanbukyoku page.

national_anthems.title: National anthems
national_anthems.html:
Each of the four great powers has a national anthem, in use by 170 AG. The texts below are English renderings. The dates and customs are the wiki's working draft and can be changed in the editor.

Fire Nation: Hi no Miyo (“The Reign of Flame”)

  • Adopted: Imperial hymn of the Empire of Tajisaki, kept as the national anthem by the Imperial Constitution of 119 AG.
  • Language: Tajisakian (English rendering below).
  • Form: A single tanka (five lines of 5, 7, 5, 7 and 7 syllables), sung slowly by massed voices.

Long may the flame-throne
burn on while the tides still turn,
until the cold peaks
are worn to drifting ember
and the sea forgets its shore.

It is sung at the opening of the National Diet, at the Fire Lord's accession, and at the close of the Day of Ash. Since the Commission on Imperial Conduct, the Veterans' League asks for the old war verses to stay dropped, while the Restoration Party wants nothing changed.

Qianchan Republic: The Charter Song

  • Adopted: Adopted by the Federal Assembly in 12 BG.
  • Language: Common Tongue.
  • Form: Eight lines, sung in unison by schools, assemblies and the army.

We raised this republic out of a hard-won peace;
its charter is our compass, its people are its source.
Let farmer, founder, soldier and scholar
keep faith with the law and with one another.
Work with courage, learn with patience, speak with candor;
many voices, one purpose, one pledge for all.
We govern ourselves and ask no one to kneel,
so may our republic endure.

Every school day in Qianchan begins with it, and every cabinet is sworn in to it. The line “ask no one to kneel” is the origin of the saying “we govern ourselves; we do not export governance”.

United Republic of Nations: Song of the Union

  • Adopted: Adopted by the National Assembly in 106 AG, four years after the Declaration of Union.
  • Language: Common Tongue, with the verses also sung in Hanwen, Tajisakian and Yanakawan on state occasions.
  • Form: Four verses and a refrain.

Verse 1

Where the old harbors faced the world
and the flags came down in spring,
we signed one name for many peoples
and called the peninsula home.

Verse 2

The cedar on the windward ridge
keeps its green through cold and storm;
so may our spirit stand unchanged
through every season of the year.

Verse 3

Over rice fields and rail-lined plains
the autumn sky is high and clear;
the lamps of the city and the sea-watch light
shine with one heart together.

Verse 4

With every hand that works, with every voice that sings,
in loyalty and in love,
let hardship be our shared and gladdened burden
and the republic our common joy.

Refrain

Many peoples, one republic,
hold it fast, from age to age.

The Council Head leads the singing at the start of each year, when the chair passes to the next seat. Each verse is dedicated in turn to a bending people, a custom that feeds the dispute over representation.

Earth Kingdom: The Unbroken Wall

  • Adopted: A court hymn of the Earth Kings, standardized after the Caldera Accord of 121 AG.
  • Language: Old court Earth Kingdom speech; the second verse is in the common tongue.
  • Form: Two verses. The second verse was added in 150 AG, when the Assembly of the Estates became fully elective.

Verse 1 (the court)

The wall stands whole, the realm is one;
three rings of stone enclose the throne.
May the granaries of earth be full,
the rivers keep their ancient course,
the King's long years be years of peace,
and the mountain's strength be strength to all.

Verse 2 (the Assembly)

Let those who till and those who trade
stand witness in the open hall;
as stone is laid on patient stone,
so may the kingdom grow in justice,
and all beneath one heaven prosper.

The first verse is sung at court and the second in the Assembly of the Estates, and the Loyalists and Reformers dispute whether both should be sung together.

See also

  • Empire of Tajisaki (Fire Nation)
  • Qianchan Republic
  • United Republic of Nations
  • Earth Kingdom

bst_siege_ends.title: Imperial armies leave Ba Sing Se
bst_siege_ends.html:
The Imperial armies have withdrawn from the approaches of the capital, ending a [[Siege of Ba Sing Se|siege]] that began on 14 February 96 AG and closed on 19 April 97 AG.

The Empire’s soldiers broke through the Outer Wall and the Inner Wall, and for one week held the Palace and the Forbidden City. They were driven out after a section of the Palace collapsed, officials of the city said.

The Palace

Inspectors have begun to assess the damage to the Palace. The collapsed section has been closed to the public, and the Forbidden City remains under guard until the inspection is complete.

The record

The [[Earth Kingdom]] and its allies in the [[Qianchan Republic]] count the result as a Coalition victory. No casualty figures have been released. The Ba Sing Se Times prints figures only when a named authority has confirmed them, and will report them when it can.

news.sub: Outer and Inner Walls stand after fourteen months
news.kick: The Siege of Ba Sing Se
deck: Outer and Inner Walls stand after fourteen months
Palace is back in the Earth King’s hands
news.src:
The Imperial armies have withdrawn from the approaches of the capital, ending a [[Siege of Ba Sing Se|siege]] that began on 14 February 96 AG and closed on 19 April 97 AG.

The Empire’s soldiers broke through the Outer Wall and the Inner Wall, and for one week held the Palace and the Forbidden City. They were driven out after a section of the Palace collapsed, officials of the city said.

## The Palace

Inspectors have begun to assess the damage to the Palace. The collapsed section has been closed to the public, and the Forbidden City remains under guard until the inspection is complete.

## The record

The [[Earth Kingdom]] and its allies in the [[Qianchan Republic]] count the result as a Coalition victory. No casualty figures have been released. The Ba Sing Se Times prints figures only when a named authority has confirmed them, and will report them when it can.

cs_consolidation.title: High Command reports orderly consolidation in the West
cs_consolidation.html:
The [[General Staff Directorate]] announces that the Imperial armies before Ba Sing Se were withdrawn in April 97 AG and consolidated for the next phase of the campaign.

The withdrawal was a decision of operational planning. Further announcements will follow.

Families of serving personnel are asked to direct inquiries to their district recruiting office. The Directorate will brief the [[National Diet]] in due course.

This statement is issued as an official communiqué and is printed in full.

rd_treaty_signed.title: A daily for the Republic
rd_treaty_signed.html:
The Republican Daily published its first edition today, seven months after the [[Treaty of Qinglan]] ended the Hundred Year War in law and recognized the [[United Republic of Nations]] as a legitimate state.

Who we are

The Daily was founded by press who covered the war for Gaozu and stayed to see it ended. In the months since, they have trained local staffers on the peninsula to write, check and set the paper, and it made more sense to found a new paper than to carry an old one across the sea.

The war ended in fact on 18 July 100 AG with the death of Ozai at the [[Battle of Qinglan Port]], but nobody signed anything until 28 April 105 AG. Five years of civil war, famine and the Yanakawan War of Independence lay between the two dates, and the Republic’s readers lived through all of them.

What we promise

The Republican Daily will report what happens next from the record. Council sessions will be quoted from the verbatim minutes, and every person named in a story will be offered a right of reply in the same edition.

qr_treaty_south.title: The south reads the treaty: peace, and a new neighbour
qr_treaty_south.html:
The Qianchan Republic joined the Coalition in 30 AG and stayed in it to the end. This paper has argued since 100 AG that the war should have been closed in law the day it closed in fact. Yesterday’s [[Treaty of Qinglan]] does that, five years late.

We do not say so to complain. We say so because the delay had a price, and the south paid part of it. Ships waited in harbors for papers that no authority could issue, because no authority could say who was at peace with whom. Contracts written before the war stayed unsettled because nobody could sign for a state that was still, in law, at war.

A new neighbour

The treaty also recognizes the [[United Republic of Nations]], born from the Empire’s former colonies. The [[Qianchan Republic]] has been a republic longer than most of the world has had the word, and it will judge the newcomer by how it keeps its borders and its trade, not by how it describes itself.

That is not unfriendly. It is how republics have always treated each other: by the record.

What we ask

We ask that the signatories publish the full text, that the offices responsible for enforcing it say plainly who is responsible for what, and that the figures on reparations and refugees be printed with the office that supplied them. This paper will print them in that way, and will say when a figure cannot be traced.

The war is over. The questions it left are not.

the_outlet_press_collective.title: The Outlet (press collective)
the_outlet_press_collective.html:
The Outlet is the international press collective of the four nations: a shared desk, wire and archive kept by the major newspapers, wire services and photo agencies of the [[Earth Kingdom]], the [[Qianchan Republic]], the [[United Republic of Nations]] and the [[Empire of Tajisaki]]. Members keep their own mastheads and their own editors. What they share is a dateline, a filing format and a code of practice.

Founding

The Outlet was founded on 19 March 187 BG. The newspapers of the day agreed to push the idea of a shared net of archives, so that a story filed in one capital could be read in all of them. It carries text only: photographs have not yet been made part of it. The idea took centuries to become the site that [[RAiKO OS]] terminals read around 190 AG.

Members

Gaozu was founded on 14 February 260 BG in Gaoling as the propaganda arm of the Beifong family. It is now the official newspaper of the government. It dates every dispatch by both calendars.

The Ba Sing Se Times was founded on 5 August 220 BG in Ba Sing Se with the help of the Avatar Kyoshi, and has been the Earth Kingdom’s paper of record ever since.

The Calderan Scire was founded on 29 January 150 BG in Caldera City, not long after the bankruptcy of the Scire, the capital’s earlier paper, which it came to replace.

The Republican Daily was founded on 3 December 105 AG by press who had covered the war for Gaozu and stayed on to see it ended. They trained local staffers on the Yanakawan Peninsula, and it made more sense to found a new paper for the new Republic than to carry an old one across the sea.

The Qianchan Report was founded on 10 June 170 AG as a politics paper for the Qianchan Republic. It widened from politics to international news, and it later gave up print to become a strictly online paper.

Photo agencies such as Zaofu Tupian, and news agencies such as the Imperial News Service, belong to the collective too and keep their own archives. Photographs travel by print plate, and the collective’s text archive carries only the caption line.

Code of practice

Every story carries a dateline, a signature or a desk credit, and the hour it was filed. Corrections run on the same page in the same type. Official statements are labelled as official statements. Casualty figures are printed only with a named authority. Each member adds rules of its own, which the collective prints beside the member’s name.

House style

Most of the archive follows the conventions of the older press: the inverted pyramid, datelines in capitals, narrow justified columns, banner headlines with italic decks, crossheads and an end mark. Stories are not written to a short limit; a report runs to at least a hundred words and usually several hundred, and a feature to a thousand or more. Members differ in small things: the order of day and month in a dateline, whether months are abbreviated, and how official statements are set.

The collective on RAiKO OS

Around 190 AG the collective’s site was read on [[RAiKO OS]] terminals. It is built to look like the web of that decade: serif headlines, small sans-serif sidebars, a search box, a printer-friendly link and a list of corrections beside the news.

raiko_os.title: RAiKO OS
raiko_os.html:
RAiKO OS is the desktop operating system sold by RepLIKA Tech Industries, in wide use around 190 AG; the release most terminals ran was version 4.2. Its look and abilities match the personal computers of the 1990s and early 2000s of our world: windowed desktops, a start menu, dial-up and early broadband networks, cathode-ray monitors, a web browser and an early web.

Terminals in the archive

The wiki’s reading terminals run RAiKO OS. Their logon screen is ceremonial: it asks for a password and has never checked one.

See also

[[The Outlet (press collective)]]

gz_grain_exchange.title: Autumn Grain Exchange Opens With Prices Held Level
gz_grain_exchange.html:
The autumn session of the Grain Exchange opened at the sixth hour with opening prices held level to those of the spring close, the Exchange Board announced.

The Board’s registrar said the granaries of the river provinces were reported full by the district offices, and that no member had asked to withdraw lots from the floor.

The Millers’ Association asked that payment terms be extended from thirty to forty-five days. The Board said it would hear the request on Monday.

* * *

The session continues until the evening bell.

the_kingdom_has_fallen.title: THE KINGDOM HAS FALLEN
the_kingdom_has_fallen.html:
Empress Hou-Ting was killed this morning when a bomb was thrown at her motorcade during the annual celebration of the founding of the Earth Kingdom. The attack set off a night of fighting in Ba Sing Se Square between the city garrison and armed rebels. It ended at 3 a.m., leaving parts of the capital burning, and the city is now under a state of emergency.

The 85th Infantry Division from Omashu was one of the units marching in the square as part of the celebration. Its company commander, Captain Kuvira Beifong, holds dual citizenship in the Qianchan Republic and the Earth Kingdom. She joined the army as a cadet and rose quickly through the ranks.

According to accounts of the fighting, the blast near the Empress’s motorcade killed her and many others and was followed by a firefight on all sides of the square. The rebels carried advanced weapons and explosives, and some used old, mechanized suits left over from the Hundred Year War. They outgunned the garrison near the royal palace. Captain Beifong and her company fought them through the night, and she took the lead in contacting other officers and units to coordinate efforts to retake the city.

Who carried out the attack has not been established. Some sources link it to the Red Lotus or the Equalist movement, which are active in the United Republic and elsewhere. At a military press conference, officials said signs of increased anarchist and Equalist activity had been seen in the weeks before the attack, and that the rebels appeared to have infiltrated the city with agents and weapons. They acknowledged that the military did not act on those warnings.

Why the warnings were missed is unclear. Some sources suggest corruption or collusion within the military ranks, though that is unconfirmed. The public is demanding an investigation and accountability for the security failure.

The succession is undecided, and the Kingdom waits to learn who will rule. Governments abroad are watching closely, fearing that the instability in Ba Sing Se could lead to a civil war.

the_kingdom_is_whole.title: THE KINGDOM IS WHOLE!
the_kingdom_is_whole.html:
Five years to the day after the Earth Queen’s assassination in this square, Generalissimo Kuvira stood on the same spot yesterday and declared the civil war over.

Her armies marched past in ranks that filled the square and spilled into the avenues beyond. Tens of thousands of citizens watched. The parade was unlike any in the Kingdom’s history. Eastern Army regulars marched beside the western divisions that once followed King Shikaei of Omashu. Behind them came republican volunteers, former provincial militias and the mountaineer division that took the northern temples. A year ago these men were in opposing camps. Yesterday they wore one insignia and carried one banner.

“This is not the triumph of one army over another,” said Chen Yulan, The Generalissimo’s spokesman

Speaking from the reviewing stand. “It is the unity of every sector of this nation. The soldier, the farmer, the clerk and the former royalist have agreed that one person can lead them through the rebuilding. They have chosen Kuvira.”

The spokesman said the accord had been reached in recent weeks by representatives of the army, the provincial councils and what he called “the remaining civic bodies of the Kingdom.” He did not say who those bodies were, how they were chosen, or whether a written agreement exists. Asked whether a vote had been held, he said “the people have spoken in the square.”

The Generalissimo addressed the crowd for twelve minutes. She promised bread, roads and a restored capital, and she called the end of the war “the beginning of the work.” She also proclaimed herself Generalissimo Minister of the Earth State, a title she said would remain until “the nation no longer needs a general to hold it together.”

Some observers abroad use a different name. Critics in several capitals have called her the Empress of the Earth Empire, a title they say better fits the powers she has gathered. Government officials rejected the label. “The Earth State has no empress,” said the spokesman. “It has a servant who has chosen to carry a heavy burden.”

Reconstruction crews began clearing the wrecked northern districts this week. Officials say the Harmonist strongholds of the central lands are under control, and the last Equalist positions in the northwest have fallen. Isolated pockets of resistance may remain in the mountain valleys. Authorities are asking citizens to report anyone sheltering armed fugitives.

Foreign delegations attended the ceremony, including envoys from the Qianchan Republic. Their governments have not yet said whether they will recognize the new title.

The Generalissimo left the reviewing stand at dusk. The lamps along the square were lit for the first time since the war began.

generalissimo_or_dictator.title: Generalissimo or Dictator?
generalissimo_or_dictator.html:
Envoys from Qianchan, the Fire Nation and the United Republic sat together at the Victory Day parade, and several said afterward that their governments had weighed an uncomfortable question. Kuvira’s “Earth State” may be the least bad option available.

The question was open on the reviewing stand. The Generalissimo had proclaimed herself Generalissimo Minister, and critics abroad call her an empress in all but name. Her armies were still marching when a Fire Nation attaché said his government “would not welcome a restored crown or a collapsed state and has no other candidates on the table.”

Qianchan’s delegation was led by Deputy Foreign Minister Shen Lihua. Speaking to correspondents afterward, she stressed that attendance did not amount to recognition. “We came to observe,” she said. “We observed an army that is disciplined, a capital that is being fed and a war that has stopped. We also observed that the same person holds the army, the ministries and the ceremony.”

Qianchan’s position has its own history. The Generalissimo is a dual citizen who trained under Qianchan doctrine, and officials in Gaoling have long admitted they are interested in what she becomes. Ms. Shen said that interest was “practical, not sentimental.”

The strongest argument for patience came from the United Republic. Ambassador Teodor Halloran told journalists that the Equalist insurgency has moved into open conflict in Republic City and across the republic’s eastern districts. President Raiko’s government has fought it for months, with Qianchan advisers and supplies helping behind the lines. “A stable Earth Kingdom does not solve our problem,” Mr. Halloran said. “An unstable one hands the insurgents a second front and a refuge.”

Mira Castellan, a correspondent for the Republican Daily who travelled with the delegation, put the dilemma more bluntly. “Every foreign capital here is doing the same sum,” she told this agency. “A strongman who keeps order, or a vacuum the Equalists and the Red Lotus would be glad to use. Nobody is saying she is good. They are saying the alternative is worse.”

The Avatar did not attend. Her aides said she remains in Republic City, occupied with the Equalist crisis, and that she sent no message to the parade. Korra’s absence was noted by delegates; several of whom said an Avatar’s presence might have carried some moral weight to the ceremony.

The Generalissimo’s office produced no evidence of the “agreement among all sectors” it announced. Diplomats said they had been given no written accord or list of signatories. Ms. Shen said her government would “watch what is built, not what is said.”

The delegations leave Ba Sing Se tomorrow. None has announced recognition of the Earth State. None has refused it either.
