cs_report_176.title: The Union’s last election: 40 seats, all in eight provinces
cs_report_176.html:
The Union won 40 seats on Feb. 2, 176 AG, down 22 from 172 AG, while The People’s Coalition took 278, its largest total in the archive. All 40 Union seats are in its eight core provinces.

The vote was held as the situation abroad worsened. Uprisings in at least seven nations had been reported by January, and the Concord of Nations had announced it would take up the question of the Equalist parties. Union candidates campaigned knowing a ban was possible.

“We are going to be on the ballot, and they are going to have to explain to our voters why we should not be,” Union leader Haruo Sakane said in Umi on Jan. 24. His party won 10 seats there, the most in any province, followed by Yahahama with nine and Kikonokawa with six.

The Union lost seats in all eight core provinces, and five provinces changed hands in total. Shinkawa, Yahahama and Takahama went from the Union to The People’s Coalition. Hoshima moved from independents to The People’s Coalition.

The People’s Coalition gained as voters moved to the largest party of the left that could not be linked to the uprisings. The SDP won 152 seats, making it the largest single party. PDP leader Daichi Oyama said the result showed “a country that wants reform without a revolution.” The Way held 128 seats.

Turnout was 69.0%, down from 72.0% in 172 AG, with about 101.5 million votes cast.

Within six weeks the Concord of Nations banned the Equalist Party, The Collective and Salvation Front and ordered the Union’s MPs to vacate their seats. The 40 seats won in this election were never filled.

cs_bombings_178.title: Bombings hit Caldera and cities across the country; snap election called
cs_bombings_178.html:
A series of bombings struck Caldera and cities across the country on Sept. 12, 178 AG, killing at least 61 people and injuring several hundred, officials said. The attacks came on the same day as bombings in capitals and major regional cities across the world, and the Lord’s council called a snap National Diet election for November.

Explosions were reported within about 40 minutes of each other in Caldera, Yahahama, Umi and four other cities. Targets included rail stations, two government depots and the offices of the provincial assembly in Takahama. The Calderan Scire has confirmed damage at all of them.

No group has claimed responsibility. The government blamed what it called “the remnants of the banned parties” within hours, and leftist networks it says survived the 176 AG ban. The Equalist Party, The Collective and Salvation Front had been dissolved by order of the Concord of Nations in March 176 AG. Former Union leader Haruo Sakane denied any link. “We have not held an office, a meeting or a bank account in two years,” he said in a statement on Sept. 13.

Foreign governments reported attacks within the same hours. Officials said explosions were recorded in capitals and regional centers on every side of the continent, and the Calderan Scire has confirmed that Equalist groups claimed several of them. Fire Nation officials called the timing “no coincidence.” The most severe fighting was in the United Republic of Nations, where the attacks were followed by an open declaration of war (see the Calderan Scire’s report from Sept. 14).

Mitsuko Aramaki, chair of NCP, said the attacks proved that the ban had been “too late and too narrow.” Daichi Oyama said the PDP would back any measure that “protects the public and keeps the Diet open.”

The council announced the snap election on Sept. 13. It will be held in November, outside the traditional Feb. 2 date. Officials said the Diet needed a new mandate to deal with security and that provinces affected by the attacks would get extra polling staff.

The election will be the first without any party of the Union. Pollsters at the Calderan Scire expect The Way and The People’s Coalition to compete for the seats vacated in 176 AG.

Curfews were in force in Caldera, Umi and Yahahama on Sunday night. Rail service to the capital resumed in the afternoon.

cs_report_178.title: Snap election after bans and bombings produces hung Diet
cs_report_178.html:
NCP and PDP together took 404 of 466 seats in the National Diet snap election in November 178 AG and formed the Reformation government. The SDP fell to 14 seats. Turnout was 85.0%, the highest in the archive.

The vote came seven weeks after bombings struck Caldera and other cities, and it was the first held without any party of the Union. The election was held outside the traditional Feb. 2 date.

The campaign was dominated by the inquiry. Investigators said on Oct. 20 that the bombings were carried out by remnants of the People’s Earth Union with help from leftist networks that survived the ban, and that members of the Diet were involved. Four of the 11 people named in warrants were still at large on election day.

NCP won 214 seats. PDP took 190. Together, the two parties govern with a margin of 170 over the 234-seat majority line, and they signed a coalition agreement on Nov. 6 that gives each a half of the cabinet.

“The country asked for order, and we are going to deliver it,” NCP chair Mitsuko Aramaki said. PDP leader Daichi Oyama said the Reformation government would “rebuild the relief accounts, the rail network and the public’s trust, in that order.”

The SDP’s collapse is the largest single-party drop in the archive. The party had held 152 seats in 176 AG. Three of its sitting members were named in arrest warrants on Oct. 20, in the inquiry into the Sept. 12 bombings, and the party expelled them. Voters moved to PDP in the provinces that had previously gone to the SDP and the Union, and to NCP in the eastern provinces.

Eleven provinces changed hands from 176 AG, including Kikonokawa, which moved from the Union to The Way, and Kiyora, Yahafurano and several others from The People’s Coalition to The Way.

With no Union on the ballot, the former Union provinces split. Umi, Yahahama, Takahama and Shirashihoro all returned majorities for NCP or PDP candidates, and turnout in those provinces was above 85%.

Haruo Sakane, the former Union leader, said in a statement that the election “was held with a third of the country’s voters unable to cast the ballot they wanted.” The government said all eligible voters could stand or vote.

The Reformation government takes office on Nov. 12. Its first act will be an inquiry into the 171 AG relief fund.

cs_investigation_178.title: Investigators trace bombings to People’s Earth Union remnants; warrants issued for Diet members
cs_investigation_178.html:
Investigators said on Oct. 20, 178 AG, that the Sept. 12 bombings were carried out by remnants of the People’s Earth Union, the movement left over from the first civil war, with help from leftist networks that survived the 176 AG ban. Courts have issued arrest warrants for 11 people, including members of the National Diet.

The findings were presented to the Lord’s council and the Diet’s security committee by the inquiry chief, Kenji Hoshiba. He said the cells that planted the devices in Caldera, Yahahama, Umi and Takahama had been formed from veterans and descendants of the People’s Earth Union that fought in the first civil war and went underground after its defeat. Some of its old couriers and depots, he said, were never dismantled.

Hoshiba said the Fire Nation attacks were timed to match the Equalist bombings abroad on the same day. Messages recovered in Umi, he said, referred to “the day of the capitals” and used the same code words as documents seized in other nations, which points to one plan coordinated across borders.

The inquiry links the cells to the banned parties through money and housing. Records seized in Umi and Yahahama show that accounts frozen by the Concord of Nations in March 176 AG were emptied weeks before the freeze, and that the money passed through shell companies owned by former Union officials. “The ban closed the offices,” Hoshiba said. “It did not close the network.”

Of the 11 warrants, six are for former Union MPs evicted from the Diet in 176 AG. Three are for sitting MPs of the SDP and two for sitting MPs of Agrarian Labor. Investigators allege the sitting members passed committee schedules and security briefings to the cells and arranged safe houses in their home provinces. The Diet voted on Oct. 20 to lift their immunity, 301 to 63.

Seven of the 11 are in custody. Four remain at large, among them one of the former Union MPs. Police said the search has focused on the border provinces.

The SDP said it had expelled its three members and would cooperate. “If this is true, they betrayed this party and the voters who sent them,” SDP chair Reiko Tanabe said. Agrarian Labor said it was reviewing the allegations against its two members.

Haruo Sakane, who is not among those named, called the inquiry “a trial by press release” and said the former Union members would answer any charge in open court. Investigators said he is a witness and not a suspect.

NCP chair Mitsuko Aramaki said the findings “proved what we said in September.” PDP leader Daichi Oyama said the government should publish the evidence in full, “so that no voter has to take any party’s word for it.”

The findings land three weeks before the snap election. Pollsters at the Calderan Scire said the SDP’s support dropped sharply in surveys taken after Oct. 20.

cs_urn_war_178.title: Equalists declare open war on the United Republic, strike Yudao and Republic City
cs_urn_war_178.html:
Equalist forces declared open war on the United Republic of Nations on Sept. 12, 178 AG, and struck Yudao and Republic City on the same day, targeting the republic’s economic and political centers. The attacks were part of coordinated bombings in capitals and regional cities around the world.

The United Republic is the heartland of the Equalist movement’s struggle, and officials in Republic City said the strikes were meant to destroy its two houses at once. Yudao is the republic’s main commercial hub and Republic City is its seat of government. Attackers hit the exchange district and the harbor works in Yudao, and the council precinct and two rail terminals in Republic City, according to accounts reaching the Calderan Scire.

The republic’s response was immediate. Security councils in both cities sealed their districts and ordered garrison units to the streets. The government said it would answer the declaration of war “with every means the republic holds.” Casualty figures have not been released. Travelers reaching the Fire Nation’s ports described fires in the Yudao exchange district and a curfew in Republic City.

The war lands on a nation already divided. Over the past several years the republic has split between those who want to negotiate with the Equalists, those who want the movement crushed, and a growing group that blames both the government and the movement for the unrest. Council sessions in Republic City have broken down twice this year. Officials in Yudao said some businesses had already moved funds abroad before the attacks.

The Equalists’ plan, according to a statement distributed in several nations, is to “cut the house of trade and the house of rule at the same time.” Analysts at the Calderan Scire said the targets suggest an attempt to damage the republic’s economy and its government together, so that neither could support the other. Whether the attacks worked is unclear. Both cities were still operating on Sept. 14, with disruptions.

The Fire Nation has offered the republic aid and is reviewing its own security. Lord’s officials said the Sept. 12 bombings in Caldera and other cities were “part of the same operation.” An inquiry into the Fire Nation attacks is under way.

The Concord of Nations will meet in an emergency session this week to discuss a joint response.

clashes_at_shu_jing.title: Clashes at Shu Jing
clashes_at_shu_jing.html:
Clashes at Shu Jing
Part ofThe early stage of the Fire Nation Civil War
Date6 October 100 – January 101 AG
LocationShu Jing industrial center, Fire Nation: the factories, rail yards and worker districts on the north bank of the river
ResultRoyalist victory. The Royalists hold the industrial center, which becomes their base for the rest of the war
Belligerents
Royalists (Restoration Government), including defected garrison unitsOzai loyalists (the Court), including units of the Flame Guard and the General Staff Directorate
Commanders and leaders
Royalists
Zuko; Iroh (negotiations); Lieutenant Colonel Mori Tatsuo (local command)		Court
Azula; Major General Hirata Gensai (field command)
Strength
Royalists
about 9,000 at the start, about 15,000 by December		Court
about 14,000 at the start, about 11,000 by January (figures vary by source)
Casualties and losses
About 4,000 killed, of whom about 1,600 were soldiers and about 2,400 civilians and factory workers

The Clashes at Shu Jing, also called the Battle of the Yards in Royalist usage and the Shu Jing disturbance in Court records, were the first fighting of the Fire Nation Civil War. From 6 October 100 AG to mid-January 101 AG, units of the same army fought one another for the factories, rail yards and worker districts of the Shu Jing industrial center, on the north bank of the river. There were no front lines in the ordinary sense, units changed sides in the middle of the fighting, and the battle was decided by who held the rail yards and the bridges, not by who held the ground around them. About 4,000 people died, of whom about 1,600 were soldiers and about 2,400 were civilians and factory workers.

The Royalists, who supported Zuko and the Diet, held the center at the end of the fighting, and Shu Jing became their base for the rest of the war. The Court, which supported Azula, lost its only substantial garrison in the north and with it the rail link between the capital and the industrial heartland. The clashes are counted as the first of the war's twenty defining battles. They showed, in miniature, the pattern that the war followed: it was fought not between two armies but by one army divided against itself, regiment by regiment and often officer by officer. Royalist sources describe the battle as the war's first decisive victory. Court records put the dead at under 1,000 and describe the fighting as a disturbance among the garrison.

Background

Shu Jing before the war

Shu Jing was the largest industrial center in the northern archipelago. It lay on both banks of a wide river about 200 kilometers from Caldera, and its steel foundries, locomotive works and munitions plants supplied a large part of the Empire's army during the Hundred Year War. Its rail yards connected the capital with the Eastern Territories and the southern ports, and the river gave it access to the sea by barge. By 100 AG it had a population of about 450,000, of whom about 120,000 worked in the foundries and works. The north bank, where the heavy industry stood, was divided into the foundry districts around the Eastgate and Canal yards, the locomotive works and the worker tenements of the Ironmonger Street district. The south bank held the administrative quarter, the Ministry of War Production's headquarters, the passenger terminal and the garrison's barracks.

The center was run by the Ministry of War Production, whose managers had built it up during the war. The garrison consisted of regular army units, among them the 3rd Rail Security Regiment, together with detachments of the Flame Guard and a security detachment of the Ministry of Truth. The foundry workers, who numbered about 30,000 in the north-bank works, had been held to their jobs by wartime regulations and were paid in part in rations. Their grievances in the final year of the war, which were chiefly about pay and the length of the shifts, had made the center one of the more restless in the Empire, though there had been no open disorder before the summer of 100.

The succession crisis

The death of Fire Lord Ozai at Qinglan Port on 18 July 100 AG opened the succession crisis that led to the war. The General Staff Directorate arranged the Privy Council's vote in favor of Azula, over the objection of the Diet, which had held that the succession should go to Zuko. Zuko left Caldera on 5 August. In the confrontation between the Diet and the Court in the same month 31 people were killed, and it became clear that no settlement would be possible. Garrisons across the Empire began declaring for one side or the other in the weeks that followed. Fuller accounts of these events are given in the article on the Fire Nation Civil War.

Shu Jing was divided from the start. The Ministry's managers and most of the foundry workers favored Zuko, who had promised to continue wartime wages and to put the Diet's veterans' bill into law. The garrison commander, Colonel Takamura Seiichi, was a Court appointee who had held the post since 98 and who regarded the Diet's resolutions as unlawful. Between August and early October the center had two sets of orders, two rationing systems and, for a week in September, two telegraph offices. The Ministry's managers continued to supply the garrison out of the center's stocks, and the garrison did not interfere with the foundries, a state of affairs that several historians have described as a truce by neglect.

Iroh, who joined Zuko in August, visited the center twice in secret in September to speak to the officers of the regional commands around the city. His principal contacts were Brigadier Ito Shigeru, who commanded the East Rail Regional Emergency Command, and Colonel Aida Ryo of the 3rd Rail Security Regiment. The meetings did not produce a declaration, but they established the channels by which the units around the city later declared for Zuko. The Court, whose agents in the center reported the visits, sent an inspection party to relieve Aida of his command in October, and its arrival was the immediate cause of the fighting.

Forces and commanders

Royalists

The Royalist force in the center was not an army in the usual sense. It consisted of the 3rd Rail Security Regiment, about 1,100 men, which declared for Zuko on 8 October; about 3,000 armed foundry workers, organized as the Works Guard under Mori Tatsuo; naval infantry detached from the river flotilla, about 600 men, who joined in the second week; and the East Rail Regional Emergency Command, an independent force of about 2,500 that declared on 19 October. The veterans' volunteer companies sent by the Diet's supporters in the south began to arrive in November and numbered about 3,000 by December. The Royalist strength was therefore about 9,000 at the start of the fighting and about 15,000 by December.

The Royalist local commander was Lieutenant Colonel Mori Tatsuo, who had been the deputy commander of the 3rd Rail Security Regiment. Mori, who was 38, had joined the army from the foundry districts of Shu Jing and had served as a staff officer during the Hundred Year War, and his connections with the workers allowed him to organize the Works Guard in the first days. Zuko, who was in the south at the time, directed the overall strategy by telegraph. Iroh was responsible for negotiations with the regional commands, and was present in the center for about a week in November.

The Court

The Court's force consisted of the Shu Jing garrison command, which had about 3,500 men, two battalions of the Flame Guard, a security detachment of the Ministry of Truth, an armored company equipped with Tessho-III tanks, and a company of Breaker Mk II power armor. Its strength was about 14,000 at the start of the fighting, including units that were later disarmed, and about 11,000 by January. Reinforcements arrived from Caldera in two detachments of the Kanbukyoku, the secret police, of which the second was turned back in November. The field command was held first by Colonel Takamura and, from December, by Major General Hirata Gensai, who was sent from the capital with orders to hold the center at any cost.

Azula directed the Court's operations from Caldera, and the records of the General Staff Directorate show that she took a close interest in the fighting at Shu Jing and issued orders by telegraph several times a day in the first fortnight. Her instructions were that the garrison hold the rail yards and the river bridges and that it not negotiate with the Royalists. These orders were obeyed by the Flame Guard and the Ministry detachments and generally disregarded by the regular units, which accounts in part for the speed with which some of them changed sides.

Equipment

Neither side had much heavy equipment in the first week of the fighting. The Court held the garrison's armored company, about 18 tanks, and its single Breaker company of eight machines. The Royalists held the foundries, which could repair vehicles but not produce them quickly. The most useful weapons in the first month were rifles, locomotives and the bridges across the river. The Royalist workers made grenades and satchel charges in the foundries from the second day, and used them against the Court's armor in the Ironmonger Street district. The Court's artillery consisted of a battery of field guns and two heavy howitzers in the fort on the south bank, which were used against the north-bank districts in December.

The armies identified themselves by armbands, which were changed more than once during the battle. The first armbands, which were improvised on 7 October from strips of cloth and red foundry rags, were worn by the Royalists. The Court's troops wore the black bands of the Flame Guard until the middle of the month, when they adopted a yellow cloth to avoid confusion with defected units that had taken black. By November the colors were changed daily, and the clash is remembered in the Fire Nation as the "fortnight of armbands."

Course

The Eastgate rail yard (6–8 October)

The first shots were fired on the evening of 6 October at the Eastgate rail yard, when the Court's inspection party, an officer of the General Staff Directorate with a platoon of Flame Guard, arrived to relieve Colonel Aida Ryo of the 3rd Rail Security Regiment for refusing the Court's orders. A crowd of several hundred workers from the evening shift had gathered outside the yard gate, having heard of the party's arrival. According to Royalist accounts, the party opened fire on the crowd when it did not disperse. Court accounts say that the regiment's sentries fired first. Eleven people died that night, among them four workers and two soldiers of the regiment, and about thirty were wounded. The inspection party withdrew to the garrison barracks on the south bank, having lost its officer.

By the morning of 7 October the regiment had sealed the yard. Aida, who had been wounded in the first exchange, was taken to the yard's infirmary, and command passed to his deputy, Lieutenant Colonel Mori Tatsuo. Mori called the regiment's officers together at six in the morning and put the question to them. About two thirds voted to resist the Court's order, and about a dozen officers left the yard in the course of the day. The regiment declared for Zuko on 8 October, in a telegram sent from the yard's signal cabin to the Royalist headquarters in the south. It was followed on the same day by the foundry committees, who voted to place the Works Guard under Mori's command.

The first week (9–12 October)

The fighting spread to the adjacent districts over the following five days. Mori, with about 400 soldiers of the regiment and about 1,000 armed workers, took the locomotive works on 8 and 9 October, and used its sheds as a base. The Court's garrison commander, Colonel Takamura Seiichi, countered by taking the main telegraph exchange on the south bank and the river bridges, which cut the city in half. The Court's control of the telegraph was of lasting importance, because it allowed the garrison to send orders to the units in the city and to cut the Royalists' communications with the south for most of the first fortnight.

On 9 October a Court armored company of about 18 tanks, with a company of infantry, attacked the Royalist line in the Ironmonger Street district from the east. The district was a quarter of narrow streets between the foundry walls and the tenements, and the tanks could not maneuver. Workers who had taken positions in the upper floors disabled the lead vehicles with charges that had been made in the foundries the day before, and the column was stopped at the cross street by the burning wrecks of its first three tanks. The Court's infantry withdrew to the river, and the company lost six of its tanks and about forty men. The Breaker company was held back by the Court's command and was not committed until 11 October, when it cleared a block of tenements but could not hold it without infantry support. Its machines were withdrawn across the river in the evening.

By 12 October neither side had a decisive advantage. The Royalists held the north bank from the Eastgate yard to the Canal yard, together with the locomotive works and the foundries. The Court held the south bank, the passenger terminal, the river bridges and the Central yard, which lay on the north bank near the water. About 700 people had died, most of them civilians who had been caught in the street fighting.

The fight for the yards (13 October – November)

From the middle of October the fighting centered on the rail yards. The Royalists held the Eastgate and Canal yards, and the Court held the Central yard and the passenger terminal. Both sides needed the line to the south: the Royalists to receive reinforcements and supplies from the Diet's supporters, the Court to bring troops from Caldera. The yards were fought over with locomotives and rolling stock as well as rifles, and a number of engines were used as rams against the barricades.

On 19 October the East Rail Regional Emergency Command, an independent force of about 2,500 that had been negotiating with both sides, declared for Zuko after a meeting with Iroh. Its commander, Brigadier Ito Shigeru, brought his troops into the city by train and took the Central yard on 21 October in a night attack in which his troops cut the Court's signal wires and entered through the coal sidings. The Court counterattacked on 24 October with a battalion of the Kanbukyoku that had been brought by rail from Caldera, and retook the passenger terminal, though not the Central yard. In the street fighting that followed, three units changed sides, two of them in the middle of a firefight, and a Royalist company was fired on by its own artillery in the Canal district.

The Royalists described the period as "the fortnight of armbands." Soldiers tied strips of colored cloth to their sleeves to avoid being shot by their friends, and the colors were changed daily. Several accounts describe officers who found themselves commanding companies that had changed sides during the night, and one battalion commander, Major Harada Isamu, is recorded to have fought on both sides in a single week. The confusion was most marked in the districts around the passenger terminal, where the lines were no more than a street wide.

In early November the Royalists cut the Court's rail connection to Caldera by blowing the Kuroishi viaduct, a stone structure about forty kilometers west of the city. The operation was carried out by a party of workers and soldiers from the locomotive works under a foundry engineer, Sakurai Daiki, who placed the charges at night under the noses of a Court patrol. The explosion destroyed two of the viaduct's five arches. It isolated the Court's garrison in the city and ended its reinforcements. A second Kanbukyoku detachment, which arrived at the viaduct on 12 November, was turned back, and the Court never again had an effective supply line to Shu Jing.

Iroh in the center (November)

Iroh spent about a week in Shu Jing in November, at the Lily House near the Eastgate yard, where he met the officers of three regional commands. His purpose was to persuade them to declare for Zuko or, if they would not, to remain neutral. He succeeded with two of the three, and the East Rail command's declaration in October was followed in November by the declarations of the North Canal and Harbor Commands. Contemporary accounts describe him as spending most of his time in the kitchen of the Lily House, where he made tea for the officers who came to see him and refused to discuss the war until they had finished it. One of the officers, who later served in the Royalist army, wrote that he had "never lost an argument so pleasantly."

The Court's agents reported Iroh's presence to Caldera, and Azula ordered the Flame Guard to arrest him. A raid on the Lily House on 14 November found the building empty, and Iroh left the center the next day under the protection of the Works Guard. The incident, which contributed to the Court's reputation among the workers for heavy-handedness, is the origin of the story that Iroh was the real author of the Royalist victory at Shu Jing. Royalist historians reject it. They point out that the military result was the work of Mori and Ito, and that Iroh's contribution was in the field of persuasion.

Winter and collapse (December – January)

The winter was the most costly period for the civilians. The foundries closed in the cold, rations were short, and the fighting moved into residential districts, where both sides used buildings as strongpoints. The Court's artillery on the south bank shelled the Works Guard's districts on at least four occasions in December, killing about 600 people. The Royalists responded by evacuating about 20,000 residents to the south by rail, using the line that had been opened from the Canal yard after the destruction of the Kuroishi viaduct had made the western line useless to the Court.

The turning point was the surrender of the Court's armored company on 17 December, after it ran out of fuel and ammunition. The company's remaining twelve tanks were handed over to the Royalists, who put them into service in the Works Guard. Hirata Gensai, who had been sent from Caldera and who had taken personal command of the garrison on 3 December, held the passenger terminal and the Ministry's headquarters with about 1,500 men until the second week of January. His defense was effective in the sense that it cost the Royalists about 600 dead in the final month, but it had no prospect of relief.

On 11 January 101, after a night assault by the Works Guard and the East Rail command on the terminal, the garrison withdrew by river to the west in barges that Hirata had assembled at the Ministry's wharf. About 300 of its soldiers stayed behind and surrendered. By 14 January the Royalists held every yard and foundry in the center. Hirata reached the Court's lines with about 1,100 men and was received at Caldera, where the General Staff Directorate regarded the defense as honorable and the result as unavoidable.

Communications and the telegraph war

The fighting at Shu Jing was accompanied from the first night by a struggle for control of communications. The center had three telegraph offices: the main exchange on the south bank, the railway telegraph in the Eastgate signal cabin, and the Ministry of War Production's private line, which ran in a cable beside the Kuroishi viaduct. The Court held the main exchange from 8 October, and used it to send orders to the regional commands and to block the Royalists' messages to the south. The Royalists answered by running a field telephone line along the river to the naval infantry's post at the estuary, from which messages were taken by boat to the southern ports.

The Eastgate signal cabin, in which Nomura Jiro kept his log, became the Royalist headquarters on 8 October. The log, which survives, records 211 telegrams sent and 340 received between 7 and 20 October. It shows that the Royalist command in the south, which was nominally under Zuko, was in fact directed by a small committee of the Diet's supporters, and that Zuko himself sent only four messages in the period, of which two concerned Iroh's movements. The log also records the first message from the East Rail command, on 11 October, in which Ito Shigeru asked, in the formal language of the army, "to be informed of the conditions on which a regional command might retain its honor."

The Court's telegraph office was equally busy. The records of the General Staff Directorate contain about 160 messages to the garrison in the first fortnight, most of them signed by Azula's secretary. They show that the Court's command did not understand the situation in the center until the third week, and that its orders, which called for the arrest of all the officers of the 3rd Rail Security Regiment and the shooting of ringleaders, were impossible to carry out. After the destruction of the Kuroishi viaduct the Court's telegraph line to the city was cut, and the garrison communicated with Caldera by courier and by heliograph until its withdrawal.

Tactics and the use of locomotives

The fighting at Shu Jing was a battle of the railway as much as of the streets, and both sides used rolling stock as weapons and as cover. The Royalists armored three engines in the locomotive works with boiler plate and used them as mobile strongpoints on the Eastgate and Canal spurs. The Court answered with two armored cars taken from the garrison's rail security detachment, which were mounted with machine guns and used in the Central yard. A number of runaway trains were sent against barricades on both sides. The best known is the coal train that was released from the Canal yard on 26 October and that destroyed the Court's barricade at the foot of the passenger terminal, at the cost of the driver's life.

The yards also determined the movement of reinforcements. The Royalist units that arrived from the south came by train, and the East Rail command used its own rolling stock to enter the city. The Court's Kanbukyoku battalions arrived on the line from the west, and were held in the Central yard until the first one had assembled its equipment. These constraints meant that the battle was largely a struggle for the switches and the signal cabins, and a handful of men could close a yard to an army. In the Canal yard, a signalman named Ohtani Gin held a switch cabin alone for eleven hours on 22 October, preventing the Court's armored cars from passing, and is remembered in the railway workers' songs.

In the streets the fighting resembled the later battles in the war, with the difference that neither side had learned the methods of urban warfare. Both used buildings as strongpoints, and both suffered heavily from the fires that spread in the tenements. The Royalists developed a system of firebreaks, created by pulling down the wooden houses at the edge of the worker districts, and the Works Guard's fire companies saved the foundry district on at least three occasions. The Court's soldiers were mostly firebenders, and used their abilities to clear rooms and barricades, which led to a number of fires that burned out of control. Royalist accounts say that the Court's firebending was the single largest cause of civilian deaths in the first week.

Political effects in the Diet and the Council

The fighting at Shu Jing had political effects well beyond the city. In the Diet, which had split between Zuko's supporters and the minority that favored accommodation with the Court, the news of the shooting at Eastgate was a factor in the vote of 14 October, in which a majority of the Diet's members who were in the south endorsed Zuko's claim. The Court's Privy Council, which had been divided over the succession, closed ranks after the loss of the center and issued a proclamation on 20 January declaring the Royalists to be rebels. The proclamation, which listed the Royalist leaders by name, remained in force for the whole war.

The effect on the regional commands was perhaps the most important. The East Rail command's declaration of 19 October was followed by those of several other commands in the following months, and the sight of a unit changing sides without a battle was taken by many of the officers as a signal that the Court could not hold the Empire. By the spring of 101, about a third of the Empire's regional commands had declared for Zuko, and about a quarter for the Court. The remainder, which included most of the Eastern commands, waited for the outcome of the spring campaign. The Court's recovery in the spring, which began with the capture of Hōryū Pass, was therefore achieved against a background of continuing defections.

Civilian experience

The workers

The foundry workers were at the center of the battle in a way that the civilians of the other early battles were not. Most of them lived within a short walk of the works, and the works were the strongpoints of the Royalist line. The foundry committees, which had been formed in the late summer to negotiate wages, were the basis of the Works Guard, and their members took up arms in the first week. The Guard was organized by shop: the rolling mill, the locomotive works and the munitions plant each formed a company, and the companies elected their own officers, subject to Mori's approval. Contemporary accounts describe a force that was poorly drilled but that knew the ground and was capable of improvising, and the use of foundry equipment as weapons, including a cart-mounted ladle that was used to pour slag on the Court's tanks, became a part of the battle's folklore.

Women formed about a third of the labor force of the north-bank works, and they were active in the defense. The records of the Works Guard list about 700 women who served in the first week, in the first-aid teams, the ammunition shops and the signal service, and a smaller number who served as riflemen. The best known is Kuwabara Haruko, a crane operator at the Canal yard, who is credited with the improvised charges that stopped the Court's armor in Ironmonger Street. She was killed on 24 October during the Court's counterattack, and a memorial to her stands in the Canal yard.

Residents

The residents of the worker districts, who numbered about 200,000, were caught between the lines. Many of the tenements were used as firing positions, and the occupants were either forced out by the soldiers or left in their rooms during the fighting. The Royalist command opened a system of shelters in the foundry cellars in the second week, in which about 40,000 people spent the nights of the October fighting. The shelters were organized by the foundry committees and fed from the works' kitchens, and they were the means by which most of the residents of the north bank survived the autumn.

The south bank, which was held by the Court until January, had a different experience. The Court's garrison closed the markets and requisitioned the stocks of the warehouses in October, and from November the south bank's food came only from the garrison's own stores. The ration was reduced to about 200 grams of bread a day in December. About 15,000 people crossed to the north bank over the river bridges during the first weeks, and a smaller number later crossed on the ice. The Royalists gave them food and shelter in the locomotive works, and several of the refugees stayed to work in the foundries.

Accounts

The best-known civilian record of the battle is the notebook of Hayakawa Misa, a clerk in the Eastgate foundry office, which also covers the First Battle of Shu Jing in 107. Her notebook for the autumn of 100 describes the first night at the Eastgate yard, the closing of the foundry gates, and the day on which the office was converted into a first-aid post. A second source is the log of the Eastgate signal cabin, kept by the signalman Nomura Jiro, which records the telegrams sent and received by the regiment in the first week. A third is the report of the Qianchan consul at Shu Jing, Mr. Fan Lisheng, whose dispatches to his government in the autumn of 100 are among the few foreign accounts of the fighting.

The accounts agree on a number of points. All of them record the confusion of the armbands. Several note that the soldiers of both sides were reluctant to fire on each other and that much of the fighting consisted of shouted negotiations across the streets. The consul's report states that "the combatants frequently knew each other by name, and in one instance two companies stopped firing in order to bury a man who had belonged to both."

Notable people

Mori Tatsuo (born 62 AG) was the Royalist local commander. A foundry worker's son from the Ironmonger Street district, he rose through the army's rail security service and was a lieutenant colonel at the start of the war. His command of the Works Guard in 100 made his reputation among the workers of Shu Jing, and in 107 he held the Ironmonger Street line in the First Battle of Shu Jing. He was killed on 14 February 117, in the Third Battle of Shu Jing. A bronze figure of him stands at the Ironmonger Street bridge.

Ito Shigeru (born 69 AG) commanded the East Rail Regional Emergency Command, with the rank of brigadier. His decision to declare for Zuko on 19 October and his night attack on the Central yard on 21 October were decisive. He rose to command the Royalist Southern Army and led it at the Siege of Caldera.

Hirata Gensai commanded the Court's garrison from December and conducted the defense of the passenger terminal. He later commanded the Court's field forces and was killed at the Ministry of Truth during the Siege of Caldera.

Takamura Seiichi, the garrison's first commander, was relieved of his command on 3 December, after the loss of the armored company's first sorties, and returned to Caldera. He was later a staff officer of the Court and was tried and acquitted at the hearings.

Aida Ryo, commander of the 3rd Rail Security Regiment, was wounded on 6 October and took no further part in the fighting. He was promoted to colonel in the Royalist army and later served as the first director of the Royalist army's railway service.

Sakurai Daiki, the foundry engineer who destroyed the Kuroishi viaduct, was a civilian employee of the locomotive works and was decorated by the Restoration Government for the operation. He was later the chief engineer of the rebuilt viaduct.

Iroh, the former general and Zuko's uncle, conducted the negotiations with the regional commands and was in the center for about a week in November. He was killed in the bombing of the Lily House on 9 March 101.

Casualties

The Royalist record gives about 4,000 dead, which is the figure used in the war's table of defining battles. The Court's records give less than a quarter of that number, and describe the events as a disturbance among the garrison in which about 900 people were killed. Estimates by later historians divide the dead into about 1,600 soldiers of both sides and about 2,400 civilians and factory workers, most of whom died in the December shelling and in the street fighting of October. Several thousand more were wounded, and about 20,000 were displaced.

The Royalist figures were compiled by the Works Guard's registry in the spring of 101 from the foundry committees' lists and the burial returns of the districts. The Court's figures are those of the General Staff Directorate's report of January 101, which counted only the garrison's own dead and which makes no mention of civilians. The Qianchan consul's dispatch of 20 January gave a figure of "between three and four thousand," and has been used by several historians as a check on the Royalist number.

Aftermath

Shu Jing became the Royalist capital in all but name. The foundries returned to production in February 101 AG, and by the spring they were repairing tanks and building rolling stock for the Royalist forces. The Restoration Government's ministries moved to the city from the south over the following months, and Zuko held his first sessions with the surviving members of the Diet at the Lily House, the teahouse and conference hall near Eastgate. It was in the Lily House that Iroh was killed on 9 March 101 AG, when a Salvationist bomb exploded during a meeting with delegates of two Regional Emergency Commands.

In the weeks after his death, the Court's spring offensive took Hōryū Pass and cut the Royalist rail link to the south. The Royalists were forced to rely on sea and Qianchan supply, which made the split of the Imperial Navy at Phoenix Island and the Southern Air Temple island chain decisive. The industrial center was attacked again in 107, 113 and 116–117 AG, in the First, Second and Third battles of Shu Jing. It was never taken.

Analysis

Historians have emphasized three features of the battle. The first is the role of the rail system. Both sides needed the line, and the possession of the Central yard and the passenger terminal was more important than the ground around them. The destruction of the Kuroishi viaduct, which isolated the Court's garrison, is regarded as the decisive act of the battle, though it was carried out by a small party of civilians and soldiers and did not involve a major engagement. The second is the importance of declarations by units. The Royalist victory came about largely because of the decisions of the 3rd Rail Security Regiment and the East Rail command, which together provided about 3,600 of the Royalists' trained troops. A smaller number of units changed to the Court, but the Court lost more than it gained.

The third feature is the role of the workers. The Works Guard, which had no training and almost no equipment on 7 October, held the north bank for three months, and its members' knowledge of the works and the streets allowed them to hold their ground against units that were better armed. Several historians have described the Guard as the only genuine popular militia of the early war. Others note that the Guard depended on the regular units for its leadership and on the Royalist government for its arms, and that its early success owed much to the Court's failure to commit its armor in the first week.

Legacy and memory

The clashes are remembered in the Fire Nation chiefly for the armbands and for the workers. The Works Guard, which began as an armed crowd at the Eastgate yard, is regarded as the first Royalist militia, and its dead are commemorated every 6 October at a memorial in the Eastgate yard, where the rails of the original gate have been preserved. Royalist veterans' groups use a red-and-white armband as their emblem. The Lily House, which was rebuilt after its destruction in 101, is a museum, and one of its rooms is devoted to the autumn of 100.

The battle has also been remembered in less official ways. The phrase "to change armbands" entered Fire Nation speech in the 100s to describe a sudden change of loyalty, and it is still used. The rail workers of the Eastgate yard, who sounded the yard's whistle for a minute on the evening of 6 October in 101, continued the practice annually, and it has been adopted by the postwar railway service as a commemoration of all the war's dead.

Historiography

Royalist accounts

Royalist accounts, which were written mostly by officers of the Works Guard and the regional commands in the late 100s and 110s, treat the battle as the war's first decisive victory. They say that the center's industry and its rail line made everything after possible, and they praise the workers and the units that declared for Zuko. They emphasize the Court's use of force against a crowd on the first night and the shelling of the north-bank districts in December. They give the Court's losses as about 1,100 and the Royalist losses as about 500 soldiers.

Court accounts

The Court's records, which survive only in part, call the events the Shu Jing disturbance and put the dead at under 1,000. They describe the first night as an act of defense by the inspection party against an armed crowd, deny that the Court's artillery shelled civilians in December, and attribute the loss of the center to the treachery of the garrison's officers. They state that the withdrawal of 11 January was an orderly operation that preserved the garrison's strength. Later Court-sympathetic authors, in particular the memoirs of Takamura Seiichi, concede that the shelling in December was ordered but argue that it was directed at military targets.

Other accounts and later assessments

Salvationist accounts, which were written much later, are limited. Several Salvationist authors point out that the committees of the later war had their origin in the foundry committees and the soldiers' councils of Shu Jing in the autumn of 100, and treat the battle as the beginning of their movement. Royalist and Court historians reject the claim, noting that the committees' formal organization dates from the winter of 106.

Historians disagree about the battle's importance. Royalist accounts treat it as the war's first decisive victory. Court accounts and some later historians say that the Royalists won a local victory in a war whose course was decided elsewhere, and that Shu Jing was held because the Court never made it a priority. Others argue that its importance was political: it was the first place in which both sides had to decide whether to fire on soldiers who had, the day before, been their own.

phoenix_island.title: Battle of Phoenix Island
phoenix_island.html:
Battle of Phoenix Island
Part ofThe early stage of the Fire Nation Civil War
Date2–9 November 100 AG
LocationPhoenix Island naval complex, home waters of the Fire Nation archipelago
ResultRoyalist victory. Defecting squadrons take the island complex, and the Imperial Navy splits
Belligerents
Royalists, with defecting squadrons of the Imperial NavyOzai loyalists (the Court), Home Fleet Command
Commanders and leaders
Royalists
Rear Admiral Minami Haruka		Court
Admiral Kuroda Ryosuke
Strength
Royalists
3 submarine flotillas (about 26 boats), 1 carrier, 9 escorts, about 6,000 personnel		Court
1 carrier, 14 escorts, the island garrison (about 4,500)
Casualties and losses
About 2,500 killed, most of them sailors and dockyard workers

The Battle of Phoenix Island was fought from 2 to 9 November 100 AG for the principal naval complex of the Fire Nation’s home waters. It was the second of the Fire Nation Civil War’s twenty defining battles. The Imperial Navy, which had eight carriers and 94 submarines at the start of the war, divided by squadron during November, and Phoenix Island was where the division turned into fighting.

The island’s dry docks, torpedo works and fuel depot passed to the Royalists after eight days, together with about a third of the submarines on its roster. The Navy never reunited. The Royalists gained a sea lane to the south and, with it, the ability to receive supplies from Qianchan through the Southern Air Temple island chain.

Background

The Imperial Navy had been the strongest in the world for most of the Hundred Year War and was the service that least wanted a civil war. Its officers had been trained by the Imperial court, but its sailors were conscripts, and its dockyard workers were drawn from the same industrial towns that favored Zuko. Through August and September 100 AG, after the Diet’s confrontation with the Court, individual ships requested instructions from both Caldera and the Royalist government at Shu Jing, and obeyed whichever order arrived first.

Admiral Kuroda Ryosuke, the commander of the Home Fleet, was loyal to Azula. Rear Admiral Minami Haruka, who commanded the island’s submarine flotillas, was not. Minami had been Iroh’s staff officer in the Ba Sing Se siege and had stayed in contact with him after his retirement. On 28 October she sent a signal, carried by a courier on the supply boat, to Royalist headquarters to say that her flotillas would declare for Zuko in the first week of November if the island’s fuel was secure.

Forces

Royalists. Third, Seventh and Ninth Submarine Flotillas (about 26 boats, Kaienha incendiary torpedoes); the carrier Shinryu; nine escorts; dockyard workers armed as the Island Guard (about 1,200).

Court. The carrier Hiryu; fourteen escorts; the island garrison, including two Flame Guard companies; Home Fleet Command staff.

The balance was uncertain at the start because neither side knew which ship would obey. Of the 94 submarines on the Navy’s roster, 26 were at Phoenix Island, and the Royalists held about two-thirds of them on the first morning.

Course

2–4 November: the signal

On the evening of 2 November Minami’s flotillas raised the red-and-white armband flag, and her boats left their berths and took up positions across the channel mouth. Kuroda ordered the escorts to open fire, and the first shots were exchanged at 21:40. Within an hour two escorts had gone over to the Royalists, and one of them rammed a Court destroyer in the dark.

The carriers did not fight each other. Shinryu’s air group, which was divided in its loyalties, flew off to the mainland on 3 November with only half its aircraft, and Hiryu’s was grounded by fuel contamination that the Royalists said was sabotage.

5–9 November: the dockyards

The fight for the dry docks and the torpedo works lasted five days. The Island Guard, workers armed with rifles from the armory, held the torpedo works against two Flame Guard assaults on 5 and 6 November. On 7 November the Court garrison’s commander was killed when a shell hit the headquarters building, and the garrison asked for terms. Kuroda refused and withdrew with the escorts and Hiryu on the night of 8 November, leaving about 1,100 sailors behind.

By 9 November the island was in Royalist hands. About 2,500 people had died, of whom about 700 were dockyard workers and about 400 were civilians from the island’s town.

Civilian accounts

About 3,000 dockyard workers lived on the island with their families. Sugimoto Ken, a dry-dock foreman who joined the Island Guard, kept a work log through the battle, and the log was later used by the Royalist naval histories. It records that the workers sealed the docks' main gate with a floating caisson on 3 November and "kept the Court's boats from the keel blocks for six days with a crane and a chain." His last entry notes that the first Qianchan supply boat tied up at the repaired quay on 12 November.

Aftermath

The Navy split by squadron in the weeks after the battle. Roughly half of the submarine force, a third of the surface fleet and one carrier ended the year under Royalist orders. The Court kept most of the battleships, the dockyards at Caldera and the larger carrier fleet, but not the loyalty of the crews. Rear Admiral Minami became the Royalists’ naval commander and later the architect of the Kumo Straits operation (see Battle of Kumo Straits).

The complex became the Royalist navy’s main base. Supply convoys from Qianchan reached it from the south through the Southern Air Temple chain.

Legacy

Phoenix Island remained the Royalists' principal naval base for the rest of the war and was the starting point for the convoys that crossed the Kumo Straits. The split of the Navy that began here was never repaired: the squadrons that had gone over to the Royalists formed the nucleus of the postwar fleet, and the officers who had stayed with the Court were tried at the accountability hearings. Minami Haruka, who died in 131 AG, is buried on the island.

Historiography

Royalist accounts describe the battle as a mutiny against an illegitimate order, in which the sailors chose the Diet. Court records call it the “Phoenix Island treason” and put the garrison’s losses at about 400, mostly from a single shell. Salvationist veterans’ memoirs describe it as the first time the Navy’s ratings, and not its officers, decided a battle, and cite it as the model for the salvation committees that later formed in the army.

horyu_pass.title: Battle of Hōryū Pass
horyu_pass.html:
Battle of Hōryū Pass
Part ofThe early stage of the Fire Nation Civil War
Date14 March – 11 May 101 AG
LocationHōryū Pass and the rail line between Shu Jing and the southern ports
ResultCourt victory. The Royalists lose the pass and their rail link to the south
Belligerents
Ozai loyalists (the Court)Royalists
Commanders and leaders
Court
Lieutenant General Sakai Renjiro		Royalists
Brigadier Ito Shigeru
Strength
Court
about 22,000, including two armored regiments, a Breaker company and air support		Royalists
about 12,000
Casualties and losses
About 9,000 killed, including about 1,800 civilians and rail workers

The Battle of Hōryū Pass was the Court’s spring offensive of 101 AG. Over eight weeks it took the mountain pass that carried the Royalists’ only rail line to the south, and cut the Royalist capital at Shu Jing off from the ports. It began five days after the death of Iroh at the Lily House and is the third of the war’s twenty defining battles.

The Court won the pass, but it did not follow up the victory. The Royalists, deprived of the railway, turned to the sea, and the Navy’s split and the Southern Air Temple island chain decided the war that the pass had been expected to decide.

Background

Hōryū Pass is a gap about 40 kilometers south of Shu Jing, where the rail line crosses the northern range through two tunnels and a viaduct. The Royalists had held it since the autumn of 100 AG. After the Clashes at Shu Jing, the line was the only way to bring Qianchan supplies, landed at the southern ports, to the industrial center.

The death of Iroh on 9 March removed the Royalists’ Chief of Staff, and the Court, which had not planned a major operation for the spring, took the chance. Lieutenant General Sakai Renjiro, who had commanded the Court’s forces in the north since September, was given two armored regiments, a Breaker Mk II company and a squadron of T-50 fighters.

Forces

Court. The 1st and 4th Armored Regiments (Tessho-III-equipped infantry and light tanks); the 2nd Breaker Company; a T-50 squadron from Caldera; two infantry divisions drawn from Flame Guard and loyal garrisons.

Royalists. The East Rail Regional Emergency Command (about 2,500); the 3rd Rail Security Regiment; Works Guard companies; naval infantry; engineer battalions with demolition charges for the tunnels.

Course

14–29 March: the lower pass

Sakai attacked on 14 March after a bombardment of the viaduct by T-50 fighters. Ito held the lower pass for two weeks with his tunnels prepared for demolition. The Court’s armor, which could not move off the track in the narrow gorge, was stopped twice at the first tunnel by anti-armor rockets and by an improvised barrier of locomotives. On 29 March the Breaker company, advancing along the cliff ledges, outflanked the tunnel mouth, and the Royalists withdrew to the upper pass.

April: the upper pass

Through April the fighting moved to the heights, where infantry on both sides fought among the signal houses and the villages of the pass. The Royalists were short of rockets, and supply trains stopped running after the Court bombed the line south of the tunnels. About 1,800 civilians, many of them rail workers’ families, died in the shelling of the villages of Upper and Lower Hōryū.

May: the demolition

On 11 May, with the Court in possession of the upper pass, Ito ordered the demolition of the second tunnel and the viaduct. The charges killed about 200 Court sappers who had entered the tunnel and brought down the viaduct. The Court held the pass, but the line through it was cut for the rest of the war.

Civilian accounts

Yamaoka Seiji, the station master at the upper pass, kept the railway's log through the battle. His entries record the last train to leave the pass on 3 May and the demolition of the first tunnel, which he watched from the signal hut. "Eleven families lived in the station cottages," he wrote. "We left with what we could carry, and the engineers walked behind us laying the charges." The station log is kept by the Railway Museum at Shu Jing.

Aftermath

The Royalists had lost the railway, and the Court had gained a pass that led nowhere. The Court’s armor was too far from its supply lines to push south, and the Royalists, who rebuilt a limited line through the coastal plain in 103 AG, shifted most of their supply to the sea. The Navy’s division, which had only recently begun, became essential. Kumo Straits and the defense of the Southern Air Temple chain followed from it.

Legacy

The pass was in Court hands but useless: the tunnels were destroyed and the Court did not have the engineers to rebuild them. The rail line was not repaired until 118 AG. The battle pushed the Royalists to rely on the sea, and the Navy's split and the Southern Air Temple island chain became the center of the war's first five years.

Historiography

Royalist histories treat the pass as a tactical defeat and a strategic gift: the Court took a position it could not use, and the Royalists were forced to build the sea route that won the war. Court accounts present it as a decisive victory that was thrown away when the General Staff refused to reinforce Sakai. Salvationist writers cite it as the first battle in which Court infantry units refused to storm a position, and note that two companies of the 4th Armored Regiment were disarmed by their own officers on 2 May.

kumo_straits.title: Battle of Kumo Straits
kumo_straits.html:
Battle of Kumo Straits
Part ofThe early stage of the Fire Nation Civil War
Date11–24 August 102 AG
LocationKumo Straits, the narrow sea lane between the southern archipelago and the Qianchan coast
ResultRoyalist victory. The southern sea lane is secured for the Royalists
Belligerents
Royalists, with defecting squadrons of the Imperial NavyOzai loyalists (the Court), Southern Squadron
Commanders and leaders
Royalists
Rear Admiral Minami Haruka		Court
Vice Admiral Tomita Haruo
Strength
Royalists
about 20 submarines, 1 carrier, 17 escorts		Court
2 battleships, 1 carrier, 22 escorts, 12 submarines
Casualties and losses
About 5,500 killed, nearly all naval personnel

The Battle of Kumo Straits was a two-week naval battle in August 102 AG for the narrow channel between the southern islands and the Qianchan coast. The Royalist and defector squadrons won it and secured the sea lane that carried Qianchan’s supplies to the Royalist government. It is the fourth of the war’s twenty defining battles.

The Court had the larger fleet but lost the battle to submarines and to its own fuel shortage. After the battle it never again sent a surface fleet into the southern channel.

Background

After the loss of the pass in 101 AG, supply by sea was the Royalists’ lifeline. Convoys left the Qianchan ports with rifles, trucks and medical stores, crossed the Kumo Straits and unloaded at Phoenix Island or at the island chain. In 102 AG the Court decided to close the straits, and Vice Admiral Tomita Haruo was given two battleships and a carrier for the purpose.

Minami, who knew the plan from a captured signal book, concentrated her submarines in the straits and asked the Qianchan navy to escort the convoys in the southern half of the passage. The Qianchan government, which had so far committed only the island garrison, agreed to provide escorts as far as its territorial waters.

Order of battle

Court (Southern Squadron). Vice Admiral Tomita Haruo; battleships Kongo and one other; one carrier; destroyers and minesweepers; a fuel tender. Short of fuel; no submarine screen.

Royalists. Minami's submarine flotillas in packs of three; escort screen of destroyers; convoys of transports. Kaienha incendiary torpedoes.

Qianchan. Escort force of the Qianchan navy as far as territorial waters. Escorts only; no part in the submarine attacks.

Course

11–15 August: the first engagement

Tomita’s squadron entered the straits on 11 August and fought a day action with the Royalist escort screen, in which the Court lost a destroyer and two minesweepers to Kaienha torpedoes. The Court’s carrier launched its air group at dawn on 12 August, but the Royalist submarines had moved their position during the night, and the strike found only empty water.

16–24 August: the submarine war

For the rest of the battle the Royalists used their submarines in packs of three to attack the Court squadron when it turned in the narrows. On the night of 18 August they sank the battleship Kongo with three torpedoes, and on 21 August they sank the Court carrier’s fuel tender, which left the carrier with two days of range. Tomita withdrew on 24 August with one battleship and the carrier under tow.

Civilian accounts

About 900 passengers, most of them Fire Nation refugees and wounded soldiers, crossed the straits on the convoys during the battle. Several kept accounts of the crossing, and the best known is the letter of Commander Shen Bao of the Qianchan escort force to his wife, written on 17 August: "We counted forty ships in the narrows that night, and not one of them showed a light. We heard the Kongo go down but no one on our deck said anything."

Aftermath

The Court’s Southern Squadron was effectively finished, and its remaining ships were reassigned to defend Caldera. The Royalists held the sea lane until the war’s end. The Qianchan government’s decision to escort convoys became the first step toward the Republic’s commitment of the two expeditionary divisions that arrived in 109 AG (see Battle of Soka Bay).

Legacy

The Southern Squadron never returned, and the Royalists' convoys crossed the straits without serious interference until the end of the war. The battle gave the submarine flotillas their reputation, and the "pack of three" became a standard Royalist tactic. The wreck of the Kongo lies in the narrows and is a protected site under the Qianchan's maritime law.

Historiography

Royalist accounts credit Minami with the victory and say the submarines sank the Court squadron. Court records say Tomita broke off the action to save his ships and claim two Royalist submarines sunk. Qianchan naval records, which are the only neutral source, support the Royalist version of the sinkings but record that the Court carrier was never in range of the convoys.

seiryu_bay.title: Battle of Seiryū Bay
seiryu_bay.html:
Battle of Seiryū Bay
Part ofThe early stage of the Fire Nation Civil War
DateMarch – June 103 AG
LocationSeiryū Bay and the Eastern Territories
ResultCourt victory. The Eastern Regional Emergency Commands are subdued
Belligerents
Ozai loyalists (the Court)Eastern Regional Emergency Commands (independent warlords); some Royalist liaison units
Commanders and leaders
Court
General Hirata Gensai		Eastern Commands
Colonel Hayashi Ukon (nominal coordinator)
Strength
Court
about 40,000 in two corps with naval support		Eastern Commands
about 30,000 in five commands, poorly coordinated
Casualties and losses
About 11,000 killed, including about 4,500 civilians

The Battle of Seiryū Bay was the Court’s campaign in the spring of 103 AG to subdue the Regional Emergency Commands in the Eastern Territories. These commands had been acting as independent warlords since 100 AG, and some of them had made agreements with the Royalists. The Court defeated them one by one between March and June, and took control of the bay and its ports. It is the fifth of the war’s twenty defining battles.

The campaign was the Court’s largest success of the early war, and it cost it the east’s food supplies, because the commands burned the harvest they could not hold.

Background

The Eastern Territories were the last Fire Nation colonies to be settled and the most heavily garrisoned. In November 100 AG the Regional Emergency Commands there declared that they would take no orders from Caldera or from Shu Jing until the question of the succession was resolved. In practice, five commands each ruled a district from a fortified port, taxed trade and fought their neighbors.

In 102 AG the Court needed the east’s rice and its ports, and General Hirata Gensai, who had commanded the garrison in the Clashes at Shu Jing and returned to the Court after his withdrawal, was given the task of ending the arrangement. Colonel Hayashi Ukon, who held Seiryū Bay, attempted to unite the five commands, and sent to Shu Jing and to the Qianchan mission for help.

Order of battle

Court (about 35,000). Eastern Army Group under General Hirata Gensai; armored regiments; amphibious flotilla of landing craft. Field guns, landing craft, tanks.

Regional Commands (about 18,000). Five commands; the three united under Colonel Hayashi Ukon held the bay (about 30 vessels and coastal batteries). Coastal batteries, small craft; little ammunition by June.

Civilians. About 400,000 in the ports and districts. Harvest burned by the commands in June.

Course

March–April: the northern ports

Hirata began in March with an amphibious landing north of the bay, which took the port of Shinsato on 14 March and cut the coastal road. The northern command surrendered after eleven days, and its troops were absorbed into the Court’s corps. The second command resisted for six weeks at the town of Tamaoki, where about 3,000 civilians were killed when the Court shelled the harbor district.

May–June: the bay

The three remaining commands joined under Hayashi in May and held the bay’s inner harbor, with coastal batteries and about 30 vessels. The Court attacked from the land side and, on 2 June, forced the harbor mouth with a flotilla of landing craft under fire. Hayashi surrendered on 17 June and was shot on 20 June.

Civilian accounts

Kitagawa Emi, a teacher in the Tamaoki harbor district, wrote a school journal during the shelling, in which the pupils copied the day's lessons from the blackboard in the shelter. The journal lists the names of 41 pupils and 7 staff who died in the bombardment. It was published in 128 AG as the Tamaoki School Record. The final entry, on the day the town surrendered, lists the names of the children who were still alive.

Aftermath

The Court controlled the east by July, but the destruction of the harvest left it short of food, and the army that had won the campaign, which was drawn from the northern garrisons, was unpaid and badly fed by the winter. Historians identify the east’s food shortage as one cause of the unrest in the units that later formed the first salvation committees. The Royalists, who could not help the commands, lost most of their remaining contacts in the east.

Legacy

The east became the Court's granary and its prison: the commands' surviving officers were sent to labor camps, and the burned harvests left the area short of food for three winters. The campaign is remembered in the east mainly for Tamaoki and for the execution of Hayashi, whose trial was not held. After the war, the accountability hearings opened an inquiry into the Tamaoki shelling.

Historiography

The Court’s record presents the campaign as the restoration of order against bandit commands. Royalist histories regard it as an unnecessary war that cost the Court its best formations and destroyed the east’s food supply. Salvationist accounts say the campaign’s dead included many of the troops who had been told they were fighting traitors and who later joined the committees.
