southern_air_temple_landing.title: Southern Air Temple Landing
southern_air_temple_landing.html:
Southern Air Temple Landing
Part ofThe early stage of the Fire Nation Civil War
Date7–19 September 104 AG
LocationThe Southern Air Temple island chain
ResultQianchan and Royalist victory. The Court landing fails and the island chain remains in Qianchan hands
Belligerents
Ozai loyalists (the Court)Qianchan (garrison and naval support); Royalists
Commanders and leaders
Court
Rear Admiral Okuda Saburo; General Hirata Gensai (overall)		Qianchan
Colonel Liao Wen (island garrison)
Strength
Court
about 8,000 in amphibious forces with two carriers		Qianchan
about 4,000 on the islands, with air and naval support
Casualties and losses
About 3,000 killed, mostly Court marines and sailors

The Southern Air Temple Landing was an amphibious operation by the Court in September 104 AG to retake the Southern Air Temple island chain, which served the Royalists as a supply base and staging area, during the early stage of the Fire Nation Civil War. The landing began on 7 September and ended on 19 September, when Rear Admiral Okuda Saburo ordered a withdrawal, leaving about 1,400 marines on the islands. About 3,000 people were killed, most of them Court marines and sailors. It is the sixth of the war's twenty defining battles.

The islands lay in the sea south of the archipelago and had been occupied since 100 AG by a garrison of the Qianchan Republic, which held them at the request of Zuko's government. The Court's landing failed against the garrison, which held the high ground on the old temple terraces, and against a Royalist submarine line and a Qianchan air group that destroyed the Court's naval support. It was the first battle in which Qianchan forces fought the Court directly, and it prepared the way for the Qianchan Congress's vote of 109 AG to send ground forces to the war (see Battle of Soka Bay). The islands remained in Qianchan hands until 120 AG, and the Court did not attempt another landing.

Background

The island chain

The Southern Air Temple island chain is a string of seven small islands and a number of rocks in the sea south of the Fire Nation archipelago, about 300 kilometers from the nearest mainland port. The largest, which is called the central island in the military accounts, is about six kilometers long and rises in a series of stone terraces to a ridge about 200 meters above the water. The terraces, which are cut into the island's seaward face, held the buildings of an Air Nomad temple, a complex of halls, dormitories, stairways and bridges that was among the southern temples of the Air Nomads. The two outer islands, about four kilometers east of the central island, are low and rocky and have a few beaches, and the four small islands to the south are largely bare.

The temple had been razed in the Air Nomad Genocide, and the chain was occupied by the Empire from 1 AG, which built forward bases and airfields on it and used it as the launching point for the invasion of Yanakawa. In 50 AG the chain was divided between the Empire and the Qianchan Navy, and the Imperial share, which had been run down during the last years of the Hundred Year War, was left with a skeleton garrison by 99 AG. The temple's buildings had been burned and partly demolished, but the stone staircases built into the cliff face, the long galleries that connected the terraces and the temple's cisterns, which collected rainwater, survived. These features made the central island an unusually good defensive position, as the Qianchan engineers noted when they surveyed it in 100.

The Qianchan occupation

The islands were occupied by Qianchan forces in the autumn of 100 AG, after the last Imperial garrison withdrew. After the Royalists lost their ports in the first weeks of the war, Zuko's government asked Qianchan to hold a base for supplies, and the Qianchan Congress approved the occupation of the chain by a small majority, on the understanding that the force would be used only to protect the base. About 1,200 troops and 800 engineers were landed in October. They repaired the Empire's old quays on the central island, built a fuel depot and storehouses in the lower temple halls, and lengthened the Imperial airfield on the eastern shelf into a usable airstrip.

The islands became a transshipment point. Cargo ships from the Qianchan ports in the south unloaded their supplies onto smaller craft, which could cross the Kumo Straits and reach the Royalist ports without being intercepted by the Court's larger warships. Over the following four years the base handled about 400,000 tons of cargo, and the Royalists estimated that about two thirds of their rifles, trucks and medical supplies had passed through it. The garrison, which was commanded from 102 by Colonel Liao Wen, grew to about 4,000 and was given an air group of about forty aircraft, which flew from the airstrip and from a second field on the mainland coast.

The Court's decision

The Court regarded the island chain as a threat to its position in the south. By 104 AG the Royalists had survived the Court's campaign of the spring of 101, they had won the Battle of the Kumo Straits in the summer of 102, and the Court's eastern campaign, which had ended in June 103 with the subjugation of the Eastern Regional Emergency Commands, had freed troops for use elsewhere. General Hirata Gensai, who had directed the eastern campaign, proposed in the winter of 103 that the freed forces be used to take the islands. His argument, which is preserved in a memorandum of the General Staff Directorate, was that the Royalists could not be starved into surrender while the base remained open, and that the garrison, which was small and had few heavy weapons, could be overwhelmed by a landing in force.

The proposal was accepted by Azula, who ordered that the operation take place before the end of the summer. Opinion in the Court was divided. The navy's staff, which had lost a battleship and a number of smaller ships at the Kumo Straits, was reluctant, and its senior officers argued that the fleet should not be risked against the Qianchan air group. Okuda Saburo, who had commanded a cruiser squadron at the Kumo Straits and who had been promoted to rear admiral after the eastern campaign, accepted the command after Hirata assured him that the Court's air arm would provide cover. The assurance was not kept.

Forces and commanders

The Court

The Court's force consisted of about 8,000 men in the amphibious forces, with two carriers, six transports, a number of landing craft and a screen of destroyers and cruisers. The ground troops were provided by the Eastern Army Group, which had fought at Seiryū Bay, and were commanded by Colonel Iwasaki Torao, a marine officer who had led the landing at Shinsato in 103. The first wave of about 2,000 marines was embarked on the transports and the landing craft, and the second wave of about 3,000 followed on the transports. The remainder were aboard the carriers and the escorts, or were in reserve at the Court's southern port.

The carriers were the Akagi, which was commanded by Captain Fukuda Eiji, and a smaller carrier, the Kaga. The Akagi had been built before the war and had an air group of about thirty aircraft, mostly fighters and dive bombers. Okuda flew his flag in the Akagi. The Court's other warships were four cruisers, ten destroyers and a number of auxiliaries. The landing craft, of which there were about 70, had been collected from the eastern ports.

Okuda, who was 52, was regarded as a competent seaman with little experience of amphibious operations. His chief of staff, Commander Nakagawa Jun, had planned the landing at Shinsato and was responsible for most of the operational detail. Hirata was in overall command of the operation, but remained at the Court's southern port, about 400 kilometers from the islands. The records suggest that he did not intend to take the field, and that he regarded the operation as one in which the navy would play the principal part.

Qianchan

The Qianchan garrison numbered about 4,000, with the air group and the naval units that were attached to it. The infantry, about 3,200 men, consisted of two battalions of the 7th Island Regiment and a battalion of marines, with a battery of 105mm guns and a number of mortars and machine guns. They were commanded by Colonel Liao Wen, a former engineer who had been in command of the base since 102. Liao, who was 47, had trained the garrison in the use of the terraces and had laid out the defense in depth in the weeks before the landing. His second in command was Major Sun Bo, an artilleryman who directed the guns and the mortars.

The air group was commanded by Captain Hua Mei, a former civilian pilot who had joined the Qianchan air arm in 99. Her aircraft were of mixed types: about 20 single-engined fighters, 12 dive bombers and a few transports. The naval support came from a small flotilla of the Qianchan navy under Commodore Ye Tao, consisting of four destroyers and some patrol craft that were based at the central island's harbor. The flotilla did not engage the Court's cruisers, and was kept in the harbor with orders to defend the quays.

The Royalists

The Royalists did not have troops on the islands, but their submarine flotillas operated in the channel. They were commanded by Captain Minami Haruka, who had been the leader of the Royalist squadrons at the Kumo Straits. Her boats, which were based at Phoenix Island, had received a warning of the Court's sailing from agents in the southern port, and had positioned three packs of three boats along the likely routes between the Court's port and the islands.

Planning and preparations

The Court's plan

The Court's plan was drawn up by Nakagawa and approved by Okuda and Hirata in July. It called for a landing in two stages. The first wave, of about 2,000 marines, would take the two outer islands and set up artillery on them, from which the guns could cover the approaches to the central island. The second wave, of about 3,000, would land on the central island's eastern beaches under the cover of the artillery and the carriers' aircraft, and would take the lower terraces and the quays. The remaining troops would be held in reserve in the transports and would be landed as needed. The planners expected the operation to take about a week and assumed that the garrison would not receive reinforcements in that time.

The plan depended on three assumptions, each of which proved false. The first was that the garrison would defend the beaches and could be defeated there. The second was that the carriers' aircraft would be able to suppress the Qianchan air group. The third was that the Royalist submarines, which were known to be in the area, would not attack the transports during the landing. Nakagawa's memoirs, which were published after the war, say that he had objected to the third assumption and had proposed an escort of destroyers around the transports, but that Okuda had overruled him in order to use the destroyers in the bombardment.

The Qianchan defense

Liao Wen's plan was based on the observation that the central island's beaches could not be defended against a landing in force, and that the terraces above them could. He had positioned his infantry on the high ground, with machine guns and mortars on the lower terraces and artillery on the ridge. The beaches were covered by fire from the terraces but were not held in strength. The temple's galleries and stairways, which connected the terraces under cover, allowed the defenders to move between positions without being seen from the sea. In the weeks before the landing his men had cleared the stairways of rubble, placed barbed wire on the beaches, and built sandbagged firing positions in the windows of the lower halls.

The outer islands were held by small detachments of about 150 men each, with orders to delay the Court and to withdraw to the central island if they were attacked in force. The detachments were provided with demolition charges for the quays and the water tanks, and with a number of mines for the beaches. The islands' defenders were reinforced on 5 September, when the Qianchan air group sent a transport with a company of marines from the mainland. The reinforcement, which had been planned for some weeks, arrived two days before the landing.

Hua Mei's air group was ordered to avoid battle with the Court's carrier aircraft until the landing had begun, and then to attack the transports and the carriers. The group's fighters were to engage the Court's air cover, and the dive bombers were to attack the ships. Hua is said to have told her pilots that they were not to expect to return, a remark that has been much quoted, but the group's losses in the battle were in fact light, about six aircraft in thirteen days.

Course

The outer islands (7–9 September)

The Court's fleet arrived off the islands on the night of 6 September and began its bombardment at first light on 7 September. The cruisers and the destroyers shelled the two outer islands for about two hours, and the carrier aircraft attacked the airstrip and the harbor at the central island. The Qianchan fighters rose to meet them, and the engagement, which lasted about forty minutes, cost the Court three aircraft and the Qianchan group two. The airstrip was cratered, but Hua's group moved its aircraft to the mainland field in the course of the morning and returned to operate from the strip in the evening, after the engineers had repaired it.

The first wave, about 2,000 marines in 40 landing craft, went ashore on the two outer islands at about eight o'clock. They met little resistance. The Qianchan detachments, which had been ordered to delay, fired on the first boats and withdrew to the central island by night in fishing boats. About 300 marines landed on the first outer island and about 1,700 on the second, which had better beaches. The islands were taken in two days, and on 9 September the marines placed a battery of 105mm guns on the second island's summit, from which it could reach the central island's eastern beaches. The Court's casualties in the operation were about 140 killed.

The central island was not attacked on the first two days. Okuda held back the second wave while the guns were being positioned, and used the interval to bring up the transports. The delay gave the Qianchan garrison time to complete its preparations, and allowed the air group to attack the Court's anchorage on the afternoon of 8 September, when it damaged one destroyer and a transport. The Court's carriers, which were at sea, did not respond.

The central island beaches (10–12 September)

The battle for the central island began on 10 September, with a bombardment by the cruisers and the battery on the outer island that lasted about four hours. The shelling destroyed the quays and the fuel depot, and set fire to the storehouses in the lower halls, but it did little damage to the defenders, who had taken cover in the galleries and the cisterns. At about noon the second wave, about 3,000 marines in 50 landing craft, went ashore on the eastern beaches under cover of a smokescreen.

The landing at the beaches followed the pattern of the previous days. The garrison let the first boats land and then opened fire from the terraces with machine guns and mortars. The marines, who were under fire from the moment they left the boats, took heavy casualties in the surf and on the sand, and a number of landing craft were hit and sunk. The survivors reached the base of the cliffs, where they sheltered in the dead ground below the lowest terrace, but they could not advance. By the evening of 10 September about 600 marines were dead or wounded, and the Court's line did not extend beyond the beach.

On 11 September the Court's command ordered an attack on the lower terraces. The marines, under the command of Colonel Iwasaki, advanced up the stairways in columns of two, supported by the guns of the outer island and by naval gunfire. The defenders held their fire until the leading men were within about thirty meters, and then fired from the windows and galleries above. The first attack was driven back with the loss of about 200 men. A second attack in the afternoon reached the first gallery, where there was a close fight with grenades and bayonets, and was thrown back in the evening.

The lower terraces (12–16 September)

On 12 September the Court's second wave, which had been held in reserve, landed on the beaches and reinforced the first. The combined force of about 4,500 marines now held the beaches and the foot of the cliffs, and Iwasaki, who had been wounded on 11 September, handed his command to Lieutenant Colonel Tsuda Kei. For the next week the fighting was concentrated on the lower terraces, where both sides used the stone staircases as fire lanes. The staircases, which were about three meters wide and had stone balustrades, could be swept by machine guns from above, and the marines were obliged to climb them in single file under fire.

The marines took the first terrace on 13 September, after a night attack in which they used the rope ladders and the drainage channels of the cliff to bypass the staircases. They held it for two days against counterattacks by the garrison, and used it as a base for an attack on the second terrace on 15 September. The second terrace, which held the main halls of the temple, was defended by Major Sun's mortar companies and by two battalions of infantry. The fighting in the halls, which were dark and full of galleries, was close and confused, and several accounts describe the marines and the defenders meeting in the corridors without warning.

The Court's attack on the second terrace was halted on the evening of 15 September. The marines, who had lost about 1,100 men since 10 September, had gained about forty meters of ground. The Qianchan garrison had lost about 400 killed and wounded and had been pushed out of the first terrace, but it held the second and third in strength and its artillery on the ridge was intact. The balance of the fighting on land, as the Court's own staff reported, was heavily in the garrison's favor.

The sea and the air (15–17 September)

The decisive actions of the battle were fought at sea and in the air. On the night of 15 September, Royalist submarines of Captain Minami's flotillas, which had been waiting off the transport anchorage, attacked the Court's ships with torpedoes. Two transports, the Tamagawa Maru and the Seiran Maru, were hit and sunk, with the loss of about 900 men, of whom about 600 were marines of the reserve. The destroyers that were nominally guarding the anchorage had been withdrawn to support the bombardment, and the submarines were able to withdraw without being detected. Minami's boats used standard torpedoes in this action and kept their Kaienha incendiary torpedoes in reserve, since the burning oil would have lit the anchorage for the Court's destroyers.

The loss of the two transports reduced the Court's strength on the islands by about a third and its reserve of supplies by about half. It also forced Okuda to move his carriers closer to the islands to protect the anchorage, which brought them within range of the Qianchan air group. On 17 September, Hua Mei's group, which had been preparing for the attack since the start of the landing, sent every aircraft it had against the carriers. The 12 dive bombers, escorted by 20 fighters, found the Akagi at about noon, and hit her with four bombs. The carrier's fuel storage caught fire, and she sank in about two hours with the loss of about 700 men, including Captain Fukuda, who stayed on the bridge. The Kaga escaped with damage.

The group lost six aircraft in the operation, mostly to the Court's anti-aircraft fire. Its survivors landed at the mainland field, where Hua, who had flown the lead aircraft, was met by the base commander. She is said to have asked whether the carrier had really sunk, and to have been told that it had. The Court's staff records, which were captured in 124, say that the news of the loss of the Akagi reached Hirata in his headquarters at the southern port on the evening of 17 September, and that he did not reply for two days.

The withdrawal (18–19 September)

Okuda, who had been rescued from the water by a destroyer, ordered the withdrawal on 18 September. The order was carried out on the following day. The transports and the landing craft, with about 2,800 marines, were evacuated from the eastern beaches on the night of 18 and 19 September, under the cover of the cruisers' guns. About 1,400 marines, who were in the forward positions on the terraces, could not be reached and were left behind. They were commanded by Lieutenant Colonel Tsuda, who had been ordered to cover the withdrawal and who, when he found that the boats had gone, held a council of his officers and decided to surrender.

The surrender took place on 20 September, when Tsuda sent a messenger under a white flag to Colonel Liao. The terms were that the marines would lay down their arms, be treated as prisoners of war and be held on the islands until the end of the war. The garrison, which had about 600 killed and wounded in the battle, accepted. The last marines, who held out in a gallery of the third terrace until 24 September, were persuaded to surrender by Tsuda. The outer islands were reoccupied by the garrison in the same week, and the battery on the second island was dismantled.

Prisoners and the islands' inhabitants

The captured marines

About 1,400 marines were taken prisoner on the islands between 20 and 24 September. They were held in the lower halls of the temple, in a compound that the garrison fenced off with wire, and were fed from the garrison's stores. The prisoners, who included about 300 wounded, were attended by the garrison's medical staff, and the severely wounded were sent to the mainland by transport. The garrison's doctors, who had treated about 400 of their own casualties, found that they had not enough bandages for all of them, and the Qianchan relief committee sent supplies in October.

The treatment of the prisoners is described in the notebook of Sergeant Oda Kenji, a marine who surrendered with Tsuda's party on 20 September. Oda, who was 24, kept the notebook in the compound from September 104 until his release in 119, and it was published in 126. It records that the garrison fed the prisoners the same rice as its own men, that the commander, Colonel Liao, visited the compound in the first week and spoke to the officers, and that the guards told the prisoners that the war was not theirs. It also records the prisoners' conditions in the later years: the compound's food was reduced in 107, when the supply line was disrupted, and in the winter of 109 about 40 of the prisoners died of dysentery.

The prisoners were not exchanged during the war. The Court refused to negotiate with the garrison, and the Royalists, who had no claim over the prisoners, did not press the point. About 200 of the prisoners joined the Royalist army in 105 and 106, and some of them served on the islands as laborers and cooks. The rest were sent home after the end of the war, in 119, and were treated by the Reformation government as returning soldiers.

Other inhabitants

The islands were not entirely a military base. About 1,500 civilians lived on the central island at the time of the landing, most of them dock workers, cargo handlers and their families, who had been recruited in the Qianchan ports to run the transshipment point. Another 600 were refugees from the Fire Nation, who had been brought to the islands by Royalist ships in 102 and 103 and who worked in the stores and the kitchens. The civilians were housed in the lower halls and in huts that had been built on the eastern shelf, and during the landing they were moved to the temple's cisterns and the interior galleries.

About 80 civilians were killed in the battle, most of them on 10 and 11 September, when the Court's bombardment hit the lower halls. A number of the dock workers formed carrying parties and brought ammunition and water to the garrison's positions, and two of them are recorded to have been killed on the stairways. The refugees' accounts, of which a small number survive, describe the battle as a week in the dark of the temple's galleries, listening to the sound of the guns. One of them, a former schoolteacher named Takeda Hana, recorded that the children of the refugees were taken by the garrison's cooks to the deepest of the cisterns, where they were told stories and given dried fruit.

The Air Nomad shrines

The temple's shrines, of which there were about 60, were not damaged further by either side. They included small altars in the galleries, carved stone figures on the stairways and a set of wind chimes in the upper hall. The garrison's soldiers, many of whom had been told of the Air Nomads by their teachers at home, treated the shrines with care, and Liao is said to have forbidden the use of the shrines for firing positions. The Court's marines, who had been told that the islands held only a small garrison, were taken aback in several accounts by the discovery of the carved figures on the stairways.

The only damage to the buildings was caused by the bombardment of the lower halls and the burning of the storehouses. The upper temple was not hit. After the battle the garrison cleaned the shrines and set up a small guarded sanctuary in the main hall, which it maintained until 120. Several visitors who came to the islands during the war, including Qianchan observers and Royalist officers, described the sanctuary as the most peaceful place that they had seen during the war.

Casualties

About 3,000 people died in the battle, according to the Royalist and Qianchan record. The Court's dead numbered about 2,700, of whom about 1,100 were killed on the islands, about 900 were lost in the two transports sunk on 15 September, and about 700 were lost in the Akagi on 17 September. The Qianchan garrison lost about 220 killed and about 380 wounded, and the civilians on the islands lost about 80 killed. The Royalists, whose submarines were not damaged, lost no men. About 1,400 marines were taken prisoner. The Court lost the carrier Akagi, two transports, two destroyers and about 30 landing craft, and its air group lost about 25 aircraft.

The Court's records give a lower figure: about 1,200 dead and 600 missing. They do not mention the loss of the transports. The discrepancy is explained by the Court's practice of counting the dead of the Akagi as casualties of a separate naval action, and by its omission of the prisoners from the casualty returns. Later historians have used the Qianchan garrison's returns, which were checked against the Court's prisoner lists after the war, as the basis for the higher figure.

Aftermath

The Court did not attempt another landing. The island chain stayed in Qianchan hands until 120 AG, and its garrison was gradually reinforced. By 107 it numbered about 6,000, and its air group had grown to about eighty aircraft. The base continued to serve as the Royalists' principal transshipment point, and the flow of cargo, which had been interrupted for a fortnight in September, rose to about 120,000 tons a year in 105 and 106.

The loss of the Akagi and the transports had lasting effects on the Court's navy. The fleet, which had already been weakened at the Kumo Straits, was without a fleet carrier until 108, and it was forced to withdraw its remaining ships to the northern ports. Okuda, who was blamed for the failure, was relieved of his command in October and posted to a shore appointment. He died in 109. Hirata, who had not taken the field, was criticized by the General Staff Directorate for the poor coordination of the air and naval forces, but he retained his position, and in the following years he commanded the Court's armies in the north.

The battle was the first in which Qianchan forces fought the Court directly, and it changed the position of Qianchan in the war. The Qianchan Congress, which had approved the occupation of the islands on the understanding that the force would be used only to protect the base, debated the battle in October. A motion by the opposition to withdraw the garrison was defeated by 261 votes to 220, and a motion by the government to increase it was passed. The debate, which was reported in the Republican Daily, was the first of a series that ended in the vote of 109 to send two expeditionary divisions to the war.

Analysis

Military historians have generally regarded the landing as a failure of planning and coordination. The Court's staff made the mistake of dividing its attention between the beaches and the terraces, and of delaying the second wave while the guns were positioned, which gave the garrison two days to prepare. The use of the destroyers in the bombardment, which left the transports without an escort, made the sinking of the transports possible. The Court's air arm was not committed in strength, and its carriers were within the Qianchan group's range for the last two days of the battle.

The garrison's defense, on the other hand, was a model of the use of terrain. Liao's decision not to defend the beaches, and to rely on the terraces and the galleries, saved his troops from the Court's naval gunfire and allowed him to fight on ground that suited his weapons. His use of the stairways as fire lanes, and of the galleries as covered communications, is described in the Qianchan staff manuals of the period. The garrison's artillery on the ridge, which was never silenced, was the decisive element. The Court's naval gunfire destroyed the quays and the storehouses, but it did not hit the guns.

The battle also showed the limits of the Court's amphibious capability. The marines of the Eastern Army Group had been trained for river and coastal operations, and had little experience of an opposed landing against a prepared defense. The landing craft, which were of an old type, were slow and vulnerable. The Court's planners did not allow for the effects of the surf on the eastern beaches, which was one of the main reasons for the high casualties in the first hours.

Legacy

The islands remained under the Qianchan flag until 120 AG and became a place of refuge for people who left the Fire Nation during the war. After 109, when the Qianchan expeditionary divisions were sent to the war, the islands were used as a staging area for the transports, and in 118 and 119 they were a collecting point for refugees from Caldera. The Court's prisoners, who were sent home after the war, spoke well of the garrison, and the battle contributed to the postwar acceptance of Qianchan as a guarantor of the armistice of 118.

The ruined Air Temple, which had been razed in the Air Nomad Genocide, was cleaned by the garrison and a small shrine was kept. After the garrison's withdrawal in 120 the islands were handed over to a trust, administered jointly by the United Republic of Nations and the Air Nomad survivors, and the temple is today a protected site. A memorial on the central island, erected in 121, lists the names of the garrison's dead and those of the Court's marines who died on the islands. It is one of the few memorials of the war that records the dead of both sides on the same wall.

Historiography

Royalist and Qianchan accounts

Royalist and Qianchan sources describe the landing as a disaster for the Court. They emphasize the sinking of the Akagi and the transports, the casualties of the first day on the beaches, and the surrender of the marines. The Republican Daily, which reported the battle from the Qianchan side, says that the Court lost six times as many men as the garrison, and argues that the battle persuaded the Qianchan Congress that the war was winnable. Qianchan military histories, in particular the work of Colonel Sun Bo, who published his account in 125, emphasize the engineering of the defense and the role of the air group.

Court accounts

Court records say that the landing was a limited operation, intended to test the islands' defenses, and that the losses were acceptable. The General Staff Directorate's report of October 104 states that the operation achieved its purpose, which was to show that the islands could be reached, and that the Court did not intend to take them. Later Court-sympathetic authors, among them Nakagawa Jun, whose memoirs appeared in 128, concede that the landing failed, but ascribe the failure to the inadequate air support that the Directorate had promised and to the decisions of Okuda in the last week.

Other accounts

The accounts of the prisoners, in particular Oda's notebook, are the main independent source, and they support the Qianchan version of events. They are generally regarded as reliable, though their authors had reason to speak well of their captors. The Air Nomad survivors' accounts of the islands in the postwar years are of a different kind: they describe the care of the garrison for the temple, and the significance of the shrine, and they are cited in discussions of the war's effects on the memory of the Air Nomads.

first_battle_of_shu_jing.title: First Battle of Shu Jing
first_battle_of_shu_jing.html:
First Battle of Shu Jing
Part ofThe middle stage of the Fire Nation Civil War
Date3 April – 19 July 107 AG
LocationShu Jing industrial center and the plain to its south
ResultRoyalist victory. The Court’s strategic reserve is destroyed
Belligerents
Ozai loyalists (the Court)Royalists, with Qianchan supply
Commanders and leaders
Court
General Hirata Gensai; Lieutenant General Sakai Renjiro		Royalists
Brigadier Ito Shigeru; Colonel Mori Tatsuo; Zuko (in the city)
Strength
Court
about 130,000 with 400 tanks, 3 Breaker companies and 120 aircraft		Royalists
about 70,000, later about 95,000, with Qianchan anti-armor and anti-aircraft stocks
Casualties and losses
About 85,000 killed, of whom about 31,000 were civilians

The First Battle of Shu Jing was the Court’s largest offensive of the early and middle war. From April to July 107 AG, armored columns, Breaker companies and bombers attacked the Royalists’ industrial base. The Royalists held, and the Court’s strategic reserve was destroyed. About 85,000 people died, making it the war’s deadliest battle to that date and the seventh of its twenty defining battles.

The battle ended the Court’s capacity for strategic offensives. The survivors of its reserve, unpaid and ill-supplied, were the first units to form the salvation committees that later took over the Court’s army (see the Fire Nation Civil War).

Background

By 107 AG the war had hardened. The Court held Caldera and the western heartland, and the Royalists held Shu Jing, whose foundries rebuilt tanks and produced rifles for about 100,000 troops. Qianchan supplies reached the city through the coastal line rebuilt in 103 AG and, increasingly, by river from the south. The Court, which had won at Seiryū Bay and Hōryū Pass but failed to follow up either, decided that the war could only be ended by taking the city.

The General Staff Directorate assembled the offensive over the winter. It drew in the divisions that had won the east, the armored regiments from the pass, three Breaker companies, 120 aircraft and the Court’s whole strategic reserve, about 130,000 troops in all. It was the largest force the Court ever put into the field.

Forces

Court. Eastern Army Group (two corps); the 1st, 2nd and 4th Armored Regiments (about 400 tanks, Tessho-III infantry); the 1st, 2nd and 3rd Breaker Companies; the 5th Air Division (T-50 fighters and B-100 bombers); Flame Guard battalions.

Royalists. First Army (three divisions); the Works Guard (about 14,000); the East Rail command; naval infantry; Qianchan anti-armor rocket stocks and anti-aircraft guns; the city’s civil defense corps.

The Court’s advantage in armor was larger than at any other point in the war, about four to one. The Royalists’ advantage was the ground: the city’s foundry districts were built of masonry and steel, with narrow streets, and tanks that entered them could be attacked from every floor.

Course

3–30 April: the plain

The offensive opened on 3 April with a bombing of the city’s rail yards and a two-day bombardment of the southern defenses. The Court’s armor crossed the plain in three columns and reached the outer suburbs by 14 April. Ito, who commanded the defense, did not try to hold the suburbs, and drew the columns into the district of the foundries.

May: the foundry districts

The battle for the foundries lasted through May. The Court advanced block by block behind its tanks, while the Royalists, fighting from the buildings, destroyed about 160 tanks with rockets and with improvised charges. On 19 May a Breaker company broke through the Ironmonger Street line and reached the river, and was destroyed by a counterattack of Works Guard companies led by Mori Tatsuo. Zuko, who was in the city, visited the line on 21 May and remained for the rest of the battle.

June–July: the breaking of the reserve

By June the Court had lost about 250 tanks and two Breaker companies, and its infantry divisions were at half strength. Its supply line was cut on 9 June, when Royalist and Qianchan-supplied aircraft destroyed the bridges over the southern river. A relief column was turned back on 22 June. On 3 July the Royalists counterattacked from the foundries and the Canal yards, and by 19 July the surviving Court troops were in retreat across the plain, under air attack.

Civilian accounts

The best civilian record is the notebook of Hayakawa Misa, a clerk in the Eastgate foundry office, who kept a daily list of the shifts, the wounded and the price of rice from April to July. The notebook was edited by her daughter and published in 134 AG. It records that the foundries kept producing rifles through the whole battle, with the night shift working by lamplight to avoid air raids, and that the rationing office on Canal Street gave out bread to anyone with a work card, "and in the last month to anyone who stood in the line."

The accounts agree that the fighting was close to the workers' homes. About 40,000 people left the city by the northern road during the battle, in columns that the Royalist air group escorted as far as the second river. Hayakawa stayed. Her last entry on the battle, for 19 July, reads: "The guns are further off. The foundry whistle blew at six, the first time since April."

Casualties

The Royalist record gives about 85,000 dead, of whom about 54,000 were soldiers. The remainder were civilians who died in the bombing and the street fighting; the city’s population fell by about 40,000 in the six months of the battle, from deaths and evacuations. The Court lost about 38,000 killed and about 40,000 wounded or captured. It is generally accepted that the Court’s strategic reserve no longer existed after July.

Aftermath

The Court never again attempted an offensive of this size. Its survivors, who had been told that the city would fall in a month, were left in the plain without pay and with little food for the autumn, and the first salvation committees formed in the divisions that had retreated from Shu Jing in the following winter. By 109 AG the committees had captured the IRB’s western complex (see Ryuusei Facility).

Shu Jing was damaged but kept its foundries. It was attacked again in 113 and 116 AG.

Legacy

The battle made Shu Jing the Royalists' symbolic capital. The Ironmonger Street line, where the Breaker company was destroyed, became the site of the Works Guard memorial, and Mori Tatsuo, who held it, was promoted to colonel and put in charge of the city's defense until his death in 117 AG. The foundry unions, which had fought as the Works Guard, kept their weapons registers and later sat on the committees that reorganized the Royalist army.

The battle also set the pattern for the later assaults on the city. The Court did not return in strength until 113 AG, and then in company with the Salvationists, who had learned from the retreat how an army could be broken and who tried to avoid the same mistakes. The three battles of Shu Jing are often read together, as a single siege in three parts, and the first is the part that is least disputed.

Historiography

Royalist histories present the battle as the turning point of the early war and credit Zuko’s presence with holding the line. Court records describe it as a reconnaissance in force that cost more than expected, and deny that the reserve was destroyed. Salvationist accounts, written by veterans of the retreat, treat the battle as the moment when the ordinary soldiers saw that the war could not be won, and they date the first committee meetings to the night of 20 July.

  • Second Battle of Shu Jing

battle_of_the_ryuusei_facility.title: Battle of the Ryuusei Facility
battle_of_the_ryuusei_facility.html:
Battle of the Ryuusei Facility
Part ofThe middle stage of the Fire Nation Civil War
Date14 October 109 AG (one day)
LocationThe Imperial Research Bureau’s western complex, near Kusanagi in the western heartland
ResultSalvationist victory. The committees capture the complex, its missiles and the Project Tetsuken stock
Belligerents
Salvationist committees, with defecting garrison troopsOzai loyalists (the Court), the complex’s security battalions
Commanders and leaders
Salvationists
committee delegates; Sergeant Major Tanaka Kenji (assault)		Court
Colonel Kageyama Soichi (security commander)
Strength
Salvationists
about 6,000		Court
about 3,500 in the complex, with armored vehicles and the Flame Guard security battalion
Casualties and losses
About 14,000 killed, including about 9,000 civilians in the research town

The Battle of the Ryuusei Facility was a one-day assault on 14 October 109 AG by committee-led units on the Imperial Research Bureau’s western complex. The committees captured it in a day, with the help of troops from the complex’s own garrison. The facility’s twelve operational Ryuusei-B2 ballistic missiles, its production line and its stock of Project Tetsuken systems gave the Salvationists their weapons. It is the eighth of the war’s twenty defining battles.

The capture turned the war into a three-sided one, and gave the movement the arms that later let it break with the Court.

Background

The Imperial Research Bureau’s western complex was the Empire’s principal weapons laboratory and production site. According to the Bureau’s 99 AG inventory, it held the Ryuusei-B2 ballistic missile program (12 operational missiles and 340 in production), the Project Tetsuken gauntlet, lightning-discharge and fire-chain systems, and the prototype Breaker Mk II power armor. The complex sat in a valley about 60 kilometers west of Caldera, with a research town of about 12,000 people.

After the First Battle of Shu Jing, committees formed in the survivors of the Court’s reserve, and by 109 AG several were in contact with the garrison’s own committee, formed by technicians and rank-and-file guards who had not been paid for seven months. The Court, which depended on the weapons, had reinforced the complex with a Flame Guard security battalion in the spring.

The facility

The western complex of the Imperial Research Bureau was a purpose-built site in the Ryuusei Valley, with a perimeter of two walls, a rail spur and the research town of Kusanagi-Shita, which housed the technicians and their families. The missile hall, which had been dug into the hillside, was the largest building. The prototype Tetsuken systems were kept in the workshops, where they had been developed by a team of about 300 engineers.

Fujiwara Daigo, an engineer who headed the Tetsuken workshop, became the chairman of the garrison's committee in the spring of 109. He had been unpaid for seven months, and he told the delegates at Kusanagi that the weapons “should belong to those who made them.” After the capture he became the technical member of the Central Salvation Committee.

Order of battle

Committees (about 6,000 and the garrison committee). Delegates from the Eastern Army Group; units from neighboring committees; the garrison's own committee. Trucks, small arms; inside knowledge of the complex.

Court (about 1,200). Flame Guard security battalion under Colonel Kageyama Soichi; a column of armor from Caldera. Tanks, field guns.

Civilians. About 12,000 in the research town. About 9,000 killed by the Court's armor.

Course

The attack was planned by about two dozen delegates from the committees of the Eastern Army Group, who met at the town of Kusanagi on 11 October. They decided to attack from within, to preserve the missiles and the production line.

At 04:30 on 14 October the garrison’s committee disarmed the guards at the main gate, and about 6,000 men from neighboring committee-led units entered the complex in trucks, as a routine relief. The Flame Guard battalion, which was in its barracks, fought for the missile hall and held it for about three hours before surrendering. The security commander, Colonel Kageyama Soichi, was killed in the fight.

The research town suffered most. A column of Court armor, sent from Caldera on the morning of the attack, shelled the town from the hills, and about 9,000 civilians were killed before the committees drove it off by midday. By evening the Salvationists held the complex and had secured the 12 operational missiles, the production line and about 400 Tetsuken sets.

Civilian accounts

The research town's dead included many technicians' families. A schoolteacher in the town, Matsuda Reiko, who was later the Central Salvation Committee's supply member, wrote a note on the morning of 14 October that was later found in the school: “The guns are on the hill. We are in the cellar of the school. I have counted forty children and they are all quiet.” After the battle she distributed the town's stock of food and joined the committees.

The Court's armored column was commanded by Colonel Okada Jun, who afterward claimed that the town had been shelled by mistake. The committees' records say that the column had fired for three hours, and that it had been ordered to destroy the complex rather than allow it to be captured.

The weapons

The Ryuusei-B2 was a liquid-fuel ballistic missile with a range of about 300 kilometers and a warhead of about 800 kilograms. The Bureau had built 340 of them by 109 AG, but only 12 were operational, because the others lacked guidance systems. The guidance systems were the work of a small team of engineers who had been unpaid and who, with the committees' help, kept the missiles in storage. The missiles were moved by rail to launch sites in the west, and about eight were still in working order in 113.

The Tetsuken system, a gauntlet that generated and directed electrical discharges, was designed to allow non-benders to fight firebenders. It was powered by a back-mounted generator that could run for about 20 minutes. About 400 sets were captured on 14 October, and the committees trained about 3,000 soldiers to use them over the following year. The system was effective against armor and against firebenders, but its generators were unreliable, and about a quarter of the sets failed in the field.

The Court's response

The Court responded to the loss with a series of reprisals. Hirata Gensai ordered the arrest of about 600 officers suspected of sympathy with the committees, and about 80 were shot. The Court also tried to retake the complex in November with a force of about 8,000, which was repulsed by the Salvationists in a three-day battle in the valley. After that the Court did not attempt to retake it.

Notable people

Colonel Kageyama Soichi, the security battalion's commander, was a Flame Guard officer who had served at the Southern Air Temple Landing. He was killed in the missile hall, leading a counterattack with about 30 men. The committees buried him with the Court's honors, and his body was later returned to his family.

Fujiwara Daigo, the engineer, was 37 at the time of the capture. He directed the committees' use of the weapons, and in 116 became a member of the Central Salvation Committee. After the war he was tried and sentenced to 12 years, and was released in 130 AG. He died in 141.

Reception in the sources

The capture is recorded in the Bureau's own files, which the committees preserved, in the minutes of the Kusanagi meeting, and in the Court's reports. The Bureau's inventories, which list the weapons, are the main source for the numbers. The Salvationists' veterans have published several accounts, of which the best known is the memoir of a technician, Ishikawa Daichi, who describes the morning of 14 October from inside the missile hall.

Aftermath

The capture gave the Salvationists weapons that no other party had, and it gave them an ideology to match: the Tetsuken gauntlets, which let non-benders fight firebenders, were distributed to the former Kern infantry, who were trained to use them. The Ryuusei missiles were not fired until 113 AG (see Second Battle of Shu Jing). The Court could no longer rely on the loyalty of its field army, which began to defect by regiment.

Analysis

The capture is usually described as the Salvationists' first political act, and as the event that changed the war from a two-sided one to a three-sided one. The committees' success came from surprise and from the cooperation of the garrison. Historians note that the committees' attack plan, which called for the avoidance of damage to the missile hall, was carried out with a precision that suggests the engineers had planned the details for months.

The 12 missiles were not used for four years. Their fuel, which was stored in the complex, had to be replaced, and the committees did not have the specialists to operate the launchers until Fujiwara's team had trained a crew. The first launch, in May 113, is described in the article on the Second Battle of Shu Jing.

Legacy

The valley is today a memorial site, and the research town has been rebuilt. The missile hall, which was damaged in 118, is preserved as a ruin. The Salvationists consider 14 October their foundation day, and the Royalist and later governments have been uneasy about the observance.

Historiography

Salvationist accounts present the capture as a revolt of the army’s own technicians and call it the first act of the committees’ government. Court records call it a mutiny and put the dead at about 2,000. Royalist histories note that the Royalists did not take part and say that the capture was the Court’s own fault, because the Court left the complex under the control of unpaid troops.
