iwakura_plain.title: Battle of Iwakura Plain
iwakura_plain.html:
Battle of Iwakura Plain
Part ofThe middle stage of the Fire Nation Civil War
Date2–19 June 110 AG
LocationIwakura Plain, a flat river basin south of Shu Jing
ResultRoyalist victory. The Court’s last major armored offensive is destroyed
Belligerents
Royalists, with Qianchan expeditionary forcesOzai loyalists (the Court)
Commanders and leaders
Royalists
General Ito Shigeru; Major General Liao Zhen (Qianchan 2nd Expeditionary Division)		Court
General Hirata Gensai
Strength
Royalists
about 90,000, including about 15,000 Qianchan troops, with anti-armor stocks and about 200 tanks		Court
about 70,000 and about 500 tanks, assembled from its remaining armored and loyal units
Casualties and losses
About 120,000 killed

The Battle of Iwakura Plain was a seventeen-day battle in June 110 AG, and the largest tank battle of the Fire Nation Civil War. The Court's last major armored offensive, led by General Hirata Gensai with about 70,000 men and about 500 tanks, met the Royalist First Army and the Qianchan 2nd Expeditionary Division on open ground south of Shu Jing and was destroyed. By the end of the battle on 19 June the Court had lost about 380 of its tanks, and the estimated number of dead was about 120,000. It is the ninth of the war's twenty defining battles.

The Court's armored strength never recovered. The Royalists, who had been on the defensive since the Court's offensive of 101, gained the strategic initiative, though at heavy cost: about half of the division strength of the First Army was lost, and the supply of Shu Jing, which fed the army, was reduced to rations for the winter of 110. The battle is regarded as the most thoroughly studied armored action in the region, and its mine doctrine, which was developed by Qianchan engineers, was used in later wars. It is also remembered for the refusals of orders by Court tank crews on 15 June, which Salvationist sources treat as the first mass refusal of the war.

Background

The Court's position in 110

By the spring of 110 AG the Court's position had worsened. In the autumn of 109 its main infantry force had been broken at the Battle of Soka Bay, where two Qianchan expeditionary divisions landed and, with the Royalist army, destroyed the Court's infantry reserve under Hirata. In the same month the committees had captured the Imperial Research Bureau's western complex in the Battle of the Ryuusei Facility, which cost the Court its stock of the Tetsuken weapons and the Ryuusei missiles, and which showed that a growing number of its units would obey committees before their officers. The units that remained loyal in name included the armored regiments, the motorized infantry divisions and the Flame Guard, which together formed the largest concentration of force that the Court still commanded.

The Court's generals were in a hurry. According to the minutes of the General Staff Directorate, the council that met in Caldera in March 110 concluded that discipline could be restored in the army only by a victory, and that the victory must be won before the Royalists and the Qianchan could bring up more troops from the south. The Directorate also believed that the committees, which were growing in the armored regiments, could not yet bring their influence to bear on operations, and that the window in which the armor could be used reliably would close within a year. The Court's treasury, which depended on the factories of Sakuragawa, could not support a long campaign.

Hirata's plan

Hirata Gensai, who had commanded at the Clashes at Shu Jing and at Soka Bay, proposed to destroy the Royalist field army in a single battle on the plain south of Shu Jing, where the Court's armor could move freely. His memorandum of 3 April, which is preserved in the Directorate's records, argued that the Royalists had committed their reserve to the defense of the industrial center and that a rapid advance from the south and the east would fix them in place and allow the Court's tanks to cut their lines to the river. The plan required about 500 tanks, two motorized infantry divisions and the 5th Air Division, and it called for the offensive to begin in the first week of June, before the rains.

Azula approved the plan on 11 April. Hirata was given command of all Court forces in the north and was promised the fuel and ammunition that he requested. The preparation took about seven weeks, and the army was concentrated at the rail towns south of the plain in the second half of May. The Directorate's records show that Hirata was concerned about the reliability of his tank crews, about a third of whom had served under officers who had since defected, and that he ordered the arrest of about thirty officers in May. He did not, however, change the plan.

The Royalist and Qianchan preparations

The Royalists learned of the Court's concentration in April, from reports of the rail traffic and from agents in the Court's staff, and they had about six weeks in which to prepare. General Ito Shigeru, who commanded the First Army, had held Shu Jing in 107 and was known for his preference for fighting from prepared positions. He was under pressure from Zuko and from the Qianchan mission to fight on the plain, which he disliked, because it deprived him of the cover of the city. He accepted the decision in the end, on the condition that the battle be fought on ground of his own choosing and that the Qianchan engineers be given the time to prepare it.

The ground that he chose was a line of low ridges south of the village of Iwakura, about 30 kilometers south of Shu Jing, which commanded the road and the rail line from the south. The plain in front of the ridges was flat and open, about twelve kilometers deep, and was crossed by a number of drainage channels and irrigation banks. The Qianchan expeditionary corps, which had been in the Fire Nation since the autumn of 109, supplied the engineers and the weapons for the defense. The preparation of the position, which is described in the sections that follow, took about six weeks and employed about 3,000 engineers and conscripted laborers.

Forces and commanders

The Court

The Court's force numbered about 70,000 men and about 500 tanks, and was organized as the Northern Armored Army under General Hirata. Its core was the 1st, 2nd and 3rd Armored Regiments, which together held about 380 tanks, and the 6th Independent Armored Brigade, with about 120. The tanks were mostly the Tessho-III, a medium tank with a 90mm gun, of which about 400 were committed. The remainder were older Tessho-II tanks with 75mm guns. The armored regiments were organized in battalions of about 45 tanks, each with a company of motorized infantry and a platoon of engineers.

The infantry of the army consisted of two motorized divisions, the 12th and the 19th, with about 28,000 men between them, who were carried in trucks and half-tracks. Both had served in the eastern campaign and had been rebuilt after the losses at Soka Bay. Their equipment was good, but their training was uneven: the 19th Division had received about 6,000 conscripts in March and April, who had not fired their rifles in a field exercise. The army also included the Flame Guard's 3rd Battalion, about 900 men, who were attached to Hirata's headquarters, and three companies of the Breaker Mk II power armor, about forty machines in all, which were to be used on the flanks.

The army's air support was provided by the 5th Air Division, which had about 70 aircraft: 30 fighters, 30 light bombers and 10 transports. Its commander, Major General Okamoto Jiro, had been a pilot in the Hundred Year War and was regarded as one of the Court's more capable air officers. The division's task was to suppress the Royalist artillery and to support the armored columns. It was able to operate from two fields south of the plain, and by June it held the fuel for about ten days of operations.

The Court's supply system was organized around the rail line from the south, and it depended on the cooperation of the rail units, which were increasingly under the influence of the committees. By 2 June the army's depots held fuel for about ten days of operations and shells for about twelve, a figure that was less than Hirata had requested. The shortfall was attributed by the Directorate to the delays in the rail traffic and by Hirata to the Directorate's neglect. Hirata's chief of staff, Colonel Ando Takeru, who later commanded the Flame Guard at Caldera, kept a diary in which he recorded that the army set out with "enough for the first week, and hopes for the second."

Command and discipline

Hirata exercised command from a headquarters train, which was positioned about 25 kilometers behind the front. His principal subordinates were Major General Ogura Shuichi, who commanded the armored regiments, Major General Tamura Hideo, who commanded the motorized infantry, and Okamoto, who commanded the air division. The relationship between Hirata and Ogura was poor. Ogura, who had served in the eastern campaign, regarded Hirata as too cautious, and he is recorded in Ando's diary as having said that "the general plans for the battle he wishes to have and not for the one he will get."

The tank crews were the army's most disaffected element. A number of the regiments had held committee meetings during the winter, and in March the Directorate ordered the dissolution of what it called "unauthorized assemblies" in the armored units. The orders had little effect. By June, the committees in the 2nd and 3rd Regiments had established informal control of the distribution of the food and fuel in their units, and the commanders, who needed the crews' cooperation, did not interfere. Hirata knew of this, and he took the view that the crews would fight as long as they believed that they were winning.

The Royalists

The Royalist force numbered about 90,000, of whom about 75,000 were Royalist troops and about 15,000 were Qianchan. The Royalist element was the First Army, under General Ito Shigeru, which had five divisions, the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 5th and 6th, and about 62,000 men. It was supported by the Works Guard's artillery regiments, which had about 120 guns and were commanded by Colonel Mori Tatsuo, who had held the Ironmonger Street line at the First Battle of Shu Jing. The remaining Royalist troops, about 13,000, were in the Reserve Corps, which was kept in the second line under Major General Aizawa Kenji and which was to counterattack when the Court's armor had been stopped.

The Royalist army had about 200 tanks, which were of the same types as the Court's but were fewer and of older models. They were used as mobile reserves behind the ridges. Their principal weapons were the anti-armor weapons that the army had developed during the previous two years. The shoulder-fired Hagane rocket, which had been developed in the foundries of Shu Jing in 108, had a range of 400 meters and a hollow-charge warhead that could penetrate the side armor of the Tessho-III at about 300 meters. It was issued in teams of three, and about 4,500 teams were in the line. The Royalist artillery included about 280 field guns and about 60 heavy guns, mostly 105mm and 150mm, with their own stocks of armor-piercing shells.

The Royalist air support was weak. The Royalists had about 25 aircraft in the area, and the principal air support came from the Qianchan air group. The Royalist command relied on the Works Guard's fire companies and the army's signal corps to maintain communications, and its field telephone network, which had been laid in the weeks before the battle, was the most extensive that the army had used.

The Qianchan expeditionary force

The Qianchan force consisted of the 2nd Expeditionary Division, with about 15,000 men, under Major General Liao Zhen, and the corps' engineers and air group. The division was a regular formation of three infantry regiments, an artillery regiment and a company of engineers. It had arrived in the Fire Nation after the landing at Soka Bay, and had been stationed at the rail town of Kuroda, south of the plain, since the winter. The 1st Expeditionary Division, which had also landed at Soka Bay, remained on the coast and did not take part in the battle.

The overall commander of the Qianchan expeditionary corps was General Han Zhiyuan, a former engineer, who supervised the preparation of the mine belts and the anti-armor defenses. Han remained at the Royalist headquarters during the battle and acted as Ito's principal adviser. The corps' air group, which was commanded by Colonel Gu Mingzhe, had about 50 aircraft, mostly light bombers and fighters, and operated from a field south of the Royalist line. The division's anti-armor weapons were of Qianchan manufacture: about 600 tripod-mounted recoilless guns, which had a longer range than the Hagane and could engage tanks at 800 meters.

The Qianchan force operated under the command of Ito, but its officers retained the right to refer his orders to the Qianchan mission. In practice this right was exercised only twice, on 12 June and 17 June, and in each case the orders were confirmed. Contemporary accounts note the good relations between Ito and the Qianchan commanders. Liao Zhen, who was 44, had been a staff officer in the Qianchan army's operations division, and he is recorded to have disagreed with Ito on a number of points but to have accepted his decisions.

The defensive position

The ground

The plain south of Shu Jing was the basin of a river that ran in a broad curve from the western hills to the sea. It was flat, with a gentle slope to the east, and it was cut by drainage channels and irrigation banks that formed a rough grid. The soil was a heavy clay that was soft after rain and hard in dry weather, and in the first week of June, when the battle began, it was dry. The villages of the plain, of which there were about forty, were small, built of timber and clay, and surrounded by rice fields that had been left unplanted in the spring. The principal road ran from the south through Iwakura village to the river crossing at Shu Jing, and the rail line ran beside it.

The ridges, which Ito chose for the defense, ran from east to west for about eighteen kilometers, and rose about 30 meters above the plain. They were covered with scrub and a few stands of pine, and they were cut by two valleys through which the road and the rail line ran. The Royalists could observe the plain from the ridges for about twelve kilometers, and the guns on the ridges could cover the whole of the approach.

The mine belts

The Qianchan engineers, under Han Zhiyuan, laid the mines in the six weeks before the battle. The belts, which ran in three lines across the plain at distances of about 3, 6 and 9 kilometers from the ridges, were of two types: a large anti-tank mine, which was laid in rows with a spacing of about 6 meters, and a small pressure mine, which was laid in the gaps and on the paths. About 300,000 mines were laid, by about 3,000 engineers and conscripted laborers working in shifts. The work was done at night, to avoid observation by the Court's aircraft, and the mines were buried and concealed with turf.

The belts were not continuous. They were laid with gaps, of about 200 meters, at intervals of about a kilometer, and the gaps were not marked. The gaps were intended to appear to a reconnaissance as the places in which the Royalists' own vehicles could cross the lines, and they were covered by pre-registered artillery fire. The tanks that entered a gap found the next belt behind it, at an angle, and were forced to halt in the killing ground. The engineers, who had learned the technique in the Qianchan border wars, called it "the corridor," and Han wrote that its purpose was "not to stop the enemy but to tell him where to go."

The anti-armor positions

Behind the belts the Royalists dug a system of anti-armor positions in depth. The forward line, about 800 meters behind the last belt, consisted of strongpoints held by companies of infantry with Hagane teams and recoilless guns, in trenches that were connected by communication trenches to the ridge. The second line, on the forward slopes of the ridge, held the artillery, the heavy guns and the tank reserves. The third line, behind the ridge, held the Reserve Corps and the supply depots.

The positions were designed to be mutually supporting and to be held against armored attack without the need for a mobile reserve. Each strongpoint had a field of fire of about 800 meters, and the fields overlapped. The trenches were deep and narrow, so that a tank could not cross them, and the strongpoints were built of timber and earth, with overhead cover against shell fire. The Royalist engineers also buried a number of command-fired charges under the road crossings and the bridges, which could be detonated by wire from the strongpoints, and which were to be used against the leading tanks.

Deception

The Royalist command also took measures to deceive the Court about the extent of the defenses. The forward belts were laid so that the gaps were visible to aerial reconnaissance, and the Royalists placed dummy tanks, built of wood and canvas, in the villages behind the ridges. A small force of tanks, about thirty, was kept in the forward area in the first week of June to draw the Court's attention, and was withdrawn on 4 June. The Court's reconnaissance reports, which were captured at the end of the battle, show that Hirata believed the Royalist line to be held by about 40,000 men and to be protected by only one belt of mines.

Course

The advance (2–5 June)

The Court's army began its advance at dawn on 2 June, after a bombardment of the Royalist forward positions by about 150 guns and an attack by the 5th Air Division on the ridges. The tanks advanced in a broad line, about 14 kilometers wide, with the Tessho-III battalions in the center and the Breaker companies on the flanks, and the motorized infantry followed about two kilometers behind. Hirata, who watched the advance from a command vehicle, had ordered the armor to advance at a steady pace of about 15 kilometers an hour, to keep its formation and to avoid halting under fire.

The first echelon, about 250 tanks, reached the outer mine belt at about nine o'clock. The belts were not marked, and the tanks did not slow down. According to the Royalist observers' reports, the first mines went off in the center of the line at about 9:10, and within ten minutes about forty tanks had been disabled. The Court's engineers, who had been ordered to advance with the leading echelon, were hit by Royalist artillery fire before they could clear a lane, and the commanders of the leading battalions, who found gaps in the belt, directed their tanks toward them. The gaps led, as the Qianchan engineers had intended, into the corridors.

The Royalist artillery opened fire at about 9:30, at a range of about 800 meters from the forward strongpoints. The Hagane teams and the recoilless guns fired on the tanks in the corridors, and the heavy guns fired on the tanks that were halted behind the belts. The Court's tanks, which were bunched in the corridors, could not turn or maneuver, and the fire from the flanks hit them on the sides, where the armor was thinnest. By noon about 90 tanks had been destroyed, and the advance of the center had halted at the second belt.

The Breaker companies on the flanks, which had been expected to cross the belts without difficulty, fared little better. The machines, which weighed about eight tons each, were slow and difficult to steer, and their wide feet spread their weight across the mines, so that some of them crossed the first belt unharmed. They were then met by the rockets of the Royalist flank guard, which hit them in the legs and the joints. Of the forty machines, 31 were lost in the first week, most of them on 2 and 3 June. The survivors, with the Flame Guard battalion, were withdrawn to the rear on 5 June.

By 5 June the Court had lost about 140 tanks, and the leading echelon was forced to halt before the second belt. Hirata, who had expected the advance to reach the ridges by the evening of the first day, ordered the army to consolidate its position and to send engineers forward to clear lanes. The engineers worked at night, under fire, and by 8 June had cleared about six lanes through the first and second belts. They lost about 600 men in the process. Meanwhile, the Royalists, who knew the lanes by observation, registered them with their artillery.

Royalist actions in the first week

The Royalists did not remain passive. On 3 and 4 June the Works Guard's artillery regiments under Mori Tatsuo shelled the Court's assembly areas and the road behind the belts, and on 5 June the Qianchan air group attacked the Court's supply trains on the rail line, destroying about 30 trucks and a fuel train. The attack, which was made at dusk by about twenty aircraft, caused a fire in the rail yards at Kuroda that burned for two days. The Court's fuel supply was reduced by about a fifth, and Hirata's staff, which had calculated on ten days of operations, now recalculated on eight.

The Royalist raiders played a part as well. A detachment of about 600 men from the Works Guard, under Captain Kuwabara Seiji, crossed the Court's lines on the night of 6 June by way of a drainage channel and attacked the supply depots at the rail town of Hamada, about 20 kilometers behind the front. The raid destroyed about 400 tons of shells and a number of trucks, and the detachment withdrew with the loss of about 80 men. Court accounts say that the raid caused only minor damage. The Royalist and Qianchan record says that it was the main cause of the Court's shortage of shells in the second week.

The reserve attack (9–11 June)

On 9 June Hirata renewed the attack. He committed the reserve armor, about 150 tanks of the 6th Independent Armored Brigade, and ordered the whole army to advance on a narrower front, of about six kilometers, around the road and the rail line. The lanes that the engineers had cleared were used for the advance. The tanks, which now moved in columns of four, reached the third belt on the afternoon of 9 June, and the leading columns passed through it at about four o'clock.

The fighting on this day and the next two was the most intense of the battle. The Court's columns reached the forward strongpoints and attacked them with fire and ramming, and a number of the strongpoints were overrun. The Royalists, who had expected this, counterattacked from the second line with the tank reserve and the infantry. The fighting spread across the plain in a series of tank duels, in which the Court's armor, which had the greater numbers, was met by the Royalist tanks, which had the advantage of position and of the support of the anti-armor weapons.

The Royalist 3rd Division, which held the sector around the road, bore the brunt of the attack. Its commander, Major General Sugiura Taro, kept his division in position for two days against a force of about 200 tanks, and he lost about 5,000 men in that time. A battalion of the 3rd Division, which held the strongpoint at the Iwakura crossroads, was cut off on the afternoon of 10 June, and held out for 36 hours with the help of the Hagane teams, who destroyed about 30 tanks. The battalion's commander, Major Takeuchi Rin, was killed on the second day. By 11 June the strongpoint had been relieved, and the Court's attack on the road had been stopped about two kilometers from the ridge.

The twelfth of June

On 12 June a Court column found a gap between two Royalist divisions and drove about 15 kilometers toward the river. It was the nearest that the Court's armor came to a breakthrough. The column, which was led by Captain Mizuno Kaito's company of 24 tanks of the 2nd Armored Regiment, was made up of about 80 tanks, and it advanced along a drainage channel and a farm track that the Court's reconnaissance had found undefended. The gap was a result of a miscalculation: the Royalist 5th and 6th Divisions, which held the line on either side of it, had each assumed that the other was responsible for the ground, and the Qianchan division, which had been in the second line, had been moved to the road the day before.

The column broke through at about nine o'clock in the morning, and in four hours it advanced about 15 kilometers, passing through two villages and overrunning a battery of Royalist field guns. It reached a point about seven kilometers from the river crossing, within sight of the pontoon bridge that carried the First Army's supplies. Mizuno, who was leading the first company, reported by radio that "the road is open," and the Court's headquarters, which had been watching the battle on its situation map, ordered the reserve to follow. The message was the high point of the Court's offensive.

The column was destroyed in the afternoon. The Qianchan 2nd Division, which Liao Zhen had moved back from the road when he had heard of the breakthrough, met it at a canal crossing with about 200 recoilless guns and Hagane teams. A team under Sergeant Wu Lian destroyed seven tanks, and was then overrun by the column's rear. Wu was killed, but her team's fire had stopped the column at the crossing, and the Qianchan air group, which arrived at about two o'clock, attacked the stalled tanks with bombs. At the same time, the Royalist engineers detonated the command-fired charges that they had buried under the bridges and the road crossings, destroying about 60 tanks in the course of the day.

By the evening the column had ceased to exist. About 60 of its tanks were destroyed, and the remainder had been abandoned or had withdrawn. Mizuno's tank was disabled by a recoilless round at the canal crossing, and he was captured with his crew. The Royalist and Qianchan accounts say that about 4,000 of the Court's soldiers were killed in the column's advance and the destruction that followed. The Court's account does not mention the column.

The fighting of 13 and 14 June

The destruction of the column did not stop the fighting. Hirata, who had been told that the road to the river was open, committed the remainder of the reserve on 13 June in an attempt to reinforce the breakthrough, and the tank battle continued across the plain for two more days. The Court's armor, which had by now lost about 250 tanks, was increasingly short of fuel and shells, and it was operating at the limit of its supply line. The Royalists' guns, which were firing at a rate of about 50,000 rounds a day, were also short of ammunition, and the Works Guard's regiments were compelled to ration their fire.

During this phase, from 9 to 14 June, about 40,000 people were killed. The majority were infantry, who were killed in the assaults on the strongpoints and in the shelling of the assembly areas, and the others were tank crews who were killed in their vehicles. The casualty rates of the Court's motorized infantry were particularly high. The 19th Division, which had been used in the assault on the Iwakura crossroads, lost about 7,000 men in two days. The Royalist 3rd Division lost about 5,000, and the Qianchan 2nd Division about 1,800.

By the night of 14 June the Court's offensive had lost its impetus. The tanks were short of fuel and shells, the crews had been in action for twelve days, and the army's morale was low. Hirata held a conference at his headquarters, at which the divisional commanders reported that their units could not attack again without a rest. He decided to hold the positions that the army had taken and to resume the attack on 16 June, after the supply trains had come up.

The committees' meeting (14 June)

On the night of 14 June, according to the Salvationist accounts, a meeting of tank crews was held in the tank park of the 2nd Armored Regiment. About 300 men took part, among them the delegates of the regiment's committees and a number of officers. The meeting, which was recorded in the minutes of the regiment's committee, discussed the situation of the army and the intentions of the command. The minutes say that the crews voted, by a large majority, not to attack again unless the army was given the fuel and ammunition that it required, and that the delegates were instructed to inform the other regiments.

The meeting is the basis of the Salvationist claim that the refusals of 15 June were organized. Court records do not mention it. Royalist and Qianchan sources, which learned of it from prisoners, regard it as a spontaneous expression of the crews' exhaustion, and point out that the committee's minutes were written after the event. Several historians have accepted a middle position: the meeting took place, and it reflected a mood that had been growing for months, but it did not plan the refusals, which began in the morning of 15 June before the delegates had returned to their units.

The Royalist counterattack and the refusals (15–17 June)

The Royalists, who had observed the signs of exhaustion in the Court's lines, counterattacked on the morning of 15 June. The First Army's reserve, with the Qianchan 2nd Division and the Royalist tank reserve, advanced from the ridges under a barrage of about 200 guns, and the Court's forward units, which had been in action for twelve days, were caught in the open. The Court's armor, which was short of fuel and shells, could not respond effectively. Several of its battalions were found by the Royalist advance with their tanks standing in the fields, their engines idle.

On the same morning, a number of Court tank crews refused to advance. The refusals, which began in the 2nd and 3rd Armored Regiments and spread to the 6th Independent Brigade, took different forms. In some units the crews simply remained at their vehicles and did not start their engines. In others they abandoned the vehicles and marched to the rear. In at least three battalions, the crews arrested their officers and put them under guard. The Court's records say that these events involved about 40 tanks. Salvationist accounts say that they involved 150 or more, and the Royalist records, which are based on the interrogation of prisoners, give a figure of about 100.

The effect of the refusals, whatever their number, was to open gaps in the Court's line. The Royalist counterattack made rapid progress. By the evening of 15 June it had retaken the strongpoints that had been lost in the previous week and had reached the Court's lines at the second belt. On 16 June and 17 June the Royalists attacked the Court's rear areas with their air group and their raiders, and destroyed a number of the remaining depots. The Court's army, which was now divided into pockets, was forced to fight in the open with fuel that was almost exhausted.

The retreat (18–19 June)

Hirata decided on 17 June to withdraw. He issued the order on the evening of the same day, and the withdrawal began on 18 June. The retreat was conducted under heavy attack from the Royalist and Qianchan aircraft, which bombed the columns on the road, and from the Royalist artillery. Many tanks were abandoned for lack of fuel, and their crews marched to the rear. By 19 June the Court's army had crossed the southern edge of the plain, leaving about 380 of its 500 tanks destroyed or abandoned. Hirata withdrew with the remnants, about 30,000 men, to the rail towns, where he reorganized the army.

The Royalist First Army did not pursue. Ito, whose troops had been in action for seventeen days and had lost about a third of their strength, ordered his divisions to hold the ridges and to advance only to the first mine belt. The Qianchan engineers began the work of marking the mine belts, and the Royalist engineers began the collection of the wrecks and the burial of the dead. The battle had ended.

Weapons and equipment

Armor

The Tessho-III, the Court's principal tank, was a medium tank of about 32 tons, with a crew of four and a 90mm gun, and its armor was about 80 millimeters on the front and 40 on the sides. It was reliable and easy to maintain, and its engine, a diesel, gave it a range of about 300 kilometers on roads. The side armor was its weakness, and the Royalist weapons were designed to exploit it. The Tessho-II, an older model, had a 75mm gun and thinner armor, and it was used mainly for reconnaissance and infantry support. Both types carried a machine gun in the turret and a second in the hull.

The Breaker Mk II, known to its crews as the "Hagane no Oni," was a one-man power armor of about eight tons, which stood about three meters high and was armed with a 40mm cannon and flamethrowers. It had been developed by the Imperial Research Bureau during the Hundred Year War, and its strength by 110 AG was about 60 percent of what it had been before the Ba Sing Se campaign, because many of its components had not been replaced. The machine was slow, about eight kilometers an hour on firm ground, and its operators were exposed to the same fire as the tanks. The Court's staff believed that its weight would allow it to cross the mine belts, a belief that was partly justified, but the Royalists' rockets hit the machines' legs and joints.

Royalist and Qianchan weapons

The Hagane rocket was a shoulder-fired weapon of about 70 millimeters, with a hollow-charge warhead, a range of about 400 meters and a weight of about 6 kilograms. It was developed in the foundries of Shu Jing in 108 by a team under the engineer Sakurai Daiki, and it was first used in the Royalist defense of the city in the winter of 109. It required two men to operate, and the teams of three, which included a loader, were trained to fire from a prepared position and to move after two shots. The Qianchan recoilless gun was a tripod-mounted weapon of about 90 millimeters, with a range of about 800 meters, and it required a crew of three. It was heavier than the Hagane but more accurate, and the Qianchan teams used it to engage the tanks at long range while the Hagane teams held the close defense.

The Royalist artillery used armor-piercing shells in the first week and high-explosive shells after that. Its heavy guns, which were placed on the ridge, fired at the tanks in the corridors at ranges of about three kilometers, and their fire was directed by observers in the forward strongpoints. The Works Guard's regiments, under Mori Tatsuo, used a system of pre-registered concentrations that had been developed for the defense of the foundry district, and they were able to fire on any point of the approach within about two minutes of a request.

The mines were of Qianchan design, and they were produced in workshops at the Qianchan ports and shipped to the Fire Nation in the first months of 110. The large mine weighed about 9 kilograms, and it contained about 5 kilograms of explosive and was fired by a pressure fuse that required about 120 kilograms. The small mine weighed about 400 grams and was designed to disable a man's foot. It was fired by a pressure of about 5 kilograms, and the Qianchan engineers laid them in the gaps in the belts to deter the Court's engineers from clearing them on foot.

Communications

The Royalist field telephone network, which was laid by the army's signal corps in the six weeks before the battle, connected the forward strongpoints to the ridge and to the headquarters at the rear. It was built of double cable, buried in shallow trenches, and it survived the Court's bombardment on the first day, with the loss of about 20 percent of its lines. The network allowed Ito to direct the battle from a command post on the ridge, and gave him information about the course of the fighting within minutes of events. The Court's army, which relied on radio, was handicapped by the interference of the Royalist jamming and by the shortage of spare parts.

Civilian experience

The evacuation

The villages of the plain, which held about 60,000 people, were evacuated in May. The Royalist administration of Shu Jing organized the movement, which was carried out by rail and by cart, and the refugees were taken to six camps on the river, near the city. The evacuation was not entirely voluntary. A number of villagers refused to leave their farms, and the army sent patrols to enforce the order. A few hundred, mostly old people, remained in their houses. They were killed in the fighting or died of exposure in the following weeks.

The camps were organized by the Royalist relief committee, with the help of the Qianchan medical mission. The refugees were housed in tents and in the halls of the Shu Jing foundries, and they were fed from the army's kitchens. The Qianchan medical officer Dr. Lin Wei, who visited the camps in the first week of June, reported that the camps held about 60,000 people and that the food and water were adequate. His report, which was published by the Qianchan Congress in 111, described the camps as orderly and the refugees as subdued, and it recorded that the sound of the guns, which could be heard in the camps, was "like a heavy door being opened and closed across the river." He added that the plain behind the camps was "as quiet as a bell after it has stopped."

The plain after the battle

The farmers began to return to the plain in the autumn of 110. The Yoshida farm, near Iwakura, was one of the first. Its owner, Yoshida Haru, who was then 41, had kept a record of the farm's work and of the family's life during the evacuation, and she described her return on 4 October. The fields were "full of iron," as she wrote, and the house, which had been used by the Royalists as a strongpoint, was a ruin. Her record, which was donated to the Shu Jing museum in 130, notes that the family found about 50 shells in the first field and a half-buried tank in the second, with the remains of its crew inside.

The mine belts made the plain unusable for farming. The Qianchan engineers, who had marked the belts, advised the returning families not to enter them, and the Royalist administration closed about 40 percent of the plain in the autumn. Several farmers, who ignored the warnings, were killed by mines in the following years, and about 40 people died in this way between 110 and 112. The clearance of the plain, which began in 112 and continued until 123, was carried out by a joint Royalist-Qianchan engineer service, and it cost about 400 lives. About 290,000 mines were recovered. Yoshida's farm was cleared in 117, and the family planted rice there in the following spring. She recorded that the first harvest was "short and sweet." Her fence posts, made of tank track pins, are in the museum.

Rear-area casualties

Civilian deaths in the battle, which numbered about 13,000, were caused mainly by the Court's air attacks on the rail towns and the camps and by the shelling of the villages along the river. The Court's bombers attacked Shu Jing's rail yards on three occasions in June, and killed about 2,500 people. The camp at Nishihara, which was near a depot, was hit by an air raid on 11 June that killed about 800 people. A further 6,000 died in the following months of the diseases that spread in the camps, mostly typhoid, and the remainder were killed in the fighting or in the mine accidents of the summer.

Prisoners and wounded

The Royalists took about 9,000 prisoners in the battle, most of them in the last three days. They were held in a camp at Shu Jing, where they were questioned by the Royalist intelligence service and by the Qianchan mission. About 2,000 of them, who had refused to advance on 15 June or who had been arrested by their own crews, were separated from the others. A number of these were later released and joined the committees. The rest were held until the end of the war, and were sent home after the armistice.

The medical services of both sides were overwhelmed. The Royalists had about 10,000 beds in the rear areas, and the Qianchan mission added about 2,000. The wounded, who numbered about 70,000 on both sides, were evacuated by rail and by cart. The Court's wounded, who were left on the plain in the retreat, were collected by the Royalists on 20 June and treated in the field hospitals. About 4,000 of them died of their wounds in the following weeks.

Notable people

Hirata Gensai commanded the Court's Northern Armored Army. Born in the Eastern Territories, he had been the Court's principal field commander since the Clashes at Shu Jing and was an armor officer by training. His belief in the single decisive battle shaped the plan, and his critics on the Court's staff said that he had never lost a battle in which he held the initiative and never won one in which he did not. After the defeat he rebuilt a smaller force in the north, and he was killed in the Siege of Caldera in 118.

Ito Shigeru commanded the Royalist First Army. He chose the ridge line and the sequence of the defense, and he directed the battle from the command post on the ridge. His preference for prepared positions and his reluctance to pursue after 19 June were criticized by some Royalist officers, who thought that the Court's army could have been destroyed. He later commanded the Royalist Southern Army at Hira, Sakuragawa and Caldera.

Han Zhiyuan was the commander of the Qianchan expeditionary corps and a former engineer. He designed the mine belts and spent the weeks before the battle with the Royalist sappers, checking the layout and the spacing of the corridors. His advice to Ito during the battle, in particular his recommendation on 12 June that the Qianchan division be moved to the canal crossing, is credited by the Royalist staff with the destruction of the breakthrough column.

Liao Zhen (born 66 AG) commanded the Qianchan 2nd Expeditionary Division. A staff officer by background, he moved his division from the road to the canal crossing on his own initiative on the morning of 12 June, on the basis of reports of a gap in the Royalist line. He is described in the Royalist accounts as quiet and exact, and his division's casualties in the battle were about 3,500 killed.

Mori Tatsuo commanded the Works Guard's artillery regiments, which provided the Royalist army with its heavy fire. His system of pre-registered concentrations allowed the army to engage the tanks in the corridors with great rapidity. He was killed in the Third Battle of Shu Jing in 117.

Ogura Shuichi commanded the Court's armored regiments, and was one of the few senior officers to oppose Hirata's plan in the Court's council. He was killed on 17 June when his command vehicle was hit by an air attack. His death is described in Ando's diary, which notes that Hirata did not attend the funeral.

Captain Mizuno Kaito (born 76 AG) commanded a company of 24 tanks of the 2nd Armored Regiment and led the column that broke through toward the river on 12 June. His company advanced about 15 kilometers in four hours. He was captured when his tank was disabled by a Qianchan team and spent the rest of the war in a prisoner camp. After the war he testified before the hearings, and described his decision to advance as "the only choice I had been given." He later became a railway clerk, and died in 148.

Sergeant Wu Lian (born 85 AG) commanded a Qianchan anti-armor team of three, which destroyed seven tanks on 12 June at the canal crossing before it was overrun by the column's rear. She was killed on the same day. She is commemorated in Qianchan as the "gunner of the river road," and a street in the capital of Qianchan is named for her. Her recoilless gun is on display in the Qianchan army museum.

Major General Sugiura Taro commanded the Royalist 3rd Division, which held the sector around the road, and he kept his division in position through two days of attack by 200 tanks. His division lost about 5,000 men. He was wounded on 11 June, and returned to command in the summer of 111.

Yoshida Haru (born 69 AG) was a farmer whose family had worked the land near Iwakura for four generations. Her record of the family's life during the evacuation and after the battle is one of the principal civilian sources. She died in 149, and the farm is now a part of the memorial park.

Casualties

The Royalist and Qianchan record gives about 120,000 dead in the battle, a figure that has been generally accepted by later historians. The Court lost about 64,000 killed, of whom about 38,000 were killed in the fighting of 9 to 14 June and about 16,000 in the retreat and the pursuit. The Royalists lost about 38,000 killed, most of them from the First Army, and the Qianchan expeditionary force lost about 5,000. About 13,000 civilians died in the camps, the rear areas and the mine accidents. The wounded numbered about 70,000.

The Court lost about 380 of its 500 tanks and about 31 of its 40 Breaker machines. The Royalists lost about 70 of their 200 tanks, about 120 guns and a large number of vehicles. The Qianchan division lost about 1,800 men on 12 and 13 June alone, and the air group lost about 12 aircraft. The Court's 5th Air Division lost about 40 aircraft, most of them to the Qianchan fighters and to anti-aircraft fire.

The figures are disputed in detail. Court records, which survive in part, give the Court's tank losses as about 150 and its dead as about 20,000, and they put the Royalist dead at 50,000. The discrepancy is largely explained by the Court's practice of counting abandoned tanks as withdrawn and the missing as survivors. The Royalist salvage returns, which list about 380 hulks recovered from the plain, provide the strongest evidence for the higher figure. The Qianchan reports, which tabulated the dead by the burial returns, give a total of about 112,000 for the soldiers, and the difference from the Royalist total is attributed to the unidentified.

Aftermath

The Court never again fielded a force of tanks of this size, and the strategic initiative passed to the Royalists. Hirata, who withdrew with about 30,000 men, reorganized his army at the rail towns, but he could not rebuild it. The Court's remaining units were largely under the control of the committees, who preferred to keep the Court's name and supply system while the war lasted. In the winter of 110 the committees in the Fourth Army formed their council, and in March 111 the army passed to the Salvationists in the mutiny at Tsurugi Bridge.

The cost to the Royalists was also heavy. About half of the division strength of the First Army was lost, and the city of Shu Jing, which supplied the army, spent the winter on rations. The army's recovery took about a year, and Ito did not launch a major offensive until the siege of Hira in 111. The Royalists also had to cope with the burial of the dead. The plain was declared a war zone in the autumn of 110, and the dead were collected in about 90 mass graves by the army's engineers and by volunteers from Shu Jing. The work took until the following spring.

The Qianchan Republic's part in the battle increased its standing in the war. The performance of the 2nd Division, and the success of the mine doctrine, were cited by the Qianchan Congress in the debate of July 110, which voted to extend the expeditionary corps' mandate. The Court, for its part, held an inquiry into the defeat. The Directorate's report, which was completed in August, blamed the commanders of the armored regiments, a number of whom were relieved, and said nothing of the shortage of fuel.

Analysis

Military assessment

Military historians usually make three points about the battle. First, the minefields. Qianchan engineers laid them to channel the tanks and not to block them, so that the Court's armor was funneled into prepared killing grounds and not simply stopped. The gaps, which made the line appear open, were the central feature of the design, and the Court's failure to detect their purpose is regarded as a failure of reconnaissance. Second, logistics. The Court had committed its armor with fuel for ten days, and by 12 June its supply trains had been attacked by Royalist raiders for a week and by the Qianchan air group for four days. The shortage of fuel, which was apparent by 9 June, prevented the Court from maintaining the pace of the attack. Third, discipline. The Court's units were no longer reliable, and the refusals of 15 June were the first sign that the Court's army would not fight on command.

Some historians also emphasize the role of the Royalist command. Ito's decision to fight on prepared ground, his use of the telephone network to control the battle, and his willingness to move the Qianchan division on the basis of the corps commander's advice are regarded as the keys to the victory. The mistake of 12 June, when the Royalist divisions each assumed that the other held the gap, is generally acknowledged, and it was the subject of an inquiry in July, which relieved the commander of the 6th Division. The gap was closed within a few hours by the Qianchan division, which was a matter of luck as much as of planning.

The question of tank numbers

The casualty figures are disputed. The Royalist and Qianchan record of 380 tanks lost is supported by the salvage returns of the Royalist First Army. The Court's figure of 150 would mean that the Court's armored force was about half the size that the Royalist order of battle assumes. Several historians have concluded that the Court's figure is a count of the tanks that were destroyed outright, and that the Royalist figure includes the tanks that were abandoned. This reading would reconcile the two counts, though it does not account for the difference in the number of dead.

Legacy and memory

The plain was declared a war cemetery in 124 AG. The burnt-out hulls were moved to a field at the edge of the plain, where they stand in rows, and the largest of them, a Tessho command tank, has been the site of the annual commemoration since 122 AG. The memorial park, which was laid out in 125, contains a museum, the Yoshida farm and a field of preserved mine belt, which visitors can walk along a marked path. The names of the dead of all three armies are carved on a long wall at the edge of the cemetery, which was completed in 130.

The battle is the most studied armored battle of the region, and its mine doctrine was used by Qianchan in its later campaigns. The expression "to go through the corridor" is used in the Fire Nation to describe a course of action that appears open but leads to disaster, and is attributed to the Qianchan engineers. The battle is also remembered in Qianchan, where Wu Lian is commemorated, and in the Fire Nation, where the refusals of 15 June are treated by the Salvationist veterans as the first act of the movement that became the committees' government.

Historiography

Royalist and Qianchan accounts

Royalist and Qianchan sources attribute the victory to the mines and the anti-armor weapons, and give the Court's tank losses at 380. They emphasize the planning of the defense, the role of the corridors and the quality of the Royalist staff work. Royalist army histories give detailed accounts of the movements of the divisions, and are the main source for the tank losses. The Qianchan reports, which were written by the expeditionary corps' staff, are the main source for the mines and for the numbers of the civilians displaced. Both sources tend to minimize the Royalist errors, in particular the gap of 12 June, which appears in the Royalist histories only as a local incident.

Court accounts

Court records say that its tanks were withdrawn in good order and that only 150 were lost. They describe the battle as an offensive that achieved its objective of destroying the Royalist forward defenses, and they attribute the withdrawal to the need to reorganize. The Court's records, which survive only in part, give an account of the preliminary orders, and are the source for the claim that the army's fuel was inadequate. Hirata's later memoirs, which were written in 116, concede the shortage but argue that the mines and the Qianchan intervention, which the Court had not expected, were the decisive factors.

Salvationist accounts

Salvationist veterans write that many Court tank crews refused to advance on 15 June, and describe the retreat as the first mass refusal of orders. Their accounts, which were written by veterans after the war, are the main source for the refusals and for the meeting in the tank park. They are generally regarded as reliable on the events of 15 June but as exaggerating the scale of the organization. Royalist historians have noted that the Salvationist accounts say little of the tanks that fought to the end, and that most of the Court's armor was lost in the fighting and not in the refusals.

  • Battle of Soka Bay
  • First Battle of Shu Jing
  • Qianchan Republic

tsurugi_bridge.title: Tsurugi Bridge mutiny
tsurugi_bridge.html:
Tsurugi Bridge mutiny
Part ofThe middle stage of the Fire Nation Civil War
Date21–24 March 111 AG
LocationThe Tsurugi Bridge over the Nagare River, on the Court’s western rail line
ResultSalvationist victory. The Court’s Fourth Army mutinies and passes to the Salvationists
Belligerents
Salvationist committees of the Fourth ArmyOzai loyalists (the Court), General Staff Directorate loyalists
Commanders and leaders
Salvationists
Fourth Army Salvation Committee (chairman Sergeant Major Tanaka Kenji)		Court
Lieutenant General Sakai Renjiro
Strength
Salvationists
about 60,000 (the Fourth Army)		Court
about 12,000 loyalist troops and the Flame Guard
Casualties and losses
About 30,000 killed, including about 10,000 civilians

The Tsurugi Bridge mutiny was a three-day battle in March 111 AG in which the Court’s Fourth Army, about 60,000 strong, seized the Tsurugi Bridge and the western rail line from loyalist troops. The army passed to the Salvationist committees, which then controlled most of the Court’s field forces. It is the tenth of the war’s twenty defining battles.

It gave the movement a field army, and ended the Court’s ability to move its forces by rail.

Background

The Fourth Army was the Court’s largest field formation in 111 AG. It had been at the front for four years, and had lost about a third of its strength at the Iwakura Plain. By the winter of 110 AG its units were short of food and boots, and had not been paid since August. The committees, which had formed after the First Battle of Shu Jing, had begun to hold meetings in most regiments.

Sakai, the Court’s commander in the west, knew the army was unreliable. In March he ordered it to withdraw across the Tsurugi Bridge, which carried the main line to Caldera, and to take up positions near the capital.

The Fourth Army

The Fourth Army had been raised in 103 AG from the divisions that survived the Eastern campaign, and by 111 AG it had about 60,000 men in six divisions. It was led by Lieutenant General Sakai Renjiro, who held the Hōryū Pass in 101 AG. Its committees were formed in the winter of 110, when the army's pay was cut. The committees elected delegates by company, and the army's committee was a council of about 300, with an executive of eleven.

The chairman of the executive was Sergeant Major Tanaka Kenji, a former foundry machinist from Shu Jing who had served in the Works Guard, defected to the Court during the Clashes at Shu Jing and then left it again after the First Battle. He became the central figure of the movement, and his role in the mutiny is the foundation of his later authority.

Order of battle

Fourth Army committees. Six divisions (about 60,000), of which about 4,000 held the bridge on 22–24 March. Captured Tetsuken lightning dischargers; infantry weapons.

Loyalists. Two Flame Guard battalions; the army staff on the west bank; a squadron of bombers; the remaining armor. Bombers, light tanks.

Civilians. Villages on both banks of the river. About 10,000 killed in the bombing.

Course

On the evening of 21 March the committees of the army’s forward divisions met at the village of Kawabata and voted to refuse the order. At dawn on 22 March they seized the bridge, and the army’s staff officers, who were on the west bank, were arrested.

The Court sent two Flame Guard battalions and a squadron of bombers on 22 March. The bombers attacked the bridge approaches for two days, and about 10,000 civilians from the villages on both banks died. The mutineers, who held the bridge with about 4,000 troops, drove off the battalions on 23 March and destroyed the Court’s remaining armor with captured Tetsuken lightning dischargers.

On 24 March the last loyalist units on the west bank surrendered. Sakai escaped with about 300 men. The Fourth Army’s committee announced that it would hold its positions, obey the Court’s orders for supply, and refuse any order to fight the Royalists.

Civilian accounts

The bombing of the bridge approaches killed about 10,000 people, most of them in the villages of Kawabata and Nagase. The schoolmaster of Kawabata, Ogawa Daisuke, kept a record of the two days: “The soldiers who held the bridge asked us to leave. We said that we had nowhere to go. They put the children in the signal house and stood outside it.” After the battle the villagers held a funeral for the dead that was attended by the army's delegates, and the village is a site of annual visits by veterans.

The bridge

The Tsurugi Bridge was a steel through-truss bridge, 340 meters long, carrying a double-track railway and a road on a lower deck. It had been built in 82 AG and was the only bridge across the river within 40 kilometers. The mutineers' first act on 22 March was to cut the cables of the demolition charges that the army's engineers had placed on the piers, a precaution of the Court's staff. The work was done by a sergeant of the engineers, Hamada Gen, who was killed at the bridge on 23 March.

The bridge was held by about 4,000 men in a perimeter on both banks, with machine guns on the bridge's towers and Tetsuken dischargers at both ends. The dischargers, which were still experimental, had been captured by the committee at the arsenal at Kawabata. They destroyed the Court's armor by short-circuiting the electrical systems of the tanks, and were used to stop two attacks by the Flame Guard.

Committees and delegates

The army's committee system was organized in three tiers. Each company elected one delegate. The delegates of each battalion elected a battalion committee of seven. The battalion committees sent two representatives each to the divisional council. The Army Council, which met at Kawabata on 21 March, included 294 delegates, and of these 211 voted to refuse the order, 62 to obey it, and 21 abstained. The minority was allowed to leave the army with their weapons on 22 March, and about 3,000 of them did so, joining the Court's forces on the west bank.

The committees' rules, which were later adopted by the Salvationists as a whole, required that all officers be elected or confirmed by the committees, that orders be written, and that the committees control the supply of food and pay. In practice the officers were retained, because the army could not operate without them. The first test of the system, during the three days of the battle, was a success.

Notable people

Lieutenant General Sakai Renjiro, the Fourth Army's commander, had been in the army for thirty years. He was on the west bank when the mutiny began and escaped with 300 men in a single truck. He later commanded the Court's forces at Sakuragawa (later Joha), and died in the Siege of Caldera.

Ogawa Chiyo, a nurse of the army's 6th Field Hospital, organized the treatment of the wounded at the bridge, including 180 civilians. Her record, which lists the patients by name, was kept by the hospital and is held in the Kawabata museum.

Reception in the sources

The mutiny is described in the army's own minutes, which the Salvationists preserved, in the Court's report to the Privy Council, which describes the events as an “insubordination at the bridge,” and in the Royalist intelligence summary of 11 April, which records the first news of the event. The minutes are the most reliable source for the dates and the vote, though they were edited after the war by the veterans' committees.

Aftermath

The committees now controlled about 60,000 troops, and most of the Court’s remaining field army was committee-led within two years. They kept the Court’s flag and its supply system, because they needed them, and they did not at first attack the Royalists. The Court was reduced to its Flame Guard, the Ministry of Truth and the cultists around Caldera.

Analysis

The mutiny was a success because it was fast and because the Court's officers on the west bank were few. The bridge was held by about 4,000 men for three days, against bombers and two Flame Guard battalions, and the loyalists failed to cross it on the first morning. Historians of the movement note that the committees' decision to refuse the order and not to attack the Court was the most important decision they made, because it kept the supply system working and allowed the army to act as a legitimate force for five more years.

The Royalists did not learn of the mutiny until 11 April. The delay is attributed to the Court's control of the telegraph and to the committees' decision not to publicize their action.

Legacy

The bridge was rebuilt in 119 AG. A plaque, placed by the veterans' committees, records the names of the 214 mutineers killed at the bridge, and the date of 22 March is observed in the western provinces as a day of remembrance. The battle is the first of the three events that the Salvationists count as their founding: the mutiny, the capture of the Ryuusei Facility and the break at Kuroshio Mills.

Historiography

Salvationist accounts present the mutiny as the largest act of soldiers’ self-government in the war, and its chairman is a hero of the movement. Court records say it was a treasonous rising by a few officers that was suppressed with minor losses. Royalist histories regard the mutiny as the event that made the Court’s defeat inevitable, and they note that the Royalists did not know of it for three weeks.
