  • Battle of Iwakura Plain
  • Siege of Hira

siege_of_hira.title: Siege of Hira
siege_of_hira.html:
Siege of Hira
Part ofThe middle stage of the Fire Nation Civil War
DateAugust 111 – July 112 AG (eleven months)
LocationHira, the Court’s main western port
ResultRoyalist victory. The port is taken after a long siege
Belligerents
Royalists, with Qianchan naval supportOzai loyalists (the Court) and Salvationist committees in the garrison
Commanders and leaders
Royalists
General Ito Shigeru; Rear Admiral Minami Haruka (naval blockade)		Court
Major General Ishida Kenzo; Salvationist committee (garrison)
Strength
Royalists
about 80,000 in the lines (about 110,000 across the siege) and about 40 warships, with a Qianchan squadron		Garrison
about 45,000, with about 300,000 civilians at the start
Casualties and losses
About 210,000 killed: about 170,000 civilians, about 25,000 Royalist and about 15,000 Court troops

The Siege of Hira was an eleven-month siege, from August 111 to July 112 AG, of the Court’s main western port. The Royalist First Army, with a blockade fleet under Rear Admiral Minami Haruka, besieged a garrison of about 45,000 troops and about 300,000 civilians. After months of bombardment the garrison ran short of food, and then ran out. The Royalists took the harbor forts in June 112 and the city surrendered on 4 July. About 210,000 people died, of whom about 170,000 were civilians. It is the eleventh of the war’s twenty defining battles and the deadliest of them for the civilian population.

The siege is remembered mainly for the famine. The fighting itself was limited. The Royalists assaulted the landward defenses once, in the first week, and again in May, and for most of the intervening months the front was a line of trenches and gun pits across the neck of the headland. What killed the city was the arithmetic of its food: who held the granaries, who held the wells, who was allowed to leave, and who was allowed to bring supplies in. Each of those questions was answered differently by the Royalist command, by the Court’s garrison commander and by the Salvationist committees inside the walls, and the disagreement between their answers is still the central dispute of the siege’s historiography.

Background

The port and its place in the war

Hira was the Court’s gateway to the west. It had the deepest harbor on the western coast, a naval dockyard that could service cruisers, and two rail lines, one running north to Caldera and one east into the farming country of the western heartland. Through it passed the western farms’ grain and the fuel that was refined at the dockyard from oil shipped up the coast. By the winter of 110 it was the only large port still under Court control that was not within reach of the Royalist army’s field forces, and it supplied the Court’s remaining armies in the north with about two-thirds of their fuel and about a third of their food.

Its loss would not by itself end the war, but the Royalist command regarded it as the Court’s last strategic reserve. Zuko’s council had argued through the autumn of 110 over whether the army should press north from Iwakura toward the Court’s remaining armor or turn west to the coast. General Ito Shigeru, who had won at Iwakura Plain, favored the coast. His reasoning, set out in a memorandum of 2 November 110, was that the Court’s armies in the north could not be fed without Hira, that they could be left to wither, and that a Royalist army that went north into the rail towns would meet the remnants of Hirata’s Northern Armored Army on ground of Hirata’s choosing. Lieutenant General Aoki Masaru, Ito’s chief of staff, added the point that the First Army had lost about half its division strength at Iwakura and needed a campaign in which it could be rebuilt as it fought, with its supplies coming by sea from the south.

The Royalist decision

The council’s decision, on 21 January 111, was to besiege Hira and not to storm it. Ito had asked for four months to prepare, and he was given seven. The preparation was largely a matter of logistics. The army’s engineers relaid the coast railway as far as the village of Oyama, about thirty kilometers from the city, and built a pier there from which Minami’s transports unloaded. Fourteen heavy guns of the Works Guard’s artillery, which had been used at Iwakura, were moved by rail in the spring and summer, and Colonel Mori Tatsuo’s artillery regiments were told to prepare gun pits that could be built in a single night. The army gathered about 12,000 tons of ammunition at Oyama before the first division moved.

The Royalist leadership also expected the civilian population to leave. Ito’s orders of June 111 said that the army would allow the inhabitants of the lower town to pass through its lines in the first two weeks of the investment, and the army prepared a reception camp near Oyama for about 40,000 people. The camp was ready on 15 August. In the event only about 20,000 civilians left the city, most of them in the first week, because the Court’s garrison closed the landward gates on 26 August on orders from Major General Ishida Kenzo, who said that the departure of the population would reveal the dispositions of the garrison to the Royalists. The reception camp, built for twice the number, never filled.

The Qianchan contribution

The Qianchan Republic’s part was naval. After Iwakura the Qianchan Congress had agreed to send a small squadron of two frigates and four patrol boats to support the Royalist blockade, under Commodore Zhou Yilan, on the condition that it would operate only outside the harbor mouth and would not engage the forts. Zhou’s ships, which arrived at Oyama on 30 August, patrolled the outer approaches, intercepted blockade runners coming from the north and gave the Royalist fleet a reserve of fuel and spare parts. The Qianchan expeditionary corps, whose divisions had held the line at Iwakura, remained in the north and took no part in the siege on land.

The Court and the committees in the west

The Court’s position in the west was weaker than its map suggested. After the mutiny at Tsurugi Bridge in March 111, most of the Fourth Army had passed to Salvationist control, and its units were reassigned by the Court’s western command to garrison duty at the coast, partly because the Court wished to remove them from the northern front and partly because it hoped that the isolation of a besieged city would restore discipline. By August 111 about 22,000 committee-led troops were inside Hira. They kept their own officers, their own stores and their own councils. The Court’s commander, Major General Ishida Kenzo, was appointed on 2 July 111, six weeks before the siege began, with instructions to hold the city to the last man. He had at his disposal about 17,000 troops whom he regarded as reliable: the Flame Guard battalions and the marine regiment that served the forts. The remaining 6,000 men of the garrison were coast artillerymen, dockyard guards and police, whose loyalties were mixed.

The committees’ position was equally constrained. They did not wish to fight the Royalists and they did not wish to surrender to them, as their delegates in the Salvationist congress had not yet decided whether the Royalists were the movement’s enemies or its allies in the struggle against the Court. The committees’ council at Hira, which was formed in the first week of August, resolved on 9 August that its troops would man the Wall in defense of the city but would not fire on Royalist forces unless the city itself was fired upon. The resolution was kept to the letter. In practice it meant that committee units on the Wall held their positions, answered Royalist fire with fire and refused to join sorties.

Forces and commanders

Royalists

General Ito Shigeru commanded the siege from a headquarters in the farmhouse at Kamiyama, on the ridge four kilometers north of the Wall. Lieutenant General Aoki Masaru, his chief of staff, ran the daily business of the army. The besieging force consisted of the First Army’s 2nd, 3rd, 5th and 9th Divisions, rebuilt after Iwakura with conscripts from the southern provinces (the shattered 1st and 6th Divisions had been merged into the new 9th, and the army was renamed the Southern Army in the autumn of 112), and the Reserve Corps under Lieutenant General Aizawa Kenji, which held the army’s rear and the reception camps. Major General Sugiura Taro’s 3rd Division, which had held the road at Iwakura, took the central sector facing the Wall’s main gate. The 2nd Division, under Major General Fujiwara Daisuke, held the northern sector from the coast to the Kitazaka road. The 5th, under Major General Kimura Tadashi, took the southern sector, which included the dockyard approaches, and the 9th, under Major General Noguchi Yuji, was held in reserve at Kamiyama and rotated into the line every six weeks.

The strength in the lines was about 80,000 at any one time. Across the siege about 110,000 men passed through the investing army, because divisions were rotated and the Reserve Corps supplied drafts. The artillery was the army’s principal weapon. Colonel Mori Tatsuo’s Works Guard regiments brought 14 heavy guns of 240mm, 60 medium guns of 150mm, and about 200 field guns and mortars. Mori’s doctrine was to fire by pre-registered concentration, and the staff at Kamiyama kept a map of about 400 numbered concentrations on the city and the forts. The engineers, under Colonel Takeda Ryo, dug about 90 kilometers of trenches and approach saps in the first five months and built the pier, the railway and the camps.

The air force played a smaller part than at Iwakura. A single air group of about 30 bombers and 40 fighters, under Lieutenant Colonel Sano Hideki, operated from the airfield at Oyama, but it was restricted by Ito’s orders to attacks on military targets, and its main work was reconnaissance and the interception of Court aircraft attempting to resupply the city by air. The Court made seven such attempts in the autumn, dropping about 90 tons of food and ammunition, of which about 30 tons fell into the Royalist lines.

The blockade fleet

Rear Admiral Minami Haruka commanded the blockade from the cruiser Shiranui. Her squadron consisted of two cruisers (the Shiranui and the Hakuryu), 14 destroyers, two submarine flotillas of eight boats each, about 14 smaller craft and a flotilla of transports and supply ships, about 40 warships in all. Minami was a careful officer, 57 years old, who had spent most of his career in the training establishment and was known for his insistence on watch-keeping and fuel discipline. The blockade was kept by a double line, an inner line of destroyers about five kilometers outside the harbor mouth, and an outer line of submarines and Qianchan patrol boats about thirty kilometers out, along the routes that blockade runners from the north were expected to use. The squadron’s captains rotated through a ten-day cycle, and the squadron’s fuel, which was the principal constraint on the blockade, was carried by the tankers that unloaded at Oyama.

The Qianchan squadron under Commodore Zhou Yilan was attached to the outer line. It consisted of the frigates Steadfast and Calm Sea and four patrol boats, and it was commanded separately from the Royalists, with its own signal arrangements, a liaison officer on the Shiranui and a standing instruction from the Qianchan Congress that its ships were not to fire on the shore.

The garrison

Major General Ishida Kenzo, the garrison commander, held the harbor forts, the dockyard and the old town on the hill with the Flame Guard battalions and the marines, a force of about 17,000. Colonel Hoshi Daigo commanded the marine regiment, which manned the forts and held the dockyard perimeter. The Flame Guard’s three battalions, under Lieutenant Colonel Date Shinji, guarded the Citadel and the headquarters. Ishida’s staff was small and mostly drawn from his old regiment, and he kept the dockyard granaries under a special guard that answered only to him.

The committee-led units numbered about 22,000 men. They were organized in nine battalions, formerly of the Fourth Army’s 11th and 14th Divisions, and they held the Wall, the lower town and the western suburbs. The battalions’ committees sent delegates to the council at the Seiryu Mill, the lower town’s largest building, and the council’s chair was Sergeant Major Nakamura Ayame, who had been the signaler of the 14th Division’s headquarters. Nakamura was elected on 5 August after the committees’ delegates failed to agree on a more senior officer. The council’s secretary was Corporal Ibuki Sho, who kept its minutes, and its supply officer was Sergeant Tsubaki Hiro, a quartermaster whose ledgers of the committees’ stocks are the main source on the committees’ food.

The remaining 6,000 men were coast artillerymen manning the forts’ guns, the dockyard’s guard, the city’s police and a small corps of military engineers who maintained the water mains. The city’s civil government, headed by the mayor, Sasaki Genji, continued to function under Ishida’s authority. Sasaki was a lawyer who had been appointed mayor by the Court in 106, and his administration issued ration cards, kept the registers of the dead and ran the municipal hospitals.

The city and its defenses

Geography

Hira stood on a rocky headland that projected about six kilometers into the sea and was about three kilometers wide at its base. The old town, with the Citadel, the governor’s palace and the temples, stood on the hill at the seaward end, about 60 meters above the water. The dockyard and the harbor lay on the southern side of the hill, sheltered from the prevailing winds, and the lower town, a grid of workshops, warehouses and tenements, spread across the flat ground between the harbor and the landward neck. About 300,000 people lived in the city at the start of the siege, including about 40,000 refugees from the northern provinces who had arrived since Iwakura, and about two-thirds of the population lived in the lower town.

The city’s water came from three sources: a reservoir in the hills north of the neck, which was cut off by the Royalists on the first day; the wells of the lower town, about 140 of them, sunk into a shallow aquifer; and the old town’s cisterns. The Royalists never shelled the wells deliberately, but the lower town was the part of the city nearest to their guns, and the wells fell into disrepair as the pumps ran out of fuel. After February most households depended on about forty wells that still worked, and the queues at them became a daily feature of the siege’s accounts.

The Wall

The landward defenses ran across the neck of the headland and were known to the Royalists as the Wall. They had been built by the Court in the decade before the war and consisted of three lines of earthworks and concrete strongpoints, about 14 kilometers in all from shore to shore, with a ditch and a belt of barbed wire in front and a line of reinforced command posts behind. The first line was held by about 8,000 men, the second by about 9,000 and the third by about 8,000, and each line had its own artillery. The main gate, through which the Oyama road entered the city, was defended by a gatehouse and two blockhouses with machine guns, and the Royalists’ staff maps showed 62 numbered strongpoints. The Wall was not a modern fortification. It lacked the depth of the Iwakura ridge and its wire was rusting, but the ground in front was open and the lines of fire were long.

The forts

The harbor was closed by a chain of five forts that the Court had built over twenty years. Fort Seigan stood on the north point, Forts Kita and Minami on the northern and southern breakwaters, Fort Hayate on the south point and the Citadel on the headland above the old town. They mounted 28 heavy coastal guns, of which 12 were 305mm pieces in armored turrets, the remainder 203mm and 150mm guns in casemates. The forts could fire on any ship approaching the harbor mouth and on the Royalist batteries at the neck, and their crews had rehearsed the engagement of ships for years. They had not rehearsed a siege. Their magazines held about 40 rounds per gun, and the replacement of ammunition from the dockyard depended on the harbor’s remaining open.

The granaries and the dockyard

The dockyard held the city’s granaries. There were six of them, concrete warehouses on the southern quay, built to hold the grain brought in by rail from the western farms, and at the start of the siege they held about 9,000 tons of grain and flour, a figure that was low for the season because the dockyard had been shipping its reserves north to the Court’s armies since the spring. It was enough to feed all 300,000 inhabitants at a full ration for about a month, or the garrison’s own 23,000 loyal troops for more than a year. Ishida placed the granaries under the marines’ guard on 20 August and ordered that the stocks were to be issued only on his authority. The dockyard’s own canteens, the forts and the Flame Guard were fed from them. The committees and the civilians were not, as the garrison’s ration scale, which Ishida issued on 3 September, provided supplies only to units “under the command of the garrison,” a phrase that excluded the committees.

The decision to exclude the committees was the origin of the famine’s politics. Ishida’s staff told him that the committees had their own stores, and in this they were partly correct. The committee battalions had brought with them the stocks of the Fourth Army’s depots, about 5,000 tons of food, which were quartered in the lower town’s warehouses. The civilian authorities, for their part, had about 3,000 tons in the municipal stores. The sum of these stocks, about 17,000 tons, was less than a fifth of what the city would need to eat at a full ration for eleven months, and from the middle of October the division of the dockyard’s grain between the garrison and the rest of the city became the chief issue between Ishida, the committees and the mayor.

Course

August–November 111: encirclement

The First Army left its assembly area at Oyama on 17 August and reached the heights north of the Wall two days later. The 2nd and 3rd Divisions took the ridge at Kamiyama against a handful of Court pickets, and by 22 August the engineers had surveyed the approaches and sited the first gun pits. The artillery opened fire on 23 August with a four-hour bombardment of the Wall’s first line. The bombardment was directed at the strongpoints and wire, and the Royalist staff had instructed the gunners to avoid the lower town, though the instruction was only partly effective because the lower town’s warehouses lay close behind the Wall and a number of shells fell short.

The assault followed on 24 August. The 3rd Division attacked the main gate sector and the 2nd Division the Kitazaka road, with about 30 tanks in support. Ito’s plan was to break the first line on the first day and to reach the second before the garrison could reinforce it. The plan failed. The wire was thicker than the staff had judged, the strongpoints were better sited than their maps showed, and the committee battalions on the Wall, though they would not fire first, returned fire promptly. The tanks, which Ito had been reluctant to commit after Iwakura, were halted by a ditch that the Court’s engineers had flooded from the harbor mains in the preceding week. The assault was renewed on 26 and 27 August with the same result. In four days the Royalists lost about 3,000 men, and Ito, who had observed the third day’s attack from the Kamiyama ridge, ordered it to be broken off. He told his staff that the army would not try the Wall again until the city had been weakened by the blockade, and the order that went to the divisions on 28 August directed them to dig in and to hold the ground they had won.

The Royalists’ siege works, which were in place by the end of September, formed three lines. The first, about 1,200 meters from the Wall at its nearest point, held the guns and the infantry reserves. The second was a system of saps that approached to within 300 meters of the Wall’s first line in the southern sector. The third, the “rear line” on the Kamiyama ridge, protected the headquarters and the railway terminus. The army’s engineers also built a double fence across the neck, about 400 meters in front of the first line, to prevent the garrison’s sorties and to control the movement of refugees. Passages were left at the Oyama road and the Kitazaka road, and the pickets at the passages had orders to direct any civilians who emerged to the reception camp.

The naval blockade closed at the same time. Minami’s ships arrived off the harbor mouth on 5 September, and the squadron’s inner line was complete on 10 September, after a night action in which the Court’s last coastal submarines were destroyed. Four boats had sortied from the harbor on the night of 9 September, under the command of Captain Ishikawa Daichi of the dockyard flotilla, in an attempt to break the line before it was established. Two were sunk by the destroyers Ayame and Umikaze and one by a depth-charge attack from the Qianchan frigate Calm Sea, which was the Qianchan squadron’s only engagement of the siege. The fourth boat returned to the harbor with its commander dead and its forward torpedo tubes flooded. The Court’s surface ships, which consisted of two old destroyers and a dozen patrol craft, remained in the harbor throughout the siege and took no part in the fighting.

The Court tried to break the blockade four times between September and the end of November. These attempts were made by blockade runners from the north, merchant vessels of 2,000 to 6,000 tons that sailed from Caldera and the rail ports at night and tried to reach the harbor mouth before dawn. Three of the four attempts were made in the first half of October, when the Royalists’ inner line was still thin, and one of them, on 11 October, put about 400 tons of grain and ammunition on the dockyard quay before the destroyers closed the harbor mouth. The others were intercepted. Of the eleven runners that sailed in the autumn, three were captured, two of them by the Qianchan patrol boats, and eight were sunk. The tonnage that reached the city in this way was about 600 tons in all, or about two days’ supply for the city at a full ration. After the failure of the last attempt, on 28 November, the Court did not try to run the blockade again by sea.

It tried by air. Between 20 September and 20 December seven flights of transport aircraft left the Court’s northern airfields for Hira, each carrying about ten tons of food, medicine and ammunition. The Royalist fighters at Oyama intercepted three of them. The remaining aircraft dropped their loads by parachute over the dockyard, the Citadel and the old town, and about 90 tons in all were dropped. About a third of this fell outside the walls, and the Royalist troops who found the canisters in the fields kept the food and sent the ammunition to the arsenal at Oyama. The airdrops stopped after the loss of a transport over the Kamiyama ridge on 20 December, in which Court records say that the crew of five and a Flame Guard liaison officer were killed.

The autumn passed with the daily routine of the siege. Mori’s guns fired a scheduled bombardment each morning and a harassing bombardment at night, and the forts replied with their heavy guns against the Royalist batteries at the neck. The counter-battery duel was the principal military event of the autumn. On 1 October the 305mm guns of Fort Seigan destroyed a Royalist battery of four 150mm guns and killed about 60 gunners, and on 19 October a salvo from Mori’s 240mm guns breached the casemate of the Citadel’s western battery and killed its crew of 31. The Royalists’ casualties from the forts’ guns, which they called the “long guns,” were about 300 a month in October and November, and the Royalist staff, which had estimated that the forts would be silenced in a month, recognized by November that they would have to be reduced by infantry.

December 111 – April 112: the famine

The city’s food ran out in December. The lower town’s stocks, which had been about three weeks’ supply at the beginning of the siege, had been stretched by rationing and by the markets that formed in the lower town’s streets, and the mayor’s ration cards had been honored at progressively smaller scales: 800 grams of grain a day in September, 500 in October, 300 in November and 150 in December. The municipal stores were emptied on 14 December. Ishida’s granaries held, at that date, about 6,000 tons, and his orders were that the stocks were to be issued only to the garrison and the dockyard.

The civilians in the lower town ate what they could find. By Christmas the city’s cats and dogs had been eaten, and by January the rats, which had multiplied in the abandoned warehouses, were being sold in the markets at ten times the price of the last flour. The people boiled the leather of belts and the harness of the dockyard’s horses, and the grass of the old town’s gardens and the parks on the hill was picked to the roots. In January people began to strip the leather from the harbor cranes’ belts and the seating of the tram cars, which they boiled for soup. The city’s water, once the pumps had stopped, came from the wells, and the queues at the surviving wells were a daily hazard because the Royalist guns fired into the lower town on the hour.

The committees fed their own troops, about 22,000 men, at a ration of about 400 grams a day, and gave some of what remained to the civilians in the districts they held. The committee council’s decision, taken on 20 December on Nakamura’s motion, was that every committee battalion would give up a quarter of its ration to the civilians of its sector, and that the soup kitchens set up in the Seiryu Mill and eleven other buildings would be run by the committees’ cooks. The kitchens issued a bowl of watery gruel to about 30,000 people a day, according to Tsubaki’s ledgers, from the end of December to the beginning of March, when the committees’ stocks gave out. Royalist intelligence estimated that the committees’ food would last six weeks and doubted that they were sharing it, and it is a matter of record that the Royalist staff noted in a report of 14 February that the lower town was “fed by the committees’ kitchens in a manner that cannot be sustained.”

Deaths began to climb in January. The first deaths were among the old and the very young, and by the end of the month the city’s hospitals, which had been operating without anesthetics or dressings since December, were turning away all but the wounded. Dr. Ono Fumiko, who directed the lower town’s main hospital in the Seiryu school, recorded 140 deaths a day in her wards at the end of January, most of them from starvation and from the pneumonia that attacked weakened patients. By the middle of February the daily toll in the city as a whole was about 800, according to the registers of the municipal burial office, which kept count until its staff were too weak to do so. The dead were collected by handcart in the mornings and taken to the pits that the municipality had dug in the Hira Cliffs’ cemetery. The burial gangs, which were fed a double ration by the mayor’s office, worked until the pits were full and, in March, buried the dead in the shell craters of the lower town.

Ishida’s garrison, by contrast, was fed. The marines and the Flame Guard received about 600 grams a day, the dockyard workers 400 and the forts’ gunners 700. The disparity was visible, and the committees’ delegates raised it with Ishida’s staff in a series of letters between 5 January and 20 February. Ishida’s replies, which were brief, said that the granaries’ stocks were the property of the Court, that they would be required for the defense of the city until the Court’s armies relieved it, and that the committees’ stocks were their own responsibility. In the last letter, of 1 March, he added that the relief of Hira was an order of the Court and that he would not diminish the garrison’s strength by a single ration.

The committees’ council debated the crisis for most of January. Its members were divided between those who wanted to seize the granaries and those who wanted to negotiate. An attempt to seize the granaries was made on the night of 22 January by a company of the 11th Division’s committee, about 140 men, who reached the southern quay before the marines opened fire. Eleven of the company were killed and the rest withdrew. Nakamura, who had not authorized the attempt, told the council on 24 January that the committees could not take the granaries without destroying the city’s defense, and the council voted, by 41 to 22, to continue to hold the Wall and to seek relief from the Royalists.

The negotiations that followed were conducted through the Royalist pickets at the Kitazaka passage. On 12 January Nakamura sent a letter to Ito by way of the pickets asking whether the Royalists would permit the committees to evacuate the city’s children. Ito replied on 18 January that the army would receive any civilians who came out, but that it could not give safe-conduct to the garrison or its families, and that it could not allow supplies to enter the city without the consent of the Court. On 25 January the Royalists opened the Kitazaka passage for four days, and about 1,500 people, most of them women and children from the committees’ districts, crossed the lines. On 29 January Ishida’s marines closed the gate behind them by occupying the Wall’s northern strongpoints, and the passage was not reopened.

The Royalist command’s attitude to the famine was the subject of an exchange of staff memoranda in February. Aoki, the chief of staff, wrote on 6 February that the army’s orders were to reduce the city and that the famine in the lower town was Ishida’s responsibility, since the Court’s granaries held enough to feed it. Major Hasegawa Ren, of the intelligence section, replied on 9 February that the intelligence of the dockyard’s granaries was “consistent and in some respects alarming,” and that the Royalist army was “the only party that can still end the famine.” His memorandum was circulated to the army’s division commanders, and the 3rd Division’s commander, Sugiura, attached a note proposing that the army open a corridor to the lower town at the Oyama road. Ito rejected the proposal, and wrote on the margin that it would “release the garrison’s ration of the city’s food and prolong the siege.”

Zuko’s visit to the lines came in March. He arrived at Oyama by rail on 11 March, accompanied by two members of his council, and spent four days at Ito’s headquarters. The visit is described in the staff diaries of Aoki and Hasegawa, which agree on its principal events. Zuko walked the lines in the Kitazaka sector, looked into the lower town through the Royalist glasses, and was told by Ito that the city’s deaths were running at about 700 a day. He asked whether the city could be relieved with supplies. Ito replied that it could be, but that the supplies would feed Ishida first. Minami, who was summoned from the blockade squadron on 13 March, advised that a relief convoy would require the opening of the blockade, which could not be done without allowing Court ships to enter, and the council agreed on 14 March that the blockade should be maintained and that the question of a limited relief should be taken up with the Qianchan Republic. The decision, which Zuko communicated to Qianchan by telegram on 15 March, led to the arrival of the relief ships in April.

The famine was complicated by typhus, which appeared in the lower town in the first week of March. It spread through the districts along the harbor’s edge, where the crowding was worst, and in four weeks it killed about 8,000 people. Dr. Ono’s hospital was converted to a fever ward, and its doctors, who had been working for three months without rest, began to die. Ono herself fell ill on 20 March and recovered, which she attributed to a bottle of antiseptic that a marine medical officer had left at the hospital’s door.

The relief ships arrived on 12 April. The Qianchan Congress, at Zuko’s request, had sent three vessels, the Peace Heron, the Sixth Harvest and the Lantern, carrying 1,500 tons of flour and about 40 doctors and nurses under Dr. Lin Wei. They had waited at Oyama for ten days while the Royalist command, the Court’s western headquarters and the committees’ council negotiated the terms of their passage. The Royalists allowed them through the blockade on 11 April, on the understanding that the Court would permit them to unload at the dockyard quay. Ishida allowed them to unload but insisted on the distribution of the flour by the garrison’s officers. Lin’s doctors reported later that about a third of the flour never reached the lower town, and that about 400 tons were taken into the granaries and issued to the Flame Guard. The lower town received about 1,000 tons, which was enough to feed about 100,000 people for three weeks.

The doctors’ own work was more effective. They set up eleven clinics in the lower town and a fever hospital in the Seiryu Mill, and in six weeks they treated about 12,000 patients, according to Lin’s report to the Qianchan Congress. The clinics’ records show that about 4,000 of these patients were children under ten. Lin wrote that the starvation she saw in Hira was “beyond anything in Iwakura,” and that the committees’ cooks, who had been working in the soup kitchens since December, were “among the bravest people I have met.” The doctors left on 26 May, a few days before the Royalist assault on the Wall, and the relief ships returned to Qianchan with about 600 sick children, whom the Royalist command allowed to be embarked on condition that they would not be returned to the city.

May–July 112: the fall

Ito’s plan for the final assault was prepared in March and approved by the council in April. It had three parts. The first was a heavy bombardment of the forts by the army’s guns and the squadron’s cruisers. The second was an attack by the 2nd Division on Fort Seigan, which Mori’s guns would prepare. The third was an assault by the 3rd and 5th Divisions on the Wall’s southern sector, to pin the garrison and to open the road to the dockyard. The assault was timed for the first week in May, when the weather in the harbor mouth was best for the cruisers, and the army’s ammunition stocks at Oyama had been rebuilt to 14,000 tons.

The bombardment began on 3 May and lasted for twelve days. The cruisers Shiranui and Hakuryu fired about 3,000 rounds of 203mm shell at the forts, and Mori’s 240mm guns fired about 11,000. Fort Seigan’s armored turrets, which had survived the autumn’s counter-battery duel, were silenced on 9 May after a direct hit on the magazine of the northern turret. On 14 May the 2nd Division attacked the fort from the landward side. The attack was costly, since the fort’s garrison of 800 marines had been fed on garrison rations and fought with determination, and the fort held for three days. It fell on 17 May. About 600 of its defenders were killed, and the 2nd Division lost about 1,400 men.

The assault on the Wall began on 20 May. The 3rd and 5th Divisions attacked in the southern sector, with the support of about 60 tanks. The ground in front of the Wall had been mined by the Court in the autumn, and the engineers cleared the mines at night, with the help of Qianchan sappers who had been lent to the army for the purpose. The committees’ battalions, which held the Wall’s southern sector, did not oppose the advance, and the first and second lines fell in two days with comparatively light casualties. On 22 May the council of the committees met in the Seiryu Mill and resolved, by 38 to 25, to withdraw the battalions from the Wall to the lower town, and not to resist the Royalists’ advance into the city’s outskirts. Nakamura, who proposed the resolution, argued that the Wall was lost and that the battalions’ lives, and the lives of the civilians in their sectors, should not be spent in its defense.

Ishida’s response was to counterattack. He committed the Flame Guard’s battalions and about 3,000 marines from the forts to a counterattack on 24 May, in an attempt to recover the southern sector of the Wall. The counterattack was beaten off with heavy loss. The Flame Guard lost about 1,100 men, and the marines about 600. Ishida, who observed the attack from the Citadel, did not repeat it, and from then on he held the dockyard, the forts and the old town with the troops he had left.

The Royalists entered the lower town’s outskirts on 1 June. Ito, who had anticipated that the lower town would be defended street by street, had ordered the divisions to halt at its edge and to wait for the committees to come to terms. The committees did not defend the lower town. By 3 June the Royalist pickets were in the streets of the lower town’s northern district, where they were met by crowds of civilians, many of whom were too weak to stand. The soldiers shared their rations with the crowds, and the army’s kitchens began to operate in the streets on 4 June. About 400 tons of food were distributed in the first week, and the daily death toll fell in ten days from about 400 to about 150.

The harbor fell on 9 June. The cruisers’ bombardment of Fort Minami and Fort Hayate had continued throughout the first week of June, and on 5 June the destroyers Ayame, Umikaze and Kamome entered the harbor mouth under the protection of the cruisers’ guns and destroyed the Court’s remaining patrol craft at their moorings. Fort Hayate surrendered on 8 June, and Fort Minami, whose garrison was reduced to about 200 men, on 9 June. The Royalist flag was raised over the harbor’s south mole on the afternoon of the 9th. Ishida, who still held the Citadel and the dockyard, had about 11,000 troops and about 4,000 tons of food.

The last weeks of the siege were taken up with negotiations. Ito offered Ishida terms on 10 June: that the garrison would be allowed to march out with its personal weapons and colors, on condition that it surrendered the dockyard and the Citadel and handed over its heavy weapons. Ishida refused on 12 June, saying that his orders were to hold the city to the last man. The offer was repeated on 20 June and on 28 June, and Ishida’s refusals grew shorter. Meanwhile the committees’ council negotiated separately. Nakamura crossed the lines at the Kitazaka passage on 15 June and spent two days at Kamiyama, where she and Aoki agreed on an arrangement for the committees’ battalions. The battalions would keep their committees and their own officers and would be held as a separate body of prisoners, under the eye of their own delegates; any man who wished could leave under safe-conduct for the Salvationist lines on the Tsurugi road, with his small arms; the wounded and sick would be treated in the Royalist hospitals; and the committees’ delegates would be present when the dockyard’s granaries were opened.

The end came on 3 July. Ishida, whose staff had begun to leave the Citadel in small groups on 29 June, summoned his remaining officers on the morning of 3 July and told them that he would not sign a surrender. He then retired to the dockyard office. His body was found there in the afternoon, with a pistol in his hand and, on the desk, a note of one line: “I have followed my orders.” The committees’ council, which learned of his death at dusk, sent Nakamura to the Citadel with a white flag, and the Flame Guard’s commander, Lieutenant Colonel Date, who was the senior surviving officer, accepted the terms on the morning of 4 July. The gates of the dockyard and the Citadel were opened at nine o’clock, and about 28,000 men laid down their weapons in the dockyard’s yards, among them about 17,000 men of the committee battalions, who marched out in their own ranks and were counted separately. About 2,000 committee men chose the safe-conduct that Nakamura had negotiated and left the city that day under arms, on the road to the north.

Civilian experience

The civilian experience of the siege is among the best documented of the war, largely because the city’s population was literate and urban, and because the committees’ kitchens, the municipal registers and the hospitals’ ledgers all kept records until their keepers died. The records suggest that the siege fell hardest on the districts nearest the Wall, where the poorest households lived, and that the dead were disproportionately the very young and the old. The city’s registers, which were reconstructed after the war from the burial returns, show that about 41,000 of the civilian dead were children under ten and about 38,000 were over sixty. Deaths among the dockyard’s workers, who had access to the canteens until January, were fewer, and deaths in the old town, where the better-off had their own stores and servants, were fewer still.

The ledger of Takahashi Setsu

The most quoted account is the record of Takahashi Setsu, a harbor crane operator who lived in Lantern Street, in the lower town’s eastern district. Takahashi, who was 41 at the start of the siege, had worked on the dockyard’s cranes for nineteen years, and when the cranes stopped for lack of fuel she took a ledger from the dockyard’s offices and began to record the deaths of her street. The ledger lists 212 names, in order of death, between December and May, with a note beside each. Many of the notes are single words: “child,” “neighbor,” “brother.” Others are longer. A note beside the name of a carpenter, Hosokawa Eiji, records that he gave his ration to his grandson for two months and “was not asked to stop.” A note beside a girl’s name, in February, says only that she “was seven and sang.” The ledger’s last entry, dated 14 May, is the name of its author, written in a different hand by a neighbor, Kuroda Mitsuko, who found Takahashi dead in her chair. Kuroda took the ledger to the Royalist kitchens in June, and it was published in 118 as The Ledger of Lantern Street.

The ledger records, in passing, the shape of a day in the lower town. Takahashi’s street, which had had 64 households, had eleven at the end. The first deaths, in December, were of the old, who gave their food to the young and did not ask for more. In January the young began to die, and in February whole households. The ledger says that the street’s children stopped playing in January and that after the third week of February “they stopped asking for food.” It notes the days on which the Royalists’ guns were loud and the days on which they were silent. It notes the arrival of the Qianchan clinics, in April, and the first day on which a child in the street was given milk.

The Hira lifeboat station

A second source is the log of the Hira lifeboat station, which rescued about 400 people from the harbor in the first months of the siege. The station’s crews, who were civilians under the harbor master’s authority, put out in whalers and small motor craft to pick up the survivors of ships sunk by the blockade, and, when the blockade closed, to bring off the families who tried to leave the city by rowing out of the harbor. The log records the rescues by name, and also the vessels that refused to take refugees: “the Royalist picket boat would not let us pass, and the crew said they had orders.” An entry for 3 October describes a boat with nineteen people, mostly women and children, that rowed out of the harbor at night and was turned back by a destroyer’s searchlight. The destroyer’s captain, whom the log does not name, “called across that he was sorry and that the harbor was closed.”

The lifeboat station’s coxswain, Mori Ichiro (no relation to the artillery colonel), kept the log until 17 January, when the station’s last fuel was exhausted. After that the station’s boats were used for the transport of the dead to the Hira Cliffs, which could be reached by water from the lower town’s eastern quay. The log’s last page, dated 20 January, records that the station had carried 61 bodies that day.

Daily life

The routine of the lower town in the winter of 111 is described in a number of other accounts, including the diaries of a schoolteacher, Matsuda Aiko, a municipal clerk, Fujii Tamotsu, and a dockyard apprentice, Ikeda Rin, who was sixteen at the beginning of the siege and eighteen at the end. These accounts agree on the principal features. The day began with the queue at the well, which formed at four in the morning, and the queue at the kitchen, which formed at five. The kitchens opened at seven and closed at ten, and those who had not been served by then did not eat until the following day. The Royalists’ morning bombardment began at eight, and the people took shelter in the warehouses’ cellars. The night bombardment kept the city awake. The people burned the furniture of the abandoned houses for heat and cooking, and by January the lower town’s wooden buildings had been stripped of their doors, floors and stairs.

The black market, which flourished in the first two months, was suppressed in January by the committees, who fined the traders and distributed their stocks. The committees’ police, who were soldiers from the battalions’ military police detachments, also guarded the wells and the kitchens and put down the food riots of 8 and 19 February, in which about 40 people were killed. The Royalists’ pickets at the Kitazaka passage reported that the number of civilians who tried to approach the lines increased in February, and that many of them were shot by Ishida’s marines before they could reach the passage.

The old town

The old town’s inhabitants, who numbered about 30,000 at the start of the siege, lived in different conditions. The district contained the temples, the palace and the villas of the city’s officials and merchants, and its households had their own stores of rice and tea. Its wells and cisterns were protected by the Citadel’s guns, and the Royalists’ shells, which fell on the dockyard and the forts, seldom reached it. The old town’s food ran short in March, but its deaths, which the burial registers put at about 7,000, were a fraction of the lower town’s. Resentment of the old town’s comparative comfort was strong in the lower town, and the committees’ newspaper, the Gate Bulletin, which was printed on a hand press in the Seiryu Mill, ran a series of articles in February on the “hill’s larder.”

Some of the old town’s residents opened their houses to the starving. The abbot of the Temple of the Harbor Moon, Sozen, turned his monastery into a kitchen and an orphanage in January and fed about 2,000 children until the temple’s stores gave out in March. The temple’s register lists 1,340 children who passed through it, of whom 910 survived. The abbot, who was 66 when the siege began, was one of those who died of typhus in March. His successor, a novice named Ryoun, who was nineteen, kept the temple’s kitchen open until the Royalists’ soldiers arrived in June.

The committees

The committees’ conduct in the siege was a principal subject of dispute in the years that followed. The Salvationist account, which was set down in the movement’s congress in 114 and in a number of memoirs, said that the committees fed about 30,000 civilians through the winter, at a cost to their own troops of a quarter of their ration, and that the soup kitchens of the Seiryu Mill and the other buildings were the only reliable source of food in the lower town. It said that the committees, which could have seized the granaries, did not do so because it would have destroyed the defense of the city, and it argued that Ishida’s refusal to share the granaries’ stocks was a crime. Tsubaki’s ledgers, which were published in 117, support the figure of 30,000 for the period from the end of December to the beginning of March and show that the committees’ stocks fell from about 5,000 tons in August to 600 tons in March.

Royalist histories deny that the committees had enough food to feed so many for so long. They cite the report of the Royalist intelligence section of 14 February, which estimated the committees’ stocks at six weeks, and they argue that Tsubaki’s ledgers, which were compiled after the war, were adjusted to support the committees’ claims. This argument has been generally rejected by historians. The ledgers’ figures for the committee stocks in August are consistent with the Fourth Army’s depot returns, which survive in the army archives, and the intelligence report’s estimate of six weeks was of the stocks that the section had seen, and not of those that it had not.

Some historians argue that the committees’ role has been inflated by their descendants, who later formed the Salvationist movement’s leadership, and they point to the committees’ failure to seize the granaries as evidence of a lack of resolve. Others note that the committees had no means of taking the granaries from the marines, who were better armed and better fed. The debate continues. Nakamura, who was questioned on the point at the accountability hearings in 119, said that she had been “in command of men who were starving and who would not fire on their own officers,” and that the choice had been between the granaries and the Wall. “I chose the Wall,” she said, “and I have never been sure I chose rightly.”

Weapons and equipment

The siege was a contest of heavy guns. The Royalists’ principal weapons were Mori’s 240mm and 150mm guns, which fired pre-registered concentrations on the Wall and the forts, and the cruisers’ 203mm guns, which were used against the forts from the sea. The Court’s principal weapons were the 305mm and 203mm coastal guns of the forts, which could reach the Royalist batteries at the neck and the ships of the blockade, and the 120mm field guns of the Wall’s artillery. Both sides used rocket artillery. The Royalists fielded two batteries of the Works Guard’s barrage rockets, which were used in the assault on the Wall in May, and the Court used its stock of coast-defense rockets against the Royalist trenches in the autumn.

The infantry fought with the standard rifles and light machine guns of the war, supplemented by the flamethrowers, satchel charges and grenades of the assault engineers. The assault on Fort Seigan was the first operation of the war in which the Royalists used a purpose-built flamethrower team, the engineers’ “fort-breakers,” who carried back-mounted fuel tanks and short-range projectors. The teams’ casualties in the assault were about 60 percent, and the engineers’ report on the operation recommended that they be used only with armor and smoke cover.

The naval war was fought with the usual weapons of the period: torpedoes, depth charges, deck guns and mines. The Court sowed a minefield in the harbor approaches in August, which cost the Royalists the minelayer Tsubame and a destroyer, the Hotaru, in October. The minefield was swept by Minami’s minesweepers in March and April, with the assistance of Qianchan craft. Minami’s submarines laid mines of their own in the approaches to the neighboring port of Ohama, to prevent its use by blockade runners.

Notable people

Major General Ishida Kenzo, the garrison commander, was 52 when the siege began. He had been a battalion commander at Shu Jing in the Clashes and had served under Hirata in the armored regiments before being transferred to the coast command in 108. He was an able but rigid officer, and the Court chose him for the defense of Hira because, as the western command’s chief of staff put it, “he does not argue.” He kept the dockyard granaries under his own guard and refused to share them. His last note, found on his desk, has been quoted in every account of the siege. Opinion of him has not softened with time: the accountability hearings found that he bore the principal responsibility for the failure to feed the city.

Sergeant Major Nakamura Ayame led the committees in the garrison. She was a signaler from the Fourth Army, 33 years old, who had joined the committee of the 14th Division’s headquarters in the spring of 111 and was elected to chair the Hira council in the first week of the siege. She negotiated the surrender with the Royalists, and she is remembered for the soup kitchens and for the council’s decision to withdraw from the Wall. She was later a member of the Salvationist congress, and in 119 she was arrested for her role in the insurgency. She was released in the amnesty of 120 and lived in Hira until her death in 141. Her statement to the accountability hearings is the most often quoted of the committees’ testimony.

General Ito Shigeru, the Royalist commander, was criticized at the time and afterward for the conduct of the siege. His defenders point out that he was under orders to reduce the city, that he offered the garrison terms three times, and that he allowed three Qianchan relief ships to pass. His critics note that he rejected Sugiura’s proposal for a corridor and that the army did not feed the city until June. Ito, who commanded the Royalist southern armies until the end of the war, wrote in his memoirs, published in 126, that the siege was “the thing I would undo if I could undo one thing.”

Rear Admiral Minami Haruka, who commanded the blockade, was an officer of the old school who regarded the blockade as a legal operation and refused to allow it to be relaxed. His advice to Zuko in March, that the blockade could not be opened without opening it to the Court, is the best-known example of his caution. He is also remembered for his decision to allow the Qianchan relief ships to pass in April, which he took on his own authority after the Royalist command had failed to reach agreement.

Dr. Lin Wei led the Qianchan medical mission. She had served in the field hospitals at Iwakura, and she spent six weeks in the lower town’s clinics. Her report to the Qianchan Congress, which was read in the Congress in June and published in the Qianchan press, was the first full account of the famine to reach the world outside the city. She later became the director of a hospital in the Qianchan capital.

Takahashi Setsu, the crane operator, is remembered for her ledger. A bronze crane, installed at the head of Lantern Street in 124, is dedicated to her and to the 212 names.

Major Hasegawa Ren of the Royalist intelligence section wrote the memorandum of 9 February that warned of the famine. He was transferred to the Royalist army’s headquarters in March and promoted in 113. He testified before the hearings that “we knew, and we did not do enough.”

Casualties

About 210,000 people died in the siege. Of these about 170,000 were civilians, and about 40,000 were soldiers. The civilian toll is the largest of any siege of the war and the largest proportion of a city’s population killed in a single operation. Of the civilian dead, the burial registers attribute about 138,000 to starvation and the diseases of starvation, about 22,000 to typhus, dysentery and other epidemics, and about 6,000 to shell fire and the collapse of buildings. The remaining 4,000 were killed in the riots of February, in attempts to leave the city, or in the fighting of May and June in the lower town.

The Court’s garrison lost about 15,000 dead. Of these about 6,000 were killed in the fighting of May and June, about 5,000 died of disease, and about 4,000 were killed by the Royalist bombardment, including the 600 killed at Fort Seigan and the 1,700 lost in the counterattack of 24 May. The Royalist armies lost about 25,000 dead. About 9,000 were killed in the three assaults of August and May, about 8,000 by the fire of the forts and in the sorties of the autumn, about 6,000 by disease in the siege lines, and about 2,000 in the blockade squadron, the majority of them in the sinking of the Tsubame and the Hotaru.

The population of the city fell from about 300,000 to about 110,000. About 20,000 left through the Royalist lines in the course of the siege, and about 170,000 died, leaving some 110,000 alive at the surrender, of whom the Qianchan doctors judged about a third to be in need of hospital care. The city’s buildings were heavily damaged. About 40 percent of the lower town’s housing was destroyed or made uninhabitable by shell fire and by the dismantling of buildings for fuel, and the dockyard’s cranes and the harbor installations were wrecked by the Court’s demolition parties in the last week of June.

Aftermath

The Royalists held the port, but the city was devastated, and the army that took it was in no condition to continue immediately. The first priority was food. Ito’s army distributed about 3,000 tons of rations in the first fortnight, and the dockyard’s granaries, when they were opened on 5 July in the presence of the committees’ delegates, were found to contain about 1,900 tons of grain and flour, enough to have fed the lower town for a month. The discovery made a deep impression on the Royalist soldiers who saw it, and it was the subject of a report by Hasegawa, which was read at the army’s headquarters on 9 July. Its conclusion, that the stocks “would have saved the lower town at any time before March,” was not contradicted by Ishida’s surviving staff.

Ito established a military administration in the city under Aizawa Kenji. It restored the water supply by the end of July, reopened the lower town’s hospitals in August and put the dockyard’s workers to work clearing the harbor in September. The army’s doctors and the Qianchan medical mission, which returned in July with two further ships, treated about 30,000 patients in the first two months. About 12,000 of the survivors died in July and August of the effects of starvation, an addition to the siege’s toll that most historians include in the figure of 170,000.

The Salvationists in the garrison withdrew to the north or were taken into Royalist custody. The committees’ battalions were held at the camp at Oyama until the autumn and released in November, when the Royalist command agreed to the committees’ demand that they be allowed to rejoin the Salvationist armies. The Flame Guard’s survivors, who numbered about 4,000, were held in the camps until the amnesty of 120. Colonel Hoshi, the commander of the marines, was tried by a Royalist court in 113 and sentenced to ten years in prison for his part in the garrison’s refusal to feed the city. He was released in 120.

The political aftermath was more significant than the military. The siege marked the point at which the Royalists, who had until then been seen as defenders of the civilian population, became responsible for the deaths of a large part of it, and the Salvationist movement’s account of the siege, in which the committees fed the city while both Ishida and Ito watched it starve, became one of the movement’s central stories. The Royalist council, which met in September 112 to review the siege, adopted a resolution that in future operations the army would open corridors for civilians and would accept the consequences for the siege’s timetable. The principle was applied at Sakuragawa and, with greater success, at Caldera, where the army organized the bread drops and the evacuation of the civilian population.

Analysis

The siege was the deadliest of the war per head of population, and the Royalist command was criticized at the time for continuing it. Military historians identify three points at which a different decision would have saved a large part of the city. The first was the decision in August 111 to rely on the civilians’ leaving, without preparing for the contingency that the garrison would stop them. The second was the decision in February 112 not to open a corridor at the Oyama road, which Sugiura had proposed and which Hasegawa’s memorandum supported. The third was the decision in March, after Zuko’s visit, to maintain the blockade, which postponed the arrival of the relief ships by about a month and, according to the Qianchan doctors’ estimate, cost about 30,000 lives.

The Court’s decisions were no less culpable. Ishida’s order to close the gates on 26 August prevented about 20,000 more civilians from leaving, and his refusal to share the granaries, which would have fed the lower town until April, was the proximate cause of most of the deaths. The Court’s western headquarters, which had issued the order to hold Hira to the last man, never sent an instruction on the feeding of the city. The Court’s records, which were recovered after the fall of Caldera, show that the headquarters had been told in November that the city’s civilians were dying and replied that “the defense of the port takes precedence over all matters of supply.”

The committees’ role has been disputed. They fed about 30,000 civilians a day for about nine weeks, which was probably the largest single act of relief in the siege, and they kept the Wall until it could no longer be held. They did not, however, seize the granaries, and the council’s decision to withdraw from the Wall in May has been criticized by some historians as hastening the city’s fall. Others argue that it saved the lives of about 10,000 men and reduced the damage to the lower town, and that the committees’ decision not to fight the Royalists was the only one consistent with their principles.

The siege is also studied as a case of the intersection of three political forces in a single place. The Royalists, who were fighting the Court, the Court, which was fighting the Royalists and distrusted the committees, and the committees, who were fighting neither and wanted the war to end, each held a part of the city and each reasoned from its own position. Their conflicting assumptions, rather than any single act, produced the famine.

Legacy

The Hira Cliffs memorial was unveiled in 119 AG. It stands on the headland above the mass graves, and it consists of a long wall of grey stone, bearing no names, only the date and a line from Takahashi’s ledger: “We stopped asking for food.” The pits of the winter of 112 are marked by low mounds, and a path leads from the memorial to the lower town’s eastern quay, where the lifeboat station’s boats took the dead to the cliffs. The lower town was rebuilt in the 120s, and the Seiryu Mill, where the committees’ kitchens operated, has been preserved as a museum. The bronze crane at the head of Lantern Street, which was installed in 124, bears the 212 names.

The siege remains one of the most disputed episodes of the war and was the subject of a specific inquiry by the accountability hearings, which reported in 121 that both the Royalist command and the Court’s garrison were responsible for the deaths. The report’s finding on the Royalist command, that it “did not use the means at its disposal to relieve a famine it had the power to end,” was accepted by the Royalist successor government, and the army’s chief of staff, Aoki, who had retired in 118, publicly accepted its conclusion. The report’s findings on the siege’s principal actors, and on the legal status of a blockade that starves a city, are the reason for the postwar rules on the protection of civilians in sieges that the Concord of Nations later adopted. Article 9 of the Concord’s convention, which obliges a besieging force to permit the passage of non-combatants and relief supplies, is commonly called the “Hira clause.”

The siege is commemorated in Hira every year on 4 July, the day of the surrender, when the city’s bells are rung for 212 strokes. It is also commemorated in Qianchan, where Lin Wei’s mission is remembered as the first modern relief operation of its kind, and in the Salvationist movement, where the committees’ kitchens are regarded as the first example of what the movement called “bread before the flag.”

Historiography

Royalist accounts

Royalist histories regard the siege as a necessary operation that was prolonged by the Court’s refusal to surrender and by its seizure of the granaries. The army’s official history, which was compiled by Aoki and published in 116, emphasizes the offers of terms, the passage of the relief ships and the army’s efforts to feed the city after June. It acknowledges the famine, but attributes it to Ishida, and it does not discuss the rejection of the corridor. Later Royalist writers, including the historian Kondo Haruki, have been more critical. Kondo’s study of 131, The Closed Gate, argues that the corridor would have saved at least 80,000 lives and that Ito’s refusal was a failure of judgment and not of intelligence.

Court accounts

Court records blame the Royalist blockade for the famine. The Court’s western headquarters, in its reports to the capital, described the siege as a battle of resistance in which the garrison held the enemy for eleven months, and it attributed the civilians’ deaths to the Royalists’ refusal to allow supplies to enter. The records, which were recovered after the fall of Caldera, show that the headquarters knew of the state of the granaries and that Ishida’s refusal to share them was reported to the Court, which took no action.

Salvationist accounts

Salvationist accounts say that both sides starved the city, and cite the committees’ refusal to fire on the Royalists as the reason the Court could not break out. The movement’s congress, in 114, adopted a resolution on the siege that blamed Ishida for the famine and Ito for “the failure to hear the city.” The accounts, which are the main source for the committees’ kitchens, are generally regarded as reliable on the committees’ actions and as less so on the numbers of those they fed, which they tend to round upward. The Salvationist literature on the siege also tends to underplay the committees’ failure to seize the granaries and the role of the Royalist relief in the final weeks.

Civilian testimony

The civilian records are the most widely read of the siege’s literature and the most important to its present-day memory. The Ledger of Lantern Street, published in 118, has been reprinted many times and is taught in the schools of Hira. The diaries of Matsuda, Fujii and Ikeda were collected in 122 in a volume that was edited by Ikeda, who became a teacher and who died in 163. Historians generally regard these sources as the most reliable account of the famine, though they note that the survivors’ testimony is inevitably weighted to the lower town, and that the voices of the old town, the dockyard’s workers and the garrison’s conscripts are underrepresented.

second_battle_of_shu_jing.title: Second Battle of Shu Jing
second_battle_of_shu_jing.html:
Second Battle of Shu Jing
Part ofThe middle stage of the Fire Nation Civil War
Date9 May – 28 August 113 AG
LocationShu Jing industrial center
ResultRoyalist victory. The Royalists survive the combined assault; first use of ballistic missiles in the war
Belligerents
Royalists, with Qianchan supplyOzai loyalists (the Court) and Salvationist committees
Commanders and leaders
RoyalistsGeneral Ito Shigeru; Colonel Mori Tatsuo; Zuko
CourtGeneral Hirata Gensai
SalvationistsCentral Salvation Committee (members not identified)
Strength
Royalists
about 110,000 with Qianchan air-defense units		Attackers
about 150,000 (Court about 50,000; Salvationists about 100,000), with 12 Ryuusei-B2 missiles and 60 Breaker Mk II
Casualties and losses
About 150,000 killed, of whom about 95,000 were civilians

The Second Battle of Shu Jing was a combined assault on the Royalist capital in the summer of 113 AG by Court and Salvationist formations. It was the war’s costliest assault on a city that held, and the first in which ballistic missiles were used. The Royalists survived, with Qianchan-supplied air defenses and reinforcements brought through the south. About 150,000 people died. It is the twelfth of the war’s twenty defining battles.

The battle established the Salvationists as a military power and ended any hope of a two-sided war.

Background

In 113 AG the Court and the committees, who commanded most of its army, had a common interest in ending the Royalist government. The Salvationists, who were still nominally under the Court’s flag, had the Ryuusei-B2 missiles and the Tetsuken systems; the Court had the air bases and the armor that remained. For the first time since 107 AG, the two forces agreed to attack the same target.

The Central Salvation Committee, which coordinated the committees, insisted that the attack be made by its own forces, and that the missiles be used only against the city’s industry. The Court agreed, because it needed the weapons.

Order of battle

Salvationists (about 100,000). Committee divisions of the western belt under the Central Salvation Committee; Tetsuken battalions; two Breaker companies; the missile battery from the Ryuusei Facility. Four Ryuusei-B2 missiles in the first strike, more over the following weeks; Tetsuken squads.

Court (about 40,000). Remaining armored regiments; the 5th Air Division; Flame Guard battalions. T-50 fighters and B-100 bombers; about a third of the air force lost by the end.

Royalists (about 90,000). First Army (three divisions); the Works Guard; the Reinforcement Corps assembled in the south; Qianchan air-defense units. Anti-aircraft guns and rockets; no defense against the missiles.

Civilians. About 600,000 in the city at the start. About 100,000 evacuated by August.

Course

9–31 May: the missiles

The battle opened on 9 May with the first ballistic-missile attack in history. The Salvationists fired four Ryuusei-B2 missiles at the foundry districts and the rail yards; they landed with a circular error of about 2,100 meters, so that they hit the city’s residential districts as often as its industry. About 11,000 people died in the first strike. The remaining missiles were fired over the following weeks, and the Royalists, who had no defense against them, evacuated about 100,000 people.

June–July: the assault

The ground assault began on 3 June with about 100,000 Salvationist troops, who advanced through the southern suburbs with Tetsuken-equipped squads and Breaker companies. They took the outer foundries in two weeks. The Court’s armor and air force attacked from the east. The Royalists, who were attacked from two sides, held the central districts and the river bridges with Works Guard and Qianchan reinforcements, who arrived by river on 28 June.

August: the relief

In August the Royalists’ reinforcement corps, which had been assembled in the south, reached the city, and the Qianchan air-defense units shot down about 70 aircraft in four days. The attackers, who were short of ammunition, withdrew on 28 August. The Salvationists took their wounded and the remaining missiles, and the Court lost about a third of its air force.

Civilian accounts

The missile strikes are described in the diary of Dr. Ishikawa Tomo, who ran the Canal Street infirmary. She recorded the first strike at 4:10 in the morning and the 311 people brought in during the first hour, and wrote that "nobody had a word for what it was, so we called it the thunder." The infirmary was hit by the second strike and rebuilt in a rail shed. Her diary, published in 131 AG, is one of the sources Qianchan archives use for the civilian dead.

Several witnesses note the evacuation. The Royalists moved about 100,000 people over the river bridges by night, and the Qianchan air group dropped leaflets telling people which districts were safe for the following day. The leaflets were often wrong, and the number of people who died on the roads is not known.

Casualties

About 150,000 people died, of whom about 95,000 were civilians, most of them killed in the missile strikes and in the fighting in the residential districts. About 60,000 attackers and about 55,000 defenders were killed or wounded. Only the longer sieges of Hira, Sakuragawa (later Joha) and Caldera cost more lives.

Aftermath

The Royalists held the city and its industry, but the Court, which had lost much of its air force, was no longer an effective military power. The Salvationists, who had fought independently, withdrew to the west, where they prepared their break with the Court in 116 AG. Missiles were used once more, at the Third Battle of Shu Jing.

Legacy

The battle introduced ballistic missiles into the war, and all three parties drew lessons from it. The Royalists built an air-defense network around their remaining industry. The Court, which had lost a third of its air force, stopped offensive air operations. The Salvationists, whose missiles had struck civilians as often as foundries, did not fire the rest of the stock, and the Central Salvation Committee later cited the error in its internal debates. The remaining missiles were expended in the Third Battle in 116 and 117 AG.

In the later history of the region the battle is remembered as the first modern attack on a civilian population from a distance. Qianchan's Congress cited it in 121 AG when it voted to ban the export of the relevant components, and the United Republic's early arms conventions refer to it as the "Shu Jing precedent."

Historiography

Royalist histories present the battle as a victory over a joint attack by the Court and a foreign-backed rebellion, and credit Qianchan air defenses. Salvationist accounts call it the first battle fought by an army of the people and describe the missile strikes as an unavoidable cost. Court records do not mention the Salvationists as a separate force. Qianchan archives record the missile strikes in detail, and are the source for the civilian dead.
