  • Ryuusei Facility
  • Siege of Hira

kaien_straits.title: Battle of Kaien Straits
kaien_straits.html:
Battle of Kaien Straits
Part ofThe middle stage of the Fire Nation Civil War
Date19–21 June 113 AG
LocationKaien Straits, the channel between the southern ports and the river mouth that serves Shu Jing
ResultCourt victory. Court submarines sink a Royalist convoy carrying the relief for Shu Jing
Belligerents
Ozai loyalists (the Court), Submarine CommandRoyalists, with Qianchan escorts
Commanders and leaders
Court
Commander Ushio Takeru (flotilla)		Royalists
Rear Admiral Minami Haruka (distant cover); Captain Aoyama Mitsuko (convoy commander)
Strength
Court
9 submarines (Kaienha incendiary torpedoes)		Royalists
a convoy of 31 ships with 6 escorts, about 22,000 relief troops and about 6,000 civilians
Casualties and losses
About 14,000 killed, of whom about 4,000 were civilians

The Battle of Kaien Straits was a three-day submarine ambush in June 113 AG, in which Court submarines sank a Royalist convoy carrying reinforcements to Shu Jing, during the Second Battle of Shu Jing. About 14,000 people died, including about 4,000 civilians who were aboard. It is the thirteenth of the war’s twenty defining battles.

The sinking delayed the relief of Shu Jing by about two months, and the city nearly fell before the remaining ships arrived. It was the Court’s last important naval success.

Background

After the first missile strikes of 9 May, the Royalist command at Shu Jing asked the south for every available soldier. A relief corps of about 35,000 was assembled at the southern ports, and was to be shipped in two convoys up the coast to the river mouth and then by river to the city. The first convoy, with Qianchan air-defense units, reached the city by river on 28 June (see the Second Shu Jing article). The second, which carried about 22,000 Royalist troops, was sunk in the straits.

It had also taken on civilians. Aoyama Mitsuko, the convoy’s commander, had agreed to take about 6,000 people from the port’s refugee camps who had relatives in the north. The convoy’s schedule was known to the Court, which had a spy in the southern harbor office.

The convoy

The second convoy was assembled at the southern port of Minato over three weeks. It consisted of 31 ships: 19 transports, three tankers, nine escorts. The transports were requisitioned merchantmen, most of them old, and the escorts included six destroyers and three corvettes. The troops aboard were the 3rd, 5th and 8th Divisions of the Relief Corps, about 22,000 men, with their field guns and about 200 trucks. The refugees, about 6,000 in all, were accommodated on the three largest transports, in holds that had been fitted with bunks.

Aoyama Mitsuko, the convoy commander, had been a merchant captain before the war and had joined the Royalist navy in 101. She was known to be a careful officer, and had opposed the carrying of civilians. Her superiors overruled her on the grounds that the refugees' relatives in the north were among the troops' own families, and that refusing them would damage morale. She signed the sailing order on 17 June with the written note that she had objected.

The Court flotilla

The Court's Ninth Submarine Flotilla was commanded by Commander Ushio Takeru, who had been given nine boats and a free hand. Ushio had been warned by his agent in Minato that the convoy would sail on one of three nights, and he placed his boats on the bottom of the straits in a line at 40-meter depth, where the escorts' sonar could not distinguish them from the rock. His crews lay on the bottom for four days, running only the minimum of machinery, and the boats' air became foul. Two commanders recorded in their logs that the crews' judgment was affected, and that they had ordered three men confined for sleeping at their stations.

Course

On 19 June the convoy entered the straits at dusk with six escorts. Nine Court submarines, which had been waiting on the bottom in the shallows for four days, attacked at 22:15. Five transports were hit in the first ten minutes. Kaienha incendiary torpedoes set fire to the oil that spread across the water, and the burning surface made rescue almost impossible.

The escorts sank two submarines the following day but were unable to protect the convoy. By the evening of 20 June, 19 of the 31 ships had been sunk, and the rest had scattered. On 21 June Minami’s covering force arrived and sank the Court flotilla commander’s boat, I-71. About 14,000 were dead or missing.

The survivors, about 17,000 troops and civilians, were taken aboard the surviving ships and landed on the river coast on 23 June. The relief corps that reached Shu Jing in August was about half the size that had been intended.

Order of battle

Royalist convoy. 19 transports, 3 tankers; 3rd, 5th and 8th Divisions of the Relief Corps (about 22,000); about 6,000 civilians. Six destroyers and three corvettes as escort.

Court (Ninth Flotilla). Nine submarines under Commander Ushio Takeru, including I-71. Kaienha incendiary torpedoes.

Royalist covering force. Rear Admiral Minami's squadron, arriving on 21 June. Cruiser, destroyers, two submarine flotillas.

Civilian accounts

About 4,000 of the 6,000 civilians aboard died. The best source is the account of Miyake Kiyoko, a sixteen-year-old who traveled to join her father in the north. Her statement, taken by the Royalist relief committee in July, says that the passengers were told to remain in the holds, and that when the first torpedoes hit the ship's lights went out. “A woman near me said the water was warm. It was the oil. Someone lit a match, I think by mistake, and then I could not see anything but light.” She was pulled from the water by a destroyer's crew after nine hours.

A second account is that of Chief Engineer Ota Gen of the transport Seiko Maru, who kept the ship's log until the ship sank. His last entry reads, “22:31. Hit forward. Hold flooding. Passengers ordered to deck. Orders to abandon given.” He was among the dead, and the log was recovered from a lifeboat.

Command responsibility

After the battle, Aoyama was subject to an inquiry, which found that she had not been negligent. She was cleared in September 113, but she resigned her commission and never returned to sea. The Royalist command's decision to carry civilians on the convoy was examined by a second inquiry in 115, which recommended that civilians never be carried on military convoys. The recommendation became a standing order, and was cited in the Concord's later conventions.

Weapons and tactics

The Kaienha incendiary torpedo was a standard weapon of the Court's submarines. Its warhead contained a mixture of oil and phosphorus that ignited on contact with water, and it was designed to burn the surface around the target. The weapon was effective against convoys, because the burning oil spread over the surface and prevented rescue, and it was condemned for the same reason. The torpedoes were fired in salvos of four, and Ushio's boats fired 52 in the first ten minutes.

The escorts' main weapon was the depth charge, which was ineffective against boats on the bottom. Their sonar was of an old design, and could not distinguish the boats from the rock. The convoy also lacked aircraft cover, because the Royalist air group was at Shu Jing. These deficiencies had been reported to the Royalist command, which did not act on the reports.

Notable people

Commander Ushio Takeru commanded the Ninth Flotilla and was killed in I-71 on 21 June. His log, recovered with the boat in 124, records the four days on the bottom. “The men are tired,” he wrote on 18 June. “They ask me whether the ships will come. I tell them that they will.”

Rear Admiral Minami Haruka, the Royalist covering force's commander, arrived on the third day and sank I-71 with depth charges. She is said to have refused a proposal to leave the survivors in the water in order to pursue the Court's boats, and she ordered the rescue.

The survivors

About 17,000 survivors were landed on the river coast on 23 June, of whom about 2,000 were civilians. They were housed in a camp at the river mouth, where the relief committee recorded their names. About 4,000 of the civilians had died, and many of the survivors were separated from their families. The committee kept a register of the missing, which listed 4,112 names. Over the following years, about 300 of the missing were found alive in other camps.

Reception in the sources

The Royalist inquiry reports, which were published in 114, are the main source for the convoy's composition. The Court's submarine logs, which were captured in 124, give an account of the attack, and show that Ushio's boats fired 52 torpedoes in all. The civilian accounts, of which Miyake's is the best known, were collected by the relief committee and published in 121.

Aftermath

The loss of the second convoy delayed the relief of Shu Jing until August, and the city came close to falling. The Court’s submarine force was nearly destroyed in the following months, and never again attacked a major convoy. The sinking is remembered in the south, where the dead were from the port districts, and a memorial stands on the beach at Kaien.

Analysis

The ambush is considered a model of submarine tactics. It succeeded because the Court knew the route and the time of sailing, and because the convoy's escorts were ill-prepared for a bottom ambush. Historians note that the use of Kaienha incendiary torpedoes against a convoy carrying civilians was condemned in the Qianchan and Royalist press, and was cited by the Court's apologists as a legitimate response to the Royalists' use of the same weapon at the Kumo Straits.

The effect of the sinking on the Second Battle of Shu Jing is a matter of dispute. The Royalist record says that the reinforcements of the second convoy would have allowed the city to counterattack in July, and that the delay cost about 20,000 lives. Some historians believe that the corps would not have arrived in time in any case.

Legacy

The memorial at Kaien Beach was unveiled in 116 AG, and is a low stone wall with 4,112 names. A second memorial, to the ship Seiko Maru, stands in the port of Minato. The date of 19 June is observed in the southern provinces as a day of mourning, and its observance is a custom of the families of the port districts. The submarine I-71 was raised in 124 AG and is on display at the maritime museum at Minato.

Historiography

Royalist accounts blame the Court spy and the convoy’s civilian passengers, and the Royalist command’s decision to carry them has been criticized. Court records describe the battle as a model submarine ambush and give the Royalist dead at 20,000. Salvationist accounts note that the convoy was carrying troops intended to defend Shu Jing against their own forces.

siege_of_sakuragawa.title: Siege of Sakuragawa
siege_of_sakuragawa.html:
Siege of Sakuragawa
Part ofThe middle stage of the Fire Nation Civil War
DateOctober 114 – August 115 AG (ten months)
LocationSakuragawa (now Joha), the Court’s principal industrial city in the western heartland
ResultRoyalist victory. The Court’s last industrial city falls
Belligerents
RoyalistsOzai loyalists (the Court) and Salvationist committee units in the garrison
Commanders and leaders
Royalists
General Ito Shigeru; Colonel Mori Tatsuo		Court
Lieutenant General Sakai Renjiro
Strength
Royalists
about 110,000		Garrison
about 70,000, about 300,000 civilians
Casualties and losses
About 190,000 killed, of whom about 140,000 were civilians

The Siege of Sakuragawa, fought at the city now known as Joha, was a ten-month siege, from October 114 to August 115 AG, in which the Royalists took the Court’s principal industrial city. It was the second-deadliest siege of the war after Caldera, and the fourteenth of its twenty defining battles. About 190,000 people died.

The city’s fall deprived the Court of its factories. It could no longer make shells or tanks, and it depended on stocks and on the committees’ goodwill.

Name

The city was called Sakuragawa during the war and is recorded under that name in all contemporary sources. After the war the Reformation government granted it a new municipal charter in 122 AG, under which it was renamed Joha in 122 AG, and it has been known by that name ever since. Postwar histories use both names, and the siege is sometimes called the Siege of Joha, especially in works written after the renaming. The wiki follows the Royalist record in using the name of the time.

Background

Sakuragawa lay on the river west of Hira, in the rice country, and had grown during the Hundred Year War into the Empire’s second industrial center. It produced most of the Court’s ammunition and vehicles. After the Royalist victory at Shu Jing in 113 AG and the failure of the combined assault, Ito proposed to take it, to end the Court’s production.

The garrison, like that of Hira, was divided. About 20,000 of its 70,000 troops belonged to committee-led units, who had no interest in dying for the Court, while the loyalist core was formed by the Flame Guard and the factories’ security battalions.

The city

Sakuragawa had about 400,000 people before the siege. It lay on both banks of a wide river, with the factories on the north bank and the residential wards on the south. The Hundred Year War had turned it into a forge: the Ministry of War Production ran 22 large works, the largest of which, the Sakura Arsenal, employed about 30,000 people. The factories were connected by an electric tramway that the workers called the Cherry Line and that was used to carry shells to the rail yards.

The garrison was commanded by General Sakai Renjiro, who had arrived in June 114 after escaping from the west bank at Tsurugi Bridge. He had about 70,000 troops, of whom about 20,000 belonged to committee-led units that refused to fight except in the defense of their own wards. Sakai accepted the arrangement, and divided the city into the loyalist north bank and the committee-held south.

Order of battle

Royalists (about 120,000). First and Second Armies; the Works Guard artillery; flamethrower and demolition companies; Qianchan-supplied air group. Heavy guns; aircraft; engineering equipment.

Court garrison (about 50,000). Flame Guard battalions; the factories' security battalions; Ministry of Truth detachments. Fortified factories; stocks of shells until March.

Committee units (about 20,000). The 11th and 14th Divisions of the Fourth Army; ward committees. Light weapons; Tetsuken sets.

Civilians. About 400,000 at the start. About 210,000 at the end.

Course

October 114 – January 115: investment

The Royalists closed the city’s landward roads between October and December, and on 20 December Qianchan-supplied aircraft destroyed the main river bridge. The factories continued to work through the autumn, with workers sleeping at their machines. By January the Royalists had begun to shell the industrial districts.

February–May 115: the winter siege

The siege tightened through the winter. The city had enough grain to last until March, but the Court’s granaries were held by the Flame Guard, and the civilians were rationed by the factories, which stopped production in February. Cholera broke out in the eastern wards in March, and killed about 22,000 people in six weeks. On 9 April the Royalists took the outer ring of fortifications, and the Court moved the remaining shell-making machinery into the cellars.

June–August 115: the fall

The final assault began on 12 June and lasted nine weeks. The Royalists advanced through the factory districts with flamethrowers and demolition charges. Many of the committee-led units withdrew in July by agreement, leaving the loyalists to defend the central district. Sakai, who was in the city, withdrew with about 8,000 men on 3 August. The city surrendered on 17 August.

The cholera

The cholera outbreak was the worst epidemic of the war. It began in the eastern wards after the pumping station was shelled on 2 March, and spread quickly because the wards' wells had been fouled by the bombing. The hospital treated about 380 patients a day in April, and the city's doctors recorded about 22,000 deaths in six weeks. The Royalists, who refused to allow a truce for the evacuation of the sick, offered to send water by road, and the first tanker reached the city on 11 April. The Court, which feared that the convoy was a ruse, delayed the delivery for three days.

Civilian accounts

The siege is documented by a diary kept by Kimura Hanae, a nurse at the Sakuragawa municipal hospital, which was published in 125 AG. Her account records the hospital’s admissions during the cholera outbreak (about 380 a day in April), the lack of clean water after the pumping station was shelled on 2 March, and a day in July when the hospital was hit by a Royalist shell. Her diary ends on 17 August with the entry: “The soldiers say it is over. We are still carrying them out.” It is the main source for the civilian death toll, which the Royalist record puts at 140,000.

The committees' withdrawal

The withdrawal of the committee units in July was negotiated by Ono Sayuri, who traveled to the Royalist lines under a white flag on 9 July. She obtained a four-day truce, during which the 11th and 14th Divisions left the south bank with their weapons and about 30,000 civilians. The Royalists agreed because they wanted to reduce the number of defenders. The committees' conduct was later cited by the Court as an act of treason, and by the Salvationists as a rescue.

Surrender

The surrender on 17 August was signed in the city hall by Colonel Hirai Takeo, who had been left in command by Sakai. About 22,000 troops surrendered, and the Royalists occupied the city the following day. The Arsenal's machinery, which had been partly destroyed, was stripped by the Royalists and shipped to Shu Jing.

The factories

The Sakura Arsenal was the Court's largest works. It produced about 3,000 shells a day in 114, and its machine shops made tank engines and gun barrels. The work was done by about 30,000 people, of whom about a third were women. The workers were organized in shifts of twelve hours, and slept in dormitories by the machines. After February the Arsenal ran out of coal, and its production ceased. The Court's order to continue was ignored by the committees' delegates, who argued that the workers could not be asked to work without food.

The factories were also the center of the committees' organization in the city. The Arsenal's committee, which had about 6,000 members, took over the distribution of food in the north bank in February, and ran the ration kitchens. The loyalists of the Flame Guard did not interfere, because they needed the workers' goodwill.

Notable people

Kimura Hanae, the nurse, was 29 at the time of the siege, and survived it. After the war she became a teacher of nursing, and in 125 published her diary. She died in 152.

Colonel Hirai Takeo, who signed the surrender, was a Court staff officer who had been left in the city by Sakai. He was tried at the hearings and acquitted, on the ground that the surrender had saved about 30,000 lives.

The fall of the north bank

The final assault began on 12 June with a bombardment of the north bank by about 400 guns. The Royalists advanced in groups of about 30 men, with flamethrowers and demolition charges, and took the factories one at a time. The fighting in the Arsenal lasted nine days, and the last defenders, about 400 men of the Flame Guard, were burned out of the foundry on 24 June. By the end of July, the Royalists held the north bank, and the loyalists were confined to the central district.

Reception in the sources

The Royalist records give a detailed account of the assault, and the Court's records of the production figures. The Kimura diary is the main civilian source. A second source, the surgeons' log of the municipal hospital, records the cholera admissions by day and was published in 127.

Aftermath

The Court lost its factories and most of its trained workers, and its remaining forces were supplied from captured stocks and from the committees. The Royalists, who held the city, did not have the strength to push on to Caldera, and in 115 AG they made their attempt on the capital by rail (see The Black Rail).

Analysis

Sakuragawa is regarded as the Royalists' most costly victory, and its closest parallel is Hira. It differs from Hira in that the deaths were caused not only by starvation but by disease, and in that the city's factories continued to work, so that the war economy of the Court was a target of the siege. The Court's decision to defend the city was a strategic mistake, because it could not be relieved, and the garrison's commander, Sakai, is blamed for it by some historians. Others note that Sakai had no choice, because the Court could not have survived without the factories.

Legacy

The Kimura diary became a school text in the postwar years. A monument to the dead, placed on the south bank in 120 AG, carries the names of 61,000 identified victims, of which about 22,000 are the cholera dead. The Sakura Arsenal was rebuilt after the war as a civilian works, and one of its halls was left as a museum. The Cherry Line tramway still runs.

Historiography

Royalist histories treat the siege as a justified operation against the Court’s arsenal, and note that the committees were allowed to leave. Court records blame the Royalists for the famine and the cholera. Salvationist accounts say that the committees negotiated their withdrawal in July to save the civilians, and cite Kimura’s diary as proof that both sides let the city starve.

the_black_rail.title: The Black Rail
the_black_rail.html:
The Black Rail
Part ofThe middle stage of the Fire Nation Civil War
Date3–28 October 115 AG
LocationThe rail belt west of Caldera, including the Black Rail embankment and the Hanazono marshalling yards
ResultCourt and Salvationist victory. The Royalist offensive on Caldera is repulsed
Belligerents
RoyalistsOzai loyalists (the Court); Salvationist committee divisions (still under the Court’s flag)
Commanders and leaders
RoyalistsGeneral Ito Shigeru
CourtGeneral Hirata Gensai
SalvationistsSergeant Major Tanaka Kenji (Fourth Army committee)
Strength
Royalists
about 100,000 with about 200 tanks and an armored train group		Defenders
about 80,000, mostly Salvationist-led, with Tetsuken systems and Breaker Mk II companies
Casualties and losses
About 95,000 killed

The Black Rail was the Royalist offensive on Caldera in October 115 AG, named for the blackened embankment of the western rail line along which it was fought. The Royalists, after taking Sakuragawa (later Joha), advanced on the capital along the railway, and were stopped about 30 kilometers from the city by Court and Salvationist forces. About 95,000 people died. It is the fifteenth of the war’s twenty defining battles.

The battle was the first in which Salvationist-led divisions fought the Royalists in the open, and it showed both the Royalists and the Court that the committees would not simply follow the Court’s orders.

Background

After Sakuragawa, Ito’s army was within reach of the capital. The Royalist command decided that the war could be ended by one more offensive in the autumn, before the winter. Armored trains were assembled from the rolling stock of Shu Jing’s works, and the offensive was to follow the main line from Sakuragawa to Caldera.

The defenders were largely committee-led. Hirata, who held the Court’s command, had few troops of his own, and the Fourth Army’s committee, led by Sergeant Major Tanaka Kenji, controlled most of the divisions on the line. Tanaka agreed to defend the line, but told Hirata that his troops would not receive orders from the Court after the battle.

The railway

The western main line ran from Sakuragawa to Caldera, a distance of about 120 kilometers, on a raised embankment through marsh and rice fields. At the Hanazono marshalling yards, about 30 kilometers from the capital, the line crossed a canal on a steel bridge and split into three branches. The yards, with their sheds and workshops, were the natural place to defend, because the embankment narrowed there and could be flooded on either side by opening the canal gates.

The Royalists' plan was to run armored trains along the embankment, with infantry marching on the roadway beside them. The trains, which Royalist engineers had built at Shu Jing, were of two kinds: gun trains carrying a 150mm gun each, and carrier trains with about 1,000 infantry in armored cars. Eight of each were assembled.

Order of battle

Royalists (about 150,000). Second Army; eight gun trains and eight carrier trains; engineer and pioneer regiments; a Qianchan air group. 150mm railway guns; armored cars.

Salvationists (about 90,000). Fourth Army divisions under Tanaka Kenji; the Ryuusei Facility garrison; Tetsuken battalions. Tetsuken lightning dischargers; prepared yard positions.

Court (about 15,000). Armored remnants and Flame Guard battalions under Hirata Gensai. Tanks held in reserve; not committed until 20 October.

Civilians. The marsh villages were evacuated by the Salvationists. About 70,000 displaced.

Course

The offensive began on 3 October, with the armored trains advancing along the embankment under cover of artillery. The first day’s advance was 12 kilometers. On 5 October the Royalists reached the Hanazono marshalling yards, and met the first Salvationist divisions, who had dug in among the yard’s sheds and who used Tetsuken lightning dischargers against the trains.

The armored trains were stopped on 7 October, when Salvationist engineers destroyed a bridge behind the lead train and a second train behind it, trapping about 4,000 Royalist troops. For the next three weeks the battle was a struggle for the embankment, in which both sides lost about 4,000 men a day. On 18 October a Royalist armored column crossed the embankment and reached the Salvationist command post, and was destroyed in a counterattack the next day.

The Royalists withdrew on 28 October, after losing about 55,000 men. The defenders’ losses were about 40,000.

Civilian accounts

The marsh villages were home to about 40,000 farmers, who were evacuated by the Salvationists in the week before the offensive. The evacuation is described by the committee's delegate Okamoto Chie, who organized the carts and the boats and wrote a report afterward. She records that the Court's officers refused to provide any transport, and that the villagers took their water buffalo with them. “An old man asked me if he would see his field again,” she wrote. “I said yes. It was not true for his field, which was under water within the week.”

The flooding of the embankment, which the Salvationists carried out on 10 October, destroyed about 8,000 hectares of rice. The cost of this decision was debated in the committees afterward, and is cited in the later criticism of Tanaka.

Command

Tanaka Kenji, who commanded the Salvationist divisions, was a sergeant major in the Fourth Army and had no formal rank above that. He took the field command on the grounds that the committees had elected him, and the Court's Hirata accepted this because he could not do otherwise. Tanaka gave his orders in writing, to the committees, which then passed them to the units. The command post was a railway signal cabin at Hanazono, where he lived for the whole of the battle.

Weapons and tactics

The Royalist gun trains carried a 150mm gun each, mounted on a flatcar behind an armored shield, with a range of about 20 kilometers. Their fire was directed by observers in forward carriers, and they could be moved along the line as needed. The carrier trains were armored cars with machine guns and light cannon, and each could carry about 1,000 men. The Royalist command believed that the trains would be impervious to small arms.

The Salvationists' main defense was the Tetsuken discharger, which could disable the trains' electrical equipment at a range of about 50 meters. They also used mines laid under the track, demolitions, and the flooding of the embankment. The yards' sheds were converted into strongpoints, with sandbagged firing positions, and the committees' engineers dug trenches along the canal banks.

Notable people

General Ito Shigeru commanded the Royalist army. He was criticized for the plan, which he had opposed, and which was ordered by the Royalist command over his objections. After the battle he was given the task of rebuilding the army.

Sergeant Major Tanaka Kenji held the command post at Hanazono, and was wounded on 18 October. He was promoted to general by the committees' congress in January.

Okamoto Chie organized the evacuation of the marsh villages, and in 116 became the committees' delegate for civilian affairs. She was arrested in 119 and released in the amnesty of 120.

Reception in the sources

The Royalist staff reports, which are the main source for the Royalist losses, describe the battle in detail. The Salvationist committee's minutes give an account of the defense. The Court's records, which claim credit for the victory, are the least reliable.

Aftermath

The Royalists retired to Sakuragawa for the winter. The battle made the Salvationists, and not the Court, the defenders of the capital, and in the following spring the committees held a congress at Hanazono, where they voted to break with the Court (see Kuroshio Mills).

Analysis

The Royalists' defeat is generally attributed to three causes: the destruction of the bridge behind the lead train on 7 October, which turned an advance into a siege; the committees' use of the Tetsuken dischargers against the trains, which neutralized the Royalists' armor; and the flooding of the embankment, which prevented the Royalists from bringing up reserves on the flanks. The Royalist command has been criticized for committing its trains without adequate infantry protection.

Legacy

The yards are a rail museum, with a preserved gun train. The congress of January 116 was held in the repaired sheds, and a plaque marks the room. The battle is regarded by the Salvationists as the beginning of their legitimacy as a government, and by the Royalists as the beginning of their awareness that the committees were a power.

Historiography

Royalist histories describe the battle as a failure caused by overextension and the loss of the bridge. Court records claim the victory for the Court’s armor, which was a small part of the force. Salvationist accounts call it the first victory of the people’s army and date the congress that followed to the same weeks.

See also

  • Siege of Sakuragawa
  • Kuroshio Mills
  • Salvationists

kuroshio_mills.title: Battle of Kuroshio Mills
kuroshio_mills.html:
Battle of Kuroshio Mills
Part ofThe late stage of the Fire Nation Civil War
Date11–13 March 116 AG
LocationThe Kuroshio Mills, the western industrial belt, and the rail towns between Hanazono and Caldera
ResultSalvationist victory. The Salvationists break with the Court and seize the western industrial belt
Belligerents
Salvationists (the committees)Ozai loyalists (the Court), Flame Guard and the Ministry of Truth
Commanders and leaders
Salvationists
Central Salvation Committee (Tanaka Kenji, Ono Sayuri, Fujiwara Daigo, Matsuda Reiko, Kuga Ren)		Court
General Hirata Gensai
Strength
Salvationists
about 120,000 under committee control		Court
about 15,000 (Flame Guard, Ministry of Truth detachments, cultists)
Casualties and losses
About 60,000 killed, including about 25,000 civilians

The Battle of Kuroshio Mills was the Salvationists’ break with the Court, in March 116 AG. In a single night of coordinated action the committees seized the mills, the rail towns and the Court’s western supply depots, and arrested or killed the Court officers attached to their units. They then used the Court’s own army against it. About 60,000 people died. It is the sixteenth of the war’s twenty defining battles.

The break ended the two-sided war. The Court never recovered its field army, and the Royalists, who had expected a negotiated end, faced a third party.

Background

After the Black Rail, the committees held a congress at Hanazono in January 116 AG. The delegates voted, by 112 to 31, to break with the Court, on the grounds that its supply system had collapsed and that the Court could no longer pay or feed the troops it commanded. The vote followed a debate in which Tanaka Kenji argued for delay and Ono Sayuri, a schoolteacher who had served as the committees’ political delegate, argued for an immediate break. The Central Salvation Committee was formed with five members: Tanaka (military), Ono (political), Fujiwara Daigo (technical, the head of the Ryuusei Facility committee), Matsuda Reiko (supply) and Kuga Ren (security).

The Court, which had learned of the vote, ordered the arrest of the committees’ leaders on 8 March. The committees acted first.

The congress

The congress at Hanazono lasted from 12 to 19 January 116 and was attended by 143 delegates, elected by regimental committees. It met in the repaired sheds of the yards, with the delegates sleeping on cots. The debate was recorded by a stenographer, whose notes were published by the Salvationists in exile in 129 AG. The most celebrated speech was Ono Sayuri's, in which she asked the delegates whether they would “serve a government that cannot feed us, or serve ourselves.” The vote to break, 112 to 31, was taken on the evening of 19 January.

The delegates agreed that the break should be made quickly and in secret. The date of 11 March was chosen by Tanaka, who calculated that the Court's plan to arrest the leaders would be carried out on 8 March, and that the committees would then have to act before the Court could reorganize.

The Central Salvation Committee

The five members had been chosen at the congress. Tanaka Kenji, the military member, was 41, a machinist from Shu Jing. Ono Sayuri, the political member, was 36, a schoolteacher from the western provinces. Fujiwara Daigo, the technical member, was 44, an engineer. Matsuda Reiko, the supply member, was 39, a former quartermaster. Kuga Ren, the security member, was 33, a former Kanbukyoku clerk who had joined the committees in 109. The Committee's decisions required a majority of three, and the record shows that Kuga voted with Tanaka in all but two of the 112 votes recorded.

Course

The coup began at 02:00 on 11 March. In about 60 garrisons and depots across the western belt, committees disarmed their officers, seized the telegraph exchanges, and sent out a printed declaration written by Ono, which announced that the Salvationists were “independent of every government that has ruled in our name.” At the Kuroshio Mills, the largest of the sites, the committee’s forces overwhelmed the Court’s security battalion in an hour and held the mills’ furnaces against two counterattacks.

Kuga Ren, the committee’s security delegate, ordered the arrest of every Court officer in the committees’ units. About 1,200 were detained, and about 400 were shot in the first three days, most of them after summary hearings. The Court counterattacked with the Flame Guard and the cultists, and was driven back. Civilian casualties, about 25,000, were mostly from the Court’s attacks on the rail towns and from the Flame Guard’s reprisals against committee supporters.

By 13 March the committees held the whole belt, and Hirata withdrew to Caldera with about 15,000 men. The Court’s western supply depots were in committee hands.

Order of battle

Salvationists. Committee units in about 60 garrisons; the Mills committee (about 4,000); the Ryuusei Facility garrison. Captured Court supplies; Tetsuken sets.

Court. Flame Guard; the cultists; the Mills security battalion (about 900); Ministry of Truth detachments. Reprisal columns.

Civilians. Rail towns of the western belt. About 25,000 killed.

Civilian accounts

The reprisals against the rail towns were recorded by the stationmaster of Oyama, Terada Keiji, who kept the station's telegraph log. On 12 March, the log notes, a Court column entered the town and shot 61 people against the station wall. “They said we had been told to cooperate,” the log reads. “We had not been told anything. We were told to hand over the telegraph and we did.” He was among those shot.

The executions of the Court officers by the committees were reported by a Qianchan observer, Mr. Zhou Ming, who described the hearings as “summaries of a few minutes” and noted that about a quarter of those shot had been the committees' own supporters, taken by mistake.

The killings

The killing of about 400 Court officers, which Kuga Ren ordered and the Committee afterward endorsed, is the most controversial act of the Salvationists. The Committee's defenders argue that the officers would have organized resistance and that the committees had no means of holding prisoners. Its critics, including some veterans, say that it began the cycle of reprisals that marked the later war. Kuga was tried for it in 121 AG.

The Mills

The Kuroshio Mills were a complex of steel mills and rolling works on the river at Kuroshio, about 50 kilometers from Caldera. They employed about 8,000 workers and supplied the Court with rails and shell steel. The mills' committee was the oldest in the western belt, and its chairman, Hamasaki Goro, was a foundry hand who had been a delegate at the Hanazono congress. On the night of 11 March, he led about 400 men of the committee through the mill's north gate, which had been opened by the night shift.

The Court's security battalion, about 900 men, was quartered in the mills' offices. It was overwhelmed in about an hour, because most of its officers were asleep, and the committee held the furnace hall against two counterattacks on 11 and 12 March. By 13 March the mills were in the committees' hands, and the furnaces were relit on 15 March.

The declaration

Ono Sayuri's declaration of 11 March was printed on the mills' presses and distributed by rail. It declared that the Salvationists were “independent of every government that has ruled in our name,” and listed the committees' demands: pay for the army, the end of the Court's requisitions, and the election of officers. It did not mention the Royalists, and its omission was interpreted by the Royalists as a hope of negotiation. The declaration was signed by the five members of the Central Salvation Committee.

Notable people

Hirata Gensai, the Court's commander, escaped from the Court's western headquarters with about 15,000 men on 13 March. He was killed at Caldera in 118.

Hamasaki Goro, the mill committee's chairman, was killed at the second counterattack, and is the first of the committees' dead to be commemorated by name.

Reception in the sources

The declaration, the congress minutes and the Committee's orders are the main primary sources. The killings are described in the Royalist intelligence reports and in the observer's account. The Court's records of the reprisals have not survived.

Aftermath

The Salvationists held the largest of the three armies, and for the first time the war was fought by three parties. The Court, which retained only Caldera and a few forts, could no longer feed its soldiers, and the Royalists, who had expected the committees to negotiate, were attacked from the west. The Salvationists went on to attack Shu Jing (see Third Battle of Shu Jing).

Analysis

The coup succeeded because it was planned over eight weeks by a small group and because the committees already held the garrisons' supplies. It failed to secure Caldera, where the Court retained its command. Historians have noted that the committees did not attack the Court's capital, which they could probably have taken, and that this decision, which they attributed to the lack of Royalist agreement, prolonged the war by two years.

Legacy

The Mills have been rebuilt as a museum. The declaration of 11 March, which Ono wrote, is read at the Salvationist memorial on the anniversary. The committees' conduct in the killings was examined by the hearings, which named the members of the Central Salvation Committee.

Historiography

Salvationist accounts present the break as a revolution carried out by soldiers and workers, and the executions as necessary. Royalist histories describe it as a military coup, and the executions as massacres; they note that Kuga Ren was tried for them in 121 AG. Court records describe the committees’ leaders as traitors and give the Court’s losses at about 3,000.

See also

  • Fire Nation Civil War
  • The Black Rail
  • Third Battle of Shu Jing
  • Salvationists

third_battle_of_shu_jing.title: Third Battle of Shu Jing
third_battle_of_shu_jing.html:
Third Battle of Shu Jing
Part ofThe late stage of the Fire Nation Civil War
Date4 December 116 – 18 March 117 AG
LocationShu Jing industrial center
ResultRoyalist victory. The Royalists hold against attacks from both the Salvationists and the Court
Belligerents
Royalists, with Qianchan support
Salvationists (the committees)
Ozai loyalists (the Court)
Commanders and leaders
RoyalistsGeneral Ito Shigeru; Colonel Mori Tatsuo; Zuko
SalvationistsTanaka Kenji (field command)
CourtGeneral Hirata Gensai
Strength
Royalistsabout 100,000
Salvationistsabout 120,000
Courtabout 8,000
Casualties and losses
About 110,000 killed, of whom about 60,000 were civilians

The Third Battle of Shu Jing was the Salvationists’ attack on the Royalist capital in the winter of 116–117 AG, with a smaller Court force attacking from the other side. The Royalists held against both, with the help of Qianchan reinforcements. About 110,000 people died. It is the seventeenth of the war’s twenty defining battles.

The Salvationists attacked the Royalists with the weapons they had captured in 109 AG, and failed to take the city. After the battle the committees’ offensive power was spent.

Background

After the break of March 116, the committees controlled the western belt and the largest army in the war. The Central Salvation Committee decided to attack Shu Jing before the Royalists could consolidate, and to try to destroy the Royalist government. Tanaka Kenji took the field command, and the Court, which could not be sure the committees would not attack it, agreed to a short-term truce and sent a small force to attack the city from the east.

The Royalists had spent the summer rebuilding. Qianchan had increased its supplies, and a division of Qianchan troops had been stationed at Shu Jing since the autumn. Zuko, who had not left the city since 113, remained.

Order of battle

Salvationists (about 120,000). Western and Northern Corps under Tanaka Kenji; Tetsuken battalions; Breaker companies. The last of the Ryuusei-B2 missiles; captured IRB systems.

Court (about 8,000). An armored group of about 4,000 with 60 tanks, two Flame Guard battalions, a four-suit Mk IV special-operations team and about 25 aircraft, sent under the truce. Destroyed within three days of its attack on 10 January.

Royalists (about 100,000). First and Third Armies; Works Guard under Mori Tatsuo; a Qianchan division; Qianchan air-defense units. Anti-aircraft guns, rockets, fortified river line.

Civilians. About 450,000 in the city. About 60,000 left by the northern road in the first weeks.

The Salvationist plan

The Central Salvation Committee met at the Kuroshio works in the last week of March 116 AG, a fortnight after the break, and decided to take Shu Jing before the Royalists could use the summer. Its reasons were military and political. The committees held the western belt and had the largest army in the war, but the army lived on the belt's own stores and the spring harvest was poor, so that it could not wait for a long war of positions. The committee's members also believed that the Royalist government was the only organization in the archipelago that could replace the Court, and that if the capital fell the Royalists' soldiers, who were mostly volunteers, would take off their badges and go home. Tanaka Kenji, who had commanded the committees' First Division at the Second Battle in 113 AG, and who now headed the committee, took the field command himself.

The plan drew on what the committees had learned from the Second Battle. Tanaka would not cross the open plain, where the Royalists' Qianchan air-defense units and long rockets had killed his assault columns in 113 AG. He would come from the west through the suburbs and the canal districts, where the buildings were low and the streets narrow, and where the Royalists' guns could not shoot without hitting the Royalists' own people. The Ryuusei-B2 missiles that remained, which he held back from three earlier opportunities, would open the battle and break the foundries, so that the Royalists would have no more rifles or rockets to produce. Fujiwara Daigo, a former Kern sergeant who had lost a hand in the Hōryū Pass, commanded the Northern Corps, which was to cut the northern road and prevent the city's relief. Ono Sayuri, the committee's political officer, served with the Western Corps, and Kuga Ren, who had been an instructor at the Imperial Research Bureau, commanded the Tetsuken battalions.

The Court was drawn in by the committees' own proposal. Hirata Gensai, who had not been able to count on the committees' loyalty since the break, heard through the Flame Guard that Tanaka meant to turn on the Court as soon as the city fell, and was willing to send a force to the east of the city as the price of a truce. The truce, which the committees and the Court kept for ten weeks, was never signed. Both sides understood it as the postponement of a fight. The Court's force was small because Hirata held back his best formations for the defense of Caldera, and the force that he sent was therefore a mixture of what he could spare: an armored group of about 4,000 men with 60 tanks, two Flame Guard battalions, a special-operations team of four Mk IV suits, and about 25 aircraft.

The Royalist defense

Ito Shigeru, who commanded the defense, had held the city for sixteen years and knew its streets better than the men who built them. His plan rested on the river. The Shu River ran through the city from north to south and the Canal yards lay on its western bank, and Ito's engineers had spent the summer of 116 AG fortifying the eastern bank with concrete positions, cellars joined by tunnels, and mined bridges. The western suburbs and the Canal yards were to be a killing ground, to be held lightly and fought for house by house, and the river line was to be held at all costs. The Royalist army in the city was about 100,000. The First Army, under Lieutenant General Nakajima Ryu, held the north and centre of the line, and the Third Army, under Major General Takeuchi Shiro, which had been rebuilt after the winter of 115 AG, held the south and the bridges. The Works Guard, under Colonel Mori Tatsuo, held the Ironmonger Street line in the centre, where the foundries met the old city, and was about 14,000 strong at the start of the battle.

The Qianchan division, which had landed at the southern docks in October, was about 9,000 men under General Wen Shaoqi. It was a regular infantry division with a battalion of rockets, and Wen, who had taken the post on the understanding that the republic did not wish to be seen to fight the war, kept it for most of the battle in reserve behind the central districts and committed it only at three crises. Its air-defense units, under Colonel Lin Haoran, were more important. Lin had about 60 guns, radar from the republic's 109 AG shipments and a signals network that linked the batteries to the Royalist airfield at Ashigara, and the committees' pilots found over Shu Jing that there was no height at which they could fly in safety. Qianchan's fighters, a squadron of about 20 aircraft on loan to the Royalists, were never at the city but were stationed at the airfield on the coast.

Zuko, who had not left the city since 113 AG, kept an office in the exchange building and was seen at the river bridges every second day through the winter. The soldiers called him the Colonel, since he wore a colonel's coat. He did not command and left the defense to Ito, but his presence, which was what the Royalists had not had in the Second Battle, was one of the reasons that no formation in the city mutinied. The Diet, which sat in the exchange until the end of January, moved to the tunnels under the foundries on 2 February, and the government's records were evacuated for the second time.

The bombardment

The battle began at dawn on 4 December 116 AG, when the Salvationists' remaining Ryuusei-B2 missiles, which Kuga had assembled on three launchers on the high ground west of the city, were fired at the foundries. Six struck within the city's limits and two fell in the river. They killed about 8,000 people in the first week, including about 1,100 workers on the morning shift of the Kaede foundry, where a missile fell on a loading bay, and burned two of the five blast furnaces of the Shu Jing works, which were not relit for a year. The Royalists, who had expected a bombardment and had put their civil defense corps in the shelters in the first days of December, lost fewer people than in 113 AG, but the foundries' output of rifles fell by about a third for the winter. The missiles were fired once. The committees had no more of them, and the three launchers were abandoned in the course of the battle for lack of spares.

The Salvationist artillery, which had better guns than the Royalists', fired on the city for eleven days. It fired on the river bridges and the foundry stacks and on the Royalist batteries in the eastern districts, and the Royalist artillery, whose commanders were under orders not to waste shells, replied sparingly. On 12 December the committees' aircraft, about 70 T-47 fighter-bombers and a handful of B-100 bombers, attacked the Qianchan batteries at the southern docks and lost 17 aircraft. The air attacks were not repeated in force.

The western suburbs and the Canal yards

The Salvationist ground assault began on 6 December. Tanaka's Western Corps advanced from the west in three columns along the canal, the old rail embankment and the road, each led by a battalion of Tetsuken-equipped squads and a company of Breaker armor. The Tetsuken gauntlets and lightning dischargers, which the former Kern infantry used with a skill that astonished the Royalists, were the most effective weapons of the offensive. A squad could clear a cellar by the fire-chain without losing a man, and a Raijin discharger, which burned out in five shots, could stop a tank column in a narrow street. The Royalist rear guards, who had been ordered to hold for as long as they could and then fall back, slowed the advance by blowing the rail embankment and mining the streets, and they did not try to stand. By 11 December the committees held the western suburbs as far as the canal.

The Canal yards, a district of rail sidings and warehouses between the canal and the river, took twelve more days. They were the last ground on the western bank and had been prepared with care. Ito had ordered the yards held by a single Works Guard battalion and a company of the Third Army, which had instructions to fall back to the bridges on the 20th, and the Salvationists, who thought the yards were the Royalists' line, expended about 5,000 men in taking them. They finished taking them on 20 December, the day the Royalists had planned to leave, and the winter put a stop to the advance. The Royalists blew the western bridges on the night of 21 December, with a Salvationist company on one of them.

The Salvationists then held the whole western bank and a front along the canal and the river of about eight kilometres, and the Royalists held the eastern bank. Neither could cross. The committees' engineers tried to build a bridge at the Ropemakers' Ford on 27 December and lost it to the Royalist batteries in an hour, and the Royalists tried to send a company across the ice on 3 January to recover the Canal yards, and lost about 200 men. Both sides settled into the cellars for the winter.

The Court's attack

The Court's force attacked from the east on 10 January, in the middle of a blizzard that grounded the Royalists' aircraft. It was commanded by Colonel Kurosawa Hisaya of the Imperial Guard, who had been told by Hirata to take the Ashigara airfield and the eastern bridges and to wait for the committees to collapse, and who had been told by the Flame Guard's commissar that he was to hold the airfield on his own account if the committees did not. Kurosawa's armored group came down the east road with its tanks in two columns and reached the eastern suburbs by noon. A special-operations team of four Mk IV suits went ahead of them, on a mission to seize the airfield. It was the first time that the Royalists had seen the Mk IV on the Shu Jing front, and the team destroyed the first Royalist line with its guns without being stopped by the Royalists' rockets.

The Court's attack failed because the Royalists did not meet it. Ito, who had known of the truce from a Qianchan intelligence report in December, had put the First Army's reserve division on the east road and mined the road. The tank columns were halted by the mines, and the Third Army's guns, which Ito had been saving, destroyed about 40 tanks on the road in a day. The Mk IV team reached the airfield on the 11th and found the Works Guard's second battalion in the hangars, with Qianchan rockets that Wen had put there on his own initiative. Three of the suits were destroyed in the hangars and the fourth, with its operator wounded, was abandoned at the perimeter. Kurosawa, who withdrew with the survivors of the column, was killed by a rocket at its head on the 12th. By the 13th the Court's force had ceased to exist as a formation, and the Flame Guard battalions surrendered in the eastern suburbs on the 14th. The Third Army took about 1,800 prisoners, and the committees, who had waited for the Court to draw off the Royalists' reserves, learned of its defeat from the radio.

Ironmonger Street

The Salvationists renewed their attack on 25 January, when the river froze. Tanaka crossed the ice at four places on the night of the 24th and 25th with about 20,000 men, and established three bridgeheads in the foundry districts on the eastern bank. The Royalists, who had expected the crossing and whose guns shot up the ice, held two of them to a depth of a few streets and lost the third, at the Ironmonger Street bridge, which the Salvationists took on the 26th and held for five weeks.

The Ironmonger Street line was the centre of the battle. It ran along a street of iron foundries and rope walks, with the old city on one side and the Kaede foundry on the other, and for five weeks the two sides fought over every building on it. The committees' Tetsuken squads took the street's cellars and the Works Guard, which had better knowledge of the buildings, took them back through the sewers. The foundries were cleared floor by floor. Mori Tatsuo, who had held the same street in 107 AG and in 113 AG, commanded it in person from a cellar behind the line, with a field telephone, and sent out the Works Guard's companies by the hour. The Royalists had about 14,000 Works Guard soldiers at the start of the battle and had about 6,000 by the middle of February. Their casualties were so high that Ito brought up two of the First Army's regiments to hold the second line, and Wen's Qianchan division, which had been behind the line, was committed on 8 February at the Kaede foundry, on the flank of the Salvationist penetration, for the first time.

The turning point of the Ironmonger Street fight was on 14 February, when Mori, who had gathered the Works Guard's last reserve and two Qianchan battalions, led a counterattack on the Canal yards' eastern end and retook the district. The counterattack succeeded, and the Salvationists, who had put about 15,000 men into the street, lost it. Mori was killed in the second hour by a Raijin discharge from a window, at the head of the column. He was 47. The street was cleared by the evening and the Works Guard's second-in-command, Captain Sasaki Aiko, took command of it. Mori's body was carried to the exchange building, where Zuko, who had not been in the line since January, kept vigil through the night.

The air war and the winter

The air war was decided by the Qianchan batteries. Lin's guns, firing proximity shells that were new to the war, shot down about 50 Salvationist and Court aircraft in January and February, and the Salvationists, who had set their hopes on the air force that they had taken from the Court, stopped flying by day on 20 February. The committees' only air raids after that were by single night bombers, which did little damage.

The cold was the other decider. The winter of 116–117 AG was the hardest in thirty years, and both armies had hunger and frostbite. The Salvationists, whose supply came across the burned plain of the west by horse sled, had half rations by the middle of February. The Royalists, who had the city's stores and Qianchan convoys on the southern road, had less to complain of, although the Works Guard's companies went hungry. About 6,000 men on both sides died of the cold in the cellars of the western bank. The district kitchens of the committees' zone ran out of flour first, and the civilians in the Salvationist-held districts, who numbered about 30,000, were the worst off. They had been told to leave in December, and many had not.

The end of the attack

The committees tried once more. On 1 March Tanaka, who had been told by the committee that he was to take the bridge by the 15th or hand over the command, attacked the Ironmonger Street bridge for the third time with the Northern Corps, which Fujiwara had brought down from the road. The assault, which was made at night with Tetsuken squads and the last Breaker company, reached the middle of the bridge before being stopped by Sasaki's Works Guard and the Qianchan rockets. About 2,500 Salvationists died in the attack. Tanaka did not renew it, and on 8 March he ordered the Western Corps to prepare a withdrawal. The retreat began on the night of the 17th, and on the 18th the last committee units left the western bank. Ito, who had no strength to pursue, let them go. The Salvationists carried about 9,000 wounded, and left behind about 11,000 dead and about 4,000 prisoners.

Civilian accounts

Nakahara Rei, a rail dispatcher at the Canal yards, wrote letters to her sister in the northern provinces through the winter, and the letters were kept by the sister's family and published in 138 AG. They describe the committees' arrival in the western suburbs, the evenings when the Salvationist and Royalist patrols passed one another in the same street without shooting, and the death of Mori Tatsuo, whose funeral procession she saw on 17 February. "The men who carried him were the same men who had carried the foundry banner," she wrote. "I think half of them were crying and the other half were already asleep on their feet."

Her letters also record the winter. Coal ran short in January and the committees' district kitchens ran out of flour before the Royalists' did. The letter of 3 March is the last, and it says only that the guns had stopped, "and the quiet is worse than the guns."

Aftermath

The Royalists held the city for the third time, and the Salvationists withdrew to the west with the loss of about 11,000 dead on the field and about 4,000 prisoners. The battle ended the committees’ ability to take the offensive in the north. The Royalists, who had lost Mori and about 15,000 soldiers, turned the following summer to destroy the Salvationist field army at the Nagare River (see Battle of Nagare River).

The reckoning in the Salvationist camp

The retreat from the western bank broke the committees' army as an offensive force. It had been the largest army in the war, and by the end of March 117 AG about a third of its soldiers had been killed, wounded or taken, and the rest were hungry, unpaid and unwilling to attack again. The Central Salvation Committee met in the second week of April at the town of Aburaya, in the west, and the meeting lasted six days. Fujiwara Daigo, who blamed Tanaka for the loss of the missiles at the beginning of the battle and for the three assaults on the bridge, demanded his removal. Ono Sayuri, who had been with the Western Corps in the Canal yards, agreed with him. Tanaka kept his seat on the committee by one vote and lost the field command to Fujiwara, who was to meet the Royalists at the Nagare River in June. The committee also decided to send a delegation to the Court, which the Court refused to receive. The Salvationists' veterans, who have argued for fifty years over whether the use of the missiles at Shu Jing was the fatal error, have generally agreed that the committee wasted a fortnight of its only real advantage on the first day of the battle.

The Court's loss

For the Court, the battle was a small but telling disaster. The detachment that Hirata had sent to the east of the city was the Court's last force outside Caldera, and Hirata, who had hoped for a quick victory in the confusion of the committees' assault, found himself with no reserve at the moment that the Royalists and the Salvationists turned to deal with him. The four Mk IV suits, which were one in eight of all that the Court had built, were lost, and the Royalists took the abandoned suit intact to Shu Jing for study. Azula, who had approved the truce and lent the Mk IV team as a pledge of her interest in it, did not reproach Hirata, but she did have Kurosawa's widow brought to the Palace and gave her a pension. The Flame Guard's commissar who had told Kurosawa to hold the airfield on his own account was shot in April, on the grounds of failing to prevent the defeat. The prisoners, who included a number of Imperial Guard officers, were given to Zuko, who held them in the exchange building for four months and released them on parole in July. They did not rejoin the Court.

The Royalist recovery

The Royalists, who had lost about 15,000 soldiers and the Works Guard's best companies, held a funeral for Mori on 17 February, two days after the battle for the Canal yards, and a second, public, funeral on 20 March, two days after the committees' withdrawal. It was the first time that Zuko spoke in public since 113 AG. He said that the dead of the street had been the city's own sons and daughters, and that those of the other side had been the same. The Works Guard, which was reorganised under Sasaki and renamed the Mori Brigade, became the Royalist army's best-known formation, and the Brigade's veterans formed the first of the Royalist veterans' societies.

The city itself, which had lost about 60,000 civilians, took three years to rebuild. The foundries were relit in the autumn, with the first of the replacement blast furnaces coming from Qianchan, and by the summer of 117 AG the rail yards had been cleared of the burned stock. The Canal yards were never rebuilt. They were laid out as a park in 123 AG and their ruined sidings were preserved. The Ironmonger Street bridge was repaired in the winter of 117 AG and the bronze of Mori was raised at its western end in 124 AG.

Legacy

The battle is remembered mainly for the death of Mori Tatsuo, who is the only commander of the war with a monument in all three parties' accounts. A bronze figure of him stands at the Ironmonger Street bridge, and his name is used for the Works Guard's successor organization. The Court's part in it is the shortest passage in any history of the war: its small force was sent in under a truce that no one at the Court had expected to last, and it was destroyed by the Royalists in three days.

For the Salvationists the battle was the end of the northern offensive. The committees turned to the south, where the Royalists were advancing, and fought the Battle of the Nagare River in June. The Central Salvation Committee has been criticized by its own veterans for the decision to spend the last missiles on Shu Jing, which they argue could have been used to hold the south.

Historiography

Royalist histories present the battle as the last attack on the Royalist capital, and name Mori Tatsuo as its hero. Salvationist accounts say that the committees were betrayed by the Court’s failure to attack in time, and by Qianchan’s intervention. Court records do not mention the truce.
