nagare_river.title: Battle of Nagare River
nagare_river.html:
Battle of Nagare River
Part ofThe late stage of the Fire Nation Civil War
Date14–30 June 117 AG
LocationThe Nagare River crossings near Tsurugi Bridge
ResultRoyalist victory. A Salvationist corps is destroyed
Belligerents
RoyalistsSalvationists (the committees)
Commanders and leaders
General Ito Shigeru; Major General Liao Zhen (Qianchan)Tanaka Kenji
Strength
about 85,000about 60,000 (the Western Corps)
Casualties and losses
About 75,000 killed

The Battle of Nagare River was a two-week battle in June 117 AG at the river crossings near Tsurugi Bridge, in which the Royalists destroyed a Salvationist corps. It was the Salvationists’ largest defeat. About 75,000 people died. It is the eighteenth of the war’s twenty defining battles.

The Salvationists lost their best field army, and the Royalists were free to move on Caldera.

Background

After Shu Jing, the committees withdrew to the Nagare River, where they held the crossings between the western belt and Caldera. The Western Corps, about 60,000 strong, was the movement’s best formation, made up of the Fourth Army and the Ryuusei Facility’s garrison. Tanaka held the bridge at Tsurugi, where the mutiny of 111 AG had begun.

Ito, who had been reinforced, proposed to cross the river at three points at once, to trap the corps against the water.

The river line

The Nagare River ran across the western belt from the northern range to the sea. It was about 200 meters wide at the Tsurugi Bridge and could be forded in dry weather at three places. The Salvationists had fortified the west bank over the spring, with a continuous trench system, wire and prepared artillery positions. The river line was about 60 kilometers long, and the Western Corps held it with about 60,000 men, or about 1,000 per kilometer.

Tanaka's plan was to hold the bridge, which could be defended by a small force, and to use the corps' reserve to counterattack any crossing. The plan depended on accurate intelligence of the Royalists' intentions. The Royalists, who had broken the Salvationist cipher in April, knew the plan.

Order of battle

Salvationists (about 60,000). The Western Corps (Fourth Army and Ryuusei garrison divisions); Tetsuken battalions; river guard regiments. Tetsuken lightning dischargers; field guns; little ammunition by late June.

Royalists (about 130,000). First, Second and Third Armies; the armored brigade; Qianchan air group and engineers. Tanks, artillery, pontoon bridges, aircraft.

Civilians. Villages along the river. About 20,000 displaced; about 8,000 killed.

Course

The Royalists crossed on 14 June, at the Tsurugi Bridge and two upstream fords, under cover of artillery and aircraft. The corps, which had been dug in along the west bank, held the bridge for three days, and its Tetsuken lightning dischargers destroyed about 40 of the Royalists’ tanks.

The upstream crossings, which were weakly held, succeeded on 17 June. The Royalists turned south behind the corps and cut its line of retreat on 21 June. For the next nine days the Salvationists, surrounded in a pocket about 20 kilometers wide, held out without food and with little ammunition. Tanaka escaped on the night of 28 June with about 4,000 men. About 25,000 surrendered on 30 June, and about 30,000 were dead.

The pocket

The pocket in which the corps was trapped was about 20 kilometers wide and 30 deep, and lay in the paddy fields between the river and the coastal road. It held the corps' headquarters, the field hospital with about 5,000 wounded, and about 12,000 civilians who had been unable to leave. The corps' commander, Lieutenant General Hayashi Gen, a former Fourth Army divisional commander, organized the defense in concentric rings, and the Royalists, who did not want to storm the pocket, reduced it by artillery and by the cutting of its water.

On the night of 28 June, Tanaka and about 4,000 men broke out to the north, leaving Hayashi in command. The breakout is controversial. Salvationist accounts say that it was ordered by the Committee, to preserve the movement's leadership. Others say that Tanaka left without informing the corps. Hayashi surrendered on 30 June, and was shot in 119 by a cell of the insurgency, after he had testified before the hearings.

Civilian accounts

The pocket is described in the notebook of Dr. Saito Hiroshi, the corps' chief surgeon, which was published in 130 AG. He records that his hospital ran out of anesthetics on 24 June, and that on the last day he and his staff operated on 90 patients. “We had nothing left to give them but our hands,” he writes. After the surrender, the Royalist medical corps took over the hospital, and Saito was permitted to continue his work. He died in 144 AG.

The Royalist plan

Ito's plan, which was drawn up in April, called for a main crossing at Tsurugi Bridge and two secondary crossings at the fords of Nagase and Oyama. The main crossing was intended to hold the Salvationists in place, and the secondary crossings to cut their line of retreat. The Royalists committed about 130,000 men, with an armored brigade, 600 guns and an air group of about 80 aircraft. They also used about 20 pontoon bridges, which were built by engineers at night.

The key to the plan was the knowledge of the Salvationist cipher, which had been broken by the Royalist signals service in April. The signals officers read the Salvationists' orders for the defense, and Ito shifted his crossing points to places that Tanaka had left weakly held. The Salvationists, who did not know that their cipher was broken, did not change their plan.

Notable people

Lieutenant General Hayashi Gen commanded the corps in the pocket, and organized its surrender. He was 49 years old, and had been a divisional commander of the Fourth Army.

Dr. Saito Hiroshi was the corps' chief surgeon. His notebook records the pocket's last week.

The surrender

About 25,000 men surrendered on 30 June. They were marched to a camp at the coastal town of Nagase, where they were held for eight months. The Royalists treated them as prisoners of war, and released about 20,000 of them in the amnesty of 120. Officers of the committees were held separately, and about 300 were tried at the hearings. The camp's record, which lists the prisoners by name, is held by the Royalist archive.

Reception in the sources

The Royalist army's reports and the signals service's records, which were published in 121, are the main sources. The Salvationist account is based on the memoirs of the survivors, of which Saito's is the best known. The Court's records do not mention the battle.

Aftermath

The Salvationists no longer had a field army capable of facing the Royalists. Tanaka withdrew to the western belt, and in August the Royalists reached the outskirts of Caldera. The siege of the capital began in the same month.

Analysis

The destruction of the Western Corps is attributed to the Royalists' superiority in numbers and to the breaking of the Salvationist cipher. Tanaka's decision to hold the river line, and not to withdraw to Caldera, has been criticized as a mistake, because it exposed the corps to encirclement. The Salvationist account that the Court withheld ammunition is supported by the Committee's records, which show that the Court's supply officers had cut deliveries to the committees in the spring, but the records also show that the corps' ammunition stocks were adequate for ten days, and that the shortage was the result of the battle itself.

Legacy

A memorial at the Tsurugi Bridge records the names of the dead of both the mutiny of 111 and the battle of 117. The Salvationists called it their Thermopylae. After the battle, the movement never again held a field army, and its later campaigns were fought by small columns. The river line is now a park.

Historiography

Royalist histories give the Royalist victory to Ito’s planning and the Qianchan troops. Salvationist accounts say that the committees were short of ammunition because the Court had withheld it, and call the battle the movement’s Thermopylae. Court records do not mention it.

See also

  • Fire Nation Civil War
  • Tsurugi Bridge
  • Third Battle of Shu Jing
  • Siege of Caldera

history_of_tajisaki_171_190.title: History of Tajisaki, 171–190 AG
history_of_tajisaki_171_190.html:
This article covers the Kingdom of Tajisaki from 171 to 190 AG. For the country as it stood in 170 AG, see Fire Nation (Kingdom of Tajisaki). For the earlier history, see History of the Fire Nation.

The history of the Kingdom of Tajisaki from 171 to 190 AG is the history of the Fire Nation’s second war in a lifetime. It began with a financial crash and a funeral abroad, and it passed through six years of fear of the left, a ban imposed by the Concord of Nations, a wave of bombings, a snap election and a government of national order, the Earth Empire’s attack of December 180, the loss of the southern islands and the destruction of the capital’s fleet and, in December 182, of the old city of Caldera itself. The country that emerged in 183 was smaller, poorer and more watchful than the one that Zuko’s daughter inherited. By 190 AG it was also, to the surprise of its own politicians, a democracy that had held every election on the appointed day.

The period had four phases. From 171 to 176 the government of Prime Minister Ryoko Sato governed through the shadow of the Earth Kingdom’s collapse and the spread of the leftist uprisings, and came to treat the Union, the left in the Diet, as a danger it could not itself remove. From 176 to 180 the Concord’s ban of the Union and the bombings of 178 broke the left and brought the Reformation government of the National Conservative Party and the Democratic Reform Party to power. From 180 to 182 the kingdom fought for its life. From 183 to 190 it rebuilt, and quarreled about the cost.

Background

The kingdom that Izumi ruled in 170 AG is described at Fire Nation (Kingdom of Tajisaki). Its essential features for this period were four. The House of Representatives had 466 members, and in the election of February 168 the People’s Coalition, a bloc of the Social Democratic Party (SDP), the Democratic Reform Party (written PDP in the Diet’s own records), Agrarian Labor and Civic Progress, had won 236 of them, the first majority of any camp in twenty-seven years. The National Conservative Party, known as the Old Guard or the Way, held 126, and the Union of the Equalist Party, the Salvation Front and the Collective held 82. The Fire Lord had changed in 168, and her father had not been seen in public since 154. The country’s external position rested on the Concord of Nations and on a wary partnership with Qianchan. And its western ports had never recovered the trust of the central government after the Joha Crisis.

The Sato government and the crash (171–172 AG)

The crash of June 171

On 8 June 171 AG, at the founding-day parade in Ba Sing Se, a bomb killed the Earth Queen, Hou-Ting, and her government lost control of the capital within a day. The exchange at Ba Sing Se, which had opened to the public that morning, lost 34 percent of its value in an hour and was closed at 10:40. By nightfall the Caldera Exchange had fallen 17 percent, the Gaoling Exchange 9 percent, and the Republic City Exchange 21 percent, and the Earth Kingdom’s bonds, which about a fifth of the Fire Nation’s banks held, were worth less than half their face value. The Bank of Tajisaki closed the Caldera Exchange for three days, a decision that the Cabinet took without consulting the Diet and that the Old Guard praised and the left condemned. The market recovered about two thirds of its fall within the month, but the banks that had lent against Earth Kingdom grain cargoes did not, and in July three Caldera houses, the Seiko Trust, the House of Aiba and the Yoshitaka Savings, failed. See Market crashes of 153 and 171 AG.

The government’s response, drawn up by Finance Minister Aya Fujimori and announced on 2 July, was the largest relief programme in the kingdom’s history. It guaranteed the deposits of the failed houses, issued 40 billion ryō of bonds, and distributed 9 billion in grain and wage support to the ports, where the Earth Kingdom’s trade had stopped. The funds were disbursed through the provincial administrations, and in four provinces, Yahahama, Umi, Takahama and Shirashihoro, which the Union’s machines controlled, through local relief boards that the Union’s officials ran. The arrangement was practical, since the boards knew the dockworkers, and it turned out to be a political mistake. The Union’s officials were not corrupt in the main, but in the winter of 171–172 the provincial auditors found about 600 million ryō of payments in the four provinces that could not be traced to a recipient. The Union said that the money had been paid in cash to families that had no bank accounts. The auditors’ report was published on 14 December, seven weeks before the election.

Aid to the Royalists

The second consequence of 8 June was the Earth Kingdom’s civil war. Within a week the kingdom had split into the Royalists, who held Ba Sing Se and the east under the Eastern Army and Omashu and the west under King Guan Shikaei’s Western Army, and the revolutionary People’s Republic of Earth, whose Equalists, Harmonists and Collective controlled the river provinces and the northern rail towns. The Fire Nation’s interest was obvious: the Earth Kingdom was its principal source of grain, its border on the Si Wong oil fields and, on the evidence of the Cabinet’s own intelligence reports, the place where a revolution would be most likely to cross the sea. The government’s policy, set by Prime Minister Sato on 20 June and approved by the Diet by 301 votes to 140, was to supply the Royalists, without sending troops.

The Fire Lord’s role was unexpected. Izumi, who had said in her speech of accession that the throne would stand “above the quarrels of the day,” asked on 22 June to be allowed to send the Royalists medical supplies and the stocks of old Hundred Year War firearms that the Tajisaki Royal Navy had held in its depots on the western coast. Her request, which was conveyed by the Grand Chamberlain, had no precedent in the constitution, and the Cabinet’s lawyers advised that it was an expression of wish and not a command. The Cabinet adopted it as policy. Between July 171 and the end of 172 about 90,000 rifles, 400 machine guns and about 2,000 tons of medical stores went to Omashu and Ba Sing Se by sea, in ships that the Navy chartered to avoid the appearance of state action, and the Fire Nation’s ports took in about 380,000 refugees from the Earth Kingdom’s coast. The firearms, most of which were thirty to sixty years old, were less valuable than the signal that the Fire Lord’s authority was behind them. The People’s Republic’s broadcasts, which began that summer, called her “the old empire’s daughter, arming the old empire’s friends.”

The election of 2 February 172

The election of 2 February 172 was held in the shadow of both events. The campaign was dominated by the relief audit and by the rallies carrying the banners of the Earth Kingdom’s revolutionary movements that had begun to appear in the western ports. The Union’s leader, Haruo Sakane, a former dock foreman from Umi who had led the party since 164, told the crowd at his last rally on 30 January that “we are a party of the Diet, not of the barricades.” The Old Guard’s chair, Mitsuko Aramaki, answered at her own rally that voters “can see the same slogans on the same flags, whatever the Union says in Caldera.” The PDP’s leader, Daichi Oyama, said that the vote was “a mandate to restore order in the relief accounts and to keep the Diet away from the street.”

The result was a defeat for the Union. It lost 20 seats and fell to 62, with the Equalist Party at 24, the Salvation Front at 24 and the Collective at 14. Its seats lay almost entirely in the eight core provinces, with Umi and Yahahama returning about half of them. The People’s Coalition gained 20 seats and won 256, with the SDP at 129, the PDP at 68, Agrarian Labor at 45 and Civic Progress at 14, and was able to govern without partners. The Old Guard held its 126, and the independents their 22. Turnout was 72 percent, with about 103.6 million votes cast, two points down from 168. Sato formed her second Cabinet on 9 February, and the Union’s leaders, who had expected a smaller loss, spent the spring arguing about whether to fire their provincial secretaries. They fired three.

Fear and the left (172–176 AG)

The uprisings abroad

The years from 172 to 176 were, for the Fire Nation, a long period of bad news from other places. The Earth Kingdom’s civil war settled into a stalemate in which the Royalists held the ports and the capital, the People’s Republic held the interior and the Western Army held the west. The Water Tribe civil war, which had begun in 170 over Chief Unalaq’s proposal to make Agna Qel’a the capital of both tribes, ended in 174 when the South, which had declared independence as the Southern Federation in 171, won its autonomy, and the old Kingdom of Two Poles was dissolved. The Fire Nation recognized the Southern Federation on 3 August 171, which the Northern chief protested, and its navy sold the Federation eighteen old destroyers on credit in 173. The United Republic, convulsed by the Equalist movement since 170, adopted the Raiko Amendment in 171 and declared the Equalists a terrorist organization, and its police fought them in the streets of Republic City for most of the decade.

The Calderan Scire’s survey of 9 June 174, “Uprisings reach the borders: what the Equalist movements want,” was the first systematic account of the movements’ common program for the Fire Nation’s readers. It found that the movements were not one organization but shared a vocabulary of abolishing hereditary privilege, breaking up landed estates and seating workers’ councils beside national assemblies, and that they differed on method. In the Fire Nation the movement’s reach was narrow. Officials counted 41 rallies in border and port provinces in the first five months of 174, most with fewer than 500 people, and eleven ended in arrests. The government’s briefings to the Diet in the same months noted leaflets at Joha, Takahama and Umi, three seized cargoes of printing type at Port Hana and the arrest of a Qianchan-born Equalist organizer, Yu Lanfen, who was deported in March 175.

The Union under pressure

The Union’s position grew steadily worse. It was the only party in the Diet that shared part of the movements’ language, and the government, under pressure from the Old Guard, began to treat it as connected to them. The ministers asked the Union to condemn the armed groups by name. Sakane’s answer on 9 June 174, that “seats in the Diet are won with ballots, and we are not responsible for what is printed in other countries,” satisfied no one. The party condemned violence in general but named no group, and its caution was read as a refusal. The Old Guard demanded a ban. Aramaki’s statement on 11 June, that “a party that will not choose between the Diet and the street has chosen already,” became the slogan of the campaign for one.

The People’s Coalition was divided. The SDP’s leaders, who had worked with the Union in the unions and the provincial assemblies for thirty years, opposed a ban, and Sato said at a meeting of the Coalition’s council on 2 July that “we do not abolish a quarter of the voters because their cousins are in trouble abroad.” The PDP, which depended on the merchants and bankers who had been hurt by the crash and were frightened by the rallies, wanted action but not a ban, and proposed in October 174 a bill that would have required parties to declare their foreign funds and affiliations. The Agrarian Labor group was split. The bill was carried by 262 to 190 in the House in March 175 and was, on the evidence of the Union’s accounts, obeyed by the Union and ignored by the movements.

The Earth Empire’s shadow

The fear of the left was joined, after 174, by a fear of the right. In the Earth Kingdom, Kuvira, who had risen to be the most powerful of the Royalist commanders, seized power in Ba Sing Se in 174 and renamed the kingdom the Earth State, killing King Shikaei, whom her propaganda said had been murdered by a Fire Nation spy. The Fire Nation’s embassy in Ba Sing Se was closed on 20 February 174, and its diplomats were expelled, and the Earth State began to broadcast to the Fire Nation’s western coast, in the Fire Nation’s own language, a daily programme of denunciation. On 30 November 176 Kuvira declared the Earth Empire. The Fire Nation’s intelligence service, which the Cabinet had reorganized in 173, reported in the summer of 175 that the State had restarted a nuclear weapons project, and in 176 that it was rearming in secret, with materials and plans drawn from Qianchan and from the Fire Nation’s own earlier work. The Cabinet’s reaction was to raise the army’s funding by 11 percent, to extend the Navy’s radar program and to seek, through the Concord, a joint warning system. It did not, until 180, think the Empire would attack.

The Concord’s ban (176 AG)

The last Union election

The election of 2 February 176 was held in this atmosphere. Turnout fell to 69 percent, with about 101.5 million votes cast, and the People’s Coalition gained 22 seats and won 278, with the SDP at 152, the PDP at 70, Agrarian Labor at 44 and Civic Progress at 12. The Old Guard won 128, and the Union fell by 22 to 40, with the Salvation Front at 16, the Equalist Party at 15 and the Collective at 9. Its seats lay in eight provinces, Umi with ten, Yahahama with nine and Kikonokawa with six being the largest groups. Yahahama, Takahama, Shirashihoro and Shinkawa all passed to the People’s Coalition. Independents won 20. It was the Union’s last election.

The ruling of 17 March

The ban came six weeks later, and not from the Diet. The Concord of Nations, meeting in Caldera City in a special session called by the Fire Nation and Qianchan under the consultation provisions of the Caldera Accord of 121 AG, voted on 17 March 176 to ban the Equalist Party, the Collective and the Salvation Front and to order the removal of their forty members from the Diet. The debate lasted four days. The Fire Nation’s delegation, led by Foreign Minister Hayato Mori, argued that the three parties were part of one network, with shared funds and a common leadership that answered to movements abroad, and presented the documents of the Public Security Bureau and the accounts of the Union’s joint secretariat. The Union’s lawyers, who were admitted to the hall but not to the vote, argued that the Concord had no jurisdiction over a member’s political parties and that the Caldera Accord contained no provision for their dissolution. The delegates accepted the first argument. The order named the three parties, barred their officers from standing for any office for twenty years, and froze their accounts pending an inquiry into links with groups abroad.

Sakane’s reaction outside the Diet was the best-known statement of his career: “This is not a ruling against a party; it is a ruling against a quarter of the voters.” He said that the Union would appeal. The Concord’s statutes did not provide for an appeal. The Old Guard and the People’s Coalition welcomed the order. Aramaki called it “the end of a long argument,” and Oyama said that the PDP would “watch every seat the Concord redistributes.” In the Diet’s non-binding motion on 15 March, the Wednesday before the ruling, several Agrarian Labor members voted against the ban and said that they would not oppose the order itself. The Union’s provincial offices in Umi, Yahahama, Takahama and Shirashihoro were sealed on 18 March, and groups of between 200 and 400 people gathered outside each. The Calderan Scire saw no violence at the sites.

The forty seats remained empty until the next general election, which left the House at 426 voting members. The Fire Nation raised its alert level in the border provinces, and the Concord’s forum, which opened in Caldera City on 14 September under the chairmanship of Fire Lord Izumi, adopted its standing charter on 17 September. Twenty-three delegations came and nineteen signed. Article 4 of the charter, which committed members to exchange information on groups that sought to overthrow a member’s order by force, was passed by 19 to 0 with 4 abstentions, after the word “leftist” that the Fire Nation had asked to add was struck. The Earth seat was left vacant. The Earth State’s delegation, led by Kuvira, which had come to claim it, was refused, and King Wu, who had written from exile to ask that it not be given to her, thanked the forum for its decision. Eleven weeks later, on 30 November, Kuvira declared the Earth Empire, and no delegation of hers came to Caldera again.

The bombings and the Reformation government (176–180 AG)

Two years without the Union

The two years that followed the ban were quieter than the government had feared and more dangerous than it knew. The Union’s leaders accepted the order. Sakane announced on 20 March 176 that the parties would dissolve rather than defy the Concord, and the Salvation Front’s congress voted, by a narrow margin, to hand its records to the Public Security Bureau. The party offices were sold or converted. The Bureau’s own assessment in the summer of 177, which was published after the war, was that the legal organization had ceased to exist and that the underground networks, which had existed beside it for years, had been left without the public face that had restrained them.

The Cabinet’s attention was elsewhere. It was occupied by the Concord’s work, by the Empire’s growing menace and by a budget crisis. The government raised the army’s funding again in 177, bought thirty jet fighters from the Tajisaki Institute’s works at Taigan and ordered the Navy’s four new cruisers, which were laid down at Port Hana in 178. It also tried, and failed, to settle the arrears of the ports. The Dockworkers’ Union’s secretary, Haruki Nomura, accepted in the spring of 177 a compromise that would have redeemed about 40 percent of the promissory notes of the reconstruction, and the Diet’s Finance Committee, under pressure from the Old Guard, cut the offer to 25 percent. The unions rejected it. The Joha curfews, which had been lifted in two districts in 175, were reimposed in three in 177.

The day of the capitals

On 12 September 178 AG, within about forty minutes of one another, bombs exploded in Caldera City, Yahahama, Umi and four other cities of the kingdom. At least sixty-one people were killed and several hundred injured. The targets were rail stations, two government depots and the offices of the provincial assembly in Takahama, and the Calderan Scire confirmed damage at all of them. No group claimed responsibility. The attacks were part of a coordinated series that struck capitals and regional cities on every side of the continent on the same day, and the most severe fighting was in the United Republic of Nations, where the bombings were followed by an open declaration of war by the Equalists on the Republic and by strikes on Yu Dao and Republic City. See Equalists declare open war on the United Republic.

The Cabinet met in the early afternoon. It blamed, within hours, “the remnants of the banned parties” and the leftist networks that it said had survived the ban. Sakane denied any link. “We have not held an office, a meeting or a bank account in two years,” he said in a statement on 13 September. Aramaki said that the attacks proved that the ban had been “too late and too narrow,” and Oyama said that the PDP would back any measure that “protects the public and keeps the Diet open.” On 13 September the Cabinet, in the name of the Fire Lord, announced that the House would be dissolved and a general election held in November, outside the traditional date of 2 February, the first such election in the kingdom’s history.

The investigation

The inquiry, which Sato placed under Kenji Hoshiba, the deputy director of the Public Security Bureau, reported on 20 October. Its findings were presented to the Cabinet and to the Diet’s security committee. The bombs had been planted, Hoshiba said, by cells formed from the veterans and descendants of the People’s Earth Union, the movement left over from the first Earth civil war that had gone underground after its defeat, with help from the leftist networks that had survived the ban. Some of the old couriers and depots had never been dismantled. The cells had timed their attacks to match the Equalists’ bombings abroad, and messages recovered in Umi referred to “the day of the capitals” and used the same code words as documents seized in other nations, which pointed to a single plan coordinated across borders.

The inquiry linked the cells to the banned parties through money and housing. Records seized in Umi and Yahahama showed that the accounts frozen by the Concord in March 176 had been emptied weeks before the freeze, and that the funds had passed through shell companies owned by former Union officials. “The ban closed the offices,” Hoshiba said. “It did not close the network.” The courts issued arrest warrants for eleven people. Six were former Union members evicted from the Diet in 176, three were sitting members of the SDP, and two were sitting members of Agrarian Labor. The inquiry alleged that the sitting members had passed committee schedules and security briefings to the cells and had arranged safe houses in their home provinces. The Diet voted on 20 October to lift their immunity, by 301 votes to 63. Seven of the eleven were in custody by election day, and four, among them one of the former Union members, were not.

The election of November 178

The election was held on 18 November, the first in the kingdom’s history without any party of the Union on the ballot and the one with the highest turnout on record, at 85 percent. The result was the largest swing of the postwar period. The National Conservative Party won 214 seats, the PDP 190, together 404 of 466, a margin of 170 over the majority line. The SDP, which had held 152 seats in 176 and whose three members had been named in the warrants and expelled, fell to 14. Agrarian Labor, Civic Progress and the independents shared the remaining 48. Eleven provinces changed hands. Kikonokawa moved from the Union to the Old Guard, Kiyora and Yahafurano from the People’s Coalition to it, and the four provinces of the Union’s old core, Umi, Yahahama, Takahama and Shirashihoro, returned majorities for NCP or PDP candidates, the PDP gaining where the SDP and the Union had been strong and the NCP in the eastern provinces. The campaign was a referendum on order. “The country asked for order, and we are going to deliver it,” Aramaki said on election night.

Sato, who had led the SDP for eleven years and whose own name had not been in the warrants, resigned as Prime Minister on 20 October, the day of the inquiry’s report, and as party leader on 19 November. Her Cabinet continued in a caretaker capacity until the new government was formed. The NCP and the PDP signed a coalition agreement on 6 November, before the vote, that gave each half of the Cabinet. Aramaki became Prime Minister on 26 November, with Oyama as Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister. The government called itself the Reformation government, a name adopted from the title of the agreement, and promised, in Aramaki’s words, to “rebuild the relief accounts, the rail network and the public’s trust, in that order.”

The Reformation government at work (178–180)

The Reformation government’s first two years were taken up with three programs. The first was security. It passed a Public Order Act in January 179 that gave the Public Security Bureau the power to detain suspects for 30 days without charge and made membership in a banned organization an offense punishable by ten years’ imprisonment. The act was carried by 391 votes to 40, and the SDP, which had only fourteen members, abstained. The second was the audit. A new Office of Relief Accounts, which Oyama created in December 178, investigated the provincial boards that had run the crash relief and recovered about 320 million ryō. The third was the Navy. The government accelerated the cruiser program, voted a supplementary budget for coastal defense in 179 and, on the Navy’s advice, began to build the radar line that was completed in January 181.

The government also made the first attempt to settle the Joha arrears. Aramaki’s offer of 11 March 179, to redeem the promissory notes of the reconstruction at 60 percent in exchange for the Dockworkers’ Union’s acceptance of a no-strike agreement of ten years, was accepted by the union’s council on 2 May by 31 votes to 24. It was the first agreement on the arrears in thirty years, and the Joha curfews were lifted on 1 July 179 for the first time since December 153. It lasted fourteen months.

The Empire’s approach

The most important fact of 179 and 180 was the one the Cabinet understood least. The Earth Empire, which had spent three years rearming in secret with materials and plans drawn from Qianchan technology and from the Fire Nation’s own earlier work, had by 180 the largest air force on the continent, an unknown quantity of the old Sōen arrays and a doctrine that placed the surprise attack above the war that followed it. The Fire Nation’s intelligence service had warned in 178 that the Empire was assembling long-range bombers. Its warnings were read in the Cabinet as the expression of the Navy’s appetite for money, and the Diet voted the coastal defense budget in 179 without the funds for the early-warning aircraft that the intelligence service had requested. The omission was to cost the Tajisaki Royal Navy its gulf squadron.

The Fire Lord’s role in these years was largely ceremonial and, on one occasion, not. On 14 March 180 Izumi received the Earth Empire’s ambassador, a general of Kuvira’s staff, at the Palace in a ceremony she had been advised to avoid, and told him, in the hearing of the Grand Chamberlain, that “the Fire Nation has learned what an empire costs, and will pay it again if it must.” The sentence was printed in the Calderan Scire and read in the Empire as a threat. It was the only public statement by a Fire Lord on a foreign government since the abdication.

The war (180–182 AG)

The declaration

The Earth Empire declared war on the United Republic of Nations on 2 December 180 AG, after two staged attacks on its western bases on 30 November and 1 December, which Marshal Xinan, Kuvira’s chief of staff, blamed on the Republic. The Republic declared war on 4 December. The Fire Nation was brought in by the same method. On 23 December Zaofu Iron Guard troops were reported ambushed on the Imperial border, and on 24 December the Empire struck Qianchan’s eastern coast and on 25 December the Zaofu–Omashu frontier. The Cabinet met in the Palace at six in the morning on 25 December and declared war the same day, by unanimous vote of the Cabinet and by 413 votes to 9 in the House, with Qianchan. The Concord of Nations, which had condemned the Empire, imposed sanctions and expelled it from membership by January 181, did not declare war. It formed a staff council in Caldera City to coordinate the allied armies, and its relief agency opened offices in the Fire Nation’s five largest ports.

The Fire Nation’s position in December 180 was worse than the Cabinet’s speeches admitted. The Navy had about 140 warships, the largest fleet on the continent, but it had no carrier and no escorts that could survive an attack by the Empire’s long-range bombers. The Air Service, which had the jets of the Tajisaki Institute’s works at Taigan, had not been told that the bombers could fly at three times the speed of sound. The radar line along the western coast was incomplete. The Army, whose twelve divisions were in the west and north, had no plan for a war in the south. The Tajisaki Royal Air Force joined the allied squadrons only in January 181, when the first jets reached the Republic’s airfields.

The Night of No Sirens

The Empire’s first strike on the Fire Nation came on the night of 2 February 181. A carrier, the CL1201, which had been hidden in the Si Wong Desert, launched three B70 bombers and twelve fighters, which flew a Mach 3 route over the mountains and the gulf and fired cruise missiles from beyond the capital’s defenses. The raiders reached Caldera City before any alarm sounded and struck the naval yards, the arsenal and the rail junction. The Palace district was not touched. At dawn the same bombers sank four cruisers and nine destroyers of the Tajisaki Royal Navy’s gulf squadron, which had put to sea to cover the yards. They killed about 3,100 sailors and about 640 civilians, and no Imperial aircraft was lost. The fleet air cover was not in the air, and the gunners of the cruisers, which were anchored off Cape Ryujin, fired at the sound. The allied staff first learned that the carrier existed from a caravan guide who had seen it in the desert on 30 January, three days before the strike.

The Diet passed emergency funds on 5 February, by 454 votes to 3. The Fire Nation’s press named the raid the Night of No Sirens, because the first sirens sounded after the first bombs. It was one of three strikes on the allied capitals, which hit Republic City on 16 February and Gaoling on 4 March. In each case the seat of government was spared, and the allies, who noted this, understood it as a warning. See Raid on Caldera City and Capital bombing campaign.

The raid’s political consequences were immediate. Aramaki told the Diet on 7 February that the intelligence service’s warnings of 178 had “been read as what they were, a request for money, and I was wrong to read them so.” She offered her resignation, which the Cabinet refused. The Navy’s commander-in-chief, Admiral Itsuki Ohara, was relieved on 12 February and replaced by Vice Admiral Naoko Shirane, the first woman to hold the post, and the Defense Staff was instructed to prepare the evacuation of the old city. By the end of February about 1.4 million people had left Caldera City for the interior. The National Service Act of 3 March 181, which restored conscription for men and women aged 18 to 30 for the duration of the war, was passed by 389 votes to 36, the first such act since 122, and the first Fire Nation conscripts reported in April.

The loss of the southern islands

The Empire’s invasion of the Fire Nation’s southern island chain began in April 181. The chain, an arc of about two hundred islands 300 to 900 kilometers south of the main islands, held the provinces of Shirashihoro, Hatsushima, Hoshima and Yahafurano and about 12 million people, and it had been garrisoned by two divisions, the 9th and 11th, and by the coast artillery of the Navy’s southern district. The Empire, which had air superiority over the islands from February and which landed from transports of its own and from fishing fleets requisitioned in the Sand Sea, took Shirashihoro first, on 14 April, and then the other provinces, in a campaign that lasted until December. The garrison commander in Hatsushima, Major General Eiji Kamimura, held the island of Hatsushima, the province’s capital, for 38 days with 7,000 men. By December the Empire held the whole chain. The Tajisaki Royal Navy, which had lost its gulf squadron and most of its trained cruiser crews, was able only to evacuate about 900,000 civilians in the first month and to sink a number of the Imperial transports.

The occupation lasted eight months and was brutal. The Empire’s administration, which was led by a Governor-General from Marshal Xinan’s staff, General Hu Tianming, with about 90,000 troops, treated the islands as a source of labor and as a base for the bombers that struck the main islands from July. It conscripted about 600,000 islanders for forced labor on airfields and fortifications, requisitioned the rice harvest and imposed a curfew on all towns. The Fire Nation’s later inquiry estimated that about 140,000 people died in the occupation, most of them of hunger and in labor camps, and that about 11,000 were executed, among them the officials, teachers and union leaders whom the Empire’s security police arrested in the first week.

The resistance was drawn from the islands’ old traditions. The southern provinces, the Union’s strongholds in Shirashihoro and Hatsushima, had a tradition of committees dating from the civil war, and the committees’ veterans, who had been told for forty years that they were the heirs of a defeated tendency, became the core of the islands’ guerrillas. The Hatsushima Sea Brigade, which had about 3,000 fighters under a former dock foreman, Tora Ibaragi, sank a number of Imperial transports in the winter of 181 with mines and fishing boats, and the Shirashihoro Committee, which assembled in October in a cave on the island of Oshiro, published a clandestine newspaper that was read by the main island’s radio listeners. The irony of the Union’s old cadres fighting the Empire in the name of the Fire Nation was noticed in Caldera. It was not, at the time, discussed.

The war at home

The Fire Nation’s main islands were at war from April 181 to December 182, and the war was in the air. Imperial bombers, which operated from bases in the Si Wong and, from the summer of 181, from the captured islands, struck the ports of Port Hana, Harbor Kuro and Shinja, the shipyards, the rail junctions and the oil refineries on the western coast in raids of ten to thirty aircraft. The allies’ interceptors, which became available in the spring of 182, brought down about one raider in six. The raids killed about 28,000 people in 181 and about 41,000 in 182, according to the inquiry, and the Fire Nation’s industries, which had been converted to war work in a year, produced about 3,400 aircraft, 31 warships and about 900 tanks in the war’s two years. Rations were introduced in June 181, and the Cabinet’s control of the grain trade, which Oyama described as “the worst necessary thing I have done,” was extended to cover the Earth Kingdom’s imports. The Concord’s relief agency, which had been established in 121, distributed about 700,000 tons of grain.

The election of 2 February 182 was held on schedule, by a decision of the Diet that Aramaki defended as “the only answer the Empire does not expect.” It was held under bombing in the western ports and without the islands, whose voters, many of them refugees, voted in the camps on the main islands, and in the islands themselves by a clandestine ballot that the committees organized and carried out of the islands by boat. The NCP won 210 seats and the PDP 196, together 406, and the SDP fell to 12, Civic Progress to 8 and Agrarian Labor to 6. Thirty-four independents were elected, the highest number since 130. Turnout fell to 66 percent, with about 100.3 million votes cast. The Reformation government continued, with the same ministers and the same programme.

The war’s politics were quiet. The government’s critics, who included Sato’s successor as SDP leader, Kenji Ishizuka, argued that the National Service Act should have been repealed in 182 and that the Public Order Act’s detentions, which reached about 11,000 in the war’s two years, had swept in union officials, journalists and, in a few cases, the families of Empire’s victims. They were not heard widely. The Diet’s inquiry into the Mutsukawa hospital attack of January 181 had reported that the guard had been too thin for a patient of that rank. See Zuko.

The December strikes

The Empire’s army broke up in December. News that Kuvira had died on 4 September, killed by the Avatar, Korra, and that the Xinan command had hidden her death and was issuing orders in her name, reached the western coast in early December. The garrisons there mutinied, the north revolted, and the Empire withdrew from the Fire Nation’s southern islands in a retreat that the Tajisaki Royal Navy, which had been rebuilt to about forty ships, was unable to oppose. The Xinan command, which had lost the army and kept the atomic units and the CL1201, decided to end the war by striking everywhere it could reach. See Collapse of the Imperial command and Strikes of December 182 AG.

The Empire’s strikes on the Fire Nation’s allies came first. An atomic bomb burst over Yu Dao on 19 December, killing about 420,000, and on 20 December atomic weapons burst over Zaofu and Gaoling. On 21 December, at about four in the afternoon, a missile fired from the Si Wong, a ballistic missile of 1.2 megatons, burst in the air over the old city district of Caldera City at a height of about 2,000 meters. The old district, the densest quarter of the city, and its government buildings were wiped off the map. About 650,000 people were killed, most of them in the first minute. The Palace was destroyed. Fire Lord Izumi, who had been evacuated from the Palace to the shelter of the old naval tunnels at Cape Ryujin eleven days earlier on the advice of the Defense Staff, which had read the intelligence service’s warning of the strikes on the allies, was unharmed, as were the Crown Prince and her husband. The Cabinet, which was sitting in session at Shinja, was also unharmed. The Diet’s hall, which had been closed in October for the dispersal of its records, was destroyed.

The Fire Nation’s response was shaped by the news from Qianchan and the western coast. Izumi’s broadcast from Shinja at midnight on 22 December, which was heard by about 80 million people, did not mention the Empire. “Caldera is not the Fire Nation,” she said. “The Fire Nation is the people who are listening to this.” The Cabinet ordered the Tajisaki Royal Navy to hold fire, and the Concord’s staff council, which had met in Caldera City until 19 December and then moved to Shinja, took up the mediation that failed on 24 December. The war ended informally on 31 December. The Earth Republic was proclaimed the same day, and the island chain, which had been abandoned in the Empire’s withdrawal, was reoccupied by the Tajisaki Royal Navy’s marines in the first week of January 183.

Reconstruction and reckoning (183–186 AG)

The new capital

The Fire Nation entered 183 with a destroyed capital, a ruined fleet, a reoccupied island chain and a government that sat in a provincial city. Shinja, which became the provisional seat of the Cabinet and the Diet on 1 January, is a port city of about six million on the northern coast, and its civic buildings housed the ministries in a rotation of three shifts until the new quarters were finished in 186. The Fire Lord and her family lived in the governor’s residence. The old district of Caldera City, which the Defense Staff’s radiation teams declared a restricted zone, was fenced off, and about 2.3 million survivors of the city’s outer districts, which had been shaken and burned but not destroyed, were returned to them in stages between March 183 and 185. The reconstruction of the capital, which the Diet voted to build on the western side of the bay, at a distance from the old district, began in 184 under the Caldera Reconstruction Authority and was in 190 about two thirds complete.

The cost of the war was counted for years. The Fire Nation’s inquiry, which reported in 185, put the dead of the two years at about 1.35 million, of whom about 650,000 died in Caldera, about 140,000 in the occupation of the islands, about 69,000 in the bombing of the western ports, about 31,000 in the fighting and in the Navy, and the rest in the ensuing fallout, famine and disease. About 1.9 million people were wounded and about 3.5 million were homeless. The Tajisaki Royal Navy had lost about 90 warships. The economy, which had contracted by about 14 percent in 181 and 182, recovered to its 170 level by 188.

The death of Zuko

Zuko had spent his last years in seclusion with a long illness. On the night of 3 January 181 an ambulance carrying him from a hospital in Mutsukawa, the old central district of Caldera City, after a bomb in the car park, was destroyed by a second bomb on the highway. Princess Kiko announced his death on 4 January. The funeral, held in Shinja on 15 January with 400,000 people on the streets, was the largest in the kingdom's history. The physicians' report, published on 30 January, recorded that the former Fire Lord had suffered from a wasting condition of the lungs for thirty years and found that the bomb, not the disease, had killed him. The Public Security Bureau blamed Imperial agents, and the Diet's inquiry into the failure of the hospital guard sat in March 181.

The Commission on the Defense of Caldera

The second reckoning was political. The Commission on the Defense of Caldera, which the Diet appointed in March 183 under Justice Ren Okabe of the Supreme Court, held public hearings for fourteen months and reported on 12 November 184. Its findings were severe. It found that the intelligence service had warned of the Empire’s bombers in 178 and that the warnings had been discounted, that the Cabinet had refused in 179 to fund the early-warning aircraft that the Navy had asked for, and that the evacuation of the old city had been delayed for twelve days by a dispute between the Defense Staff and the Ministry of the Interior over who should give the order. It also found that the Palace had been warned of the missile strike on the allies’ cities on 19 December and that the evacuation of the Fire Lord on 10 December had been ordered on the strength of a Qianchan intelligence report, not the Fire Nation’s own. The Commission’s recommendations included a new alert system, a ministry of civil defense and the permanent seating of the Tajisaki Royal Navy’s radar service in the Defense Staff.

Aramaki, who had said in 181 that the failure was hers, resigned on 20 November, the day after the report was published. The NCP chose as its new chair the former Foreign Minister, Sora Hamada, and the coalition agreed that Oyama would become Prime Minister. Oyama’s government, which was formed on 28 November, kept the Reformation government’s name and most of its Cabinet. Its first act was the Civil Defense Act of December 184, which created the ministry and an alert system of sirens, radios and shelters in the twenty largest cities.

The archive and the left

A third reckoning was slower and more unsettling. In the summer of 184 the allied forces that entered Ba Sing Se found the Earth Empire’s intelligence archive, and among its papers a file that the Fire Nation’s officials read only in 185. It was a record of the Empire’s intelligence section’s operations in the Fire Nation from 175 to 180. It showed that the Empire had funded and equipped the cells of the People’s Earth Union remnants that had set off the bombs of 12 September 178, that two of its agents had been placed in the Union’s Umi secretariat in 176, and that the Empire’s purpose had been to provoke the ban of the left, to bring a government of the right to power in Caldera and so to divide the allies. The file named, among the Fire Nation’s politicians, none. It did say that the party offices’ sealing in 176 and the election of 178 “fulfilled the intended purpose of the operation.”

The Cabinet withheld the file for a year, and it was published on 14 June 186 by the Diet’s Committee on Security, over the government’s objection, by 233 votes to 175. The revelation did not rehabilitate the Union, whose ban remained, and the Concord, which considered the file, did not revise its ruling. It did change the politics of the left. The SDP’s new leader, Kenji Ishizuka, argued that “the ban we welcomed was written in another country’s office,” and the party’s numbers began, slowly, to recover. The Union’s remaining leaders, among them Sakane, who had retired to Umi, were not touched. Sakane died in 187.

The election of 186

The election of 2 February 186 was the last held under the old party names, which the Party Registration Act of 187 altered, though the press kept the abbreviations. The NCP won 205 seats, the PDP 197, and the SDP 12, Civic Progress 8 and Agrarian Labor 6. Thirty-eight independents were elected. Turnout fell to 62 percent, with about 96.3 million votes cast, the lowest in the archive, a result that the political scientists of the Academy of Caldera attributed to “exhaustion.” The Reformation government continued under Oyama. No province changed hands.

The politics of memory (186–190 AG)

The Earth Union and the Xinan Dominion

The world that emerged from the war was divided into the successors of the Empire. The Earth Republic, proclaimed on 31 December 182 by the revolting army, merged in 184 with the free cities and the Si Wong confederation into the Earth Union, which the Fire Nation recognized on 3 April 184. The Xinan Dominion, which held the Earth Kingdom’s eastern heartland from Ba Sing Se and the Empire’s remaining bases in the Si Wong, did not. The Fire Nation had no relations with it. The Dominion’s capital, its leadership and the extent of its holdings were unknown to the Fire Nation’s intelligence service, which reported in 188 that the Dominion had reassembled about 30 atomic weapons from the Empire’s stocks and that it kept the CL1201 flying. See Xinan Dominion.

The National Alliance

The politics of the later 180s was dominated by a new current. The National Alliance, which was registered on 14 March 188, was founded by Natsume Sakura, a former Defense Staff officer who had become a radio commentator during the war and whose nightly broadcast, The Wall at the Door, was heard by about thirty million people. Its program had five points: a deterrent, which meant the abandonment of the Concord’s non-nuclear protocol; conscription in peacetime; a permanent ban on the left, written into the constitution; the sealing of the ports to refugees; and the abolition of the Concord’s powers over the Diet. The party’s supporters were drawn from the NCP’s right wing, from the veterans of the war and from the families of Caldera’s dead. The Old Guard, whose leader Hamada had been a member of the Concord’s delegation, did not know whether to oppose it or to absorb it.

The SDP’s recovery, which began in 186, was the other current. It drew on the memory of the islanders. The returning guerrillas of the Hatsushima Sea Brigade and the Shirashihoro Committee, who had fought for their islands under the red flag of the committees, were honored in the Diet in 185 in the first official acknowledgment of the committees’ role in the nation’s defense, and the SDP, which Ishizuka led, was the only party that supported a pension for the islanders. The Union’s ban was not touched. The SDP’s success in the south, which extended in 190 to Umi, Yahahama and Takahama, was a vote for a party that had opposed the ban and been right about the left, and not for the Union’s return.

The northern pole and the Earth Union City strike

Two events from outside the kingdom marked the last years of the decade. On the night of 20 December 189, the Northern Water Tribe’s capital, Agna Qel’a, saw 37 minutes of unexplained light and a magnetic surge that the Qianchan Meteorological Institute logged as nine pulses at four-minute intervals. The Tajisaki Institute’s seismologists recorded the pulses at the instruments on the southern chain, and the Fire Sages’ Great Sage said that “the spirits have spoken in the north.” The Fire Nation made no statement. The Avatar’s discovery of spirit energy, which she kept secret, is not a subject of the Fire Nation’s official record. See Northern pole disturbance of 189 AG.

At 7:42 in the morning on 18 October 190, the Xinan Dominion destroyed Earth Union City, in the Si Wong, with an atomic weapon of about 36 kilotons. The Dominion’s defense ministry announced the strike on state radio as a lawful act against an “illegal occupation” of its oil fields. The Concord met in emergency session the following day, and its relief agency counted 112,000 dead and 70,000 missing. The Fire Nation, whose oil comes from the Si Wong under the Si Wong Accord, received the news with particular alarm. Oyama’s Cabinet met in Shinja on 19 October and ordered the closing of the Fire Nation’s airspace to Xinan aircraft, the suspension of all fuel and grain sales to the Dominion, which were small, and the sending of two Tajisaki Royal Navy hospital ships and four transports with 6,000 tons of relief to the Earth Union’s northern ports. The Fire Nation accepted about 40,000 refugees. Izumi’s statement on 20 October, which was read in the Diet, said only that “the Fire Nation knows what this was.” The Concord’s emergency session was the first since 182. See Strike on Earth Union City.

The election of 190

The election of 2 February 190 was the first held after the Party Registration Act, and the first in which the National Alliance stood. The result was a hung House. The NCP won 168 seats, down 37, the PDP 150, down 47, the SDP 45, up 33, and the National Alliance, which won a few distinct strongholds in the west and north, 38. Agrarian Labor won 14, Civic Progress 12 and independents 39, among them Tora Ibaragi of Hatsushima, the sea brigade’s commander, who was elected with the highest personal vote in his province. Turnout rose to 66 percent, with about 104.7 million votes cast. The NCP led in the west and north, the PDP in the center and the east, and the SDP in the south. The press first reported that the People’s Coalition, which had shed the old names, held 246 seats, a figure that included the independents it had counted in 186. The correct figure was 221, thirteen short of the 234 that a majority required.

The coalition that followed took six weeks to form. The NCP and the PDP, which together held 318 seats, would have continued the Reformation government, and the Old Guard’s leaders pressed for it. Oyama, whose party had lost a quarter of its seats and who regarded the National Alliance’s rise as a rebuke to the arrangement he had led, refused. On 15 March he formed a Cabinet of the PDP, the SDP, Agrarian Labor and Civic Progress, with the support of 22 independents, which commanded 243 seats. It was the first government since 178 without the Old Guard, and the first in which the SDP had held office since the fall of Sato. The Old Guard and the National Alliance formed the opposition together, which, with 206 seats, was the largest ever.

Society and economy, 171–190 AG

Population and cities

The Fire Nation’s population, about 214 million in 170 AG, fell by about 1.35 million in the war and by about 3 million more through the emigration and the births that were not conceived, and recovered to about 211 million by the census of 188, helped by about 2.1 million immigrants and refugees from the Earth Kingdom and the Earth Union. The island chain’s population fell from about 12 million to about 10.6 million and has not recovered. The country’s cities were reshuffled: Caldera City’s proper population, 8 million in 170, was about 5.1 million in 190, and Shinja, which took the largest share of the capital’s refugees, grew to about 9 million. Harbor Kuro and Port Hana, rebuilt after the bombing, are in 190 among the most modern ports in the world.

The economy

The kingdom’s output, which contracted by about 14 percent between 180 and 182, recovered by 188, and its structure changed. The war industries, which had been converted to war work in 181 and kept at scale under the Reformation governments, produced in 190 about 38 percent of the country’s manufacturing output, from aircraft and radar sets to shipbuilding and electronics. The reconstruction of Caldera City, which the Diet funded through a ten-year reconstruction bond, accounted for about 4 percent of output a year from 185 to 189. The public debt, which had stood at about 38 percent of output in 170, rose to about 96 percent by 184 and fell to 71 percent by 190. The Si Wong Accord, which had made oil the kingdom’s principal strategic dependence, was renegotiated in 186 and again in 188, and in 190 the Cabinet’s suspension of sales to the Dominion put its own supply, about 60 percent of liquid fuel, under strain for the first time since 100. The volcanic and fission programs, which the Cabinet expanded in 187, supplied by 190 about 52 percent of the country’s electricity.

The arrears of the ports were never fully settled. The Joha agreement of 179, which lasted fourteen months, was broken in September 180 when the Dockworkers’ Union struck over the first wartime pay cuts, and was not repeated. The Joha curfews, lifted in July 179, were reimposed in the autumn of 180 and again, in two districts, in 189. The islands’ pension, which the SDP proposed in 185 and the Diet passed, in a reduced form, in 187, was the only redistributive measure of the decade.

Security and the armed forces

The armed forces, which had been about 420,000 strong in 170, numbered about 1.4 million at the end of 182 and about 640,000 in 190, a figure that includes about 90,000 conscripts. The National Service Act of 181, which was extended each year until 184 and then reduced to a six-month term for those between 18 and 22, remained on the books in 190, and was a subject of the 190 election. The Tajisaki Royal Navy was rebuilt around eight new cruisers and, for the first time since the Empire, two carriers, the Hakuryu and the Ryujin, laid down in 184 and 186. The Defense Staff, under the Civil Defense Act, was given control of the alert system, and the Public Security Bureau, under the Public Order Act, which was renewed every two years until 189 and then allowed to lapse by the Diet, was the principal organ of internal security. The kingdom had no nuclear weapons in 190 and had signed the Concord’s protocol against them, a position that the National Alliance wished to overturn and that the Cabinet, with the support of the SDP and the Civic Progress Party, refused to.

The kingdom in 190 AG

In October 190 the Kingdom of Tajisaki was governed by Fire Lord Izumi, aged about sixty-nine, and Prime Minister Daichi Oyama of the PDP, whose Cabinet of the PDP, the SDP, Agrarian Labor and Civic Progress held 243 of 466 seats with the help of the independents. The Crown Prince was Iroh, and the Fire Lord’s younger daughter, Kiko, who had married Kei Seinaka in 175, was the country’s best-selling singer and, since the war, the host of a monthly radio program on which survivors of Caldera read the names of the dead. The provisional capital was Shinja, and the new capital at Caldera was two thirds finished. The House of Lords, which had been at Caldera and was destroyed with it, met in the Shinja Assembly Hall.

The Union remained banned. The National Alliance, the Old Guard and the PDP disagreed about almost everything except the Dominion, which all three regarded as the principal threat. Relations with Qianchan, which had suffered the destruction of Gaoling and Zaofu, were the warmest of the kingdom’s history. Relations with the United Republic, whose capital had fallen and whose government had been driven from Yu Dao by the same strikes, were those of two countries that had lost cities to the same enemy. The Earth Union was a friend, the Southern Federation an ally and the Kingdom of Agna Qel’a a neighbor with which there was no quarrel. The Concord of Nations, which met in Shinja at the time of the strike on Earth Union City, was the main instrument of the kingdom’s foreign policy.

Historiography

The Fire Nation’s writing on the period divides along the line of the Union’s ban. The official histories of the Reformation government, among them the Cabinet Office’s The Two Wars, which Oyama commissioned in 185, treat the ban as a necessary step in the defense of the realm, the bombings of 178 as the work of the underground and the war as the consequence of the Empire’s ambition. The historians of the left, among them Itsuki Namiko of the Academy of Caldera, whose The Closed Door was published in 187, argue that the ban was a mistake, that the Empire’s file shows that the bombings were provoked and that the Cabinet’s sealing of the party offices made the Union’s members into the enemy that the Empire wanted. Historians of the right, among them Taro Mizushima, answer that the Empire’s file shows only that the Empire was a clever enemy, that the cells existed and that the Concord’s ban was lawful.

The war’s memory is divided differently. The Night of No Sirens is remembered as the failure of the state, and the survivors of the old city, who gather each year on 21 December at the fenced edge of the restricted zone, as the nation’s principal mourners. The islanders’ memory, which was not acknowledged officially until 185, is of an occupation that the mainland ignored. The Caldera Memorial, a field of 650,000 small stones in the bay’s western park, was dedicated on 21 December 189 by the Fire Lord, who read out the names of the first hundred. The reading took four hours.

ee_concord_war_opening_180.title: Opening phase of the Earth Empire–Concord War
ee_concord_war_opening_180.html:
Opening phase of the Earth Empire–Concord War
Period2 December 180 AG to early January 181 AG
TheatresZaofu and the Foggy Swamp; Qianchan; the eastern United Republic (Yanakawa, Tawaraza and the two straits); Mutsukawa (Caldera City); Republic City; Lake Laogai
BelligerentsEarth Empire, against the United Republic of Nations, Qianchan and the Kingdom of Tajisaki
LeadersEmpress Kuvira; Fire Lord Izumi, President Zhu Li and President Haatao
Notable eventsBombing of Zaofu and death of Suyin Beifong (24 December 180); the allied declarations and alliance (25 December); the Mutsukawa hospital attack and death of Zuko (3 January 181); the Kuchuya scroll
StatusBlended with the draft novel To the East; see "Reconciliation with the main article"

The opening phase of the Earth Empire–Concord War covers the first weeks of the war, from the declaration of 2 December 180 AG to the death of Zuko in January 181 AG. It is drawn from the draft novel To the East and fitted to the main article's dates. It follows Empress Kuvira's war cabinet, the western allies' emergency governments, and the Avatar's party as they move from Republic City to the Fire Nation and then to the Qianchan coast. The dates of the novel have been moved to those of the main article, Earth Empire–Concord War, and the points where the two accounts differ are listed at the end.

Background

The Empire declared the war on 2 December 180 AG in a speech from the square at Ba Sing Se. Kuvira invoked Emperor Chin the Great and said the Avatar had killed his heir and left an empire without one to collapse. She declared war on the remnants of the old Earth Kingdom, the western nations and the Avatar. She named the United Republic a puppet of the Kingdom of Tajisaki and the Federal Republic traitors occupying the west coast near Omashu. She promised to answer Tajisaki's naval supremacy with numbers and battleships. Her soldiers answered with a raised right arm and bent wrist and the chant "Hail Kuvira!"

In the weeks after the declaration Kuvira sent an ultimatum to Republic City, claiming a uranium-235 weapon and giving the city until noon of the following day. It lapsed without a strike on the city, whose first raid came on 16 February 181. President Zhu Li answered it by mobilising the reserves. The Tajisaki Royal Navy sent Crown Prince Vice Admiral Iroh to coordinate the Republic's naval defence. Recalled Army-General Bumi took the Centre Army Group and Army-General Uzu the East Army Group, with Defence Secretary Kirvik in the cabinet and the exiled King Wu in the city. Some of the Tajisaki scientists who had once refused Ozai's bomb order had been shot and the rest had fled to the Federal Republic, which the allies later saw as the source of the Empire's expertise.

The Empire's war cabinet

The Empire's war room lay in a secret underground complex in the Forbidden City, rebuilt after the second siege of Ba Sing Se in the green and brown of the new regime. A large wall map showed the Empire's forces and targets, and a round metal table carried the controls from which the Empress and her generals ran the war. Its generals reported to Kuvira in turn at the height of the western offensive of late December.

The southern commander reported that Zaofu had been levelled: about 40 per cent of its structures were gone, but the metal domes held and the defenders were trapped inside them. He asked for more firepower or earthbenders to breach them. The air commander reported that the Federal capital, Qianchan, was about half wrecked, with its airbases, airports and factories out of commission. The south-eastern commander reported the capture of Xiandong, Tengcheng and Shinzui with few losses. Kuvira named the Foggy Swamp and Zaofu region the key to the south and ordered the domes broken and the city taken.

Against the United Republic the Empire had taken the two straits that joined its territory by air superiority, and had sunk ten ships of the Tajisaki Royal Navy and the Republic's navy in a few hours. Its staff did not know whether the heavy traffic in the Yasato Sea, with civilian cargo ships halted in Republic and Tajisaki ports, meant a counter-attack or a blockade. On the ground, paratroops, amphibious landings and earthbending assaults had taken cities in eastern Yanakawa at a medium cost.

Atomic weapons

The Empire's staff reported a test of an atomic device in the remote Si Wong Desert, and said the yield and radiation matched its predictions. The generals claimed five bombs in storage and hoped for twenty within the month. The allies treated the claim as a threat, and the main article records that the device tested was a small one and that the first real strikes came only in late 182 AG, after the larger test of the autumn of 181. Some aircraft and ships were fitted with bomb racks and launchers, and some pilots and sailors had been trained to carry them. The generals chose Republic City, Yu Dao and Takagawa as the targets in the United Republic and Zaofu, Qianchan and Jinshan in the south, with backups still under discussion. Kuvira ordered the bombs prepared for deployment. None of these strikes was made in 180 AG.

Lake Laogai

Lake Laogai had been turned into a bunker holding the Dai Li and the State Security Bureau. There Kuvira killed the Red Lotus member Aiwei. She claimed she had made a bargain with the Red Lotus to kill the queen, and had his body dumped as if it were an Equalist killing. The State Security Bureau of Ba Sing Se later gave the order to kill Zuko.

Zaofu

Imperial bombers hit Zaofu on 24 December 180 AG, the day before Qianchan and Tajisaki declared war. A blast in the city hall killed Suyin Beifong. Her daughter Opal was dug out of the wreckage with shrapnel wounds to her legs and waist, and was carried to safety by ship by Fire Lord Izumi, who told her of her mother's death on deck. The metal domes at the edge of the city held, trapping the defenders but keeping them alive. The Empire's southern assault stalled at the Foggy Swamp, where the swamp benders refused to yield and the Qianchan press reported that Kuvira had made no progress through it. Opal was later treated at the Shizu City Hospital in January 181, with Izumi paying her medical costs from her own purse in gratitude to Suyin for her work in advancing the technology of mankind. Qianchan's radio reported on 26 December that Opal had been evacuated and that her location was classified.

Shiza

See Shiza.

Shiza (also written Shizu) is a strategic port on the coast of the Southern Air Temple region. It had been a stronghold of the Imperial remnants until the Qianchan Federal Republic took it in a campaign of air strikes, naval bombardment and ground assault. The Federal army built a network of bases there as a staging ground. Loyalists who refused to surrender launched desperate attacks and were cut down by machine guns in the streets. Reserves from the city were loaded with their mecha equipment onto a cargo ship for the mainland while the Avatar's party was stuck in traffic at a bridge. The party left from there on a fuelled flying boat.

Qianchan

On the evening of the first raids on the south the Federal capital was gripped by chaos. The roads were clogged with civilians trying to leave, anti-air batteries ringed the city, and the Imperial air force outnumbered them. A surprise raid set the industrial district alight. Firefighters, many of them earthbenders, built barriers and tunnels to rescue trapped workers. At the airfields the main runway was cratered, and engineers worked to repair it with earthbending. The Federal air force's only chance lay with vertical take-off aircraft, launched from underground hangars, which were outclassed by the Imperial fighters. Airships carried the casualties and evacuees to safety. President Haatao (also written Haato) spoke on the evening of 25 December to say that Federal forces were holding.

The eastern front

In the last week of December, on the eastern edge of the United Republic, the war became an urban fight in a ruined city. A Republic machine-gun section, drawn from conscripts including a violinist and a factory worker, ambushed an Imperial truck column at about 180 m. An Imperial infantry fighting vehicle silenced the gun, and a Republic squad leader destroyed it with three PT-23 rocket-propelled grenades. Then a headquarters report warned of unidentified mechanised units, Kuvira's new suits. They wore the Empire's hybrid power armour, a mix of the Tiejia-III and the Breaker Mk III No. 2. They were clad in black plates, stood over six feet tall, had helmets like a diver's with glowing green eyes and carried heavy machine guns, miniguns and aircraft cannon. They threw boulders and were immune to earthbending and to infantry weapons. They caught the squad in a cabin in the forest and killed it.

The Republic's colonel told President Zhu Li that no one could explain how the suits had been built in secret over the previous five years. Zhu Li ordered the army's development team to produce a matching suit, whatever the cost.

In her broadcast, Zhu Li said that the Empire had declared war on the Republic and on its ally Qianchan, south of the Si Wong Desert. She said Tajisaki had sent land and naval forces. She listed the lost cities of the Tawaraza region: Ikiyo, Shimajiri, Masnda, Hikanigoka and Gaipan. She reported massacres by Kuvira's metalbending army in the two south-eastern straits and said the reserves had been mobilised again. She recalled the ten-year war from 100 to 110 AG against the Ozai loyalists and the Earth Kingdom's attempts to reincorporate the Republic, which she said gave the country its founding. She promised to fight to the last.

The alliance

On 25 December 180 AG, when all three had declared war, the western leaders, Izumi, Zhu Li and Haatao, announced a joint alliance against the Empire in a statement. They pledged military, economic and diplomatic support to one another and respect for each other's sovereignty. The press welcomed it, though some minority groups and parties said it risked more violence and doubted the members' motives.

Mutsukawa hospital attack

In early January 181 AG the Earth Empire's spy ring learned that Zuko, former Fire Lord and then ambassador of peace, lay in a coma on the locked third floor of a hospital in Mutsukawa, the old central district of Caldera City, a building he had himself built during the civil war. Zuko was suffering from tuberculosis, the "wasting condition of the lungs" of the physicians' later reports. A spy posing as a doctor confirmed his location, photographed the building with a camera disguised as a pen and crossed the border to report.

On Kuvira's orders and those of the State Security Bureau, the ring, in two teams, entered the hospital in disguise. Royal Guards turned them back from the third floor. The Bravo team set a bomb in the car park beside the stairs, intending to clear the floor. The blast cut power and sent the guards, and Zuko's wife Mai and granddaughter Princess Kiko, down the stairs with him under a sheet. The Alpha team had taken an ambulance and loaded him into it at the dock. Mai was refused entry. The ambulance was blown up on the highway shortly after, with a mushroom-shaped fireball. The spies jumped clear and were collected by a van. The attack came on the night of 3 January. In the early hours of 4 January Kiko gave an emergency broadcast confirming Zuko's death and asking for a minute of silence. The papers named Kuvira's spies or leftist radicals as suspects. The funeral at Shinja followed on 15 January, with about 400,000 people on the streets.

The Avatar's party

With Kuvira's ultimatum in force, Avatar Korra and her friends were sent to the Fire Nation by supersonic plane. Mako was chief of police and Asami ran Future Industries, and Bolin worked in films. They landed at Mutsukawa International Airport, the old city airport in Caldera City, where Princess Kiko met them and took them to the palace. Zuko gave Korra the letter from Avatar Aang about energybending and the scroll on Kuchuya Island, then collapsed. Zuko was killed the next night, and after the funeral they flew an old NY-13 Zeong, refitted by a Fire Nation mechanic, over the Huiyeong Ocean to Kuchuya, where a bare tree opened a spirit portal. In the Spirit World a note on a tree told Korra the scroll was buried under her feet. She dug it up with earthbending and said there was little time. Bolin was told by Izumi that Opal lay in a hospital in Shiza and left at once. The others joined him there and left for the mainland that night.

Home front

On 26 December 180 AG the Republic City morning radio host Honah Lee read the news. She reported the death of Suyin, Haatao's speech, the alliance and the checkpoints and spy fears in the city. On 4 January the same station reported Zuko's death. Republic City by then ran on war footing, with armoured patrols, identity checks and rumours of saboteurs.

Reconciliation with the main article

The novel has the war two days old on 10 August 180 AG. The wiki keeps the main article's declaration of 2 December 180 and moves the novel's events to the dates above. Suyin's death and the first Zaofu raid come on 24 December 180, the day before the allies declare war. The domes of Zaofu hold in 180 and stay standing until the atomic strike of 20 December 182. Zuko's assassination moves from 28 December 182 to 3 January 181, and the Household's later account of a quiet death is dropped. Kuvira's atomic threat is a test and an ultimatum in 180, and no atomic weapon is used until late 182. Kuvira remains alive until 4 September 182, as in the main article.
